blocks.text: Circle. The perimeter of a circle has its own name: the circumference. If the circle has radius $r$ and diameter $d = 2r$, then $$\text{Circumference} = 2\pi r \quad \text{or} \quad \pi d.$$ You can use either formula; choose the one that fits what you know.

Example 7. Calculate the perimeter of a circle of radius 7cm. Use $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$. fig-11 shows a circle with radius 7cm. Using $\text{Perimeter} = 2\pi r$: $$= 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7$$ $$= 2 \times 22$$ $$= 44\mathrm{cm}$$ We can check with $\pi d$. Since $r = 7\mathrm{cm}$, the diameter $d = 2 \times 7 = 14\mathrm{cm}$, and $$\frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 22 \times 2 = 44\mathrm{cm}.$$ The circumference is 44cm.

blocks.caption: A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked 7cm.

blocks.text: Example 8. The circumference of a circle is 440cm. Find its radius. Use $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$. fig-13 shows a circle with unknown radius $r$. Using $\text{Circumference} = 2\pi r$: $$440 = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r$$ $$440 = \frac{44r}{7}$$ Cross multiply: $$440 \times 7 = 44r$$ $$3080 = 44r$$ Divide both sides by 44: $$\frac{44r}{44} = \frac{3080}{44}$$ $$r = 70\mathrm{cm}$$ The radius of the circle is 70cm.

blocks.caption: A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked $r$.

blocks.text: Example 9. A rope is wound 50 times round a cylinder of radius 25cm. How long is the rope? Use $\pi = 3.14$. fig-12 shows the rope wound round the cylinder. One complete turn of the rope is the circumference of the cylinder, so the length of rope in one turn is the circumference. $$\text{Circumference} = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25$$ $$= 157\mathrm{cm}$$ The rope goes round 50 times, so the total length of rope is $$157\mathrm{cm} \times 50 = 7850\mathrm{cm}.$$ The rope is 7850cm long.

blocks.caption: An upright cylinder with a rope wound round it, drawn as a series of turns spiralling down the body from the top face to the base.

blocks.text: Combined shapes. Some shapes are made of straight sides and a curved arc. For these, find the length of the curved part and add it to the straight sides. A quarter circle is one quarter of a full circle, so its curved length is $$\frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r.$$

Example 10. Calculate the perimeter of the shape below. fig-14 shows a quarter circle: an upright side and a base, each 4.9cm, joined by an arc. First find the length of the curved part. The arc is a quarter of a circle of radius 4.9cm: $$\text{curved length} = \frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9$$ $$= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{44}{7} \times 4.9 = \frac{11}{7} \times \frac{49}{10}$$ $$= \frac{11 \times 7}{10} = \frac{77}{10} = 7.7\mathrm{cm}$$ Now add the two straight sides: $$\text{Perimeter} = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\mathrm{cm}$$ The perimeter of the shape is 17.5cm.

blocks.caption: A quarter circle: an upright side and a base meeting at a right angle, each marked 4.9cm, with an arc closing them from the top of the upright to the end of the base.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a square of sides 8cm.
practice.worked_solution: Perimeter of a square $= 4L = 4 \times 8\mathrm{cm} = 32\mathrm{cm}$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a rectangle of length 7cm and breadth 4cm.
practice.worked_solution: $\text{Perimeter} = 2(L + b) = 2(7 + 4) = 2(11) = 22\mathrm{cm}$.

practice.prompt: What is the perimeter of a regular pentagon with sides 5cm?
practice.worked_solution: A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides, so $\text{Perimeter} = 5 \times 5\mathrm{cm} = 25\mathrm{cm}$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a parallelogram whose base is 6cm and sides 5cm.
practice.worked_solution: The parallelogram has two sides of 6cm and two of 5cm: $\text{Perimeter} = 2(6 + 5) = 2(11) = 22\mathrm{cm}$.

practice.prompt: The circumference of a circle is 22cm. Find the radius of the circle. Use $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.
practice.worked_solution: $22 = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}$. Cross multiplying, $22 \times 7 = 44r$, so $154 = 44r$ and $r = \frac{154}{44} = 3.5\mathrm{cm}$.

practice.prompt: A rectangle is such that its length is twice its breadth. If the breadth is $d$, find the total length of the sides of the rectangle.
practice.worked_solution: Length $= 2d$ and breadth $= d$, each occurring twice. So the total length of the sides is $2(2d) + 2(d) = 4d + 2d = 6d$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a regular hexagon with sides 5cm.
practice.worked_solution: A regular hexagon has 6 equal sides, so $\text{Perimeter} = 6 \times 5\mathrm{cm} = 30\mathrm{cm}$.

practice.prompt: Calculate the perimeter of the figure below: a base of 9cm, a right side of 5cm, and a top made of two 1cm straight pieces joined by a semicircular arc. Use $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.
practice.worked_solution:
The semicircular arc has diameter 7cm, so radius $3.5\mathrm{cm}$, and its length is $\pi r = \frac{22}{7} \times 3.5 = 11\mathrm{cm}$.

Now add the straight sides: base 9cm, right side 5cm, and the two 1cm top pieces:

$$9 + 5 + 1 + 1 = 16\mathrm{cm}$$

Total perimeter $= 16 + 11 = 27\mathrm{cm}$.

sections_json.title: Plane Shapes: Their Types, Properties, Similarities and Differences

blocks.text: Plane shapes are shapes that lie flat on a surface, so they are also called two-dimensional shapes (2-D shapes). The plane shapes you will meet include the triangle, the square, the rectangle, the parallelogram, the trapezium, the circle and other polygons. A polygon is any closed shape that has three or more straight sides. Let us look at each family of plane shapes, its properties, and how the shapes are similar to or different from one another.

Look at the three triangles in fig-01: the isosceles, the scalene and the equilateral. Their names tell you how their sides compare. - An isosceles triangle has two adjacent sides equal (the two slanted sides carry a single tick each). Its base angles are equal, and it has one line of symmetry. - A scalene triangle has no side equal to another — each side carries a different number of ticks (one, two, three). No angle is equal to another, and it has no line of symmetry. - An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal (a single tick on each side). All three angles are equal, each measuring $60^\circ$, and it has three lines of symmetry. So the key differences come down to how many sides are equal: an equilateral has three equal sides, an isosceles has two, and a scalene has none.

blocks.caption: Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text: Now compare the square and the rectangle in fig-02. Each has a right-angle mark at every corner, so both have all angles equal, each measuring $90^\circ$, and both have two pairs of parallel sides. The difference lies in the sides. - A square has all four sides equal (a single tick on every side). It has four lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other at a right angle. - A rectangle has only two opposite sides equal — the two longer sides carry a single tick each and the two shorter sides a double tick each. It has two lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other but not at a right angle.

blocks.caption: Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

blocks.text: Finally, compare the parallelogram and the trapezium in fig-03. - A parallelogram has two pairs of opposite sides equal and parallel (its two horizontal sides carry a single arrow and its two slanted sides a double arrow). Its opposite angles are equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonals divide it into two equal triangles. - A trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides (the two parallel sides carry a single arrow each, and one diagonal is drawn in). Its opposite angles are not equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles. The great difference between them is the number of parallel sides: a parallelogram has two pairs, a trapezium has only one pair.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

blocks.text:
Polygons come in many forms, and each is named by its number of straight sides. The table below lists the common polygons, their number of sides, and how many triangles each can be divided into by drawing diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices.

| Name of polygon | Number of sides | Number of triangles ($n-2$) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (or undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

The rule that produces the third column is simple: take the number of sides $n$ and subtract $2$. A hexagon has 6 sides, so it divides into $6-2=4$ triangles; a pentagon has 5 sides, so it divides into $5-2=3$ triangles.

Worked example — triangles in a polygon How many triangles can a heptagon be divided into if you draw diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices? Solution. A heptagon has 7 sides. Use the rule: number of triangles $= n-2 = 7-2 = 5$. So a heptagon divides into 5 triangles, which matches the table.

practice.prompt: How many triangles can an octagon be divided into if you draw diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices?
practice.worked_solution: An octagon has 8 sides. Number of triangles $= n-2 = 8-2 = 6$.

practice.prompt: Name the triangle whose three sides are all equal, and state the size of each of its angles.
practice.answer: It is an equilateral triangle, and each of its three angles measures 60°.

practice.prompt: Which of the square and the rectangle has four lines of symmetry?
practice.answer: The square has four lines of symmetry; the rectangle has two.

practice.prompt: State one difference between a parallelogram and a trapezium.
practice.answer: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides, while a trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides.

practice.prompt: How many sides does a dodecagon have, and into how many triangles can it be divided?
practice.answer: A dodecagon has 12 sides and divides into 10 triangles.
practice.worked_solution: Number of triangles $= n-2 = 12-2 = 10$.

blocks.text:
A circle is a plane shape with no corners: every point on its boundary is the same distance from its centre. The curved line that forms the round boundary of the circle is its **circumference**. fig-04 shows two labelled circles so you can see each part sitting on a real circle.

- The **centre** is the point in the middle of the circle.
- The **radius** (plural *radii*) is any straight line joining the centre to the circumference. In the second circle of fig-04 a radius is drawn from the centre out to the circumference, and the right-hand bounding line of the sector below is also a radius.
- A **chord** is any straight line joining two points on the circumference. The second circle in fig-04 has a chord drawn near the top.
- The **diameter** is any chord that passes through the centre of the circle. In the first circle of fig-04 the diameter is drawn straight across through the centre. Because it goes through the centre, it is the longest chord a circle can have, and it is twice as long as the radius.
- An **arc** is a curved part of the circumference. In the first circle of fig-04 a part of the circumference is marked and named the arc.

The figure also shows three more parts:
- A **segment** is the region of the circle cut off by a chord — the shaded part above the chord in the second circle.
- A **sector** is the region bounded by two radii and the arc between them — the shaded part below in the second circle, whose two straight sides are both radii.
- A **tangent** is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point, as shown touching the right side of the second circle.

blocks.caption: Two labelled circles. The first has the diameter drawn across it and a radius from its centre to the circumference, with the arc and the circumference labelled. The second has a chord near the top with the segment above it shaded, a shaded sector below with its right-hand bounding line labelled Radius, and a tangent touching it on the right.

practice.prompt: Name the straight line that joins the centre of a circle to its circumference.
What do we call a chord that passes through the centre of the circle?
A straight line drawn across a circle joining two points on its circumference is called a ______.
The curved part of the circumference between two points on a circle is called an ______.
If a circle has a radius of 5 cm, how long is its diameter?
practice.worked_solution: The diameter is twice the radius, so 2 × 5 cm = 10 cm.

practice.prompt: Which part of a circle is the region bounded by two radii and the arc between them? Which part is the region cut off by a chord?
practice.answer: The region bounded by two radii and the arc between them is a sector; the region cut off by a chord is a segment.

practice.prompt: A straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point is called a ______.

sections_json.title: Finding the Perimeter of Plane Shapes

blocks.text:
The perimeter of a shape is the distance all the way round it. To find it you simply add the lengths of every side. For a straight-sided shape, this means adding each side once. For a circle, the perimeter has a special name — the circumference — and you find it using the radius (or diameter) and the number π (pi), which is about $\frac{22}{7}$ or 3.14.

Because some shapes have equal sides, you can often write a short formula instead of adding each side separately. Work through the examples below to see how each shape's perimeter is found.

Example 1 — a square. A square has four equal sides. In fig-05 each side is marked $L$ and measures 15cm. Its perimeter is four lengths added together: $$L + L + L + L = 4L$$ $$= 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 4(15) = 60\text{cm}.$$ Example 2 — a rectangle. A rectangle has two long sides $L$ and two short sides $b$. In fig-06, $L = 10\text{cm}$ and $b = 7\text{cm}$. Adding all four sides: $$P = L + b + L + b = 2L + 2b = 2(L + b)$$ $$= 2(10 + 7) = 2(17) = 34\text{cm}.$$ Example 3 — a missing side. Sometimes you are given the perimeter and one side and must find the other. Suppose a rectangle has perimeter 60cm and length 17cm (fig-07). Write the perimeter formula and solve for $b$: $$P = 2L + 2b$$ $$60 = 2(17) + 2b$$ $$60 = 34 + 2b$$ Collect like terms: $$60 - 34 = 2b$$ $$2b = 26$$ Divide both sides by 2: $$b = 13\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A rectangle with both long sides marked $L = 17$cm and both short sides marked $b$.
A rectangle with both long sides marked $L$, the top one also 10cm, and both short sides marked $b$, the right-hand one also 7cm.
A square, named *Square* at its left, with all four sides marked twice — $L$ and 15cm.

blocks.text: Example 4 — a trapezium. A trapezium has four sides, usually of different lengths. In fig-08 they are $a = 11\text{cm}$, $b = 9\text{cm}$, $c = 5\text{cm}$ and $d = 4\text{cm}$. The perimeter is all four added: $$P = a + b + c + d$$ $$= 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29\text{cm}.$$ Example 5 — a parallelogram. A parallelogram has opposite sides equal: two of length $a$ and two of length $b$ (fig-09, where $a = 9\text{cm}$ and $b = 5\text{cm}$). So $$P = a + a + b + b = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b)$$ $$= 2(9 + 5) = 2(14) = 28\text{cm}.$$ Example 6 — a regular hexagon. A regular hexagon has six equal sides. In fig-10 each side is 5.2cm, so $$P = 6 \times 5.2 = 31.2\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A regular hexagon, named above the drawing, with each of its six sides marked 5.2cm.

A parallelogram with a single arrow on each of its four sides: the two horizontal ones both lettered $a$, the lower also measured 9cm, and the two slanted ones both lettered $b$, the right-hand one also measured 5cm.
A trapezium with each side lettered and measured: the top $c$, 5cm; the left $b$, 9cm; the right $d$, 4cm; the base $a$, 11cm.

blocks.text: Example 7 — a circle. The perimeter of a circle is its circumference, found with either formula: $$C = 2\pi r \quad\text{or}\quad C = \pi d.$$ In fig-11 the radius is 7cm, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$: $$C = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 = 2 \times 22 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Using $\pi d$ instead: since $d = 2r = 2 \times 7 = 14\text{cm}$, $$C = \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 22 \times 2 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Example 8 — a rope wound round a cylinder. One turn round the cylinder is one circumference. With radius 25cm and $\pi = 3.14$, $$C = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25 = 157\text{cm}.$$ Wound 50 times, the rope's total length is $$157 \times 50 = 7850\text{cm}.$$ Example 9 — the radius from the circumference. If the circumference is 440cm, find $r$ ($\pi = \frac{22}{7}$): $$440 = 2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}.$$ Cross-multiply: $$440 \times 7 = 44r \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3080 = 44r.$$ Divide both sides by 44: $$r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked 7cm.

blocks.text: Example 10 — a quarter circle. The shape in fig-14 is made of two straight sides of 4.9cm each and a curved part that is one quarter of a full circle. Its perimeter is the two straight sides plus that curved part. First find the curved part. It is $\frac{1}{4}$ of a full circumference: $$\frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9$$ $$= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{44}{7} \times 4.9 = \frac{11}{7} \times \frac{49}{10}$$ $$= \frac{11 \times 7}{10} = \frac{77}{10} = 7.7\text{cm}.$$ Now add the straight sides and the curved part: $$P = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A quarter circle: an upright side and a base meeting at a right angle, each marked 4.9cm, with an arc closing them from the top of the upright to the end of the base.
An upright cylinder with a rope wound round it, drawn as a series of turns spiralling down the body from the top face to the base.
A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked $r$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a square with sides of 8cm.
practice.worked_solution: A square has four equal sides, so $P = 4 \times 8 = 32\text{cm}$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a rectangle of length 7cm and breadth 4cm.
What is the perimeter of a regular pentagon with sides of 5cm?
practice.worked_solution: A regular pentagon has five equal sides, so $P = 5 \times 5 = 25\text{cm}$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a parallelogram whose base is 6cm and whose sides are 5cm.
practice.worked_solution: Opposite sides are equal, so $P = 2a + 2b = 2(6) + 2(5) = 12 + 10 = 22\text{cm}$.

practice.prompt: The circumference of a circle is 22cm. Find its radius $(\pi = \frac{22}{7})$.
practice.worked_solution: $C = 2\pi r$, so $22 = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}$. Cross-multiply: $22 \times 7 = 44r$, so $154 = 44r$, giving $r = \frac{154}{44} = 3.5\text{cm}$.

practice.prompt: A rectangle is such that its length is twice its breadth. If the breadth is $d$, find the total length of the sides of the rectangle.
practice.worked_solution: Length $= 2d$ and breadth $= d$. Perimeter $= 2(\text{length} + \text{breadth}) = 2(2d + d) = 2(3d) = 6d$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a regular hexagon with sides of 5cm.
practice.worked_solution: A regular hexagon has six equal sides, so $P = 6 \times 5 = 30\text{cm}$.

practice.prompt: A trapezium has sides 11cm, 9cm, 5cm and 4cm. Find its perimeter.

sections_json.title: Cubes and Cuboids: Faces, Edges and Vertices

blocks.text: Around you are solid shapes that take up space. A box, a dice, a brick and a matchbox are all three-dimensional shapes, which means they have length, width and height. In this section you will look closely at two of them: the cube and the cuboid. To describe either one, you need three key ideas. • A face is one of the flat surfaces of the shape. • An edge is where two faces meet — the straight line between them. • A vertex (plural: vertices) is a corner, where edges meet. Let us see how these appear on a cube. A cube is the shape of a dice. Every one of its faces is a square, and all its faces are the same size. Count them: a cube has 6 faces. Where the faces meet, there are straight edges, and a cube has 12 edges — all of them the same length. Where the edges meet, there are corners, and a cube has 8 vertices. Now picture a cuboid, the shape of a brick or a box of cereal. A cuboid also has flat faces, but they are rectangles, and not all of them are the same size: the front and back are identical, the two sides are identical, and the top and bottom are identical. Like a cube, a cuboid has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. The difference is that the edges of a cuboid are not all equal — there are three different lengths (length, width and height), and each length is repeated four times. So a cube and a cuboid are actually close cousins: both have 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. What separates them is that every face of a cube is an equal square, while a cuboid has rectangular faces that may differ in size.

Worked example 1
A dice is a cube. State the number of faces, edges and vertices on it.

Solution
A cube has 6 square faces. It has 12 edges, all of equal length. It has 8 vertices (corners). So the dice has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

Worked example 2
A cereal box is a cuboid. It has length 30 cm, width 10 cm and height 20 cm.
(a) How many faces does it have, and what shapes are they?
(b) How many edges of length 30 cm does it have?

Solution
(a) A cuboid has 6 faces, and they are rectangles.
(b) The length 30 cm appears four times, on the four edges that run along the length of the box. So there are 4 edges of length 30 cm.

practice.prompt: Write down the number of faces, edges and vertices of a cube.
practice.answer: A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

practice.prompt: A brick is a cuboid. (a) How many faces does it have and what shape is each face? (b) A cuboid has edges of three different lengths — length, width and height. How many edges of each length does it have?
practice.answer: (a) 6 faces, each a rectangle. (b) 4 edges of each length, so 4 length-edges, 4 width-edges and 4 height-edges.
practice.worked_solution: A cuboid has 6 faces, all rectangles. Its edges come in three lengths (length, width, height). There are 12 edges in total, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4 edges of each length.

practice.prompt: A cube and a cuboid both have the same number of faces, edges and vertices. State these three numbers, and explain the one way in which a cube is different from a cuboid.
practice.answer: Both have 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. The difference is that every face of a cube is an equal square, while the faces of a cuboid are rectangles that may differ in size (and the edges of a cube are all equal, while a cuboid has three different edge lengths).
practice.worked_solution: Count on the shapes: each has 6 flat faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. In a cube all six faces are identical squares and all edges are equal. In a cuboid the faces are rectangles and not all edges are equal — there are three lengths, each repeated four times.

sections_json.title: Pyramids and Cones: Faces, Edges and Vertices

blocks.text:
A pyramid is a three-dimensional shape with one flat base and triangular side faces that all meet at a single point called the apex. The name of a pyramid tells you the shape of its base. For example, a pyramid with a triangular base is a triangular pyramid, and one with a square base is a square pyramid.

Every pyramid is described by three properties:
- Faces: the flat surfaces. A square pyramid has a square base plus four triangular side faces, so 5 faces in total.
- Vertices: the corners where faces meet. A square pyramid has 5 vertices — the 4 corners of the base and the apex.
- Edges: the straight lines where two faces meet. A square pyramid has 4 edges around the base and 4 edges slanting up to the apex, so 8 edges in total.

No matter what shape the base is, a pyramid always has just one apex, and its side faces are always triangles.

A cone is like a pyramid whose base is a circle instead of a polygon. A cone has:
- Faces: a cone has one flat circular base and one curved surface. The curved surface is not a flat face, so a cone is described as having 1 face.
- Vertices: a cone has one vertex, the pointed apex at the top.
- Edges: a cone has one edge, the circle where the curved surface meets the flat base.

The two key things to remember about a cone are that its base is a circle and its one curved surface slides up to a single point. Because the base is curved, a cone has only one edge (the circle), unlike a pyramid which has several straight edges.

Example: Count the faces, edges and vertices of a triangular pyramid.

Step 1 — Identify the base. The base is a triangle, so the pyramid has 1 triangular base.
Step 2 — Count the side faces. There is one triangular side face for each side of the base, so 3 side faces.
Step 3 — Add the faces together. 1 base + 3 side faces = 4 faces in total.
Step 4 — Count the vertices. The base triangle has 3 corners, and there is 1 apex on top, so 3 + 1 = 4 vertices.
Step 5 — Count the edges. The base has 3 edges and each corner of the base connects to the apex, giving 3 more edges. So 3 + 3 = 6 edges.

So a triangular pyramid has 4 faces, 4 vertices and 6 edges.

Example: Describe the faces, edges and vertices of a cone.

Step 1 — Look at the base. The base of a cone is a circle, so the cone has 1 flat face.
Step 2 — Look at the rest of the shape. The curved surface wraps around from the base up to the point, so that is 1 more surface.
Step 3 — Count the edges. The only edge is the circle where the curved surface meets the base, so the cone has 1 edge.
Step 4 — Count the vertices. The cone has one point at the top, so it has 1 vertex.

So a cone has 1 face, 1 edge and 1 vertex.

practice.prompt: A pyramid has a square base. How many faces, vertices and edges does it have in total? Write your answer as three numbers, e.g. "x faces, y vertices, z edges".
practice.worked_solution: A square pyramid has 1 square base and 4 triangular side faces, so 1 + 4 = 5 faces. It has 4 base corners plus 1 apex, so 4 + 1 = 5 vertices. It has 4 edges around the base and 4 slanting edges to the apex, so 4 + 4 = 8 edges.

practice.prompt: Explain in one sentence what shape the side faces of any pyramid are, and what shape the base of any cone is.
practice.answer: The side faces of any pyramid are triangles, and the base of any cone is a circle.

practice.prompt: A cone is sometimes said to have "one face, one edge and one vertex." In your own words, identify each of these three parts of a cone.
practice.answer: A cone has 1 face, 1 edge and 1 vertex.
practice.worked_solution: The one face is the flat circular base (the curved surface is not counted as a flat face). The one edge is the circle where the curved surface meets the base. The one vertex is the single pointed apex at the top of the cone.

blocks.text:
A three-dimensional shape is solid, so it has three measures: length, breadth (width) and height. When we study a solid shape, we look at its faces, its edges and its vertices (corners). Learning these three things for a shape lets you recognise it and tell it apart from other shapes.

A face is a flat surface of the shape. An edge is a line where two faces meet. A vertex (plural: vertices) is a corner, where edges meet.

Let's look at a cuboid first. A cuboid is a box whose faces are rectangles — think of a brick, a book or a matchbox. Every cuboid has the same properties:
• Faces: 6
• Edges: 12
• Vertices: 8

Notice that not all the faces of a cuboid look the same, because a cuboid's faces are rectangles of different sizes. But it still always has exactly 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

Now look at a cube. A cube is a special cuboid: every one of its faces is a square, and all the squares are the same size. Think of a dice. Because a cube is just a cuboid with equal square faces, it has the same counts:
• Faces: 6
• Edges: 12
• Vertices: 8

So both a cube and a cuboid have 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. The difference between them is the shape of their faces: a cube's 6 faces are all equal squares, while a cuboid's faces are rectangles (not all the same).

Let's work through the properties of a cube, then a cuboid.

A cube has 6 faces. Count them: front, back, top, bottom, left and right — that is 6. Each of these faces is a square, and they are all the same size.

A cube has 12 edges. The front face has 4 edges, and the back face has 4 edges, and there are 4 edges joining the front to the back — 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.

A cube has 8 vertices — one at each corner, top and bottom, front and back: 4 on top and 4 on the bottom.

A cuboid has exactly the same counts: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. The only difference is the shape of its faces. A cuboid's faces are rectangles (for example a front that is taller than it is wide), and opposite faces are the same size. In a cube all six faces are equal squares.

So when you are asked for the properties of a cube or a cuboid, answer with the three counts — faces, edges and vertices — and, for a cube, add that all its faces are equal squares.

practice.prompt: 1. How many vertices has a cuboid?
practice.worked_solution: A cuboid has 4 corners at the top and 4 corners at the bottom, so 4 + 4 = 8 vertices in total.

practice.prompt: 2. How many edges has a cube?
practice.worked_solution: A cube has 4 edges on the top face, 4 edges on the bottom face, and 4 vertical edges joining the top to the bottom. 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 edges.

practice.prompt: 3. A box of chalk is the shape of a cuboid. List its number of faces, edges and vertices.
practice.answer: A cuboid (the chalk box) has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.
practice.worked_solution: Every cuboid — a chalk box, a book or a brick — has the same three counts: 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

practice.prompt: 4. A dice is in the shape of a cube. How many faces does it have, and what shape is each face?
practice.answer: A cube has 6 faces, and every face is a square (all the same size).
practice.worked_solution: A cube is a cuboid whose 6 faces are all equal squares, which is why a dice — a cube — has 6 square faces.

blocks.text: In the last section you looked at cubes and cuboids — shapes built from flat square and rectangular faces. Now meet two more three-dimensional figures: pyramids and cones. Both are built from a flat base that rises up to a single point, but their sides are very different. A pyramid has a flat base that is a polygon (a triangle, a square, a pentagon, a hexagon, and so on), and every other face is a triangle. All these triangular faces meet at one point at the top, called the apex (or vertex). A pyramid is named by the shape of its base: a pyramid with a square base is a square pyramid, one with a triangular base is a triangular pyramid, and one with a hexagonal base is a hexagonal pyramid. A cone has a flat circular base, and instead of triangular faces it has one curved surface that tapers smoothly up to a single point, the apex. So while a pyramid is made entirely of flat faces, a cone has exactly one curved face. Let's list their properties side by side.

Here are the properties to know for each figure. Square pyramid (a pyramid with a square base):
  • It has 5 faces: 1 square base and 4 triangular faces.
  • It has 8 edges.
  • It has 5 vertices: the 4 corners of the square base plus the apex.
Hexagonal pyramid (a pyramid with a hexagonal base):
  • It has 7 faces: 1 hexagonal base and 6 triangular faces.
  • It has 12 edges.
  • It has 7 vertices: the 6 corners of the hexagon base plus the apex.
Cone:
  • It has 2 faces: 1 circular base and 1 curved surface.
  • It has 0 edges (no straight edges at all).
  • It has 1 vertex: the apex.
Spot the pattern for a pyramid: if the base is a polygon with n sides, the pyramid has n triangular faces plus the 1 base (so n + 1 faces in total), n + 1 vertices, and 2n edges. Check it against the square pyramid: n = 4, so faces = 5, vertices = 5, edges = 8. That works! And the hexagon: n = 6, so faces = 7, vertices = 7, edges = 12.

Worked example — listing the properties of a pentagonal pyramid A pentagonal pyramid has a pentagon (5 sides) for its base. Faces. It has 1 pentagonal base and 5 triangular faces that rise to the apex. So the number of faces is 5 + 1 = 6. Vertices. It has the 5 corners of the base plus the 1 apex, so 5 + 1 = 6 vertices. Edges. Using the pattern, edges = 2 × n = 2 × 5 = 10. Check by counting: the base is a pentagon (5 edges), and each of the 5 corners sends an edge up to the apex (5 more edges). That gives 5 + 5 = 10 edges. So a pentagonal pyramid has 6 faces, 6 vertices and 10 edges.

practice.prompt: A hexagonal pyramid has a hexagon for its base. List all its properties: how many faces, how many vertices and how many edges does it have?
practice.answer: 7 faces (1 hexagonal base and 6 triangular faces), 7 vertices (6 base corners plus the apex), and 12 edges.
practice.worked_solution: The base is a hexagon, so n = 6. Faces = n + 1 = 7. Vertices = n + 1 = 7. Edges = 2n = 2 × 6 = 12.

practice.prompt: A tetrahedron is a pyramid with a triangular base. How many vertices does a tetrahedron have?
practice.answer: 4 vertices: the 3 corners of the triangular base plus the 1 apex.
practice.worked_solution: n = 3 for a triangle. Vertices = n + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4.

practice.prompt: A cone has how many faces, edges and vertices?
practice.answer: 2 faces (1 circular base and 1 curved surface), 0 edges, and 1 vertex (the apex).

blocks.text:
Three-dimensional shapes are shapes that have length, breadth and height. Because they have all three of these, they are called **solid shapes**. They can be regular or irregular. A cube of sugar, a can drink and a matchbox are regular shapes; a stone or a tree is an irregular shape.

Two important solids you will meet are the **cube** and the **cuboid**. Before we list their properties, make sure you know three words that we use to describe any solid shape:

- A **face** (or surface) is one of the flat surfaces of the shape. A face may be flat or curved.
- An **edge** is a line where two faces meet. An edge may be straight or curved.
- A **vertex** is a point corner where edges meet. (More than one vertex are called **vertices**.)

### Properties of a cube

A cube is a solid in which **all six faces are squares** of the same size. Look at fig-01 — a cube drawn as a see-through solid, with two equal squares joined corner to corner. The properties of a cube are:

1. It is a solid state.
2. It has **6 square faces**.
3. It has **12 edges**.
4. It has **8 vertices**.

blocks.caption: A cube drawn as a see-through solid: two equal squares, the nearer one offset down and to the right of the farther one, with the four pairs of corresponding corners joined.

blocks.text:
### Properties of a cuboid

A cuboid is a solid like the one in fig-02, drawn wide and shallow. Its faces are **rectangles**, not all of them equal. The properties of a cuboid are:

1. It has **6 faces**.
2. It has **12 edges**.
3. It has **8 vertices**.

In fig-02 the leader lines name three parts for you: the top **face**, a **vertex** (the nearer top-right corner, where edges meet) and an **edge** (the nearer right-hand vertical line where two faces meet).

blocks.caption: A cuboid drawn the same way, wide and shallow, with three leader lines to the right naming the top face, the nearer top-right corner and the nearer right-hand vertical edge.

blocks.text:
**Worked example.** How many edges does a cube have, and what shape are its faces?

A cube has **12 edges** and its faces are all **squares**. Because all six faces are squares of the same size, the cube is the solid whose faces are all equal squares.

practice.prompt: How many vertices does a cuboid have?
How many edges does a cube have?
A cube and a cuboid both have the same number of faces. How many faces does each one have?
In your own words, what is the difference between the faces of a cube and the faces of a cuboid?
practice.answer: A cube has 6 square faces, all of the same size; a cuboid has 6 faces that are rectangles, not all equal.

blocks.text:
You already know the difference between a cube and a cuboid. Now we meet two more solids: pyramids and cones.

A pyramid is named according to the shape of its base. Look at fig-03: a pyramid with a triangular base is called a triangular based pyramid. Because it has four triangular faces, it is also called a tetrahedron (from the Greek for "four faces"). fig-04 shows a square based pyramid, fig-05 a pentagonal based pyramid, and fig-06 a rectangular based pyramid. In every pyramid, the base is a flat polygon and the slanted faces meet at a single point at the top called the apex.

Count the faces, edges and vertices of each pyramid carefully, and you find this pattern:

| Shape | Faces | Edges | Vertices |
|---|---|---|---|
| Triangular based pyramid | 4 | 6 | 4 |
| Square based pyramid | 5 | 8 | 5 |
| Pentagonal based pyramid | 6 | 10 | 6 |
| Rectangular based pyramid | 5 | 8 | 5 |

A cone (fig-07) is a different solid, with a round base and a pointed top. It has two faces — one curved face and one flat circular face. It has one edge (the circular rim where the two faces meet) and one vertex (the pointed apex).

blocks.caption: Two drawings side by side. On the left an upright cone: an elliptical base with the two slant sides running up from the ends of the ellipse to the apex. On the right a cone lying on its side, apex at the left, its two slant sides reaching a narrow upright ellipse whose top and bottom then continue as two parallel lines to a second narrow ellipse further right.
A rectangular based pyramid, drawn like the square one but on a base wider than it is tall.

A pentagonal based pyramid. The base is drawn as a pentagon standing on one side with its fifth vertex uppermost, and the apex above is joined to that vertex, to the two vertices either side of it, and to the lower-right vertex — four edges from the apex, the last of them crossing the face of the solid.
A square base pyramid. The base is drawn as an upright rectangle and the apex above is joined to all four of its corners, so two edges run outside the rectangle and two cross it.
A triangular base pyramid. The base triangle is drawn in perspective, its third vertex raised into the middle of the figure, and the apex above is joined to all three base vertices.

blocks.text:
Let's work out the properties of a square based pyramid by looking at fig-04.

Step 1 — Faces. The base is a square, and four triangular faces slant up from the four sides of the square to the apex. So there are 5 faces.

Step 2 — Edges. The base has 4 edges, and each corner of the base is joined to the apex by one more edge, giving 4 more. So there are 4 + 4 = 8 edges.

Step 3 — Vertices. There are the 4 corners of the base plus the apex at the top. So there are 5 vertices.

So a square based pyramid has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices, which matches the table.

practice.prompt: How many vertices has a tetrahedron?
practice.worked_solution: A tetrahedron is a triangular based pyramid. From the table, a triangular based pyramid has 4 vertices.

practice.prompt: A pentagonal based pyramid — how many faces, edges and vertices does it have?
practice.worked_solution: From the table, a pentagonal based pyramid has 6 faces, 10 edges and 6 vertices.

practice.prompt: Write down the number of faces, edges and vertices of a cone.
practice.answer: A cone has 2 faces (one curved, one flat), 1 edge and 1 vertex.

sections_json.title: Cubes and Cuboids: Faces, Edges and Vertices

blocks.text: Three-dimensional shapes are shapes that have length, breadth and height. Because they have all three, they are called solid shapes. Some of them are regular, like a cube of sugar, a can drink or a match box; others are irregular, like a stone or a tree. To describe any solid shape, you use three words: - A face (or surface) is a flat or curved side of the shape. - An edge is a line where two faces meet. It may be straight or curved. - A vertex is a point corner where edges meet. The plural is vertices. Count these parts on the cube in fig-01 and you will find its properties.

blocks.caption: A cube drawn as a see-through solid: two equal squares, the nearer one offset down and to the right of the farther one, with the four pairs of corresponding corners joined.

blocks.text: Properties of a cube A cube is a solid whose every face is a square. Look at the cube drawn in fig-01 — two equal squares joined by four straight edges. 1. It is a solid shape. 2. It has 6 square faces. 3. It has 12 edges. 4. It has 8 vertices. Properties of a cuboid A cuboid is like a cube but its faces are rectangles, so it can be wide and shallow rather than equal in every direction. The cuboid in fig-02 shows you a face, a vertex and an edge. 1. It has 6 faces. 2. It has 12 edges. 3. It has 8 vertices. So a cube and a cuboid both have 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. They differ in their faces: every face of a cube is a square, while the faces of a cuboid are rectangles.

blocks.caption: A cuboid drawn the same way, wide and shallow, with three leader lines to the right naming the top face, the nearer top-right corner and the nearer right-hand vertical edge.

blocks.text: Let's check that you can find these properties on the picture. Take the cube in fig-01. Run your eye over it: count the squares that make it up — there are 6. Count the straight lines where two squares meet — there are 12 of them. Count the point corners where three edges meet — there are 8. These three numbers, 6, 12 and 8, are the properties you should always be able to recall for both a cube and a cuboid.

practice.prompt: How many vertices has a cuboid?
practice.worked_solution: A vertex is a point corner where edges meet. Count the corners of the cuboid: 4 on the nearer face and 4 on the farther face, giving 8 in all.

practice.prompt: How many edges has a cube?
practice.worked_solution: An edge is a line where two faces meet. On the cube, count 4 edges on the top face, 4 on the bottom face and 4 vertical edges joining them — 12 in all.

practice.prompt: Copy the cuboid in fig-02 onto your paper and label one face, one edge and one vertex on it.
practice.answer: Your drawing should show a wide, shallow cuboid with a rectangle labelled 'face', one point corner labelled 'vertex' and one straight line where two faces meet labelled 'edge', exactly as in fig-02.
practice.worked_solution: Draw a cuboid the way fig-02 shows it: two rectangles, the nearer one offset down and to the right of the farther one, with the four pairs of corresponding corners joined. Then pick one flat side and label it 'face', pick one point corner and label it 'vertex', and pick one line where two faces meet and label it 'edge'.

blocks.text: A pyramid is a solid shape that narrows from a flat base up to a single point called the apex. A pyramid is named according to the shape of its base. For example, a pyramid whose base is a triangle is a triangular based pyramid, and one whose base is a square is a square based pyramid. Because the name always tells you the base, you can work out many of the properties without drawing anything.

Three things describe a solid shape: - Faces — the flat surfaces that make up the shape. - Edges — the lines where two faces meet. - Vertices — the corners where edges meet (one corner is a vertex). Here are the properties of four pyramids. Notice that the numbers depend on the base. | Shape | Faces | Edges | Vertices | |---|---|---|---| | Triangular based pyramid (tetrahedron) | 4 | 6 | 4 | | Square based pyramid | 5 | 8 | 5 | | Pentagonal based pyramid | 6 | 10 | 6 | | Rectangular based pyramid | 5 | 8 | 5 | A triangular based pyramid has a triangle for its base, so it has four faces altogether: the triangular base plus three triangular sides. It is also called a tetrahedron.

Now consider the cone. A cone has a circular flat base and a curved face that rises to a point, the apex. Its properties are: - It has two faces — one curved face and one flat face (the circular base). - It has one edge — the circular rim where the curved face meets the flat base. - It has one vertex — the pointed apex. So unlike a pyramid, a cone has only one flat face and only one vertex, because its side is curved rather than made of flat faces.

Worked example — naming and listing properties A solid has a pentagon for its base and a single apex above it. Name the solid and list its faces, edges and vertices. Step 1. The name comes from the base. The base is a pentagon, so this is a pentagonal based pyramid. Step 2. Look up its properties. From the table, a pentagonal based pyramid has 6 faces, 10 edges and 6 vertices. Answer: Pentagonal based pyramid — 6 faces, 10 edges, 6 vertices.

blocks.caption: A triangular base pyramid. The base triangle is drawn in perspective, its third vertex raised into the middle of the figure, and the apex above is joined to all three base vertices.
A square base pyramid. The base is drawn as an upright rectangle and the apex above is joined to all four of its corners, so two edges run outside the rectangle and two cross it.

A pentagonal based pyramid. The base is drawn as a pentagon standing on one side with its fifth vertex uppermost, and the apex above is joined to that vertex, to the two vertices either side of it, and to the lower-right vertex — four edges from the apex, the last of them crossing the face of the solid.
A rectangular based pyramid, drawn like the square one but on a base wider than it is tall.

Two drawings side by side. On the left an upright cone: an elliptical base with the two slant sides running up from the ends of the ellipse to the apex. On the right a cone lying on its side, apex at the left, its two slant sides reaching a narrow upright ellipse whose top and bottom then continue as two parallel lines to a second narrow ellipse further right.

practice.prompt: A solid has a square for its base and a single apex above it. Name the solid and state how many faces, edges and vertices it has.
practice.answer: Square based pyramid; it has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices.
practice.worked_solution: The name comes from the base shape, so a square base gives a square based pyramid. From the properties table, a square based pyramid has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices.

practice.prompt: How many vertices does a tetrahedron have?
practice.worked_solution: A tetrahedron is another name for a triangular based pyramid. Its properties are 4 faces, 6 edges and 4 vertices, so it has 4 vertices.

practice.prompt: State the number of faces, edges and vertices of a cone. Identify which face is curved and which is flat.
practice.answer: A cone has 2 faces, 1 edge and 1 vertex. It has one curved face and one flat face (the circular base).
practice.worked_solution: A cone has a flat circular base and a curved side that rises to a point. The curved side and the flat base make 2 faces. The circular rim where they meet is 1 edge, and the pointed apex is 1 vertex.

practice.prompt: A pyramid has 6 faces, 10 edges and 6 vertices. What is the shape of its base?
practice.answer: Its base is a pentagon, so it is a pentagonal based pyramid.
practice.worked_solution: The properties 6 faces, 10 edges and 6 vertices match the pentagonal based pyramid in the table, and a pentagonal based pyramid is named for its pentagon base.

sections_json.title: Cylinders and Spheres: Their Shapes and Properties

blocks.text: Look around your home and you will see objects with familiar 3D shapes. A tin of baked beans and a drinking glass are cylinders. A football and an orange are spheres. In this section we look closely at these two shapes and learn how to tell them apart by their properties.

Properties of a cylinder A cylinder is a solid with two flat circular faces and one curved surface that joins them. Let us count its parts carefully using a tin can: • Faces: a cylinder has two faces — the circular top and the circular bottom. The curved part that wraps around the sides is not counted as a flat face; it is a curved surface. • Edges: an edge is where two faces meet. The curved surface meets each circular face along a circle, so a cylinder has two curved edges (the rim of the top and the rim of the bottom). • Vertices: a vertex is a corner, where edges meet at a point. A cylinder has no vertices — there is no sharp corner anywhere on it. • Curved surface: the cylinder has one curved surface joining the two flat circular faces. So a cylinder has 2 faces, 2 curved edges, 1 curved surface and 0 vertices.

Properties of a sphere A sphere is a perfectly round solid, like a ball. Every point on its surface is the same distance from its centre. • Faces: a sphere has no flat faces. Its whole surface is one curved surface. • Edges: a sphere has no edges. There is no line where two surfaces meet. • Vertices: a sphere has no vertices. There are no corners at all. • Curved surface: a sphere has one curved surface that covers the whole shape. So a sphere has 0 faces, 0 edges, 0 vertices, and 1 curved surface. Because it rolls in every direction, a sphere is sometimes called a "perfectly round" solid.

Comparing the two shapes Here is a quick way to remember the difference. Both a cylinder and a sphere have one curved surface and no vertices. But a cylinder has two flat circular faces and two curved edges, while a sphere has no flat faces and no edges at all. So when you see a solid with a round flat top and a round flat bottom, it is a cylinder; when you see a solid that is round all over with no flat part, it is a sphere. A useful check: imagine resting the shape on a table. A cylinder can stand still on its flat circular end, but a sphere will roll away — it has no flat surface to rest on.

Worked example 1 A can of soup has a flat circular top, a flat circular bottom, and a curved side that joins them. How many faces, edges and vertices does it have? Think: the two flat circular parts are the two faces. The curved side is a curved surface, not a flat face. The curved surface meets the top along a circle and meets the bottom along another circle, giving two curved edges. There are no corners anywhere. Write: faces = 2, curved edges = 2, vertices = 0.

Worked example 2 Classify each solid as a cylinder or a sphere: (a) a tennis ball, (b) a roll of sticky tape. Think: a tennis ball is round all over, with no flat face and no edges — it is a sphere. A roll of sticky tape has a flat circular top and a flat circular bottom joined by a curved surface — it is a cylinder. Write: (a) sphere, (b) cylinder.

practice.prompt: How many faces, edges and vertices does a cylinder have?
practice.answer: A cylinder has 2 faces (two flat circles), 2 curved edges, and 0 vertices.
practice.worked_solution: Count the flat circular top and bottom as the two faces. The curved side is not a flat face. Where the curved surface meets each circular face there is a curved edge, so there are 2 edges. There are no corners, so there are 0 vertices.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a sphere: an ice cream cone, a beach ball, a coin? Explain why.
practice.answer: A beach ball is a sphere, because it is round all over with no flat faces and no edges. A cone and a coin have flat surfaces.
practice.worked_solution: A sphere has no flat faces and no edges, only one curved surface. A beach ball fits this. A coin has two flat circular faces, and a cone has a flat circular base, so neither is a sphere.

practice.prompt: A solid has two flat circular faces and one curved surface. What is the name of this solid?
practice.worked_solution: A cylinder has exactly two flat circular faces (top and bottom) joined by one curved surface. A sphere has no flat faces, so the solid described must be a cylinder.

practice.prompt: Complete the table for a sphere: faces, edges, vertices, curved surfaces.
practice.answer: A sphere has 0 flat faces, 0 edges, 0 vertices, and 1 curved surface.
practice.worked_solution: A sphere is perfectly round all over. It has no flat face anywhere, so 0 faces; no line where surfaces meet, so 0 edges; no corners, so 0 vertices; and its entire outside is one curved surface.

practice.prompt: Name one object in your home shaped like a cylinder and one shaped like a sphere.
practice.answer: For example, a drinking glass is a cylinder and an orange is a sphere. (Any similar correct examples are accepted.)
practice.worked_solution: A cylinder has a flat circular top and bottom joined by a curved surface (e.g. a glass or a tin). A sphere is round all over with no flat face (e.g. an orange, a football).

blocks.text:
Let's meet two more three-dimensional shapes that you see all around you: a cylinder and a sphere.

A cylinder is the shape of a tin of baked beans, a drum, or a drinking glass. Its two ends are identical circles, and the curved surface joining them is smooth and straight along its length. A cylinder has two flat faces (the circular ends), one curved face, and no corners. The line that runs down the middle of the curved face, from the centre of one circle to the centre of the other, is the height (or length) of the cylinder, and the radius of either end is the radius of the cylinder.

A sphere is perfectly round, like a football, a globe, or a marble. It has just one curved face, with no flat faces, no edges and no corners. Every point on the surface of a sphere is exactly the same distance from its centre, and that distance is the radius of the sphere.

So remember: a cylinder has two flat circular faces and one curved face; a sphere has only one curved face and nothing flat at all.

Now we turn to finding how much space a three-dimensional shape takes up. That space is called its volume, and it is measured in cubic units, such as cubic centimetres (cm³).

A cube is a shape whose every face is a square, so all its edges are the same length. If each edge is s units long, then its volume is s × s × s, written as s³. For example, a cube with edges 3 cm long has volume 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cm³.

A cuboid is like a box: its opposite faces are equal rectangles. If it has length l, breadth b and height h, then its volume is l × b × h. A cuboid 5 cm long, 4 cm wide and 2 cm high has volume 5 × 4 × 2 = 40 cm³.

A prism is a shape that has the same cross-section all the way through from one end to the other. The cross-section is the flat shape you see when you cut straight across the prism. A cuboid is one kind of prism, and so is a triangular prism, whose cross-section is a triangle. The volume of any prism is found the same way: the area of the cross-section multiplied by the length of the prism.

Volume of a prism = area of cross-section × length.

Worked example 1: Finding the volume of a cube
A cube has edges 4 cm long. Find its volume.

Step 1: A cube's volume is edge × edge × edge.
Step 2: 4 cm × 4 cm × 4 cm = 64 cm³.
Answer: The volume is 64 cm³.

Worked example 2: Finding the volume of a cuboid
A cuboid is 8 cm long, 5 cm broad and 3 cm high. Find its volume.

Step 1: A cuboid's volume is length × breadth × height.
Step 2: 8 cm × 5 cm × 3 cm = 120 cm³.
Answer: The volume is 120 cm³.

Worked example 3: Finding the volume of a triangular prism
A prism has a triangular cross-section with base 6 cm and height 4 cm, and the prism is 10 cm long. Find its volume.

Step 1: Find the area of the triangular cross-section. The area of a triangle is ½ × base × height, so ½ × 6 cm × 4 cm = 12 cm².
Step 2: Multiply the cross-section area by the length of the prism: 12 cm² × 10 cm = 120 cm³.
Answer: The volume is 120 cm³.

practice.prompt: Name one shape from this lesson that has only a single curved face and no flat faces, and say how many faces, edges and corners a cylinder has.
practice.answer: A sphere has only one curved face and no flat faces. A cylinder has two flat circular faces, one curved face, and no corners (and no edges that are corners, though the rims are circles).
practice.worked_solution: A sphere is perfectly round, so its entire surface is a single curved face. A cylinder is like a tin or drum: its two ends are flat circles (two flat faces), the curved side is one more face, and because all the faces meet along smooth curves rather than sharp points, it has no corners.

sections_json.title: Cylinders and Spheres: Knowing Their Shapes

blocks.text:
You have already worked with shapes like cubes, cuboids, pyramids and cones. Now we meet two more solid (three-dimensional) shapes: the cylinder and the sphere. A solid shape is described by its faces, edges and vertices, so to identify a shape we count and name these parts carefully.

Start with the **cylinder**. Think of a tin of baked beans, a drinking straw, or a roll of toilet paper. A cylinder has:

- **Two circular faces** – one at the top and one at the bottom. These two circles are exactly the same size, and they lie flat and parallel to each other.
- **One curved surface** – the smooth, rounded wall that joins the two circles together.
- In total, a cylinder has **three faces**: two circular faces plus the one curved surface.
- A cylinder has **no vertices** – you will not find a sharp corner or point on it.
- A cylinder has **no straight edges** either, because the circular rims are curved, not straight.

So when someone asks how many faces a solid cylinder has, the answer is **three**: two circular faces and one curved surface.

Now think of a **sphere**. Picture a football, a marble, or an orange. A sphere is perfectly round – every point on its surface is the same distance from its centre. A sphere has:

- **Exactly one curved surface**, and no flat faces at all.
- **No edges** and **no vertices** – there is nothing sharp anywhere on it.

So the key difference between the two shapes is this: a cylinder has flat circular faces (two of them) and a curved surface, while a sphere is one smooth curved surface with no flat faces, no edges and no vertices.

**Worked example 1 – a cylinder**

Look at a solid cylinder. Let's count its parts step by step.

1. Hold the cylinder so you can see the top. There is a circular face. Flip it over – there is another circular face at the bottom. That gives **2 circular faces**.
2. Run your hand around the wall that joins the top to the bottom. That smooth rounded wall is the **curved surface** – **1 curved surface**.
3. Add them together: 2 circular faces + 1 curved surface = **3 faces** in total.
4. Finally, look for corners. A cylinder has **no vertices**, and it has **no straight edges**.

So a solid cylinder has **3 faces** (2 of them circular) and **no vertices**.

**Worked example 2 – a sphere**

Take a sphere, like a football.

1. Feel the whole surface. It is smooth and curved all over, with no flat part – so it has **1 curved surface** and **no flat faces**.
2. Look for any corner, edge or point. There are none – a sphere has **no vertices** and **no edges**.

So a sphere has just **1 face** (a curved one) and **no vertices**.

The two worked examples show the difference clearly: the cylinder uses two flat circular faces plus a curved surface, while the sphere is one smooth curved surface with nothing flat and nothing sharp.

practice.prompt: How many circular faces does a solid cylinder have?
practice.answer: 2 (two). A solid cylinder has two circular faces – one at the top and one at the bottom – plus one curved surface.

practice.prompt: A cylinder has how many faces in total?
practice.answer: 3 faces: two circular faces and one curved surface.
practice.worked_solution: Count the flat parts first: the top circle is one face and the bottom circle is another, giving 2 faces. Then add the curved wall that joins them, which is 1 more face. So 2 + 1 = 3 faces in total.

practice.prompt: How many faces, edges and vertices does a sphere have?

sections_json.title: Finding the Volume of Cubes, Cuboids and Prisms

blocks.text:
Volume tells you how much space a three-dimensional shape takes up. To measure it, think of filling the shape with little cubes. For a cuboid, you can picture it as rows of unit cubes.

A cuboid has three measurements: its length, its width (also called its breadth) and its height. To find its volume, you multiply all three together:

**Volume of a cuboid = length × width × height**

A cube is a special cuboid where the length, width and height are all equal. If the side of the cube is called \(s\), then its volume is:

**Volume of a cube = \(s \times s \times s = s^3\)**

So a cube of side 4 cm has volume \(4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64 \text{ cm}^3\).

A prism is a three-dimensional shape with two identical parallel faces (its bases) and sides that are rectangles or parallelograms. For any prism, you can find its volume by working out the area of the base first, then multiplying by the height of the prism:

**Volume of a prism = area of base × height**

A cuboid is itself a prism whose base is a rectangle, so this same rule works for it too: the area of its rectangular base is length × width, and multiplying by the height gives length × width × height.

Remember the units: if the measurements are in centimetres, the volume is in cubic centimetres, written cm³; if in metres, it is cubic metres, m³.

**Example 1: Volume of a cuboid**

Find the volume of a cuboid that is 8 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high.

Volume = length × width × height
= 8 × 4 × 3
= 32 × 3
= 96 cm³

**Example 2: Volume of a cube**

What is the volume of a cube of side 5 cm?

Volume = \(s^3 = 5 \times 5 \times 5\)
= 25 × 5
= 125 cm³

**Example 3: Volume of a prism**

A triangular prism has a base with area 10 cm² and a height of 7 cm. Find its volume.

Volume = area of base × height
= 10 × 7
= 70 cm³

It has no edge and no vertex — there is nothing sharp on a sphere at all. 3. It has one curved surface only.

sections_json.title: Finding the Volume of Cubes, Cuboids and Prisms

blocks.text:
Volume is the amount of space a three-dimensional shape takes up, and we measure it in cubic units such as cm³, m³ or mm³. To find the volume of any solid that has a flat base and straight vertical sides, we can multiply the area of the base by the height of the shape.

For a cuboid, the base is a rectangle, so the area of the base is length × breadth. Multiplying that by the height gives the volume:

Volume of a cuboid = length × breadth × height = lbh

A cube is a special cuboid where all three edges are the same length, so length = breadth = height = l. Its volume is therefore:

Volume of a cube = length × length × length = l³

Example 1. Calculate the volume of a cuboid of length 3 cm, breadth 2 cm and height 8 cm.

Solution:

Volume of a cuboid = length × breadth × height

length = 3 cm, breadth = 2 cm, height = 8 cm

Volume = 3 cm × 2 cm × 8 cm = 48 cm³

So the volume of the cuboid is 48 cm³.

Example 2. The volume of a cuboid is 24 cm³. If the base is 6 cm by 2 cm, find the height of the cuboid.

Solution:

Volume of a cuboid = length × breadth × height

length = 6 cm, breadth = 2 cm, height = ?

Volume = 24 cm³

So 24 cm³ = 6 cm × 2 cm × h

24 cm³ = 12 cm² × h

To find h, divide both sides by 12 cm²:

24 cm³ ÷ 12 cm² = h

h = 2 cm

So the height of the cuboid is 2 cm.

Example 3. Calculate the volume of a cube of side 3 cm.

Solution:

Volume of a cube = l³

V = (3 cm)³ = 3 cm × 3 cm × 3 cm = 27 cm³

So the volume of the cube is 27 cm³.

A prism is a solid with a uniform cross-section, meaning the same shape runs all the way along its length. For example, the prism in fig-03 is a triangular prism: its end is a triangle, and that triangle runs back 10 m along the prism. Its base does not have to be a rectangle, so we use the general rule:

Volume of a prism = area of base × height

Here "base" means the cross-section that is repeated, and the "height" is how far that shape runs along the prism.

blocks.caption: A triangular prism lying on its rectangular face. The triangular end has a base of 5 m and a height of 3 m, and the prism runs back 10 m.

blocks.text:
Example 4. In fig-03, the triangular prism has a triangular end with a base of 5 m and a height of 3 m, and the prism runs back 10 m. Calculate its volume.

Solution:

First find the area of the triangular base.

Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height = ½ × 5 × 3 = 7.5 m²

Now multiply by the distance the prism runs back:

Volume of prism = area of base × height = 7.5 m² × 10 m = 75 m³

So the volume of the prism is 75 m³.

practice.worked_solution: Volume = length × breadth × height = 5 m × 2 m × 3 m = 30 m³.

sections_json.title: Volume of a cube, a cuboid and a prism

blocks.text:
Volume is the amount of space a shape takes up. For a cuboid — a box with a rectangular base — you find the volume by multiplying the length, the breadth and the height:

$$\text{Volume of a cuboid} = \text{length} \times \text{breadth} \times \text{height} = lbh$$

You can also think of it as the area of the base times the height. Since the base is a rectangle of area $l \times b$, multiplying by the height $h$ gives $lbh$.

A cube is a cuboid whose length, breadth and height are all the same. If each side is $l$, then:

$$\text{Volume of a cube} = l \times l \times l = l^3$$

For a prism — a solid with a constant cross-section — the volume is the area of the base (the end face) times the height:

$$\text{Volume of a prism} = \text{area of base} \times \text{height}$$

You use whichever end face is constant, find its area, then multiply by how far the prism runs back.

**Example 1. Find the volume of a cuboid of length 3 cm, breadth 2 cm and height 8 cm.**

$$\text{Volume} = L \times b \times h$$

Length $= 3\text{ cm}$, breadth $= 2\text{ cm}$, height $= 8\text{ cm}$.

$$\text{Volume} = 3\text{ cm} \times 2\text{ cm} \times 8\text{ cm} = 48\text{ cm}^3$$

So the cuboid holds $48\text{ cm}^3$.

---

**Example 2. The volume of a cuboid is $24\text{ cm}^3$. If its base is 6 cm by 2 cm, find its height.**

$$\text{Volume} = L \times b \times h$$

Length $= 6\text{ cm}$, breadth $= 2\text{ cm}$, height $= h$ (unknown).

$$24\text{ cm}^3 = 6\text{ cm} \times 2\text{ cm} \times h$$

$$24\text{ cm}^3 = 12\text{ cm}^2 \times h$$

Divide both sides by $12\text{ cm}^2$:

$$\frac{24\text{ cm}^3}{12\text{ cm}^2} = \frac{12\text{ cm}^2 \times h}{12\text{ cm}^2}$$

$$2\text{ cm} = h$$

So the height is $2\text{ cm}$.

---

**Example 3. Find the volume of a cube of side 3 cm.**

$$\text{Volume of a cube} = l^3$$

$$V = (3\text{ cm})^3 = 3\text{ cm} \times 3\text{ cm} \times 3\text{ cm} = 27\text{ cm}^3$$

---

**Example 4. Find the volume of the triangular prism**, where the triangular end has a base of 5 m and a height of 3 m, and the prism runs back 10 m.

First find the area of the triangular base:

$$\text{Area of triangle} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 3 = 7.5\text{ m}^2$$

Then multiply by the length of the prism (10 m):

$$\text{Volume of prism} = \text{area of base} \times \text{height} = 7.5\text{ m}^2 \times 10\text{ m} = 75\text{ m}^3$$

blocks.caption: A triangular prism lying on its rectangular face. The triangular end has a base of 5 m and a height of 3 m, and the prism runs back 10 m.

practice.worked_solution: Volume of a cuboid $= L \times b \times h = 5\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m} = 30\text{ m}^3$.

practice.worked_solution: Volume of a cube $= l^3 = (4\text{ cm})^3 = 4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64\text{ cm}^3$.
