blocks.text:
Parallel lines are straight lines that stay the same distance apart all along their length, so they never meet, no matter how far you draw them. In a pair of parallel lines, the arrowheads drawn on each line point the same way.

To construct a line parallel to a given line through a chosen point, you can use two simple tools: a ruler and a set square. The set square is the triangle-shaped ruler; the secret is that its edges are already perfectly square to one another, so sliding it along a ruler keeps the same direction.

Here is the plan. You already have a line drawn on your page and a point P where you want the parallel line to pass. Put one edge of the set square along your given line. Hold your ruler firmly against another edge of the set square, like a track. Then slide the set square along the ruler until its edge touches the point P. Draw your line along that edge — it is parallel to the first line.

The important habit is to keep the ruler completely still while the set square slides. If the ruler moves, the direction changes and your new line will not be parallel.

Worked example — construct a line through a point P parallel to a given line AB.

Step 1: Draw a straight line and label its ends A and B. Mark a point P anywhere above the line where you want the new line to run.

Step 2: Place one edge of your set square flat along line AB. The set square should sit so it leans on the line.

Step 3: Hold your ruler against the long sloping edge of the set square, pressing it down so it cannot move. This ruler is your track.

Step 4: Slide the set square along the ruler until its bottom edge touches the point P. Do not let the ruler slip.

Step 5: Draw a straight line along the bottom edge of the set square, through P, and past it on both sides.

Step 6: Check your work — put the set square back on line AB and slide it again. If it lands exactly on your new line, you have drawn a true parallel. Mark both lines with matching arrowheads.

practice.prompt: You are given a straight line. Use a ruler and a set square to construct a line parallel to it through a point P marked above the line. List the three things you must do, in order, to keep your new line parallel.
practice.answer: 1. Place one edge of the set square along the given line. 2. Hold the ruler firmly as a track against another edge of the set square so it cannot slip. 3. Slide the set square along the ruler to P and draw along its edge.
practice.worked_solution: The three essential steps are: put the set square's edge on the given line; lock the ruler against the set square as a track; slide the set square to P and draw. The ruler must stay still while the set square slides, otherwise the direction changes.

practice.prompt: After constructing your parallel line, you slide your set square back along the ruler to check your work. What does it mean if the set square's edge lies exactly on the line you just drew?
practice.answer: It means the line you drew is correctly parallel to the given line, because sliding the set square along the same track reproduced the same direction.
practice.worked_solution: Sliding the set square along the ruler reproduces the same direction every time, so if it lies exactly on your new line, that line has the same direction as the original — it is parallel. If it does not land exactly, the ruler moved during construction and you should try again.

practice.prompt: While you are sliding the set square towards point P, your hand nudges the ruler and it turns slightly. Explain in one sentence why your new line will no longer be parallel.
practice.answer: Because the ruler is the track that fixes the direction, so if it turns, the set square slides in a new direction and the line you draw is no longer parallel to the original.
practice.worked_solution: The ruler sets the direction of the slide. The whole method only works because sliding the set square along a still ruler preserves the original direction. If the ruler turns, the preserved direction changes too, so the drawn line is not parallel.

sections_json.title: Drawing Lines That Meet at Right Angles

blocks.text: Two lines are perpendicular when they meet at a right angle — that is, the angle between them is exactly 90°. You can check your work with your protractor, but you can also construct a perpendicular line using only a ruler and a pair of compasses, which gives an exact right angle every time. To construct a perpendicular, you only need two moves with your compass: draw arcs, then join the points where those arcs cross. Here is the whole idea. Suppose you have a straight line AB and you want to draw a line through a point P on it that stands straight up at a right angle. The secret is that the point where two equal arcs cross is always the same distance from the two centres of those arcs — and that balance is exactly what makes the join come out at 90°. When you practise, always keep your compass opening unchanged as you swing each arc. If you keep the same opening, your arcs stay true and your right angle comes out cleanly.

Worked example 1 — a perpendicular at a point on the line Construct a line perpendicular to AB through the point P that lies on AB. Step 1. Put the point of your compass on P and open it to any width. Draw one arc that crosses AB on the left of P and another that crosses AB on the right of P. Call the two crossing points C (left) and D (right). Now PC = PD, because you used the same compass opening. Step 2. Keep the compass at that same opening. Put the point on C and swing a large arc above P. Without changing the opening, put the point on D and swing another large arc above P. Let the two arcs meet at a point Q. Step 3. Draw the straight line from P through Q. Because QC = QD and PC = PD, the line PQ stands exactly at a right angle to AB. Your protractor will read 90° at P.

Worked example 2 — a perpendicular dropped from a point not on the line Construct a line from the point P that meets the line AB at a right angle, where P is not on AB. Step 1. Put your compass on P and open it wide enough that an arc will cross AB in two places. Swing one arc that cuts AB at C on one side and D on the other. Step 2. Now put the point of the compass on C and open it a little more than half of CD. Swing an arc below AB. Without changing the opening, put the point on D and swing another arc below AB. Let them meet at Q. Step 3. Draw the line from P through Q. It crosses AB at a right angle, so the distance from P straight down to AB is the shortest possible. Check with your protractor: the angle where your new line meets AB is 90°.

practice.prompt: Draw a horizontal line AB about 6 cm long and mark a point P in the middle of it. Using only a ruler and compasses, construct the line through P that is perpendicular to AB. What is the angle where your new line meets AB?
practice.answer: The angle is exactly 90° (a right angle), so the constructed line is perpendicular to AB.
practice.worked_solution: Put the compass point on P and draw two small arcs, one crossing AB on each side of P. Keep the same opening, put the point on each crossing in turn, and swing two larger arcs that meet above P. Draw the line from P through that meeting point. The new line makes a 90° angle with AB, so it is perpendicular.

practice.prompt: A point P is drawn above a line AB, not touching it. You want to drop a perpendicular from P down to AB. Put the steps in order: (a) swing an arc centred at P that cuts AB in two places; (b) draw the line from P through the meeting point of the two lower arcs; (c) from each cutting point, swing equal arcs that meet below AB. Write the correct order as three letters.
practice.worked_solution: First the arc from P cuts AB in two places (a). Then, from those two places, equal arcs meet below the line (c). Finally you join P to the meeting point (b). The order is a, c, b.

sections_json.title: Cutting a Line Segment in Half with a Compass

blocks.text: When you "bisect a line segment", you cut it exactly into two equal halves. The point where it is cut is called the midpoint. You can find that midpoint with a ruler, but a much more reliable way is to do it by construction with a compass — and that is what this revision pack is about. The idea is simple. If you draw a compass circle that passes through both ends of your segment, then the point halfway between those two ends is exactly the centre of that circle. To be sure, we draw two overlapping circles (one centred at each end), and the midpoint of the segment lies on the straight line joining the two points where the circles cross. Here is the full method, step by step. You need only a ruler (for drawing straight lines) and a pair of compasses. Step 1. Draw your line segment AB. Step 2. Put the point of the compass on A, open it a little more than half of AB, and draw a large arc (or circle) so it swings well above and well below the line. Step 3. Keeping the compass opening exactly the same, put the point on B and draw another arc, the same size. The two arcs should cross each other at two points — one above the line and one below it. Step 4. Draw a straight line through those two crossing points. Where this new line cuts AB is the midpoint of AB. The new line you have drawn is called the perpendicular bisector of AB, because it crosses AB at a right angle and at its exact middle. The single point where the two lines meet is the midpoint.

Worked example: Bisect a segment 8 cm long. Suppose AB is 8 cm long and you want its midpoint. 1. Draw AB, 8 cm long, with A on the left and B on the right. 2. Open your compass to about 5 cm — clearly more than half of 8 cm (half of 8 cm is 4 cm, so 5 cm works). Put the point on A and swing a large arc above and below the line. 3. Keep the compass opening at 5 cm. Put the point on B and swing a matching arc. The two arcs meet at a point above the line, call it C, and a point below the line, call it D. 4. Draw a straight line through C and D. It will cross AB at the midpoint M. 5. Measure: AM should be 4 cm and MB should be 4 cm. Because the opening (5 cm) was bigger than half the segment, this works even if you do not measure AB first. Check: the two halves AM and MB are equal, and the line CD meets AB at a right angle. You have bisected the segment.

practice.prompt: A line segment PQ is 10 cm long. Using your compass and ruler only, bisect PQ and mark the midpoint M. What is the length of PM?
practice.answer: PM = 5 cm, because the midpoint splits PQ into two equal halves of 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm each.
practice.worked_solution: Draw PQ = 10 cm. Open the compass to more than half of 10 cm (for example, 6 cm). Draw an arc from P above and below the line, then, keeping the same opening, draw an arc from Q. The arcs cross at two points; draw a straight line through both crossing points. Where that line meets PQ is M. Since M is halfway along a 10 cm segment, PM = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.

practice.prompt: A segment XY is 6 cm long. You bisect XY to find its midpoint, then you bisect one of the two halves again. How long is each of the smallest pieces?
practice.answer: The smallest pieces are 1.5 cm each.
practice.worked_solution: First bisection splits XY = 6 cm into two equal pieces of 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm each. Bisecting one 3 cm piece splits it into two equal pieces of 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 cm each. So the smallest pieces are 1.5 cm long.

blocks.text:
A right angle measures exactly 90°. It is the corner you see in a square or the corner of a sheet of paper. Using only a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses, you can draw a perfect 90° angle without guessing.

Here is the method to construct a 90° angle at a chosen point P on a straight line. Keep your pencil sharp, and do not change the compass opening unless the steps tell you to.

1. Draw a straight line and mark a point P on it.
2. With P as the centre, draw an arc (a part of a circle) that cuts the line at two points, one on each side of P. Call them A and B.
3. Open the compass a little wider — more than half the distance from A to B.
4. With A as the centre, draw an arc above the line.
5. Keeping the compass exactly the same opening, with B as the centre, draw another arc above the line to cut the first arc. Call the point where they meet C.
6. Use your ruler to join P to C, and extend the line.

The line PC meets the original line at right angles. The two lines are perpendicular, so the angle between them is exactly 90°.

Why does this work? The arcs drawn from A and B have equal radius, so C is the same distance from A as it is from B. That means C sits exactly above the middle of the segment, and the line joining it to P stands straight up — at right angles to the line below.

Construct a 90° angle at the point P on the line below.

Step 1: Draw a straight line and mark a point P somewhere on it.

Step 2: Put the point of your compass on P and draw an arc that crosses the line on both sides of P. Label these crossings A (left) and B (right). Notice that A and B are the same distance from P.

Step 3: Widen the compass so its opening is more than half of AB. Put the point on A and draw an arc above the line.

Step 4: Without changing the compass opening, put the point on B and draw another arc above the line. The two arcs meet at a point C.

Step 5: Place your ruler against P and C, and draw a straight line through both points, extending it a little past C.

The line PC now stands at right angles to the original line, so the angle at P is exactly 90°. To check, you can fit the corner of your set square or a sheet of paper into the angle — it should sit perfectly.

practice.prompt: List the compass and pencil steps, in order, that you would use to construct a 90° angle at a point P on a straight line.
practice.answer: 1. Put the compass point on P and draw an arc cutting the line at two points A and B. 2. Widen the compass to more than half of AB. 3. Draw an arc above the line from centre A. 4. Keeping the same opening, draw an arc above the line from centre B to meet the first arc at C. 5. Draw the line from P through C. The angle at P is 90°.
practice.worked_solution: The construction needs three centres: first P to mark A and B, then A and B to locate C. After the first arc fixes A and B, open the compass wider so the arcs from A and B cross above the line. The meeting point C is then joined to P.

practice.prompt: In the construction of a 90° angle, you draw two arcs above the line — one from centre A and one from centre B. Why must the compass opening be the same for both of these arcs?
practice.answer: So that the point C where the arcs meet is the same distance from A as it is from B. That places C directly above the middle of the line, making the angle at P exactly 90°.
practice.worked_solution: Equal radii from A and B mean C lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, so the line PC is perpendicular to the line, giving a 90° angle. If the openings differed, C would not be centred and the angle would not be exactly 90°.

practice.prompt: A student marks a point P on a line and draws the first arc with centre P, getting points A and B. She then keeps the same small compass opening to draw arcs from A and B, but the two arcs do not meet above the line. What has she done wrong, and how should she fix it?
practice.answer: Her compass opening is too small — the arcs do not reach each other. She should widen the compass so its opening is more than half of AB, then draw the arcs from A and B again.
practice.worked_solution: The first arc from P may be any size, but the arcs from A and B must be opened wider than half of AB, otherwise the two arcs have too small a radius to cross above the line. Widening the compass fixes it.

practice.prompt: Using a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses, construct a 90° angle at a point P on a straight line. Then use the corner of your set square or a sheet of paper to check that the angle you drew is exactly 90°.
practice.answer: The construction should show a straight line, a point P on it, and a second line through P standing at right angles to the first. The corner of a set square or paper should fit into the angle exactly.
practice.worked_solution: Follow the five steps: mark P, arc from P to get A and B, widen the compass, arc from A, arc from B to meet at C, then join P to C. Check the corner of a set square fits snugly in the angle, confirming 90°.

blocks.text:
An angle of 60° is one of the special angles you can draw using only a ruler and a pair of compasses. You do not need a protractor at all. The trick is that a 60° angle is one corner of an equilateral triangle — a triangle in which all three sides are equal, so all three angles are equal too. Since the three angles of any triangle add up to 180°, each angle in an equilateral triangle is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°.

So, to draw a 60° angle, you simply build an equilateral triangle. Here is the plan:

1. Draw a straight line, and mark a point on it. Call this point A. This is where your angle will sit.
2. Open your compasses to any convenient length. Keep this opening the SAME for the whole construction.
3. Put the compass point on A and draw an arc that crosses the line on one side of A. Call the crossing point B. The distance AB is your compass opening.
4. Keep the compasses at the same opening. Put the point on B and draw an arc that crosses the first arc (above the line). Call the crossing point D.
5. Draw a straight line from A through D.

The angle between the line AB (the original line) and the line AD is exactly 60°. You have constructed a 60° angle! You can check why it works: D lies on the arc drawn from A, so AD equals your compass opening; D also lies on the arc drawn from B, so BD equals your compass opening. And AB equals your compass opening too. So triangle ABD has all three sides equal — it is equilateral — and its angle at A is 60°.

Worked example: Construct a 60° angle at point A on a line.

Step 1 — Draw a horizontal line and mark point A on it.

Step 2 — Open your compasses to a convenient width, say 4 cm. Put the compass point on A and draw an arc that cuts the line on the right. Where it cuts the line, mark point B. So AB is now 4 cm long.

Step 3 — Keep the compasses at exactly 4 cm. Put the point on B and draw an arc above the line so that it crosses the first arc. Mark the crossing point D.

Step 4 — Draw a straight line from A through D. The angle DAB is 60°.

Check: AB is 4 cm (your compass opening). Point D lies on the arc drawn from A, so AD is also 4 cm. Point D also lies on the arc drawn from B, so BD is 4 cm as well. All three sides of triangle ABD are equal, so it is equilateral. That means each of its angles is 60°, so the angle at A is 60°.

practice.prompt: Construct a 60° angle at a point A on a straight line using only a ruler and compasses. Then measure it with your protractor (if you have one) to check it is about 60°.
practice.answer: You should end with an angle between your original line and the final line of about 60°. The two arcs above the line cross at a point D, and the line from A to D makes the 60° angle.
practice.worked_solution: Draw a line and mark A. With compasses at a fixed opening, mark B on the line from A, then C on the line from B. Keeping the same opening, draw arcs from B and C that cross above the line at D. Draw A to D. Since AB = BC = AD (all equal to your compass opening), triangle ABD is equilateral, so the angle at A is 60°.

practice.prompt: In your construction of a 60° angle, the point where the two arcs cross above the line is labelled D. Why is the angle at A exactly 60° and not some other size? Explain using the idea of a triangle.
practice.answer: Because triangle ABD is equilateral: AB, BD and AD are all the same length (each equals your compass opening). Every angle of an equilateral triangle is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°, so the angle at A is 60°.
practice.worked_solution: All three sides of triangle ABD are the same length, so it is equilateral. The three equal angles add to 180°, so each is 60°. The angle at A is one of them.

sections_json.title: Constructing Parallel Lines with a Set Square and Ruler

blocks.text: Two straight lines are parallel when they always stay the same distance apart, so they never meet no matter how far you extend them. The two rails of a railway track are parallel, and so are the two upright sides of a ladder. You already know how to draw a straight line with a ruler. Now you will learn how to construct a line that is parallel to a line you have already drawn, using two simple tools: a set square and a ruler.

The trick is to let the set square slide along the ruler, keeping the ruler fixed. Because the set square is a right-angled triangle, when you slide it its edge never changes direction — so the line you draw is parallel to the one you started with.

To construct a line through a point P that is parallel to a given line AB:

1. Draw the given line and label its ends A and B. Mark clearly the point P through which the new parallel line must pass.
2. Place the set square so that one of its straight edges lies exactly on top of the line AB.
3. Hold the ruler firmly against the side of the set square, so that the ruler does not move.
4. Keeping the ruler pressed against the table, slide the set square along the ruler until its edge reaches point P.
5. Now hold the set square firmly and draw a straight line along its edge through P.

The line you have drawn through P is parallel to AB.

Construct a line through point P that is parallel to the given line AB.

Step 1 — Draw a line about 8 cm long and label its ends A and B. Mark a point P about 3 cm above the middle of the line.

Step 2 — Place the set square so one of its straight edges lies exactly on line AB. The edge must touch the line along its whole length.

Step 3 — Hold the ruler firmly against the side of the set square, keeping it fixed in position.

Step 4 — Slide the set square up the ruler until its edge passes through point P.

Step 5 — Press the set square firmly and draw a straight line through P along its edge. Label this new line.

Check your work: measure the gap between AB and your new line at two different places with your ruler. The two gaps should be equal. That is the sign that the two lines are parallel — they stay the same distance apart, so they will never meet.

practice.prompt: Draw a straight line AB about 8 cm long. Mark a point P about 3 cm above the line. Using only a set square and a ruler, construct the line through P that is parallel to AB. Write down, in order, the steps you took.
practice.answer: You placed the set square with one edge exactly on AB, held the ruler against the side of the set square, slid the set square along the ruler until its edge reached P, and drew the line through P. The line you drew is parallel to AB.

practice.prompt: Draw a line CD about 6 cm long. Mark a point Q below the line. Construct the line through Q that is parallel to CD using a set square and ruler. Now measure the gap between the two lines at two different places. What should you find, and what does this tell you?
practice.answer: The two gaps you measured should be equal. This is exactly the test for parallel lines: they stay the same distance apart everywhere, so they can never meet.

practice.prompt: Draw a line AB about 7 cm long. Mark a point P above the line and a point Q below the line. Construct a line through P parallel to AB, and a separate line through Q parallel to AB. What do you notice about the three lines, and why?
practice.answer: All three lines are parallel to one another. The line through P and the line through Q are each parallel to AB, so all three run at the same angle and never meet one another.

blocks.text:
Two lines are perpendicular when they meet at a right angle — that is, at exactly 90°. You have seen this idea when drawing squares, rectangles and right angles. With your mathematical set you can draw a perpendicular to any straight line, and you do it with just a ruler and a set square. Here is the key idea. Your set square has one corner that is a perfect right angle, and the two edges that meet at that corner are perpendicular to each other. If you slide one of those edges along a straight line, the other edge always stays at 90° to it. So, wherever you stop, the edge that is not lying on the line is a perpendicular line — you just draw along it. To draw a perpendicular to a given line:
  1. Place the ruler so one of its long edges lies exactly along your given line. Hold it still.
  2. Place the set square so that one of its shorter edges lies flat against the ruler, with the right-angle corner pressed against the ruler's edge.
  3. Draw along the other short edge of the set square. This edge is at right angles to the line, so the line you draw is perpendicular to it.
Mark the point where the two lines meet and label the right angle so you can see it is 90°.

Example. Draw a line AB, and then construct a perpendicular to it. Step 1. Draw the line AB with your ruler and label its ends A and B. Step 2. Place your ruler so one long edge lies exactly along AB. Hold the ruler firmly so it does not slip. Step 3. Place your set square against the ruler, with its right-angle corner pressed to the ruler's edge and one of its short edges lying flat along the ruler. Step 4. Slide the set square along the ruler until the edge you will draw from is where you want the perpendicular to stand, then press it down. Step 5. Draw a line along the other short edge of the set square. Extend it with your ruler so it is clearly a straight line crossing AB. Step 6. Mark the point where the two lines meet, and draw a small square in the corner to show the right angle. The line you have drawn meets AB at a right angle, so it is perpendicular to AB. Check your work by looking at the corner: the two lines form a clean 90° angle.

practice.prompt: Draw a horizontal line PQ on your page. Using your ruler and set square, construct a line perpendicular to PQ that passes through a point you choose on PQ. Name the point where the two lines meet.
practice.answer: Your constructed line meets PQ at a right angle. The point where the two lines cross is the point you chose on PQ. Check that the two lines form a clean 90° corner.
practice.worked_solution: Lay the ruler's edge along PQ. Press the set square's short edge against the ruler, slide it to your chosen point, hold it firm, and draw along the other short edge. The drawn edge is perpendicular to PQ because it follows the set square's right-angle corner.

practice.prompt: Draw a line segment AB. Construct a perpendicular to AB at its midpoint — that is, halfway between A and B. Measure the four angles where your new line crosses AB. What do you notice about them?
practice.answer: All four angles where the perpendicular crosses AB are equal and each is 90°.
practice.worked_solution: Measure AB, mark its midpoint, then place the ruler along AB and slide the set square to the midpoint. Draw along the set square's other short edge. Each of the four angles where the two lines cross is a right angle, 90°, because the two lines are perpendicular.

sections_json.title: Cutting a Line Exactly in Half

blocks.text:
When you draw a line, you can find its midpoint by measuring with a ruler. But in construction we find that point using only your mathematical set — a pair of compasses and a straight edge. This is called **bisecting** the line segment: cutting it into two equal halves.

To bisect a line segment you draw a line that crosses it at its exact middle and meets it at a right angle. That line is called the **perpendicular bisector** of the segment. The point where it crosses the segment is the midpoint, and it splits the original segment into two equal parts.

Here is the idea. A point that is the same distance from the two ends of a segment must lie on the line that cuts the segment exactly in half. So we find two such points — one above the segment and one below it — and join them. The line through those two points is the perpendicular bisector, and where it crosses the segment is the midpoint.

Let us bisect a line segment AB.

1. Draw the segment AB with your ruler. Leave a little space above and below it, because the compass work happens there.

2. Put the point of your compasses on A. Open them so the gap is more than half the length of AB — clearly more than half, not just a little. Draw an arc that passes above and below the segment, near where the middle will be.

3. Without changing the compass opening, move the point to B. Draw a second arc. The two arcs meet at two points: one above the segment and one below it.

4. With your ruler, draw a straight line through the two points where the arcs crossed. This line crosses AB at its midpoint. Label that point M.

The segment is now cut into two equal halves: AM and MB are equal in length, and the line you drew meets AB at a right angle.

practice.prompt: Draw a line segment CD that is 8 cm long. Bisect it with your compasses and ruler. Mark the midpoint M. What are the lengths of CM and MD?
practice.answer: CM = 4 cm and MD = 4 cm. The perpendicular bisector cuts the 8 cm segment exactly in half.
practice.worked_solution: 1. Draw CD = 8 cm. 2. Put the compass point on C, open the compass more than 4 cm (more than half), and draw an arc above and below the segment. 3. Without changing the opening, put the point on D and draw another arc, so the arcs cross above and below. 4. Draw a straight line through the two crossing points. It meets CD at its midpoint M. Half of 8 cm is 4 cm, so CM = 4 cm and MD = 4 cm.

practice.prompt: When you bisect a line segment, why must the compass opening be more than half the length of the segment (not exactly half, and not less than half)?
practice.answer: If the opening is less than half, the two arcs drawn from the two ends cannot reach each other, so they do not cross and there is no point to join. If it is exactly half, the arcs only touch at one point on the segment, so you cannot draw the perpendicular bisector through it. Opening it more than half makes the arcs cross in two places, one above and one below, giving the two points needed to draw the bisector.

practice.prompt: You bisect a line segment and label the midpoint M. State two things that are always true about the line you drew that crosses the segment at M.
practice.answer: It passes through the exact midpoint M of the segment, and it meets the segment at a right angle (90°). Because of that it is called the perpendicular bisector.

blocks.text:
A right angle is the angle that measures exactly 90°. You meet it at the corner of a page, a doorframe or a set square. You can build one yourself using only a ruler and a pair of compasses.

The key idea is this: if a line stands straight up on another line, the two angles it makes at the meeting point are both right angles. We say the standing line is *perpendicular* to the first line, and the angle where they meet is 90°. So constructing a 90° angle is the same as constructing a perpendicular to a line at a chosen point on it.

Here is the plan. You start with a line and mark a point where the right angle should sit. Then you draw a sequence of compass arcs — some cutting the line, some rising above it — and the last point where two arcs meet gives you the direction of the perpendicular. A final line drawn from that point to your marked point completes the right angle.

Worked example — construct a 90° angle at point O on a line.

Use a sharp pencil, a ruler and a pair of compasses. Keep the radius of your compasses steady while you use it.

Step 1. Draw a straight line across your page. Mark a point O on it. This is where the right angle will sit.

Step 2. Place the compass point on O. Open the compasses to any convenient radius — about half the width of your page works well. Draw a complete circle with centre O. Where that circle crosses your straight line, you get two points; label them A (on the left) and B (on the right). The distances OA and OB are equal because they are both radii of the same circle.

Step 3. Put the compass point on A. Without changing the radius, draw a large arc above the line, roughly in the middle. Make it long enough that a second arc can cross it.

Step 4. Now put the compass point on B. Still without changing the radius, draw another arc above the line so that it crosses the arc from Step 3. Label the point where the two arcs cross C.

Step 5. Use your ruler to draw a straight line from C to O. This line is perpendicular to your original line, so it stands straight up on it.

Step 6. Check your work: the angle between the original line and the line OC — on either side of O — should look like the corner of a page. Measure it with a protractor if you have one; it should read 90°.

Why this works: the compasses were kept at the same radius throughout, so OA = OB = AC = BC. With all four sides equal, figure AOBC is a rhombus, and the line OC is the perpendicular bisector that splits the straight angle AOB of 180° exactly in half, giving 90° on each side.

practice.prompt: On a fresh line, mark a point O and construct a 90° angle at O using your ruler and compasses only. Then check your angle by measurement.
practice.answer: Your construction should show a perpendicular line standing on the original line at O, and the angle between them should measure 90° with a protractor.
practice.worked_solution: Follow the worked example: draw the line and point O; draw a circle centred on O to cut the line at A and B; keeping the same radius, draw an arc from A and a crossing arc from B above the line, meeting at C; draw OC. The line OC is perpendicular to the original line, so the angle at O is 90°.

practice.prompt: In the construction of a 90° angle, the compasses are kept at the same radius in every step. Explain in one or two sentences why this matters.
practice.answer: Keeping the radius the same makes OA = OB = AC = BC, so the figure formed is a rhombus whose diagonal OC splits the straight angle of 180° in half, giving 90° on each side.

blocks.text: An angle of 60° is one you will meet again and again, because it sits inside equilateral triangles and regular hexagons. The good news is that you can draw it with just your compass and ruler — no protractor needed. The secret is the equilateral triangle hiding inside the construction: when you make three arcs of the same radius that join end to end, the angle they enclose is exactly 60°.

Construct an angle of 60° at the point A on a line.

Step 1. Draw a straight line and mark a point A on it. This is where the 60° angle will sit.

Step 2. Open your compass to any convenient radius. Put the point of the compass on A and draw an arc that crosses the line. Call the point where the arc meets the line B. The radius AB is your working radius.

Step 3. Without changing the radius, put the compass point on B and draw a second arc, cutting the first arc. Call the point where the two arcs cross C.

Step 4. Use your ruler to join A to C with a straight line.

The angle BAC is 60°. Why? Because AB, BC and AC are all equal — each is the same compass radius — so triangle ABC is equilateral, and every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°.

practice.prompt: Draw a straight line, mark a point A on it, and construct an angle of 60° at A using only your compass and ruler. After you have finished, check the two arcs you drew had the same radius and that you joined A to the point where the arcs crossed.
practice.answer: A correct construction shows an angle at A of 60°. Your two compass arcs must have the same radius, and the line from A should run to the point where those two arcs cross. If it does, the angle is exactly 60°.
practice.worked_solution: Draw line AB, then swing an arc from A across the line (meeting it at B). Keeping the radius unchanged, swing a second arc from B so it crosses the first (at C). Join A to C. Since AB = BC = AC (all one compass radius), triangle ABC is equilateral, so angle BAC = 60°.

practice.prompt: Explain, in your own words, why the construction you just did gives an angle of 60° rather than, say, 45° or 90°. What must stay true about your compass radius for this to work?
practice.answer: The three sides AB, BC and AC are all equal because each is made with the same compass radius. A triangle with three equal sides is equilateral, and every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°. The radius must stay the same (unchanged) throughout the construction, or the sides will not be equal and the angle will not be 60°.

sections_json.title: Drawing Parallel Lines with a Set Square and Ruler

blocks.text: Two lines are parallel when they run side by side and never meet, no matter how far they are extended. This section shows you how to draw a line through a given point that stays parallel to a given line, using only your set square and ruler.

Here is the method for the problem: construct a line through point $P$ parallel to the line $AB$. Step 1. Place the set square so that one of its edges lies exactly along $AB$ (fig-01). Step 2. Place the ruler firmly against one of the other edges of the set square. If you are right-handed, rest the ruler against the left-hand edge (fig-02). The ruler just holds the set square in place — its own slope does not matter, so the ruler may lean however is comfortable for you (fig-03). What matters is that the set square does not turn. Step 3. Hold the ruler firmly and slide the set square along the ruler towards $P$. Keep sliding until the edge that was lying on $AB$ reaches $P$ (fig-04, fig-05). Step 4. Draw a line along that edge of the set square, through $P$. Because the set square only slid without turning, that edge keeps the same direction as it had on $AB$ — so the new line is parallel to $AB$.

blocks.caption: The same slide as fig-04, made against the leaning ruler of fig-03. The set square is drawn twice: once with its edge on $AB$, and once slid along the ruler until that edge passes through $P$. The two positions are congruent and point the same way — sliding along a held ruler moves the set square without turning it — so the edge through $P$ stays parallel to $AB$. The arrow gives the direction of the slide, along the ruler's edge, and the right angle is marked in both positions.

The vertical ruler held fixed, with the set square drawn twice — once with its edge on $AB$ and once higher up, its edge on a second line parallel to $AB$ — and an arrow between the two positions pointing up along the ruler.

The same set square on $AB$ as in fig-02, with the ruler moved to rest against its sloping edge instead of its upright one. The set square has not moved; only the ruler has, so it now leans across $AB$, running from lower left to upper right. The right angle is still where the edge on $AB$ meets the short upright edge, and it is marked there. The ruler's inclination does not affect the construction. The set square is drawn at one particular size, and with its right angle at one particular end; neither is part of the method. Any set square works, either way round, so long as one edge lies along $AB$ and the ruler rests against another.

The same set square on $AB$, with the ruler now drawn as a long strip lying along the set square's downward edge. The right angle marked at the corner is the set square's own, between the edge lying along $AB$ and the edge running down from it.

Line $AB$, with a point $P$ marked above it. A set square is drawn below $AB$ with one edge along the line: the right angle is at the left end of that edge, one leg runs down from it, and the hypotenuse closes back to a point on $AB$ to the right.

blocks.text: Worked example. Construct a line through point $P$ that is parallel to the line $AB$. Working through it: 1. Lay one edge of your set square exactly along $AB$. The edge must touch the whole line, and the right-angle corner sits at one end of that edge (fig-01). 2. Hold your ruler against the set square so it cannot slip — against the upright (left-hand) edge if you are right-handed (fig-02). Keep the ruler still from here on. 3. Slide the set square along the ruler, up towards $P$, without letting the set square turn. Stop as soon as the edge that was on $AB$ passes through $P$ (fig-05). 4. Draw a line along that edge through $P$. This line is parallel to $AB$. Check your work: the two lines should look exactly side by side — the new line through $P$ never leans towards or away from $AB$.

practice.prompt: In the construction of a line through $P$ parallel to $AB$, what must you do in Step 2 before you slide the set square, and why?
practice.answer: Place the ruler firmly against one of the set square's other edges (the left-hand edge if right-handed) and hold it still, so that when the set square slides along it, the set square does not turn.
practice.worked_solution: The ruler acts as a fixed track. If the ruler moved or the set square turned as it slid, the edge would no longer keep the direction it had along $AB$, and the final line through $P$ would not be parallel to $AB$.

practice.prompt: While sliding the set square along the ruler towards $P$, what tells you to stop, and what do you then draw?
practice.answer: Stop when the edge of the set square that was lying on $AB$ reaches $P$; then draw a line along that edge through $P$.
practice.worked_solution: The set square slides without turning, so the edge that matched $AB$ keeps the same direction. When that edge passes through $P$, drawing along it gives the line through $P$ parallel to $AB$.

practice.prompt: Construct a line through point $P$ that is parallel to the line $CD$, where $C$ and $D$ are the two end points of your line and $P$ is a point marked above it. Use your set square and ruler, and describe the three moves you make.
practice.answer: The final line drawn through $P$ is parallel to $CD$. The three moves are: (1) place one edge of the set square exactly along $CD$; (2) hold the ruler firmly against another edge of the set square; (3) slide the set square along the ruler until the edge reaches $P$, then draw the line through $P$ along that edge.
practice.worked_solution: Set the set square's edge on $CD$, brace the ruler against another edge and hold it still, then slide the set square up the ruler until the original edge passes through $P$. Drawing along that edge gives the line through $P$ parallel to $CD$, because the slide kept the edge parallel to $CD$.

blocks.text: Two lines are said to be **perpendicular** to each other when they meet at a right angle — that is, an angle of exactly **90°**. Look at fig-06: line $XY$ crosses line $AB$, and the small square mark drawn at the crossing shows the right angle between them. Because the angle at the crossing is a right angle, the two lines are perpendicular. Whenever you see that little square mark at a crossing, it is telling you the angle is $90^\circ$.

blocks.caption: Line $AB$ with a second line $XY$ crossing it, $X$ above and $Y$ below, and a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant at the crossing.

blocks.text:
**Construct a line perpendicular to line $AB$ at point $Q$, using a set square and a ruler.**

**Step 1.** Draw a line and label its ends $A$ and $B$ (fig-07). Mark a point $Q$ somewhere on the line. This is the point where your new line must cross $AB$ at a right angle.

**Step 2.** Place the edge of the set square along line $AB$, and let the edge of the ruler rest against the hypotenuse of the set square (fig-08). The ruler is now held still — it will guide the slide in the next step.

**Step 3.** Pressing firmly on the ruler, slide the set square down along the hypotenuse side until the third edge of the set square touches point $Q$. Keeping it there, draw a line $XY$ along that edge (fig-09). 

Line $XY$ now crosses $AB$ at $Q$ with a right angle marked between them, so $XY$ is perpendicular to $AB$.

blocks.caption: Line $AB$ with $XY$ now drawn across it, $X$ above and $Y$ below, and a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant.

Line $AB$ with the set square standing on it as a narrow right-angled triangle: a short base along $AB$, the upright edge rising from the right end of that base with the right angle marked there, and the hypotenuse closing back down to the left.
A plain line with a stroke at each end, labelled $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right.

practice.prompt: Two lines meet at a crossing and the small square mark is drawn in the corner of that crossing. What does that square mark tell you about the angle between the two lines?
practice.answer: The square mark shows that the angle between the two lines is a right angle, exactly $90^\circ$, so the lines are perpendicular to each other.

practice.prompt: A line $XY$ crosses line $AB$ at point $Q$ with a right angle at the crossing. What do we call lines $XY$ and $AB$? Write down the steps you would follow with a set square and a ruler to draw $XY$.
practice.answer: $XY$ and $AB$ are perpendicular to each other.
practice.worked_solution: Steps: (1) Draw line $AB$ and mark point $Q$ on it. (2) Place the edge of the set square along line $AB$ and rest the ruler against the hypotenuse of the set square. (3) Pressing firmly on the ruler, slide the set square down along the hypotenuse until its third edge touches point $Q$, then draw line $XY$ along that edge.

blocks.text:
To **bisect** a line segment means to divide it into two equal halves. When a segment $AB$ is bisected, the point where it is cut — call it $M$ — is its **midpoint**, and the two parts $AM$ and $MB$ are exactly the same length, so $AM = MB$.

You can bisect a line segment using only a pair of compasses and a ruler. Here is how.

1. Draw the segment $AB$ (fig-10).
2. Open your compasses so that the radius is about $\frac{3}{4}$ of the length of $AB$. Keep this radius the same for the whole construction.
3. Put the sharp point of the compasses on $A$ and draw two arcs: one arc above $AB$ and one arc below it.
4. Keeping the same radius, put the sharp point on $B$ and draw two more arcs, one above and one below, so that they cut the first two arcs. The arcs crossing above meet at a point $P$, and the arcs crossing below meet at a point $Q$ (fig-11).
5. Join $P$ to $Q$ with your ruler.
6. The line $PQ$ crosses $AB$ at $M$. Because the arcs were all drawn with the same radius, $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$, so $AM = MB$. The line $PQ$ also meets $AB$ at a right angle ($90^\circ$), shown by the right-angle mark in fig-12.

The secret of the whole construction is the single compass radius: drawing every arc with the same opening is what makes the crossing points $P$ and $Q$ sit exactly above and below the middle of $AB$.

blocks.caption: The same arcs with $P$ joined to $Q$, the joining line crossing $AB$ at its middle at $M$ and carrying a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant.
The segment $AB$ with arc pairs crossing above and below it, the upper crossing labelled $P$ and the lower one $Q$. Each crossing is drawn as a small X where an arc from $A$ meets an arc from $B$.
The line segment $AB$, a stroke at each end, $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right.

blocks.text:
**Worked example — bisecting a segment**

Suppose you want to bisect a segment $AB$ drawn on your page.

- Set your compasses to about $\frac{3}{4}$ of the length of $AB$ and do not change this radius.
- Place the point on $A$. Draw one arc above $AB$ and one arc below it.
- Place the point on $B$ with the same radius. Draw one arc above and one below so they cut the arcs from $A$.
- The crossing above is $P$; the crossing below is $Q$ (fig-11).
- Rule a straight line through $P$ and $Q$.
- Where this line meets $AB$ is $M$, the midpoint. Check it in fig-12: $AM = MB$, and $PQ$ stands on $AB$ at $90^\circ$.

practice.prompt: What does it mean to bisect a line segment $AB$?
practice.answer: It means to divide $AB$ into two equal halves, so the point of bisection $M$ is the midpoint and $AM = MB$.

practice.prompt: When bisecting a line segment $AB$, what should you keep the same about your compasses for all four arcs you draw?
practice.answer: The radius (the compass opening) must stay the same for every arc, set to about $\frac{3}{4}$ of the length of $AB$.

practice.prompt: Draw a segment $AB$. Bisect it using your compasses and ruler. Name the midpoint $M$, and state the two equal lengths you have created and the angle at which your bisecting line meets $AB$.
practice.answer: The bisecting line meets $AB$ at $M$, so $AM = MB$, and it meets $AB$ at $90^\circ$.
practice.worked_solution: Open the compasses to about $\frac{3}{4}$ of $AB$ and keep that radius. From $A$ draw an arc above and an arc below $AB$. With the same radius, from $B$ draw an arc above and an arc below so they cut the first arcs; the upper crossing is $P$, the lower is $Q$. Rule a line through $P$ and $Q$. Where it crosses $AB$ is the midpoint $M$, giving $AM = MB$, and the two lines meet at $90^\circ$.

blocks.text:
A 90° angle is a right angle — the kind of corner you see at the junction of a horizontal line and a line rising straight up from it. You can build one using only your compasses and a ruler. The idea is to draw a perpendicular from a point on your line: a perpendicular is simply a line that meets another line at a right angle, so the angle it makes is exactly 90°.

You will need your mathematical set, and you should already know how to draw a straight line. Let's set out the construction.

**Worked example — constructing angle 90° at a point on a line**

We will construct angle 90° at a point on the line $AB$, following the figure (fig-13).

**Step 1.** Draw a straight line $AB$ and mark a point $C$ on it, where the 90° angle is to be constructed.

**Step 2.** With the compasses at $C$, draw an arc that cuts the line at two points. Call these points $D$ and $E$.

**Step 3.** Open the compasses WIDER than the distance $DC$ — the width used in step 2 will not work, because arcs drawn at that width meet only at $C$ itself. With the compasses at $D$ at this new wider setting, draw an arc above the line.

**Step 4.** Keeping the compasses at the wider setting of step 3, place them at $E$ and draw another arc, cutting the first arc at $F$.

**Step 5.** Join $C$ to $F$ with your ruler.

**Step 6.** The line $CF$ is perpendicular to $AB$, so $\angle FCB = 90^\circ$.

In fig-13 you can see the finished result: the perpendicular $CF$ rises from a point near the middle of the line, the right-angle mark sits at its foot, and the two small strokes cross each other near the top of $CF$. The little square at the foot of the perpendicular is the right-angle mark — it shows the angle is 90°.

blocks.caption: A line with a stroke at each end, $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right, and four short strokes standing on the line, a pair towards $A$ and a pair towards $B$. A perpendicular rises from a point near the middle, with a right-angle mark at its foot, and two short strokes cross each other near its top.

practice.prompt: Construct angle 90° at a point $C$ on a straight line $AB$, using your compasses and ruler. In your construction, what is the special name given to the line you draw through $C$ and $F$?
practice.answer: The line $CF$ is a perpendicular to $AB$ — that is why $\angle FCB = 90^\circ$.

practice.prompt: In the construction of angle 90°, after drawing the first arc from $C$ that cuts the line at $D$ and $E$, you must open the compasses wider than $DC$ before drawing the next two arcs. Why is the step-2 width not enough for these arcs?
practice.answer: Because arcs drawn at the step-2 width from $D$ and $E$ meet only at $C$ itself, so they would not give a point $F$ above the line to join to $C$.

practice.prompt: Draw a line $AB$, mark a point $C$ on it, and construct the perpendicular to $AB$ at $C$ following the six steps. What is the measure, in degrees, of the angle between $AB$ and the perpendicular you drew?

blocks.text: You already know how to draw straight lines. Now you will use a pair of compasses to construct an angle of exactly 60° — one of the most useful angles in construction, because it is the angle inside an equilateral triangle. The key idea is that an equilateral triangle has all three sides equal, and all three angles are 60°. So if you can draw a triangle whose three sides are equal, you have drawn three 60° angles without measuring a single one. The compass does the work for you: wherever you draw two arcs with the same radius, you are marking off equal distances. Here is how the construction works, using figure fig-14 as your guide. You start with a line segment $BC$ and mark a point $X$ on it. One compass radius is chosen once and used for every arc — that is what keeps the distances equal.

blocks.caption: The line $BC$ with $B$ at the left, a stroke marking $X$ part way along, a long arc swung from $B$ through $X$ and up to the left, a shorter arc swung from $X$ cutting it, and a straight line from $B$ to that crossing.

blocks.text: Worked example — construct an angle of 60° at point B. Step 1. Draw a line segment $BC$. Open your compasses to any convenient radius. Place the point on B and swing an arc that cuts $BC$ at a point you call X. In fig-14, X lies part way along the line, and the long arc from B swings up to the left through X. Step 2. Keep the compasses at the same radius — do not change the opening. Place the point on X and swing a second arc. This arc cuts the first arc at a point A. (In fig-14 the shorter arc from X cuts the long arc from B at A.) Step 3. Draw a straight line from B to A. The angle $\angle ABC$ (the angle at B between the line BA and the line BC) is exactly 60°. Why is this correct? Because BX and XA are both drawn with the same compass radius, and BA joins B to A — so all three sides BX, XA and BA are equal. That makes triangle BXA equilateral, and every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°. The angle you have constructed at B is $\angle XBA$, which is exactly that 60°.

practice.prompt: Follow the three steps to construct an angle of 60° at B on a line segment BC. In your construction, why must the second arc (drawn with centre X) use exactly the same radius as the first arc (drawn with centre B)?
practice.answer: The second arc must use the same radius so that the distance XA equals the distance BX. Since BA joins B to A as well, all three sides BX, XA and BA become equal, making triangle BXA equilateral — and an equilateral triangle has all angles 60°. The angle you construct at B is therefore exactly 60°.
practice.worked_solution: Draw BC, place compass point on B and swing an arc to cut BC at X. Without changing the radius, place the point on X and swing a second arc to cut the first at A. Join BA. Because the radius was kept the same, BX = XA, and BA is the same straight distance again, so triangle BXA is equilateral and $\angle XBA = 60°$.

practice.prompt: In the construction of a 60° angle, you first swing an arc from B that cuts the line at X, then swing a second arc from X. What point is marked where the second arc cuts the first arc, and what figure does joining B to that point complete?
practice.answer: The second arc cuts the first arc at A. Joining B to A completes triangle BXA, which is equilateral (all three sides equal), so the angle at B between BA and BC is 60°.
