sections_json.title: Constructing a Parallel Line Through a Point

blocks.text: Two lines are parallel when they run side by side and never meet, no matter how far they are extended. A railway track is a good picture: the two rails stay the same distance apart all the way along. In this section you will construct a line that passes through a given point $P$ and is parallel to a given line $AB$. You will need a set square and a ruler — the same tools you use for drawing lines. The set square does the work of keeping the new line parallel; the ruler simply holds the set square steady while you slide it.

Example: Construct a line through the point $P$ so that it is parallel to $AB$. Step (a) — place the set square on the line. Place a set square so that one of its edges lies exactly along $AB$ (fig-01). Take care to line the edge up with the line the whole way along it. The point $P$ is marked above the line, where the new line must pass. Step (b) — hold the set square with the ruler. Place the ruler along one of the set square's other edges (fig-02). If you are right-handed, use the edge on your left; if left-handed, the other one. It does not matter which edge you choose, and the set square can be used either way round, so long as one edge lies on $AB$ and the ruler rests against another edge of it (fig-03). The ruler's slope across the page does not affect the construction — the ruler is only there to hold the set square still. Step (c) — slide the set square to $P$ and draw. Hold the ruler firmly in place with one hand. With the other hand, slide the set square along the ruler towards $P$ (fig-04). Slide it until the edge that was lying on $AB$ reaches $P$ (fig-05). Because you slid the set square without turning it, this edge stays parallel to $AB$ the whole time. Draw a line along that edge of the set square, through $P$. That line is parallel to $AB$.

blocks.caption: The same slide as fig-04, made against the leaning ruler of fig-03. The set square is drawn twice: once with its edge on $AB$, and once slid along the ruler until that edge passes through $P$. The two positions are congruent and point the same way — sliding along a held ruler moves the set square without turning it — so the edge through $P$ stays parallel to $AB$. The arrow gives the direction of the slide, along the ruler's edge, and the right angle is marked in both positions.

The vertical ruler held fixed, with the set square drawn twice — once with its edge on $AB$ and once higher up, its edge on a second line parallel to $AB$ — and an arrow between the two positions pointing up along the ruler.

The same set square on $AB$ as in fig-02, with the ruler moved to rest against its sloping edge instead of its upright one. The set square has not moved; only the ruler has, so it now leans across $AB$, running from lower left to upper right. The right angle is still where the edge on $AB$ meets the short upright edge, and it is marked there. The ruler's inclination does not affect the construction. The set square is drawn at one particular size, and with its right angle at one particular end; neither is part of the method. Any set square works, either way round, so long as one edge lies along $AB$ and the ruler rests against another.

The same set square on $AB$, with the ruler now drawn as a long strip lying along the set square's downward edge. The right angle marked at the corner is the set square's own, between the edge lying along $AB$ and the edge running down from it.

Line $AB$, with a point $P$ marked above it. A set square is drawn below $AB$ with one edge along the line: the right angle is at the left end of that edge, one leg runs down from it, and the hypotenuse closes back to a point on $AB$ to the right.

practice.prompt: Describe, in your own words, the steps you would take to construct a line through a point $P$ that is parallel to a line $AB$.
practice.answer: Place a set square with one edge exactly along $AB$. Hold it steady by placing the ruler along another edge of the set square. Holding the ruler firmly, slide the set square along the ruler until the edge that was on $AB$ reaches $P$. Draw a line along that edge through $P$ — it is parallel to $AB$.

practice.prompt: While you slide the set square along the ruler towards $P$, why must you hold the ruler firmly and slide the set square without turning it?
practice.answer: Holding the ruler firmly keeps the slide straight. Sliding without turning the set square keeps its edge at the same angle as $AB$, so that edge stays parallel to $AB$ — and the line you draw through $P$ is therefore parallel to $AB$.

blocks.text:
Two lines are said to be **perpendicular** to each other when they meet at a right angle — that is, at an angle of $90^\circ$. In fig-06, the line $XY$ crosses the line $AB$, and the small square mark in the upper right corner of the crossing tells you the two lines meet at a right angle. Wherever you see that little square, the lines are perpendicular.

You can draw a perpendicular line yourself using just a set square and a ruler. A set square is a flat triangular piece of plastic with one corner that is exactly a right angle, and the edge that faces that corner is called the hypotenuse. Here is how to use it.

blocks.caption: Line $AB$ with a second line $XY$ crossing it, $X$ above and $Y$ below, and a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant at the crossing.

blocks.text:
**Construct a line perpendicular to line $AB$ through a point $Q$ on it.**

**Step 1.** Draw a line $AB$, as in fig-07, and mark a point $Q$ on the line.

**Step 2.** Place the edge of the set square on the line $AB$, as shown in fig-08. Let the edge of the ruler meet the hypotenuse of the set square. The set square stands on the line with one upright edge rising from it and a marked right angle there.

**Step 3.** Pressing firmly on the ruler so it does not slip, slide the set square down along the hypotenuse side until the third edge touches the point $Q$. Then draw a line $XY$ along that edge.

The line $XY$ you have drawn crosses $AB$ at point $Q$, and the right-angle mark at the crossing (fig-09) shows the two lines meet at $90^\circ$. So $XY$ is perpendicular to $AB$.

blocks.caption: Line $AB$ with $XY$ now drawn across it, $X$ above and $Y$ below, and a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant.

Line $AB$ with the set square standing on it as a narrow right-angled triangle: a short base along $AB$, the upright edge rising from the right end of that base with the right angle marked there, and the hypotenuse closing back down to the left.
A plain line with a stroke at each end, labelled $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right.

practice.prompt: 1. Two lines are perpendicular when they meet at what angle?

2. Draw a line $AB$ and mark a point $Q$ on it. Using your set square and ruler, construct a line through $Q$ that is perpendicular to $AB$. What small mark should you add at the crossing to show the lines are perpendicular?
practice.answer: You should add a small right-angle square in one quadrant of the crossing, showing the lines meet at $90^\circ$.
practice.worked_solution: Place the edge of the set square on line $AB$, let the ruler meet the hypotenuse, slide the set square along until its third edge touches point $Q$, and draw line $XY$. Mark the little square at the crossing.

blocks.text: To bisect a line segment means to divide it into two equal halves. When you bisect the segment AB, you find its midpoint M, the point exactly halfway along it, so that AM = MB. You do this with a pair of compasses and a ruler.

Bisect the line segment AB. Step 1. Open your pair of compasses so that the radius is about 3/4 of the length of AB.

Step 2. Place the sharp point of the compasses on A. Draw two arcs — one above and the other below the middle of AB.

Step 3. Keeping the same radius, place the sharp point on B. Draw two arcs so that they cut the first arcs at P (above) and Q (below).

Step 4. Join P to Q with a ruler.

The line PQ crosses AB at M. M is the midpoint of AB, so AM = MB. Notice also that PQ meets AB at 90° — the two lines cross at a right angle.

blocks.caption: The line segment $AB$, a stroke at each end, $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right.
The segment $AB$ with arc pairs crossing above and below it, the upper crossing labelled $P$ and the lower one $Q$. Each crossing is drawn as a small X where an arc from $A$ meets an arc from $B$.
The same arcs with $P$ joined to $Q$, the joining line crossing $AB$ at its middle at $M$ and carrying a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant.

practice.prompt: Draw a line segment CD and bisect it with your compasses and ruler. What can you say about the two parts of CD after you have bisected it?
practice.answer: The bisecting line cuts CD at its midpoint, so the two parts are equal in length — you can write CM = MD, where M is the midpoint.
practice.worked_solution: Open the compasses to about three-quarters of the length of CD. Draw two arcs from C (one above, one below), then keep the same radius and draw two arcs from D that cut them at P and Q. Join P to Q; where it crosses CD is the midpoint M, so CM = MD.

practice.prompt: When you bisect the segment AB, the line PQ crosses AB at M. Write down the relationship between AM and MB, and the angle at which PQ meets AB.

blocks.text: To construct a 90° angle you only need a ruler and a pair of compasses. You build the perpendicular on an existing line, and where a perpendicular meets the line it makes a right angle, which measures 90°. Begin by drawing a straight line AB and marking a point C on it. This is the point where the 90° angle is to be made, and it is where the perpendicular will stand. 1. With the compasses resting at C, draw an arc that crosses the line at two points on either side of C. Call those points D and E. (See fig-13: the two short strokes on the line towards A and the two towards B mark where these arcs touch the line.) 2. Now open the compasses WIDER than the distance DC. This matters: the width you used in step 1 will not work, because two arcs drawn at that width from D and E would meet only at C itself. 3. With the compasses at this new, wider setting, place the point at D and draw an arc above the line. 4. Keeping the compasses at that same wider setting, move the point to E and draw another arc, cutting the first one at a point F. 5. Join C to F with a ruler. The line CF is perpendicular to AB, so the angle between CF and the line — written ∠FCB — is 90°.

blocks.caption: A line with a stroke at each end, $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right, and four short strokes standing on the line, a pair towards $A$ and a pair towards $B$. A perpendicular rises from a point near the middle, with a right-angle mark at its foot, and two short strokes cross each other near its top.

blocks.text: Constructing ∠FCB = 90° Draw the line AB and mark point C on it. With the compasses at C, swing one arc to cut the line at D and E on either side of C. Now open the compasses wider than DC. From D, draw an arc above the line. Without changing the compass width, move to E and draw another arc that cuts the first at F. Join C to F with a straight line. The result looks like fig-13: a perpendicular rises from a point on the line, marked with a small right-angle square at its foot, and two short arcs cross near its top where the two wider arcs met. Because CF is perpendicular to AB, the angle ∠FCB is exactly 90°.

practice.prompt: When you construct a 90° angle on a line AB at point C, you first draw an arc from C that cuts the line at D and E. Then you must open the compasses wider than DC before drawing the arcs from D and E. Why is the wider opening necessary?
practice.answer: If the compasses were left at the width DC, the two arcs drawn from D and E would meet only at C itself, so they would not give you a point F above the line to join to C. Opening wider makes the two arcs cut each other at a point F above the line.

practice.prompt: A line AB is drawn with point C marked on it. To construct a right angle at C, name, in the correct order, the four compass steps you take, and say what you draw last with a ruler.
practice.answer: 1. With the compasses at C, draw an arc that cuts the line at D and E. 2. Open the compasses wider than DC, and from D draw an arc above the line. 3. Keeping the same wider width, from E draw another arc to cut the first at F. 4. Join C to F with a ruler.
practice.worked_solution: The order matters. First fix the two cut points D and E on the line with one arc from C. Then, with a wider compass opening (wider than DC), draw an arc from D above the line, keep the width, and draw a second arc from E that crosses the first at F. Finally use the ruler to draw CF, which is perpendicular to AB and makes ∠FCB = 90°.

blocks.text:
Here you will learn to construct an angle of exactly 60° using only a ruler and a compass. The secret is to swing two arcs of the same radius, because an equilateral triangle has all three angles equal to 60°.

You already know how to draw a straight line. Now you need your compass set to one convenient radius and kept at that same radius for both arcs.

Construct angle 60° at point B on line BC.

**Step 1 — Draw the base line.** Draw a line segment BC, with B at the left end and C further along to the right. Set your compass to a convenient radius.

**Step 2 — First arc.** Put the compass point on B (the centre) and draw an arc that cuts BC at a point X. Keep the compass at this same radius — do not change it.

**Step 3 — Second arc.** Put the compass point on X (your new centre) and, with the *same radius*, draw another arc that cuts the first arc. Call the point where the two arcs meet A.

**Step 4 — Join.** Use your ruler to draw the straight line from B to A.

The angle between BA and BC at B is exactly 60°. This works because in triangle ABX, all three sides BX, XA and AB are equal — they are all the same compass radius — so it is an equilateral triangle, and every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°.

blocks.caption: The line $BC$ with $B$ at the left, a stroke marking $X$ part way along, a long arc swung from $B$ through $X$ and up to the left, a shorter arc swung from $X$ cutting it, and a straight line from $B$ to that crossing.

practice.prompt: Construct an angle of 60° on a fresh line, working carefully through the four steps. When you have joined the last line, use your protractor to check that the angle at the endpoint really is 60°.
practice.answer: Your constructed angle should measure 60° when checked with a protractor. If it does not, repeat the construction keeping the compass radius the same for both arcs — changing the radius between the arcs is the most common reason the angle is wrong.
practice.worked_solution: Draw a base line BC with B on the left. With B as centre, swing an arc to cut BC at X. Keeping the compass at the same radius, swing a second arc with X as centre to cut the first arc at A. Join B to A. Triangle ABX is equilateral because AB = BX = XA, so angle ABC = 60°.

blocks.text:
Every day, you come across lots of facts and figures — how many goals a team scored, the temperature outside, the price of bread, your scores in a test. When these pieces of information are gathered together, we call them data. Statistics is the part of mathematics that deals with collecting data, organising it, and making sense of it. Why do we need statistics? Its main purpose is to help us make decisions based on facts instead of guesswork. For example, a shopkeeper who records which snacks sell best each week can decide which ones to stock more of. A school that records how many students are absent each day can see when illnesses spread and take action. A football coach who notes how many goals each player scores can pick the strongest team. Statistics does three main jobs:
  • Collecting data — gathering facts from a source, such as a survey or a tally.
  • Organising data — putting the facts in order so they are easy to read, often in a table.
  • Interpreting data — reading the organised facts to answer questions and draw conclusions.
In this section you will learn the purpose of statistics and how to read the information that is laid out in a table.

Worked example 1 — reading a table A class recorded how each student travelled to school one morning. The results were put into a table.
Way of travellingNumber of students
Walking14
Bicycle8
Bus6
Car4
Question: Which way of travelling was used by the most students? Answer: Walking. The table shows 14 students walked, and no other row has a bigger number, so walking was the most common way. The table lets us answer this question at a glance. If the same facts were just a long jumbled list of words, we would have to count through everything again. Organising the data in a table is what makes the information useful.

The purpose of statistics is not just to count things — it is to use the counts to decide and predict. When data is set out in a table, you can quickly find the biggest value, the smallest value, the total, and the difference between values. These simple readings let you answer real questions. The steps you follow are:
  1. Read the headings of the table to know what each column and row mean.
  2. Compare the numbers to answer the question — look for the largest, the smallest, or the total.
  3. State your conclusion in a full sentence that uses the data you read.
Remember that a conclusion is only trustworthy when it comes from the data shown. If a number is not in the table, you cannot invent it.

Worked example 2 — comparing values in a table A fruit seller recorded how many of each fruit he sold on Saturday.
FruitFruits sold
Apples25
Oranges30
Bananas18
Mangoes12
Question 1: How many more oranges than mangoes were sold? Answer 1: 30 − 12 = 18, so 18 more oranges were sold. Question 2: How many fruits were sold altogether? Answer 2: 25 + 30 + 18 + 12 = 85 fruits. Question 3: Which fruit should the seller order more of next week? Answer 3: Oranges, because they had the largest number sold (30). The table tells him which fruit people wanted most.

practice.prompt:
A shop recorded the number of drinks sold on Friday.

| Drink | Drinks sold |
|-------|-------------|
| Water | 40 |
| Juice | 25 |
| Soda | 30 |
| Tea | 15 |

(a) Which drink sold the most?
(b) How many drinks were sold altogether?
practice.answer: (a) Water, because 40 is the largest number in the table. (b) 40 + 25 + 30 + 15 = 110 drinks.
practice.worked_solution:
(a) Look down the "Drinks sold" column and find the biggest number. The numbers are 40, 25, 30 and 15; the biggest is 40, which belongs to Water.
(b) To find the total, add all four numbers: 40 + 25 = 65, 65 + 30 = 95, 95 + 15 = 110. So 110 drinks were sold altogether.

practice.prompt:
A teacher recorded the number of students in each house for a sports competition.

| House | Number of students |
|-------|--------------------|
| Red | 45 |
| Blue | 55 |
| Green | 50 |

(a) Which house has the fewest students?
(b) How many more students are in Blue than in Red?
(c) If the teacher wants to reward the house with the most students, which house should she reward?
practice.answer: (a) Red, because 45 is the smallest number. (b) 55 − 45 = 10 more students. (c) Blue, because it has the most students (55).
practice.worked_solution:
(a) Compare the numbers 45, 55 and 50. The smallest is 45, which is Red.
(b) Subtract the smaller from the larger: 55 − 45 = 10. So Blue has 10 more students than Red.
(c) The house with the most students is the one with the largest number, 55, which is Blue. The table lets the teacher decide using the facts instead of guesswork.

sections_json.title: Reading Stories from Tables of Data

blocks.text:
When a survey or count is finished, the results are often long lists of numbers that are hard to take in at a glance. A table gathers those results into neat rows and columns so that we can see patterns, compare values, and answer questions quickly. Tables turn a messy pile of facts into a clear picture. To read a table, look first at the heading, which tells you what was counted. Then read the row labels down the left and the column labels across the top. Where a row and a column meet, the number in that box is the answer to the question the two labels ask together. Here is an example. The table below shows the favourite sport chosen by students in one school, with the number of students who chose each sport. | Favourite sport | Number of students | |---|---| | Football | 40 | | Basketball | 25 | | Swimming | 20 | | Athletics | 15 | | Total | 100 | Three questions you can answer from this table:
  • How many students chose swimming? Look along the "Swimming" row to the number column: 20.
  • Which sport was most popular? The row with the biggest number is Football (40), so football was the most popular.
  • How many students took part altogether? The Total row at the bottom says 100.
A "Total" row or column is a great help: it lets you check that all the parts add up, and it gives you a whole to compare each part against.

The word statistic is about collecting, organising and making sense of facts in numbers. Tables are one of the clearest ways to organise data. When you analyse a table, you look carefully at the numbers to spot what is most common, what is least common, and how the parts compare. When you interpret it, you explain in words what the numbers mean. A good way to work through a table is to answer questions in this order:
  1. What does the table count? Read the heading and the labels.
  2. How much is each part? Read the number in each row or column.
  3. What is the total? Add the parts or read the total row.
  4. What is the pattern? Compare the parts to find the biggest, the smallest, and how they differ.
Following these steps turns a table of numbers into a sentence you can say aloud, like "Twice as many students walk to school as come by bicycle."

Worked example The table below shows how students in a class travel to school each day. | How students travel | Number of students | |---|---| | Walk | 30 | | Bicycle | 15 | | Bus | 10 | | Car | 5 | | Total | 60 | Let's analyse and interpret it step by step. Step 1 — What does the table count?
The heading tells us the number of students using each way of travelling to school. Step 2 — How much is each part?
Walk: 30, Bicycle: 15, Bus: 10, Car: 5. Step 3 — What is the total?
The Total row reads 60. Check: 30 + 15 + 10 + 5 = 60. ✓ Step 4 — What is the pattern?
Walking is the most common way (30), and travelling by car is the least common (5). Walking is used by twice as many students as bicycling (30 = 2 × 15). Interpretation in words: Most students in the class walk to school, and very few come by car.

practice.prompt: The table below shows how many books students in a library borrowed in one week. | Type of book | Number borrowed | |---|---| | Story books | 45 | | Science books | 20 | | History books | 15 | | Poetry books | 10 | | Total | 90 | (a) How many science books were borrowed? (b) Which type of book was borrowed the most? (c) Which type of book was borrowed the least? (d) How many books were borrowed altogether? (e) Write one sentence interpreting what the table tells you.
practice.answer: (a) 20 science books. (b) Story books (45, the biggest number). (c) Poetry books (10, the smallest number). (d) 90 books altogether. (e) Example: Most books borrowed were story books, and poetry books were borrowed the least.
practice.worked_solution: (a) Look along the "Science books" row to the number column: 20. (b) The row with the largest number is Story books at 45, so story books were borrowed most. (c) The row with the smallest number is Poetry books at 10. (d) The Total row reads 90; check 45 + 20 + 15 + 10 = 90. (e) Compare the parts: the largest is story books and the smallest is poetry books, so we can say most borrowed were story books and fewest were poetry books.

practice.prompt: The table below shows the number of pupils in a school who chose each school club. | School club | Number of pupils | |---|---| | Drama | 35 | | Music | 30 | | Art | 25 | | Chess | 10 | | Total | 100 | (a) Which club was chosen by the fewest pupils? (b) How many more pupils chose Drama than Music? (c) How many pupils chose Art or Chess together? (d) What fraction of the whole school chose Music?
practice.answer: (a) Chess (10 pupils). (b) 5 more pupils chose Drama (35 − 30 = 5). (c) 35 pupils chose Art or Chess together (25 + 10 = 35). (d) 30 out of 100, which is 3/10 (thirty hundredths).
practice.worked_solution: (a) The smallest number in the table is 10, which belongs to Chess. (b) Drama has 35 and Music has 30; the difference is 35 − 30 = 5. (c) Add the Art and Chess rows: 25 + 10 = 35. (d) Music has 30 pupils out of a total of 100, so the fraction is 30/100 = 3/10.

blocks.text: Every day you are surrounded by numbers. The number of students in your class, the scores in a test, the number of bottles in a crate, the ages of people in your family — all of these are pieces of information. On their own, scattered here and there, they are not very useful. But when you collect them, organise them and make sense of them, they become powerful. That is what statistics is about. Statistics is the method of collecting and organising information so that it can be understood and used. It helps us answer questions like: How many? How many more? How many altogether? What is the most common? Why do we need statistics? Because raw information, on its own, tells us very little. Once we collect it and put it in order, we can see what is happening, compare things, and make good decisions. Suppose a shopkeeper wants to know which drink sells best. If he just watches customers, he might guess. But if he counts and organises the sales in a table, he knows for certain which one to order more of. That is the purpose of statistics: to turn scattered information into something clear and useful.

Statistics is made of two main actions: collecting information and organising it. Collecting means gathering the information from where it is. You might count the number of girls and boys in your class, or ask everyone their favourite colour. Organising means putting the collected information in a neat, ordered form, usually in a table, so that it is easy to read. Watch how collecting and organising work together. A teacher wants to know how many students are in each of two arms of Class 1. She counts: 24 students in 1A and 27 students in 1B. She has collected the information. Now she organises it in a table: | Class | Number of students | |-------|--------------------| | 1A | 24 | | 1B | 27 | Now the information is clear at a glance. You can see at once that 1B has more students than 1A, and you can add to find that together they have 24 + 27 = 51 students. That is the whole point of statistics — collecting the facts and organising them so the answers become obvious.

Let's work through collecting and organising information together. Example. A group of friends wants to know how many red, blue and green pencils they have altogether. Amina counts and finds 8 red pencils, 5 blue pencils and 7 green pencils. First, the information is collected: Amina has counted 8 red, 5 blue and 7 green. Next, it is organised in a table so that it is easy to read: | Colour of pencil | Number of pencils | |------------------|-------------------| | Red | 8 | | Blue | 5 | | Green | 7 | Now the organised table lets us answer questions easily. How many pencils are there altogether? Add the column: 8 + 5 + 7 = 20 So there are 20 pencils in total. The table also shows that red pencils are the most common (8) and blue pencils are the fewest (5). This is exactly why we collect and organise information: scattered counts become a clear picture.

practice.prompt: Define statistics in your own words.
practice.answer: Statistics is the method of collecting and organising information so that it can be understood and used.

practice.prompt: A fruit seller counts the fruit she has: 15 oranges, 12 mangoes and 9 pawpaws. Organise this information in a table.
practice.worked_solution: Collect the counts: 15 oranges, 12 mangoes, 9 pawpaws. Organise them into a table with one row for each fruit and a column showing the count.

practice.prompt: Using your table from the previous question, state how many fruits the seller has altogether, and name which fruit is the fewest.
practice.answer: Altogether there are 15 + 12 + 9 = 36 fruits. The pawpaws, with 9, are the fewest.
practice.worked_solution: Add the organised counts: 15 + 12 + 9 = 36. Compare the counts in the table: 9 is the smallest, so pawpaws are the fewest.

sections_json.title: Organising Data with Tally Marks and Frequency Tables

blocks.text: Raw data on its own is hard to read. If you are asked how many of your classmates are 12 years old, you do not want to count through a long, jumbled list every time. So we organise data into a table. Two tools help us do that: tally marks and a frequency table. Tally marks are a quick way to count how many times each value appears. You draw one stroke for each item. When you reach the fifth, you draw it across the four like this: 𝍸 (four strokes, then the fifth crossing them). That makes groups of five, so you can count them in fives at the end. A frequency table sets out each value together with the number of times it appears. The table has columns for the value, the tally marks, and the frequency (the count). Once the table is built, you can answer questions about the data just by reading the table.

Worked example. A class was asked how many pets each student owns, and these were the answers: 3, 1, 2, 0, 2, 3, 1, 2, 0, 3, 2, 1, 2 Let us build a frequency table. Step 1 — List the values. The values that appear are 0, 1, 2 and 3. Write them in a column in order, smallest first. Step 2 — Tally. Go through the list one answer at a time and make a tally mark beside that value: - 0 appears twice: 𝍇 - 1 appears three times: 𝍇 (three strokes) - 2 appears five times: 𝍸 - 3 appears three times: 𝍇 Step 3 — Count the tally marks. Remember that a crossed group 𝍸 counts as five. So the frequencies are: 0 has 2, 1 has 3, 2 has 5, 3 has 3. Step 4 — Write the frequency table. | Number of pets | Tally | Frequency | |---|---|---| | 0 | 𝍇 | 2 | | 1 | 𝍇 | 3 | | 2 | 𝍸 | 5 | | 3 | 𝍇 | 3 | Now we can read answers straight from the table. How many students own 2 pets? The frequency for 2 is 5. How many students answered altogether? Add the frequencies: 2 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 13 students.

practice.prompt:
Prepare a frequency table for the following data:

1, 1, 3, 4, 4, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 1, 2
practice.answer:
The frequency table is:

| Number | Tally | Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 𝍇 | 3 |
| 2 | 𝍇 | 3 |
| 3 | 𝍸 | 4 |
| 4 | 𝍇 | 3 |

Total = 13
practice.worked_solution: List the values in order: 1, 2, 3, 4. Go through the data and tally each occurrence. 1 appears three times, 2 appears three times, 3 appears four times (a crossed group of five is not needed since four is fewer than five), and 4 appears three times. Add the frequencies to check: 3 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 13, which matches the 13 numbers in the data.

A frequency table for the ages of students in a club is shown below.

| Age | Tally | Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| 11 | 𝍸 | 5 |
| 12 | 𝍸 𝍇 | 7 |
| 13 | 𝍸 𝍇 | 6 |
| 14 | 𝍇 | 3 |

(a) How many students are 12 years old?
(b) Which age has the highest frequency?
(c) How many students are in the club altogether?

sections_json.title: What Statistics Is and What It Is For

blocks.text: When you count the pencils in your pencil case, or the number of learners in your class, you are dealing with information. That information — the facts or numbers you collect — is called data. Data are facts or information collected for a particular purpose. Statistics is the science of collecting, organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting data. Let us look at each of those words: - Collecting means gathering the facts or information you need. - Organising means putting that information into some order, so it is easy to read. - Presenting means showing the information clearly, for example in a table. - Analysing means studying it carefully to see what it tells you. - Interpreting means explaining what the information means. So statistics is the whole process of working with data — from collecting it, right through to explaining what it shows.

Why do we bother with all of this? Statistics is important because it helps us to: - Collect information — gather the facts we need in an orderly way. - Organise information — arrange the facts so they are easy to manage and read. - Compare information — put facts side by side and see how they are alike or different. - Make decisions — use the facts to choose sensibly, rather than guessing. - Present information clearly — show the facts so that other people can understand them at a glance. In short, statistics gives us a reliable way to handle information, so that the choices we make are based on real facts.

Think about the facts of your own class. The number of boys and the number of girls are pieces of data — facts collected about your class. When you write them in a table so they are easy to read, you are organising the data. When you look at the two numbers and say which group is larger, you are comparing the information. And if you use that comparison to decide, say, how many chairs the class needs, you have used statistics to make a decision. One set of data can pass through every part of statistics in just a few steps.

practice.answer: Statistics is the science of collecting, organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting data.

practice.answer: Data are facts or information collected for a particular purpose.

practice.answer: Any three of: it helps us to collect information, organise information, compare information, make decisions, and present information clearly.

sections_json.title: Collecting Data with Tally Marks and Building a Frequency Table

blocks.text:
When we want to answer a question like "How many cars pass our school each morning?" we first have to gather the information. That gathered information is called **data**. Data can be collected in four main ways:

1. **Observation** — you watch and note down what you see.
2. **Counting** — you count things, such as the number of students present.
3. **Interview** — you ask people questions and record their answers.
4. **Questionnaire** — you hand out a set of written questions for people to answer.

Once the data is collected, it can be a jumbled list, which is hard to read. So we tidy it up using **tally marks** and a **frequency table**.

A **tally mark** is a single stroke (|) used to record one item. To make counting easy, every fifth item is marked by drawing a stroke across the previous four, like this: **||||**. A group of five tally marks is always drawn as four vertical strokes with one stroke across them. Each group stands for 5.

A **frequency table** is a table showing how many times each item occurs in a set of data. The number of times an item appears is called its **frequency**.

To build a frequency table, you go through your data one item at a time. Each time you meet an item, add a tally stroke next to it. When an item reaches five strokes, you close the group by drawing the fifth stroke across. At the end, count the strokes in each row and write that number as the total (frequency).

**Worked example — recording vehicles with tally marks**

Two students collected the same data about the vehicles that passed their school:

bus, car, car, car, lorry, bicycle, bicycle, car, car, lorry, bicycle, car

This jumbled list is hard to read, so let us record it with tally marks and show it in a table.

Work through the list one vehicle at a time and add a stroke each time:

- **car** appears 6 times. Its tally is one group of five plus one more: **|||| |**.
- **bus** appears 1 time. Its tally is **|**.
- **lorry** appears 2 times. Its tally is **||**.
- **bicycle** appears 3 times. Its tally is **|||**.
- **motor bike** appears 0 times, so it gets no tally marks.

Now we count the strokes in each row to find the total:

| Vehicles | Tally | Total |
|---|---|---|
| car | |||| \| | 6 |
| bus | \| | 1 |
| lorry | \|\| | 2 |
| bicycle | \|\|\| | 3 |
| motor bike | | 0 |

This table shows at a glance which vehicle was most common (car, with 6) and which was least common (motor bike, with 0). The "Total" column is the frequency of each vehicle.

**Worked example — a frequency table of favourite colours**

A class of students was asked for their favourite colour. The results were counted and written as a frequency table:

| colour | frequency |
|---|---|
| Red | 18 |
| Blue | 20 |
| Green | 14 |
| Yellow | 16 |
| White | 15 |
| Pink | 30 |

This table shows how many students chose each colour. The frequency of a colour is just the number of students who chose it. For example, the frequency of **Pink** is 30, which means 30 students said pink was their favourite. Reading the table, we can compare the colours at a glance: Blue (20) and Pink (30) were chosen more than Green (14).

blocks.text: Every day you gather facts and figures around you — how many students were in class, how many bottles of water were sold, how many goals your favourite team scored. These facts and figures are called data. Data are facts or information collected for a particular purpose. Statistics is the science of collecting, organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting data. When you count the pupils present in the morning and write their names in a register, you are collecting data. When you sort those names by class or by age, you are organising it. Statistics brings a clear order to information so that it becomes useful to you.

Why do we bother with statistics at all? Statistics helps us in five important ways: - (a) Collect information — gather the facts you need. - (b) Organise information — put the facts into a sensible order. - (c) Compare information — see how one set of facts stands against another. - (d) Make decisions — use the facts to choose sensibly. - (e) Present information clearly — show the facts so others can understand them at a glance. Consider a shopkeeper who sells oranges. Each day she counts how many oranges she sells (collecting information), and writes the daily totals in her notebook one after another (organising information). By looking at her notes she can compare Saturday's sales with Monday's (comparing information), and then she decides how many oranges to buy for next weekend (making decisions). When she wants to show her progress to her boss, she draws a simple table or chart so the figures are clear at a glance (presenting information clearly). Every one of these steps is statistics at work.

practice.answer: Data are facts or information collected for a particular purpose.

sections_json.title: Recording Data with Tally Marks and Frequency Tables

blocks.text:
Statistics is built on data — the facts and numbers you gather when you count or record something. Before you can study data you have to collect it, and there are four common ways to do that:

1. **Observation** — you watch and note down what you see.
2. **Counting** — you count the items one by one.
3. **Interview** — you ask someone a question and record their answer.
4. **Questionnaire** — you give someone a written list of questions to answer.

Once you have collected your data, you need a neat way to record it as it comes in. That is where **tally marks** are used. A tally mark is a single stroke that stands for one item. You add one stroke for each item you collect, and every fifth stroke is drawn across the previous four. So five items are written as a bundle of four strokes with a fifth crossing them. Grouping the marks in fives makes counting fast, because you can count the bundles of five and then the leftovers.

Suppose you stand by the road and note the vehicles that pass, in this order:

bus, car, car, car, lorry, bicycle, bicycle, car, car, lorry, bicycle, car

You record each vehicle with a tally mark under its name as it passes. When you finish, your tally looks like this:

| Vehicles | Tally | Total |
|---|---|---|
| car | \|\|\|\|/ \| | 6 |
| bus | \| | 1 |
| lorry | \|\| | 2 |
| bicycle | \|\|\| | 3 |
| motor bike | | 0 |

Let's check the tally. **car** appears six times in the data, so it earns one full group of five (four strokes with the fifth across them) and one more mark on its own — that is 6, and the total column shows 6. **bus** appears once, **lorry** twice, and **bicycle** three times, so each gets the matching number of marks. **motor bike** never appears, so it gets no marks and its total is 0. Add the totals and you get 6 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 0 = 12, which matches the 12 vehicles listed.

When your tally is complete, you can present it in a **frequency table**. A frequency table is a table showing how many times each item occurs in a set of data. It brings all the totals together into one clear summary.

Here is a frequency table showing the favourite colours of a group of students:

| colour | frequency |
|---|---|
| Red | 18 |
| Blue | 20 |
| Green | 14 |
| Yellow | 16 |
| White | 15 |
| Pink | 30 |

The **frequency** is simply how many students chose that colour. Reading this table, you can immediately see that Pink is the most popular colour (30 students chose it) and Green is the least popular (only 14 chose it). A frequency table lets you read the whole set of data at a glance, so you can compare items and answer questions about the data easily.

practice.prompt: State three methods of collecting data.
practice.answer: Any three of: observation, counting, interview, questionnaire.

practice.prompt: Prepare a frequency table for the following data: 1, 1, 3, 4, 4, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 1, 2.
practice.worked_solution: Count how many times each number appears. The number 1 appears three times, 2 appears three times, 3 appears four times, and 4 appears three times. So the frequency table lists each distinct number with its tally marks and its total, and the totals add to 3 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 13, which matches the number of data values.

practice.prompt:
A class recorded the favourite colours of its students in the frequency table below:

| colour | frequency |
|---|---|
| Red | 18 |
| Blue | 20 |
| Green | 14 |
| Yellow | 16 |
| White | 15 |
| Pink | 30 |

(a) How many students chose Pink?  (b) Which colour was chosen by the fewest students?
practice.answer: (a) 30 students chose Pink.  (b) Green, chosen by 14 students, was the fewest.

sections_json.title: The Right Order: Working Through Algebraic Expressions

blocks.text: An algebraic expression is a sentence of mathematics built from letters (like x and y) and numbers, joined by operations such as +, −, × and ÷. For example, 2x + 3 and 4(x − 1) + 5 are both algebraic expressions. When an expression has more than one operation, you cannot simply work from left to right. Everyone must get the same answer, so mathematicians agree on one fixed order to follow. The order is often remembered with the word BODMAS: • Brackets — work out anything inside brackets first • Orders — powers, such as x², next • Division and Multiplication — from left to right • Addition and Subtraction — from left to right, last The same order is used in algebra as with plain numbers. The letters simply stand in for numbers, so they follow exactly the same rules. Whenever you see brackets, deal with them first — and remember that a number written next to a bracket, like 3(x + 2), means multiply everything inside by that number (this is called expanding the bracket).

Example 1 — Multiplication before addition Simplify 2 + 3 × 4x. There is no bracket and no power here. BODMAS says multiplication comes before addition, so do the 3 × 4x first. 3 × 4x = 12x. Now add: 2 + 12x. So 2 + 3 × 4x = 2 + 12x. We cannot add the 2 and the 12x together because one is a plain number and the other has an x, so the expression is now as simple as it can be. Example 2 — Removing a bracket Simplify 4(2x − 3). The bracket is first, and the 4 outside multiplies both terms inside. 4 × 2x = 8x, and 4 × (−3) = −12. So 4(2x − 3) = 8x − 12. Example 3 — Brackets then collecting like terms Simplify 3x + 2(x + 5) − 7. Step 1 — the bracket: 2(x + 5) = 2x + 10. The expression becomes 3x + 2x + 10 − 7. Step 2 — collect the x-terms: 3x + 2x = 5x. Step 3 — collect the numbers: 10 − 7 = 3. So 3x + 2(x + 5) − 7 = 5x + 3.

The order of operations also helps with word problems. A word problem describes a situation in sentences, and you turn it into an algebraic expression using a letter for the unknown. Read carefully, decide which operation each phrase points to (for example, "more than" means add, "times" means multiply, "the difference" means subtract), then simplify using BODMAS. Here is a useful way to think about it: if a problem mentions a total built from separate parts, brackets often hold one part so it is dealt with before the rest of the expression.

Example 4 — A rectangle A rectangle has length (x + 4) cm and width 3 cm. Write a simplified expression for its perimeter. The perimeter of a rectangle is twice the length plus twice the width: Perimeter = 2(length + width) = 2((x + 4) + 3). Work inside the bracket first: (x + 4) + 3 = x + 7. Now expand: 2(x + 7) = 2x + 14. So the perimeter is 2x + 14 cm. Example 5 — A shopping problem A pencil costs x naira and a pen costs 5 naira more. Amina buys 3 pencils and 2 pens. Write a simplified expression for the total cost. A pen costs x + 5 naira. 3 pencils cost 3 × x = 3x naira. 2 pens cost 2 × (x + 5) = 2x + 10 naira. Total = 3x + 2x + 10 = 5x + 10 naira. So the total cost is 5x + 10 naira.

practice.prompt: Simplify 6 + 2 × 3x. Remember which operation comes first.
practice.worked_solution: Multiplication comes before addition. 2 × 3x = 6x, then add the 6: 6 + 6x.

practice.prompt: Simplify 4(2x − 3) + 5x.
practice.worked_solution: Expand the bracket first: 4(2x − 3) = 8x − 12. The expression becomes 8x − 12 + 5x. Collect like terms: 8x + 5x = 13x. So the answer is 13x − 12.

practice.prompt: Simplify 3x + 2(x + 5) − 7.
practice.worked_solution: Bracket first: 2(x + 5) = 2x + 10. The expression becomes 3x + 2x + 10 − 7. Collect x-terms: 3x + 2x = 5x. Collect numbers: 10 − 7 = 3. Answer: 5x + 3.

practice.prompt: A rectangle has length (2x + 1) cm and width 4 cm. Write a simplified expression for its perimeter.
practice.worked_solution: Perimeter = 2(length + width) = 2((2x + 1) + 4). Work inside the bracket: (2x + 1) + 4 = 2x + 5. Expand: 2(2x + 5) = 4x + 10. So the perimeter is 4x + 10 cm.

practice.prompt: A box weighs x kg. A crate weighs 3 times as much as the box plus 2 kg more. Write a simplified expression for the weight of the crate.
practice.worked_solution: Three times the box is 3 × x = 3x kg, and 2 kg more is added last. So the crate weighs 3x + 2 kg.

blocks.text: Brackets hold terms together, and often an expression is easier to work with once you have either taken the brackets away or grouped terms inside a new pair of brackets. Both moves follow the same simple idea: whatever sits right in front of a bracket multiplies every single term inside it. Removing a bracket When a letter or number stands in front of a bracket, multiply it by each term inside, then drop the brackets: - 3(x + 2) = 3·x + 3·2 = 3x + 6 - 2(b − 5) = 2·b − 2·5 = 2b − 10 When a minus sign stands in front of a bracket, you change the sign of every term inside and then drop the brackets. Think of the minus as −1 multiplying each term: - −(a + 4) = −a − 4 - −(2y − 3) = −2y + 3   (the −3 becomes +3) Inserting a bracket To put terms back into a bracket, find the largest factor that divides every term, write it in front of the bracket, and divide each term by it: - 6x + 9: 3 divides both terms, so 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3). - 8p − 4: 4 divides both terms, so 8p − 4 = 4(2p − 1). Simplifying after removing brackets Once the brackets are gone, finish by collecting the like terms — add or subtract the terms that have the same letter (and the plain numbers on their own). For example, 3x + 6 + 4x − 4 becomes (3x + 4x) + (6 − 4) = 7x + 2. Work carefully, one sign at a time, and you will always end with a tidy expression.

Example 1: Remove the brackets and simplify 4(x + 3) + 2(x − 1) Remove each bracket first, multiplying the number in front by every term inside: 4(x + 3) = 4x + 12   and   2(x − 1) = 2x − 2 So the expression becomes: 4x + 12 + 2x − 2 Collect the like terms. The x-terms: 4x + 2x = 6x. The plain numbers: 12 − 2 = 10. Answer: 6x + 10

Example 2: Remove the brackets and simplify 5a − (2a + 3) The bracket is preceded by a minus sign, so change the sign of every term inside and drop the brackets: −(2a + 3) = −2a − 3 The expression becomes: 5a − 2a − 3 Collect the like terms: 5a − 2a = 3a. The number −3 has no a to join, so it stays. Answer: 3a − 3 Example 3: Insert a bracket to write 12m − 8 as a product Find the largest factor of both terms. 12m and 8 are both divisible by 4, so bring 4 out in front: 12m ÷ 4 = 3m   and   8 ÷ 4 = 2 Answer: 4(3m − 2). Check by removing the bracket: 4·3m − 4·2 = 12m − 8, which matches.

practice.prompt: Remove the brackets and simplify: 4(x + 3) + 2(x − 1)
practice.worked_solution: 4(x + 3) = 4x + 12 and 2(x − 1) = 2x − 2. The expression is 4x + 12 + 2x − 2. Collect like terms: 4x + 2x = 6x and 12 − 2 = 10, so the answer is 6x + 10.

practice.prompt: Remove the brackets and simplify: 7a − (3a + 2)
practice.worked_solution: The minus in front of the bracket changes every sign inside: −(3a + 2) = −3a − 2. So 7a − 3a − 2 = 4a − 2.

practice.prompt: Remove the brackets and simplify: 2(3b + 1) − 3(b − 4)
practice.worked_solution: 2(3b + 1) = 6b + 2 and −3(b − 4) = −3b + 12. The expression is 6b + 2 − 3b + 12. Collect like terms: 6b − 3b = 3b and 2 + 12 = 14, so the answer is 3b + 14.

practice.prompt: Insert a bracket to write 8x − 12 as a product.
practice.worked_solution: The largest factor of 8x and 12 is 4. Bring 4 out: 8x ÷ 4 = 2x and 12 ÷ 4 = 3, so 8x − 12 = 4(2x − 3). Check: 4·2x − 4·3 = 8x − 12.

practice.prompt: A rectangle has length (2x + 3) cm and width 4 cm. The perimeter is found by removing the brackets in 2(2x + 3) + 2(4). Simplify this expression.
practice.worked_solution: Remove the brackets: 2(2x + 3) = 4x + 6 and 2(4) = 8. The expression is 4x + 6 + 8. Collect like terms: 4x stays, and 6 + 8 = 14, so the perimeter is 4x + 14.

blocks.text: A word problem gives you a story, and your job is to turn the story into algebra, work with the expression you build, and then answer the question the story is asking. You already know how to simplify algebraic terms by collecting like terms and applying the order of operations. Word problems simply ask you to spot which operation (add, subtract, multiply, divide) the words are describing, and to use a letter for the unknown amount. The key moves are these: 1. Read the problem and decide what the unknown is. Give it a letter, such as x or y. 2. Write each sentence of the story as part of an algebraic expression. 3. Simplify the expression by collecting like terms. 4. Use the final answer to answer the original question. Some phrases give you strong clues: • "more than", "add", "sum of" → addition • "less than", "difference", "take away" → subtraction • "times", "product of", "twice", "three times" → multiplication • "shared equally", "divided between" → division

Example 1 — One unknown. A number x is increased by 5, and the result is then tripled. Write an expression for the final amount. Step 1: The unknown is the number x. Step 2: "increased by 5" means x + 5. Step 3: "tripled" means multiply by 3, so put the whole thing in brackets: 3(x + 5). Step 4: Expand the bracket: 3x + 15. So the final expression is 3x + 15.

Example 2 — Two unknowns in one story. Amina has y oranges. Her brother has 3 more than twice as many oranges as Amina. Write, in terms of y, how many oranges her brother has. Step 1: Amina has y oranges. Step 2: "twice as many as Amina" means 2y. Step 3: "3 more than" that means add 3: 2y + 3. So her brother has 2y + 3 oranges.

Example 3 — A word problem you simplify then evaluate. A rectangle has length x cm. Its width is 2 cm less than its length. (a) Write an expression for the perimeter of the rectangle. (b) Find the perimeter when x = 6. Step 1: Length = x cm. Width = 2 cm less than length, so width = x − 2. Step 2: Perimeter = length + width + length + width = 2 × length + 2 × width. So perimeter = 2x + 2(x − 2). Step 3: Expand the bracket: 2x + 2x − 4 = 4x − 4. Step 4: When x = 6, perimeter = 4(6) − 4 = 24 − 4 = 20 cm. So (a) the perimeter is 4x − 4 cm, and (b) it is 20 cm when x = 6.

Notice how a single word problem can combine everything: building the expression from the words, then simplifying it by expanding brackets and collecting like terms, and sometimes putting in a value for the letter at the end. Keep your steps in the same order every time, and check that your final expression actually answers the question asked — not just the algebra you did.

practice.prompt: A number n is decreased by 7, and the result is then multiplied by 4. Write an expression for the final amount.
practice.worked_solution: Decreased by 7 means n − 7. Multiply the whole result by 4, so bracket it: 4(n − 7). Expand: 4n − 28.

practice.prompt: Bala is m years old. His sister is 4 years younger than twice his age. Write, in terms of m, how old his sister is.
practice.worked_solution: Twice Bala's age is 2m. Four years younger means subtract 4: 2m − 4.

practice.prompt: The length of a rectangle is y cm and its width is 3 cm more than the length. (a) Write an expression for the perimeter of the rectangle. (b) Find the perimeter when y = 5.

sections_json.title: Getting the Order Right in Algebra

blocks.text: When an algebraic expression mixes several operations, you cannot work from left to right in any order you like. The result depends on the order in which you carry them out. So algebra follows one agreed set of rules. Do the operations in this order: 1. Brackets first — work out what is inside them. 2. Order / Of — powers like ² or ³. 3. Division and Multiplication — from left to right. 4. Addition and Subtraction — from left to right. A handy way to remember the order is BODMAS: Brackets, Of/Order, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction. The trick in algebra is that you first deal with multiplication and division wherever they appear, before you do any adding or subtracting. Then you combine like terms. Let's see this in action.

Worked example 1 Simplify 4n + 3n × 10. Here there are no brackets and no powers, so Division and Multiplication come first. The only multiplication is 3n × 10. 3n × 10 = 30n So 4n + 3n × 10 = 4n + 30n. Now do the addition: 4n + 30n = 34n. Answer: 34n Notice that if you had added 4n + 3n first (getting 7n) and then multiplied by 10, you would have got 70n — which is wrong. The multiplication must be done before the addition.

Worked example 2 Simplify 32 + 8x ÷ 2. Again, there are no brackets. Division and Multiplication come before Addition and Subtraction. The only division is 8x ÷ 2. 8x ÷ 2 = 4x So 32 + 8x ÷ 2 = 32 + 4x. There is nothing more to add — 32 and 4x are not like terms, so the answer is left as 32 + 4x. Answer: 32 + 4x

Worked example 3 Simplify 3 × 5x + 4x ÷ 2. No brackets, no powers. Division and Multiplication come first, from left to right. 3 × 5x = 15x, and 4x ÷ 2 = 2x. Now do the addition: 15x + 2x = 17x. Answer: 17x

Worked example 4 Simplify 7 × 3a − (3a + 5a) × 2. Brackets come first. Inside the bracket: 3a + 5a = 8a. So the expression becomes 7 × 3a − 8a × 2. Now Division and Multiplication come before the subtraction. Work from left to right: 7 × 3a = 21a, and 8a × 2 = 16a. Now do the subtraction: 21a − 16a = 5a. Answer: 5a

Now try these yourself. Work them out on paper first, then check your answers below. Remember to deal with brackets first, then multiplication and division, and only then addition and subtraction — combining like terms as you go.

practice.prompt: Simplify 36y ÷ 6 + y + 2 × 4y.
practice.worked_solution:
No brackets. Division and multiplication come first:
36y ÷ 6 = 6y, and 2 × 4y = 8y.
The expression becomes 6y + y + 8y. All three are like terms, so add them: 6y + y + 8y = 15y.

practice.prompt: Simplify 4x + 2 × 6x.
practice.worked_solution:
Multiplication first: 2 × 6x = 12x.
Then 4x + 12x = 16x.

practice.prompt: Simplify 5 × 3a − 2 × 3a.
practice.worked_solution:
Multiply first: 5 × 3a = 15a, and 2 × 3a = 6a.
Then subtract: 15a − 6a = 9a.

practice.prompt: Simplify (2y + 4y) × 3 − 14y.
practice.worked_solution:
Brackets first: 2y + 4y = 6y.
Then multiply: 6y × 3 = 18y.
Then subtract: 18y − 14y = 4y.

blocks.text: Brackets group terms together so that we know which parts of an expression belong together. When you want to simplify an expression that has brackets in it, the first thing to do is remove the brackets — and the sign just in front of a bracket decides how the terms inside come out. Think of a bracket as a box. If a plus sign sits in front of the box, then every term inside the box keeps its own sign exactly as it is. You can lift the lid and write the terms down unchanged. If a minus sign sits in front of the box, then the box is being subtracted from everything before it. To take the whole box away, every term inside must change sign: a plus becomes a minus, and a minus becomes a plus. Once every bracket has been removed, you finish by collecting the like terms — the terms that carry the same letter.

Example 1: Simplify $(12a - 7) + (4 - 5a)$ There is a plus sign before the first bracket, so remove it unchanged: $12a - 7$. There is also a plus sign before the second bracket, so remove it unchanged too: $4 - 5a$. Put it all together: $$12a - 7 + 4 - 5a$$ Now collect the like terms. The $a$-terms are $12a$ and $-5a$: $$12a - 5a = 7a$$ The number terms are $-7$ and $+4$: $$-7 + 4 = -3$$ So the answer is: $$\boxed{7a - 3}$$ Example 2: Simplify $(8x - 2y) - (9x - 4y)$ The first bracket has a plus sign in front, so it comes out unchanged: $8x - 2y$. The second bracket has a minus sign in front. Every term inside must change sign: - $9x$ becomes $-9x$ - $-4y$ becomes $+4y$ So we write: $$8x - 2y - 9x + 4y$$ Collect the like terms. The $x$-terms are $8x$ and $-9x$: $$8x - 9x = -x$$ The $y$-terms are $-2y$ and $+4y$: $$-2y + 4y = 2y$$ So the answer is: $$\boxed{-x + 2y}$$

practice.worked_solution:
The first term, $12$, has no bracket. The bracket $(7 - 2f)$ has a minus sign in front, so change every sign: $7$ becomes $-7$ and $-2f$ becomes $+2f$. The bracket $(3 - f)$ also has a minus sign in front, so $3$ becomes $-3$ and $-f$ becomes $+f$.

So we get:
$$12 - 7 + 2f - 3 + f$$

Collect the number terms: $12 - 7 - 3 = 2$.
Collect the $f$-terms: $2f + f = 3f$.

Answer: $2 + 3f$.

practice.prompt: Simplify $(8a - 5) + (14 - 3a)$.
practice.worked_solution:
Both brackets have a plus sign in front, so remove them unchanged:
$$8a - 5 + 14 - 3a$$

Collect the $a$-terms: $8a - 3a = 5a$.
Collect the number terms: $-5 + 14 = 9$.

Answer: $5a + 9$.

practice.prompt: Simplify $(6p + 9) - (4p - 2)$.
practice.worked_solution:
The first bracket has a plus sign in front, so it comes out unchanged: $6p + 9$.
The second bracket has a minus sign in front, so change every sign: $4p$ becomes $-4p$ and $-2$ becomes $+2$.

So we get:
$$6p + 9 - 4p + 2$$

Collect the $p$-terms: $6p - 4p = 2p$.
Collect the number terms: $9 + 2 = 11$.

Answer: $2p + 11$.

blocks.text:
Word problems describe a situation in everyday words, and your job is to turn those words into an algebraic expression before you simplify it. To do that, look for two things: the unknown amount (the letter) and the relationship that connects the amounts.

Suppose a pen costs h naira and a crayon costs ₦20 less than a pen. The pen's cost is h, so the crayon costs h − 20. If the question asks for the cost of a crayon and a pen together, you add the two: h + (h − 20). Now simplify by collecting like terms: h + h − 20 = 2h − 20. So both items cost (2h − 20) naira.

The key steps are always the same:
1. Decide what the letter stands for (the unknown amount).
2. Write the other amount in terms of that letter, using the words that tell you the relationship — "less than" means subtract, "more than" means add, "twice" means multiply by 2.
3. Combine the expressions you have written and simplify by collecting like terms.

Envelopes cost d naira per pack. Four notepads cost ₦20 more than a pack of envelopes. Find the total cost of a pack of envelopes and a notepad.

Step 1 — Decide what the letter stands for. The pack of envelopes costs d naira.

Step 2 — Write the other amount. The notepads cost ₦20 more than a pack of envelopes, so they cost d + 20 naira. Since there are four notepads and they cost the same each, one notepad costs (d + 20) ÷ 4.

Wait — read the question carefully. It asks for the total cost of a pack of envelopes and a notepad, so you need one notepad, not the set of four. One notepad costs (d + 20) ÷ 4, which we write as (d + 20)/4.

Step 3 — Add and simplify. Total = d + (d + 20)/4.

To add these you need a common denominator of 4. Write d as 4d/4:
Total = 4d/4 + (d + 20)/4 = (4d + d + 20)/4 = (5d + 20)/4.

So the total cost of a pack of envelopes and one notepad is (5d + 20)/4 naira.

practice.prompt: A pen costs h naira and a crayon costs ₦20 less than a pen. (a) Find the cost of a crayon. (b) Find the total cost of a crayon and a pen.
practice.worked_solution: The pen costs h. The crayon costs ₦20 less, so it costs h − 20. Together they cost h + (h − 20) = h + h − 20 = 2h − 20 naira.

practice.prompt: A pen and a pencil altogether cost x naira. If a pen costs y naira, find the cost of 3 pencils.
practice.worked_solution: The pen and pencil together cost x, and the pen costs y. So one pencil costs x − y naira. Three pencils cost 3 × (x − y) = 3(x − y) naira.

practice.prompt: Tunde has m marbles. His sister has twice as many marbles as Tunde. Write an expression for the total number of marbles they have together.
practice.worked_solution: Tunde has m. His sister has twice as many, so she has 2m. Together they have m + 2m = 3m marbles.

sections_json.title: The Order of Operations in Algebra

blocks.text:
When you simplify an algebraic expression, you must work through it in a fixed order, not just left to right. The rule to remember is: **multiply and divide before you add and subtract**, and always deal with anything inside **brackets** first.

Here is how the order goes:

1. Work out anything inside **brackets** first.
2. Then do **multiplication** and **division** from left to right.
3. **Last** do **addition** and **subtraction** from left to right.

You already know how to add and subtract like terms, and how to multiply and divide them. This section is about putting those skills together in the right order so you get one correct answer.

**Example 1 — numbers first, to see the order**

Simplify (a) $18 - 6 \times 2$,  (b) $6 - 18 \div 3$,  (c) $6 \times 2 - 2 - 40 \div 4$.

**(a)** $18 - 6 \times 2$

Multiply before subtracting:
$$= 18 - 12$$
$$= 6$$

**(b)** $6 - 18 \div 3$

Divide before subtracting:
$$= 6 - 6$$
$$= 0$$

**(c)** $6 \times 2 - 2 - 40 \div 4$

Do the multiplication and division first:
$$= (6 \times 2) - 2 - (40 \div 4)$$
$$= 12 - 2 - 10$$
$$= 10 - 10$$
$$= 0$$

**Example 2 — the same order with letters**

Simplify (a) $3x \times 2 + 5x$,  (b) $17y - 5 \times 2y$.

**(a)** $3x \times 2 + 5x$

Multiply first:
$$= 6x + 5x$$

Then add the like terms:
$$= 11x$$

**(b)** $17y - 5 \times 2y$

Multiply first:
$$= 17y - 10y$$

Then subtract the like terms:
$$= 7y$$

**Example 3 — brackets come first**

Simplify (a) $7x \div x + 5$,  (b) $4x - (6 \div 3)$,  (c) $(24x \div 6) + x + (1 \times 5x)$.

**(a)** $7x \div x + 5$

Divide first. Since $7x \div x = 7$:
$$= 7 + 5$$
$$= 12$$

**(b)** $4x - (6 \div 3)$

Work out the bracket first: $6 \div 3 = 2$.
$$= 4x - 2$$

**(c)** $(24x \div 6) + x + (1 \times 5x)$

Do each bracket first. $24x \div 6 = 4x$, and $1 \times 5x = 5x$.
$$= 4x + x + 5x$$

Now add the like terms from left to right:
$$= 5x + 5x$$
$$= 10x$$

practice.prompt: Simplify $4n + 3n \times 10$.
practice.worked_solution: Multiply first: $3n \times 10 = 30n$. Then add the like terms: $4n + 30n = 34n$.

practice.prompt: Simplify $32 + 8x \div 2$.
practice.worked_solution: Divide first: $8x \div 2 = 4x$. $32$ and $4x$ are not like terms, so they cannot be combined. The answer is $32 + 4x$.

practice.prompt: Simplify $3 \times 5x + 4x \div 2$.
practice.worked_solution: Multiply and divide first: $3 \times 5x = 15x$ and $4x \div 2 = 2x$. Then add the like terms: $15x + 2x = 17x$.

practice.prompt: Simplify $36y \div 6 + y + 2 \times 4y$.
practice.worked_solution: Divide and multiply first: $36y \div 6 = 6y$ and $2 \times 4y = 8y$. Now add the like terms from left to right: $6y + y = 7y$, then $7y + 8y = 15y$.

blocks.text:
When an algebraic expression has brackets in it, you can often make it simpler by removing them. Removing a bracket means writing the terms inside it without the bracket, but the sign right before the bracket tells you what to do.

Keep these hints in mind:

- If a bracket has terms inside it, see whether you can simplify those terms first.
- A $+$ sign in front of a bracket does not change the signs of the terms inside. When you remove the bracket, every term keeps its own sign.
- A $-$ sign in front of a bracket changes every sign inside it: each $+$ becomes $-$ and each $-$ becomes $+$.

After removing the brackets, collect the like terms together and add or subtract them as you already know how.

Let us see the effect of a $+$ sign and a $-$ sign in front of a bracket.

Simplify:
(a) $a + (b + c)$
(b) $a + (b - c)$
(c) $2a - (3b - c)$

Solution

(a) The $+$ before the bracket leaves the signs alone, so
$$a + (b + c) = a + b + c.$$

(b) Again a $+$ sits before the bracket, so the signs stay the same:
$$a + (b - c) = a + b - c.$$

(c) Here a $-$ sign is before the bracket, so every sign inside changes: $3b$ is positive inside, and it becomes $-3b$; $c$ is negative inside, and it becomes $+c$. So
$$2a - (3b - c) = 2a - 3b + c.$$

Now remove the brackets and then collect like terms.

Simplify:
(a) $a + (a - b)$
(b) $6x + (3 - x)$
(c) $(3a + 2) + (5a + a)$

Solution

(a) Remove the bracket (the $+$ keeps the signs), then collect the $a$ terms:
$$a + (a - b) = a + a - b = 2a - b.$$

(b) Remove the bracket, then gather the $x$ terms:
$$6x + (3 - x) = 6x + 3 - x = 6x - x + 3 = 5x + 3.$$

(c) Remove the bracket, then collect the $a$ terms:
$$(3a + 2) + (5a + a) = 3a + 2 + 5a + a = 3a + 5a + a + 2 = 9a + 2.$$

A $-$ sign before a bracket changes every sign inside it. Watch for this in each step.

Simplify:
(a) $5x - (3y + z)$
(b) $10d - (9c - 4d)$
(c) $(6x - y) - (4x - 5y)$

Solution

(a) The $-$ before the bracket changes $+3y$ into $-3y$ and $+z$ into $-z$:
$$5x - (3y + z) = 5x - 3y - z.$$

(b) The $-$ changes $+9c$ into $-9c$ and $-4d$ into $+4d$:
$$10d - (9c - 4d) = 10d - 9c + 4d = 10d + 4d - 9c = 14d - 9c.$$

(c) Remove the first bracket as it is (the $+$ in front of it changes nothing), and change the signs inside the second bracket because a $-$ stands before it:
$$(6x - y) - (4x - 5y) = 6x - y - 4x + 5y = 6x - 4x + 5y - y = 2x + 4y = 2(x + 2y).$$

practice.prompt: Remove the brackets and simplify: $(12a - 7) + (4 - 5a)$
practice.worked_solution: The $+$ before the bracket keeps the signs: $12a - 7 + 4 - 5a$. Collect like terms: $12a - 5a - 7 + 4 = 7a - 3$.

practice.prompt: Remove the brackets and simplify: $(8x - 2y) - (9x - 4y)$
practice.worked_solution: The first bracket keeps its signs; the $-$ before the second bracket changes $+9x$ to $-9x$ and $-4y$ to $+4y$. So $8x - 2y - 9x + 4y = 8x - 9x + 4y - 2y = -x + 2y$.

practice.prompt: Remove the brackets and simplify: $12 - (7 - 2f) - (3 - f)$
practice.worked_solution: Each $-$ before a bracket changes every sign inside. So $12 - 7 + 2f - 3 + f$. Collect the numbers and the $f$ terms: $12 - 7 - 3 + 2f + f = 2 + 3f = 3f + 2$.

practice.prompt: Remove the brackets and simplify: $(8a - 5) + (14 - 3a)$
practice.worked_solution: The $+$ before the bracket keeps the signs: $8a - 5 + 14 - 3a$. Collect like terms: $8a - 3a + 9 = 5a + 9$.

blocks.text:
A word problem often describes a quantity in words and asks you to write it with a letter, then combine the parts. The key is to let each letter stand for one thing, read the problem slowly to decide whether to add or subtract, and then simplify the expression you build.

Think of it like this: the problem names some objects (a pen, a rubber, the boys and girls in a class) and tells you how their costs or numbers are related. You turn each sentence into algebra, one piece at a time, and then put the pieces together. As you go, keep the naira sign (₦) with every cost, and when you are asked for a total, add all the parts and simplify by collecting like terms.

Example 1 A pen costs ₦P and a pencil costs ₦15 less than a pen. (a) Find the cost of a pencil. (b) Find the cost of a pen and a pencil. Solution A pencil costs 15 naira less than the pen, so take 15 away from P: (a) Cost of a pencil = ₦(P − 15). (b) A pen and a pencil together means we add the two costs: Cost of pen + cost of pencil = ₦P + ₦(P − 15) = ₦P + ₦P − ₦15 = ₦2P − ₦15 = ₦(2P − 15). So a pen and a pencil together cost ₦(2P − 15).

Example 2 A pencil costs ₦x and a rubber costs ₦40 more than a pencil. (a) Find the cost of a rubber. (b) Find the cost of a pencil and a rubber. Solution A rubber costs 40 naira more than the pencil, so add 40 to x: (a) Cost of a rubber = ₦(x + 40). (b) Cost of a pencil and a rubber: ₦x + ₦(x + 40) = ₦(x + x + 40) = ₦(2x + 40). So a pencil and a rubber together cost ₦(2x + 40).

Example 3 In a class there are x boys and y girls. This semester 5 boys join and 3 girls leave the class. How many students are now in the class? Solution Start with the total: total number of students = number of boys + number of girls. Boys: 5 join, so the number of boys becomes x + 5. Girls: 3 leave, so the number of girls becomes y − 3. Total number = (x + 5) + (y − 3) = x + 5 + y − 3 = x + y + 5 − 3 = x + y + 2. So there are now x + y + 2 students in the class.

practice.prompt:
A pen costs ₦h and a crayon costs ₦20 less than a pen.

(a) Find the cost of a crayon.
(b) Find the cost of a crayon and a pen.
practice.worked_solution: A crayon costs 20 naira less than the pen, so cost of a crayon = ₦(h − 20). A crayon and a pen together = ₦(h − 20) + ₦h = ₦h − ₦20 + ₦h = ₦2h − ₦20 = ₦(2h − 20).

practice.prompt: Envelopes cost ₦d per pack, and a notepad costs ₦20 more than a pack of envelopes. Find the total cost of a pack of envelopes and a notepad.
practice.worked_solution: A pack of envelopes costs ₦d. A notepad costs 20 naira more, so it costs ₦(d + 20). Total = ₦d + ₦(d + 20) = ₦(d + d + 20) = ₦(2d + 20).

practice.prompt: A pen and a pencil together cost ₦x. If a pen costs ₦y, find the cost of 3 pencils.
practice.worked_solution: Out of the total ₦x, the pen costs ₦y, so one pencil costs ₦x − ₦y = ₦(x − y). Three pencils cost ₦3 × (x − y) = ₦3(x − y).

findings_text:
lo-t2w09-01: "The order is:

1. **Brackets** — work out anything inside brackets first.
2. **Multiplication and division** — from left to right.
3. **Addition and subtraction** — from left to right." — This is stated as the full order of operations, but it leaves out the 'of/order' or indices/powers step, which comes after brackets and before multiplication and division. A learner following this rule would not know how to handle expressions containing powers or 'of', so the rule is incomplete as a definition.
later_round_findings: lo-t2w09-01: "2. **Of (or powers/indices)** — evaluate any 'of' or powers next." — This bullet states as a fact that 'of' is the same kind of operation as powers/indices and gives it a separate priority in the order of operations. 'Of' is not an algebraic operation and is not used or taught anywhere in the lesson evidence or the examples; powers/indices are also not part of the taught work. The rule is therefore unsupported for this lesson.

lo-t2w09-02: "Both are preceded by a plus, so no signs change:" — In the example $(3a + 2) + (5a + a)$, the first bracket is at the start of the expression and has no written plus sign before it, so saying both brackets are preceded by a plus contradicts the expression shown.

lo-t2w09-02: "The first bracket is preceded by a plus and the second bracket is also preceded by a plus, so no signs change:" — In $(12a - 7) + (4 - 5a)$, the first bracket begins the expression and is not preceded by a plus sign, so this statement contradicts the printed expression.

lo-t2w09-02: "Both brackets are preceded by a plus, so no signs change:" — In $(8a - 5) + (14 - 3a)$, the first bracket begins the expression and has no plus sign before it, so the statement contradicts the printed expression.

lo-t2w09-03: "Here is the plan to follow for any word problem:

1. Read the story and decide which item the letter stands for.
2. Write that item's value using the letter.
3. Write every other item as the letter, plus or minus a number, depending on the words "more than" or "less than"." — The plan is presented as valid for any word problem, but the section's own worked examples contradict it: the class-size problem uses two different letters (x boys and y girls) and combines them into x + y + 2, and the notepad problem requires dividing (d + 20) by 4 rather than writing every other item as the letter plus or minus a number. A learner following this plan could not solve those problems from the stated steps.

blocks.text:
When you simplify an algebraic expression, you cannot just work from left to right. You must follow the order of operations, which tells you which part to work out first.

The correct order is:

1. **Brackets** — work out anything inside them first.
2. **Multiplication and division** — do these from left to right.
3. **Addition and subtraction** — do these from left to right.

You already know how to add, subtract, multiply and divide algebraic terms. Order of operations tells you the order in which to apply those skills. In an expression like $3x \times 2 + 5x$, you must multiply before you add, so you deal with $3x \times 2$ first and only then combine the $x$ terms.

**Example 1.** Find the value of each expression by following the order of operations.

(a) $18 - 6 \times 2$

Multiplication comes before subtraction, so work out $6 \times 2$ first.

$18 - 6 \times 2 = 18 - 12 = 6$

(b) $6 - 18 \div 3$

Division comes before subtraction, so work out $18 \div 3$ first.

$6 - 18 \div 3 = 6 - 6 = 0$

(c) $6 \times 2 - 2 - 40 \div 4$

Deal with the multiplication and division first, then subtract from left to right.

$6 \times 2 - 2 - 40 \div 4 = 12 - 2 - 10 = 10 - 10 = 0$

**Example 2.** Simplify the following expressions.

(a) $3x \times 2 + 5x$

Multiply first: $3x \times 2 = 6x$. Then add the $x$ terms.

$3x \times 2 + 5x = 6x + 5x = 11x$

(b) $17y - 5 \times 2y$

Multiply first: $5 \times 2y = 10y$. Then subtract.

$17y - 5 \times 2y = 17y - 10y = 7y$

**Example 3.** Simplify the following expressions.

(a) $7x \div x + 5$

Division comes before addition. $\frac{7x}{x} = 7$, then add $5$.

$7x \div x + 5 = 7 + 5 = 12$

(b) $4x - (6 \div 3)$

Work out the bracket first: $6 \div 3 = 2$. Then subtract.

$4x - (6 \div 3) = 4x - 2$

(c) $(24x \div 6) + x + (1 \times 5x)$

Work out each bracket first: $24x \div 6 = 4x$ and $1 \times 5x = 5x$. Then add all the $x$ terms.

$(24x \div 6) + x + (1 \times 5x) = 4x + x + 5x = 5x + 5x = 10x$

practice.prompt: Simplify: $4n + 3n \times 10$
practice.worked_solution: Multiply first: $3n \times 10 = 30n$. Then add: $4n + 30n = 34n$.

practice.prompt: Simplify: $32 + 8x \div 2$
practice.worked_solution: Divide first: $8x \div 2 = 4x$. Then add: $32 + 4x$. There are no $x$ terms to combine with $32$, so the answer is $32 + 4x$.

practice.prompt: Simplify: $3 \times 5x + 4x \div 2$
practice.worked_solution: Multiply first: $3 \times 5x = 15x$. Divide next: $4x \div 2 = 2x$. Then add: $15x + 2x = 17x$.

practice.prompt: Simplify: $36y \div 6 + y + 2 \times 4y$
practice.worked_solution: Work out the division and multiplication first: $36y \div 6 = 6y$ and $2 \times 4y = 8y$. Then add all the $y$ terms from left to right: $6y + y + 8y = 7y + 8y = 15y$.

blocks.text:
When an expression contains brackets, you can remove them and then collect the like terms. Three hints will guide you every time:

- Always try to simplify the terms inside the bracket first.
- A $+$ sign just before a bracket does **not** change the signs of the terms inside the bracket when the bracket is removed.
- A $-$ sign just before a bracket **changes every sign** inside the bracket when the bracket is removed: each $+$ becomes $-$ and each $-$ becomes $+$.

Here is what that looks like in the simplest case. In $a + (b + c)$, the plus before the bracket leaves the signs alone, so $a + (b + c) = a + b + c$. In $a + (b - c)$ the same rule applies: $a + (b - c) = a + b - c$.

But in $2a - (3b - c)$, the minus before the bracket flips both signs inside: $3b$ keeps its term but its sign becomes $-3b$, and $-c$ becomes $+c$. So $2a - (3b - c) = 2a - 3b + c$.

Simplify the following.

(a) $6x + (3 - x)$

The plus before the bracket leaves the signs alone, so
$6x + (3 - x) = 6x + 3 - x$.
Collect the like terms: $6x$ and $-x$ are both in $x$, so
$6x - x + 3 = 5x + 3$.

(b) $(3a + 2) + (5a + a)$

Remove the brackets without changing any signs:
$3a + 2 + 5a + a$.
Collect the like terms: $3a + 5a + a = 9a$, so the answer is
$9a + 2$.

(c) $10d - (9c - 4d)$

The minus before the bracket flips both signs inside: $-9c$ and $+4d$.
So $10d - 9c + 4d$.
Collect the like terms: $10d + 4d = 14d$, so
$14d - 9c$.

(d) $(6x - y) - (4x - 5y)$

Remove the first bracket as it is. The second bracket is preceded by a minus, so $4x$ becomes $-4x$ and $-5y$ becomes $+5y$:
$6x - y - 4x + 5y$.
Collect the like terms: $6x - 4x = 2x$ and $-y + 5y = 4y$, so
$2x + 4y$.

practice.prompt: Simplify $(12a - 7) + (4 - 5a)$.
practice.worked_solution:
No signs change when the brackets are removed:
$12a - 7 + 4 - 5a$.
Collect the like terms: $12a - 5a = 7a$ and $-7 + 4 = -3$.
So the answer is $7a - 3$.

practice.prompt: Simplify $(8x - 2y) - (9x - 4y)$.
practice.worked_solution:
Remove the first bracket as it is. The second bracket is preceded by a minus, so $9x$ becomes $-9x$ and $-4y$ becomes $+4y$:
$8x - 2y - 9x + 4y$.
Collect the like terms: $8x - 9x = -x$ and $-2y + 4y = 2y$.
So the answer is $-x + 2y$.

Remove the first bracket: the minus before it flips $7$ to $-7$ and $-2f$ to $+2f$. Remove the second bracket: the minus flips $3$ to $-3$ and $-f$ to $+f$.
So we get $12 - 7 + 2f - 3 + f$.
Collect the number terms: $12 - 7 - 3 = 2$. Collect the $f$ terms: $2f + f = 3f$.
So the answer is $2 + 3f$.

practice.prompt: Simplify $(8a - 5) + (14 - 3a)$.
practice.worked_solution:
No signs change when the brackets are removed:
$8a - 5 + 14 - 3a$.
Collect the like terms: $8a - 3a = 5a$ and $-5 + 14 = 9$.
So the answer is $5a + 9$.

blocks.text:
A word problem tells a short story, and your job is to turn that story into an algebraic expression. You do this by deciding which part of the story is your unknown (the letter), then writing the other costs or numbers in terms of it. You already know how to add, subtract, multiply and divide algebraic terms, and you know how to remove brackets and simplify. A word problem just asks you to use those skills on a story.

Here is the plan to follow for any word problem:

1. Read the story and decide which item the letter stands for.
