sections_json.title: Pyramids and Cones: Naming Them and Counting Their Parts

blocks.text:
A pyramid is named after the shape of its base. A triangular base gives a triangular based pyramid, a square base gives a square based pyramid, a pentagonal base gives a pentagonal based pyramid, and a rectangular base gives a rectangular based pyramid. The apex is the single point above the base, and every other corner of the base is joined up to that apex. Every pyramid is built from the same three parts:
  • Faces — the flat surfaces. A pyramid has its base plus one triangular face for each side of the base.
  • Edges — the lines where two faces meet.
  • Vertices — the corners where edges meet.
The table below shows the counts for the four pyramids you can see in the figures. | Shape | Faces | Edges | Vertices | |---|---|---|---| | Triangular based pyramid (tetrahedron) | 4 | 6 | 4 | | Square based pyramid | 5 | 8 | 5 | | Pentagonal based pyramid | 6 | 10 | 6 | | Rectangular based pyramid | 5 | 8 | 5 | Notice the pattern: each time the base gains one more side, the faces, edges and vertices each go up by one.

The cone is a different shape from a pyramid. Its parts are:
  • Two faces — one curved face (the sloping side) and one flat face (the base).
  • One edge — the single circular line where the curved face meets the flat base.
  • One vertex — the apex, the point at the top.
So a cone has 2 faces, 1 edge and 1 vertex. You can see the upright cone and the cone lying on its side in fig-07.

blocks.caption: Two drawings side by side. On the left an upright cone: an elliptical base with the two slant sides running up from the ends of the ellipse to the apex. On the right a cone lying on its side, apex at the left, its two slant sides reaching a narrow upright ellipse whose top and bottom then continue as two parallel lines to a second narrow ellipse further right.

blocks.text: Let's name and count the parts of a square based pyramid. Name it. The base is a square, so the shape is called a square based pyramid. Count the faces. There is the square base, and one triangular face for each of the four sides of that base. So it has 1 base + 4 triangular faces = 5 faces. Count the edges. The base has 4 edges, and each of the 4 triangular faces reaches up to the apex, adding 4 slanting edges. So it has 4 + 4 = 8 edges. Count the vertices. There are 4 corners on the base plus the apex = 5 vertices. So a square based pyramid has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices — exactly what the table says.

blocks.caption: A triangular base pyramid. The base triangle is drawn in perspective, its third vertex raised into the middle of the figure, and the apex above is joined to all three base vertices.
A square base pyramid. The base is drawn as an upright rectangle and the apex above is joined to all four of its corners, so two edges run outside the rectangle and two cross it.

A pentagonal based pyramid. The base is drawn as a pentagon standing on one side with its fifth vertex uppermost, and the apex above is joined to that vertex, to the two vertices either side of it, and to the lower-right vertex — four edges from the apex, the last of them crossing the face of the solid.
A rectangular based pyramid, drawn like the square one but on a base wider than it is tall.

sections_json.title: Cubes and Cuboids: Faces, Edges and Vertices

blocks.text:
A **three dimensional shape** has length, breadth and height, so it takes up space. That is why these shapes are also called **solid shapes**. The cube and the cuboid are two of these solid shapes. Before we count their parts, let us fix three words you will need.

- A **face** (or surface) is one of the sides of the shape. A face may be flat or curved.
- An **edge** is a line where two faces meet. It may be straight or curved.
- A **vertex** is a point corner where edges meet. The plural of vertex is **vertices**.

**The cube.** A cube is a solid shape whose faces are all equal squares. Look at **fig-01**: a cube drawn as a see-through solid, with one square offset from another and their corners joined. Count its parts carefully.

- It has **6 square faces** — the six equal squares that cover it.
- It has **12 edges** — the straight lines where the faces meet.
- It has **8 vertices** — the 8 point corners where the edges meet.

A cube is a **regular** solid shape: its faces are all the same shape and size.

blocks.caption: A cube drawn as a see-through solid: two equal squares, the nearer one offset down and to the right of the farther one, with the four pairs of corresponding corners joined.

blocks.text:
**The cuboid.** A cuboid is also a solid shape with six faces, but its faces are rectangles rather than equal squares. In **fig-02** the cuboid is drawn wide and shallow, and three leader lines name its parts: the top **face**, a **vertex** (the point corner), and an **edge** (the line where two faces meet).

Count its parts in the same way:

- It has **6 faces**.
- It has **12 edges**.
- It has **8 vertices**.

The cube and the cuboid share the same numbers of faces, edges and vertices. What makes them different is that every face of a cube is an equal square, while a cuboid's faces are rectangles (usually of two or three different sizes).

blocks.caption: A cuboid drawn the same way, wide and shallow, with three leader lines to the right naming the top face, the nearer top-right corner and the nearer right-hand vertical edge.

How many edges has a cube?

practice.answer: A cube has 6 square faces. A cube's faces are all equal squares, while a cuboid's faces are rectangles (so they are not all equal squares).

sections_json.title: Pyramids and Cones: Faces, Edges and Vertices

blocks.text:
A pyramid is named by the shape of its base. The base is the flat face it stands on, and from every corner of that base one straight edge runs up to a single point at the top, called the apex. Look at the triangular base pyramid in fig-03: its base is a triangle, so it is a triangular based pyramid. Its special name is a tetrahedron.

The square based pyramid in fig-04, the pentagonal based pyramid in fig-05 and the rectangular based pyramid in fig-06 are all named the same way — by what their base is.

Every pyramid has faces, edges and vertices, and you can count them. Remember: a face is a flat surface, an edge is where two faces meet, and a vertex is a corner where edges meet. Here is how the count works out:

| Shape | Faces | Edges | Vertices |
|---|---|---|---|
| Triangular based pyramid | 4 | 6 | 4 |
| Square based pyramid | 5 | 8 | 5 |
| Pentagonal based pyramid | 6 | 10 | 6 |
| Rectangular based pyramid | 5 | 8 | 5 |

A cone (fig-07) is different. It is round, so it has a flat circular base and a curved face that narrows up to one point. Altogether a cone has two faces — one curved face and one flat face — one edge (the rim of the circular base), and one vertex (the point at the top).

blocks.caption: Two drawings side by side. On the left an upright cone: an elliptical base with the two slant sides running up from the ends of the ellipse to the apex. On the right a cone lying on its side, apex at the left, its two slant sides reaching a narrow upright ellipse whose top and bottom then continue as two parallel lines to a second narrow ellipse further right.
A rectangular based pyramid, drawn like the square one but on a base wider than it is tall.

A pentagonal based pyramid. The base is drawn as a pentagon standing on one side with its fifth vertex uppermost, and the apex above is joined to that vertex, to the two vertices either side of it, and to the lower-right vertex — four edges from the apex, the last of them crossing the face of the solid.
A square base pyramid. The base is drawn as an upright rectangle and the apex above is joined to all four of its corners, so two edges run outside the rectangle and two cross it.
A triangular base pyramid. The base triangle is drawn in perspective, its third vertex raised into the middle of the figure, and the apex above is joined to all three base vertices.

blocks.text:
Let's name a solid and then count its parts.

Example 1 — Name the solid with a square base. Its base is a square, so it is a square based pyramid. From the table, a square based pyramid has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices.

Example 2 — How many edges does a pentagonal based pyramid have? Its base is a pentagon (five sides). Reading the row for the pentagonal based pyramid: 6 faces, 10 edges, 6 vertices. So it has 10 edges.

Example 3 — A cone has a curved face and a flat circular base. The flat base meets the curved face along one circular rim. So a cone has 2 faces, 1 edge and 1 vertex.

practice.prompt: Draw a hexagonal base pyramid (a pyramid whose base has six sides) and list its properties. How many faces, edges and vertices does it have?
practice.answer: A hexagonal based pyramid has 7 faces, 12 edges and 7 vertices.
practice.worked_solution: The pyramid is named by its base, so a hexagonal base gives a hexagonal based pyramid. Its base is a hexagon (6 sides). A pyramid with a base of n sides has n + 1 faces (the n triangular side faces plus the base), 2n edges, and n + 1 vertices. With n = 6: 6 + 1 = 7 faces, 2 × 6 = 12 edges, and 6 + 1 = 7 vertices.

practice.prompt: How many vertices does a tetrahedron have? What kind of base does it have, and how is it named?
practice.answer: A tetrahedron has 4 vertices. It has a triangular base, so it is also called a triangular based pyramid.
practice.worked_solution: A tetrahedron is a triangular based pyramid, and the triangular based pyramid row of the table shows 4 faces, 6 edges and 4 vertices — so it has 4 vertices.

practice.prompt: How many faces, edges and vertices does a cone have?
practice.answer: A cone has 2 faces (one curved face and one flat circular base), 1 edge and 1 vertex.

sections_json.title: Cylinders and Spheres, and Finding Volume

blocks.text: Solid shapes are all around you — tins, balls, boxes, and bricks. In this section you will get to know two of them well (the cylinder and the sphere), and then find the volume of three solid shapes: the cube, the cuboid and the prism.

Cylinders
A cylinder looks like a tin of tomatoes or a drinking can. Its key properties are:
• It has two flat circular faces — one at the top and one at the bottom — and they are the same size.
• It has one curved surface that joins the two circles.
• If you cut it straight across, the slice is always a circle the same size (its cross-section is a constant circle).
• It has no vertices (corners).
• Its height is the distance between the two circular faces.

Spheres
A sphere looks like a ball — a football or a marble. Its key properties are:
• It is perfectly round.
• Every point on its surface is the same distance from its centre. That distance is called the radius.
• It has no flat faces, no edges and no vertices at all.
• No matter how you slice it, a cut gives you a circle.

Volume
Volume measures how much space a solid takes up. You work it out by multiplying a shape's length, width and height, and you answer in cubic units (like cm³, meaning centimetres cubed).

• Cube — all its edges are equal. Volume = side × side × side, or side³.
• Cuboid — a box with three different lengths. Volume = length × width × height.
• Prism — a shape with a cross-section that is the same all the way through (for example, a triangular prism). Volume = area of the cross-section × length.

Worked Example 1 — the volume of a cube
Find the volume of a cube whose side is 4 cm.

Volume of a cube = side × side × side
= 4 × 4 × 4
= 64 cm³

So the cube takes up 64 cubic centimetres of space.

Worked Example 2 — the volume of a cuboid
A cuboid is 5 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm high. Find its volume.

Volume of a cuboid = length × width × height
= 5 × 3 × 2
= 30 cm³

The order of the three measurements does not matter — you always multiply them together.

Worked Example 3 — the volume of a prism
A triangular prism has a triangular cross-section with area 12 cm², and its length is 6 cm. Find its volume.

Volume of a prism = area of cross-section × length
= 12 × 6
= 72 cm³

The prism holds 72 cubic centimetres.

practice.prompt: A drinks tin is in the shape of a cylinder. How many flat faces does it have, and what shape are they?
practice.answer: It has two flat faces, and both are circles.
practice.worked_solution: A cylinder has two circular faces (one on top and one at the bottom) plus one curved surface joining them. So it has two flat faces, and they are circles.

practice.prompt: Which solid shape has no flat faces, no edges and no vertices? Name one thing in your home that has this shape.
practice.answer: A sphere. One example is a ball or an orange.
practice.worked_solution: A sphere is perfectly round: every point on its surface is the same distance from its centre, and it has no flat faces, edges or vertices. Any ball, marble or orange is a sphere.

practice.prompt: Find the volume of a cube whose side is 5 cm.
practice.worked_solution: Volume of a cube = side × side × side = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 cm³.

practice.prompt: A cuboid is 8 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high. Find its volume.
practice.worked_solution: Volume of a cuboid = length × width × height = 8 × 4 × 3 = 96 cm³.

practice.prompt: A triangular prism has a triangular cross-section of area 15 cm² and a length of 4 cm. Find its volume.
practice.worked_solution: Volume of a prism = area of cross-section × length = 15 × 4 = 60 cm³.

blocks.text:
Before we measure shapes, let's make sure we know them. A cylinder is like a tin or a drum: it has two flat, circular faces (top and bottom) that are the same size and face each other, and one curved surface that joins them. Its two circular faces are identical and lie flat and parallel to each other. A sphere is perfectly round like a ball or an orange: it has just one surface, the whole outside is curved, and there is no flat face, no edge and no corner. From the centre of a sphere, every point on its surface is exactly the same distance away.

Now for the main job of this section: finding volume. The volume of a solid is the amount of space it takes up, and we measure it in cubic units such as cm3 or m3. For a box-shaped solid, the volume is found by multiplying its three measurements together.

A cube is a box where every edge is the same length. If one edge is length s, then:

Volume of a cube = s × s × s = s3

A cuboid is a box where the faces are rectangles, and its three edges can all be different lengths — length l, breadth b and height h. Then:

Volume of a cuboid = l × b × h

Many solids are prisms. A prism is a solid with the same cross-section all the way through — think of a Toblerone bar, a pipe, or a wedge of cheese. For any prism:

Volume of a prism = area of cross-section × length

So once you can work out the area of the shape at the end, you multiply it by how long the prism is.

Example 1 — Volume of a cube. A cube has edges of length 4 cm. Find its volume.
Volume = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. So the volume is 64 cm3.

Example 2 — Volume of a cuboid. A box measures 5 cm long, 3 cm broad and 2 cm high. Find its volume.
Volume = 5 × 3 × 2 = 30. So the volume is 30 cm3.

Example 3 — Volume of a prism. A prism has a triangular end with an area of 8 cm2, and it is 6 cm long. Find its volume.
Volume = area of cross-section × length = 8 × 6 = 48. So the volume is 48 cm3.

Notice the pattern: a cube and a cuboid are actually special prisms, because their cross-section is the same all the way through. For a cuboid, that cross-section is a rectangle, so its area is length × breadth, and multiplying by the height again gives length × breadth × height.

practice.prompt:
1. Look at these two solids. Which one is a cylinder and which one is a sphere?
   (a) A solid with two identical flat circular faces and one curved surface.
   (b) A perfectly round solid with only a curved surface and no flat faces.
practice.answer: (a) is a cylinder; (b) is a sphere.

practice.prompt: 2. A cube has edges of length 6 cm. Find its volume.
practice.worked_solution: For a cube, volume = s × s × s. Here s = 6, so volume = 6 × 6 × 6 = 216. The answer is 216 cm³.

practice.prompt: 3. A cuboid is 7 cm long, 4 cm broad and 3 cm high. Find its volume.
practice.worked_solution: For a cuboid, volume = length × breadth × height = 7 × 4 × 3 = 84. The answer is 84 cm³.

practice.prompt: 4. A prism has a triangular cross-section with an area of 5 cm² and it is 9 cm long. Find its volume.
practice.worked_solution: For a prism, volume = area of cross-section × length = 5 × 9 = 45. The answer is 45 cm³.

practice.prompt: 5. A rectangular box is 10 cm long, 6 cm broad and 5 cm high. How many cubes of edge 1 cm can fit inside it?
practice.answer: Its volume is 10 × 6 × 5 = 300 cm³, so 300 one-cubic-centimetre cubes fit inside.
practice.worked_solution: Each 1 cm cube takes up 1 cm³. The volume of the box is length × breadth × height = 10 × 6 × 5 = 300 cm³, so 300 of the small cubes fit inside.

blocks.text:
You already know the properties of cubes, cuboids, pyramids and cones. Now let's look at two more solid shapes: the cylinder and the sphere. These are three-dimensional figures, and each has its own set of properties. A cylinder is a solid shape with two flat circular faces and one curved surface joining them. Picture a tin of milk or a roll of paper towel. Its properties are:
  • It has two circular faces, one at the top and one at the bottom.
  • The two circular faces are equal in size — they are identical circles.
  • It has one curved surface that wraps around and joins the two circles.
  • It has two edges — each edge is the circle where a circular face meets the curved surface.
  • It has no vertices (corners).
So when you count the faces of a cylinder, you get two flat circular faces and one curved face. Altogether a cylinder has three faces: two flat circles and one curved surface.

Before we go further, see if you can name the properties of a sphere yourself. A sphere is a perfectly round solid shape — think of a ball, a football, or an orange. Write down what you think its properties are, then read on to check. A sphere's properties are:
  • It has no faces.
  • It has no edges.
  • It has no vertices.
  • It has one curved surface that covers the whole shape.
  • Every point on its surface is the same distance from its centre.
Unlike the cylinder, which has flat circular faces, the sphere is curved all over — that is why it has no flat faces, no edges and no corners.

Let's compare the two shapes side by side. Question: A solid cylinder has how many faces? Solution: A cylinder has two flat circular faces (one at the top, one at the bottom) and one curved surface that joins them. So altogether it has three faces: 2 circular faces + 1 curved face = 3 faces. Question: How many circular faces does a solid cylinder have? Solution: The two flat faces are the circular ones. So a solid cylinder has two circular faces. Question: How many faces does a sphere have? Solution: A sphere is curved all over, so it has no flat faces at all — it has zero faces (just one curved surface covering the whole shape).

practice.prompt: A solid cylinder has how many faces altogether?
practice.answer: 3 faces (2 circular faces and 1 curved surface)
practice.worked_solution: The cylinder has a top circle, a bottom circle, and one curved surface wrapping around to join them. So 2 + 1 = 3 faces.

practice.prompt: How many circular faces does a solid cylinder have?
practice.worked_solution: The two flat faces of the cylinder are the circles at the top and at the bottom, so there are exactly two circular faces.

practice.prompt: State the number of faces, edges and vertices of a sphere.
practice.answer: A sphere has 0 faces, 0 edges and 0 vertices. It has one curved surface covering the whole shape.
practice.worked_solution: A sphere is curved all over, with no flat faces and no corners, so it has no faces, no edges and no vertices.

practice.prompt: A cylinder has some vertices. How many?
practice.worked_solution: A vertex is a corner where edges meet. A cylinder has only circular edges and no corners, so it has no vertices.

sections_json.title: Finding Volume: Cubes, Cuboids and Prisms

blocks.text:
Volume is the amount of space a solid takes up. For a cube or a cuboid, the volume is found by multiplying the three dimensions together: length × width × height.

A **cuboid** is a box with rectangular faces. Its volume is:

Volume = length × width × height

A **cube** is a special cuboid where all three edges are the same length, so its volume is simply:

Volume = side × side × side

You can think of it this way: the bottom face of a cuboid has area length × width, and the height tells you how many of those layers of unit cubes stack up. So the volume is just the area of the base multiplied by the height. This same idea works for any prism: a prism has a shape at the front and back that is the same all the way through, so

Volume of a prism = area of base × height

For a cuboid the base is a rectangle, so area of base = length × width, which gives length × width × height.

**Example 1 — cuboid.** Find the volume of a cuboid 8 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high.

Volume = length × width × height = 8 × 4 × 3 = 96

So the volume is 96 cm³.

**Example 2 — cube.** Find the volume of a cube with edges 4 cm.

Volume = side × side × side = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64

So the volume is 64 cm³.

**Example 3 — prism.** A prism has a triangular base. The base has area 12 cm² and the prism is 5 cm long. Find its volume.

Volume = area of base × height = 12 × 5 = 60

So the volume is 60 cm³.

practice.prompt: Calculate the volume of a cuboid 8 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high.
practice.worked_solution: Volume = length × width × height = 8 × 4 × 3 = 96, so the volume is 96 cm³.

practice.prompt: Calculate the volume of a cuboid with dimensions 5 m by 2 m by 3 m.
practice.worked_solution: Volume = 5 × 2 × 3 = 30, so the volume is 30 m³.

practice.prompt: What is the volume of a cube of 4 cm × 4 cm × 4 cm?
practice.worked_solution: Volume = side × side × side = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, so the volume is 64 cm³.

practice.prompt: A rectangular tank is 6 m long and 2 m wide, and it holds 36 m³ of water. How deep is the water in the tank?
practice.worked_solution: Volume = length × width × depth, so 36 = 6 × 2 × depth = 12 × depth. Divide both sides by 12: depth = 36 ÷ 12 = 3. The water is 3 m deep.

blocks.text:
Let's look closely at two three-dimensional shapes you meet all the time: the cylinder and the sphere. A cylinder is the shape of a tin or a drum — straight sides with a round top and a round base. A sphere is the shape of a ball or an orange — perfectly round.

Look at the cylinder in fig-01. It has a flat circular top and a flat circular base, and between them one face that curves all the way around the sides. So a cylinder has two circular faces and one curved face. Count them together and you find it has three faces altogether. Run your finger along the rim of the top circle: that is one curved edge, and the rim of the base circle is another. So it has two curved edges. Notice, too, that there is no sharp corner anywhere on a cylinder — no point where three or more edges meet. That means a cylinder has no vertex at all.

Now look at the sphere in fig-02. A sphere is a single curved surface, with nothing flat on it. There are no edges and no vertices anywhere on it. Finally, turn the sphere any way you like: it looks the same from every direction, so we say it is symmetrical from all directions.

blocks.caption: A sphere drawn as a circle with an ellipse across its middle to show the curved surface.
A cylinder drawn upright: an ellipse for the top face, two vertical sides falling from its ends, and a curve closing the base.

blocks.text:
Let's identify the properties of a cylinder together, one by one.

Look again at the cylinder in fig-01. Ask yourself four questions.

First, what faces does it have? You can see a flat circle at the top and a flat circle at the bottom, and the curved side running between them. That is two circular faces and one curved face — three faces in total.

Second, does it have any vertices? A vertex is a sharp corner where edges meet. Run your eye around the whole cylinder: there is no sharp corner anywhere. So it has no vertex.

Third, does it have any edges? An edge is a line where two faces meet. Where the curved face meets the top circle, there is a curved rim — that is one curved edge. Where it meets the base circle, there is another. So it has two curved edges.

Now do the same for the sphere in fig-02. Ask the same questions. It has only one face, and that face is curved — there is no flat circle anywhere. With no flat face meeting a curved one, there are no edges. And with no edges, there is no sharp corner, so there is no vertex either. Finally, spin the sphere: it looks the same from every direction, which is why we say it is symmetrical from all directions.

So you can list the properties of each shape in the same way: count the faces, count the edges, count the vertices, and note any special feature such as the cylinder's curved faces and edges, or the sphere's symmetry.

practice.prompt: How many circular faces does a solid cylinder have?
practice.answer: Two — one circular top face and one circular base.
practice.worked_solution: A solid cylinder has a flat circular top and a flat circular base, so it has two circular faces.

practice.prompt: How many faces does a cylinder have altogether?
practice.answer: Three — two circular faces and one curved face.
practice.worked_solution: Count the flat circular top, the flat circular base, and the curved face that runs between them: that gives three faces altogether.

practice.prompt: State how many edges and how many vertices a sphere has.
practice.answer: A sphere has no edges and no vertices.
practice.worked_solution: A sphere is one single curved surface with nothing flat on it. Since edges form where faces meet and vertices form where edges meet, a sphere has neither.

practice.prompt: A pupil says a cylinder has one curved face and two curved edges. Is the pupil right about the edges?
practice.answer: Yes — the two curved edges are the rim of the top circle and the rim of the base circle.
practice.worked_solution: Each rim is a line where the curved face meets a circular face. There is one such rim at the top and one at the base, so the cylinder has two curved edges.

sections_json.title: Volume of a Cube, a Cuboid and a Prism

blocks.text:
Volume tells us how much space a three-dimensional shape takes up, and it is measured in cubic units like cm³, m³. For a cuboid, think of it as a box that is made of layers of cubes stacked up. If you know the area of the base (how many cubes cover the floor of the box) and how many layers high it is, you can find the volume.

**Volume of a cuboid** = area of base × height = length × breadth × height, often written simply as **V = l × b × h** or **V = lbh**.

**Volume of a cube** is the same idea, but a cube has every edge the same length. So its volume is length × length × length, written as **V = l³**.

A prism is a solid whose two ends are identical. For any prism, you can again find the volume by multiplying the area of one end (the base) by the length it runs back: **Volume of a prism = area of base × height**. For a triangular prism, the base is a triangle, so you first find the area of that triangle using area = ½ × base × height of the triangle, then multiply by how far the prism runs.

**Example 1.** Calculate the volume of a cuboid of length 3 cm, breadth 2 cm and height 8 cm.

Volume of cuboid = l × b × h.

length = 3 cm, breadth = 2 cm, height = 8 cm.

Volume = 3 cm × 2 cm × 8 cm = 48 cm³.

**Example 2.** The volume of a cuboid is 24 cm³. Its base is 6 cm by 2 cm. Find its height.

Volume of cuboid = l × b × h.

length = 6 cm, breadth = 2 cm, height = h.

Volume = 24 cm³.

So 24 cm³ = 6 cm × 2 cm × h.

24 cm³ = 12 cm² × h.

Divide both sides by 12 cm²:

24 cm³ ÷ 12 cm² = h, so h = 2 cm.

**Example 3.** Calculate the volume of a cube of side 3 cm.

Volume of cube = l³.

V = (3 cm)³ = 3 cm × 3 cm × 3 cm = 27 cm³.

**Example 4.** fig-03 shows a triangular prism lying on its rectangular face. The triangular end has a base of 5 m and a height of 3 m, and the prism runs back 10 m. Find its volume.

First find the area of the triangular end (the base of the prism):

Area of triangle = ½ × base × height = ½ × 5 m × 3 m = 7.5 m².

Now multiply by the length the prism runs:

Volume of prism = area of base × height = 7.5 m² × 10 m = 75 m³.

practice.worked_solution: V = l × b × h = 8 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm = 96 cm³.

What is the volume of a cube measuring 4 cm × 4 cm × 4 cm?
practice.worked_solution: V = l³ = (4 cm)³ = 4 cm × 4 cm × 4 cm = 64 cm³.

blocks.text: Two common three-dimensional shapes are the cylinder and the sphere. You can tell each one apart by the faces, edges and vertices it has. The cylinder Look at the cylinder in fig-01. Think of a tin or a drum. A cylinder has a top and a bottom that are both circular, and a curved wall joining them. Its properties are: 1. It has two circular faces and one curved face. 2. It has no vertex (no pointed corner). 3. It has two curved edges — the two circles where the curved face meets each circular face. 4. It has three faces altogether. The sphere Look at the sphere in fig-02. Think of a ball. Its whole surface is curved, with no flat parts at all. Its properties are: 1. It is symmetrical from all directions — however you turn it, it looks the same. 2. It has no edge and no vertex. 3. It has one curved surface.

Where each circular face meets the curved face, there is a curved edge, so it has two curved edges in total. Because a cylinder has no pointed corner, it has no vertex.

practice.prompt: How many circular faces does a solid cylinder have?
practice.worked_solution: A solid cylinder has a circular top and a circular bottom, so it has 2 circular faces.

practice.prompt: State how many edges and how many vertices a sphere has.
practice.answer: A sphere has no edge and no vertex.
practice.worked_solution: The whole surface of a sphere is one curved surface with no flat parts, so there are no edges where flat faces meet and no pointed vertices.

sections_json.title: Finding the Volume of a Cube, Cuboid and Prism

blocks.text:
Volume measures how much space a solid takes up. For the solids you meet here, volume is found the same way every time: multiply the area of the base by the height. The only difference is how you work out that base area.

A cuboid is a box with rectangular faces. Its base is a rectangle, so:

Volume of a cuboid = area of base × height = length × breadth × height = l × b × h.

A cube is a special cuboid where length, breadth and height are all equal. If the side is l, then:

Volume of a cube = l × l × l = l³.

Worked example — finding the volume of a cuboid
Calculate the volume of a cuboid of length 3 cm, breadth 2 cm and height 8 cm.

Volume of cuboid = l × b × h
length = 3 cm, breadth = 2 cm, height = 8 cm
Volume = 3 cm × 2 cm × 8 cm = 48 cm³.

Worked example — finding the height of a cuboid
The volume of a cuboid is 24 cm³. Its base is 6 cm by 2 cm. Find its height.

Volume = l × b × h
24 cm³ = 6 cm × 2 cm × h
24 cm³ = 12 cm² × h
Divide both sides by 12 cm²:
24 cm³ ÷ 12 cm² = h
h = 2 cm.

Worked example — finding the volume of a cube
Calculate the volume of a cube of side 3 cm.

Volume of cube = l³
V = (3 cm)³ = 3 cm × 3 cm × 3 cm = 27 cm³.

Worked example — finding the volume of a prism
A prism has two identical ends. The volume of a prism is still:

Volume of prism = area of base × height.

Consider a triangular prism (fig-03) whose triangular end has a base of 5 m and a height of 3 m, running back 10 m.

First find the area of the triangular end (the base of the prism):
Area of triangle = ½ × b × h = ½ × 5 × 3 = 7.5 m².

Then multiply by the length of the prism:
Volume of prism = 7.5 m² × 10 m = 75 m³.

practice.worked_solution: Volume = l × b × h = 5 m × 2 m × 3 m = 30 m³.

practice.worked_solution: Volume of cube = l³ = 4 cm × 4 cm × 4 cm = 64 cm³.
