practice.worked_solution: Volume = l × b × h, so 36 m³ = 6 m × 2 m × h = 12 m² × h. Divide both sides by 12 m²: h = 36 m³ ÷ 12 m² = 3 m.

blocks.text:
Two lines are parallel when they run side by side and never meet, no matter how far they are extended. You can tell they are parallel because they keep the same distance apart all along their length. In a diagram, parallel lines are often marked with matching little arrows.

In this section you will learn how to draw a line through a given point that is parallel to a given line, using only a ruler, a set square, and a pencil. The set square is the triangle-shaped tool with a right angle (a 90° corner) at one end. It does the important job for us: because its straight edge stays fixed against the ruler, we can slide it along without turning it, and the lines it draws stay parallel.

Here is the idea behind the method. When you draw any straight line and then draw another line that cuts across it (called a transversal), the two lines are parallel exactly when the angles they make with that crossing line are equal. In the construction below we use this fact in a simple mechanical way: sliding a set square along a ruler keeps its edge at the same angle the whole time, so the line you draw is always at the same angle to the ruler — and that guarantees the new line is parallel to the first.

Worked example: Construct a line through the point P that is parallel to the line AB.

Step 1 — Draw the given line AB and mark the point P anywhere off it. Keep P a sensible distance away, not too close and not too far.

Step 2 — Place your set square so that one of its straight edges lies exactly on top of the line AB.

Step 3 — Keeping the set square pressed down firmly, place your ruler against the other straight edge of the set square so the ruler touches it along its whole length. Hold the ruler very still.

Step 4 — While holding the ruler in place, slide the set square along the ruler towards P. Do not let it twist or lift: it must stay pressed against the ruler the whole time.

Step 5 — When the top edge of the set square reaches P, keep it there and draw a straight line through P along that edge. This new line is parallel to AB.

Step 6 — Mark the new line with a little arrow (the same style of arrow as on AB) to show the two lines are parallel.

Because you slid the set square without turning it, the edge you drew along stayed at exactly the same angle to the ruler as the line AB was. That equal angle is what guarantees the two lines are parallel.

Let us look at the reasoning once more, because it is the whole secret of the construction.

Imagine a line CD drawn across the line AB (so CD cuts AB at some point). Now imagine the same line CD drawn across your new line. If the angle that CD makes with AB is exactly the same as the angle that CD makes with the new line, then the two lines are parallel. This is what we depend on.

In the set-square method, the ruler plays the part of CD: it is the fixed reference line that both AB and your new line cross. When you slide the set square along the ruler without turning it, you are drawing a line that meets the ruler at exactly the same angle that AB meets the ruler. Same crossing line, same angle — so the two lines must be parallel.

A useful check when you finish: parallel lines are the same distance apart everywhere. Use your ruler to measure the gap between AB and the new line at two different places. If both measurements are equal, your construction has worked.

practice.prompt: Draw a straight horizontal line and label it AB. Choose a point P above the line, about halfway along it. Using only a ruler and a set square, construct a line through P that is parallel to AB. Explain in one sentence why the method works.
practice.answer: You slide the set square along the ruler without turning it, so the new line meets the ruler at the same angle as AB. Because the new line and AB make equal angles with the same crossing line (the ruler), the two lines are parallel. Check by measuring the gap in two places — the distances should be equal.
practice.worked_solution: Place the set square so one straight edge lies on AB. Rest the ruler against the other edge and hold it still. Slide the set square along the ruler up to P without twisting it, then draw a straight line through P along the set square's edge. The line through P is parallel to AB.

practice.prompt: Line XY is drawn slanting downwards. Construct a line through a point Q, placed below and to the right of the line, that is parallel to XY. What single thing must you avoid doing while sliding the set square, and why does that matter?
practice.answer: You must avoid letting the set square twist or lift away from the ruler while you slide it. If it twists, its edge no longer keeps the same angle to the ruler, so the line you draw would meet the ruler at a different angle and would not be parallel to XY.
practice.worked_solution: The method works for a slanting line exactly as for a horizontal one: put the set square's edge on XY, rest the ruler against the other edge and hold it firmly, slide the set square down to Q without turning it, and draw the line through Q. The equal angles with the ruler guarantee parallelism.

practice.prompt: Two students each draw a line through point P. Student A slides the set square along the ruler without turning it. Student B turns the set square a little as it slides. Only one of the two lines is guaranteed parallel to the original line. Which student, and why?
practice.answer: Student A's line is guaranteed parallel, because keeping the set square at the same angle to the ruler makes the new line meet the ruler at the same angle as the original line. Student B turned the set square, which changes that angle, so the line is not guaranteed to be parallel.
practice.worked_solution: Equal angles with the same crossing line (the ruler) give parallel lines. Student A preserves the angle by sliding without turning; Student B changes the angle by turning, so the equal-angle condition no longer holds.

sections_json.title: Drawing a Perpendicular Line with Ruler and Compass

blocks.text:
A perpendicular line is a line that meets another line at a right angle — an angle of exactly 90°. Think of the corner of a sheet of paper, or the way the two arms of a plus sign (+) cross each other. When two lines are perpendicular, we can mark the right angle with a small square drawn at the corner.

In construction work you often need to draw a perpendicular line. You will learn two situations:
1. Dropping a perpendicular from a point that lies above a line, down to meet the line.
2. Erecting (raising) a perpendicular at a point that lies on the line itself.

Both methods use only a ruler and a compass, and both rely on the same simple idea: the point you want lies exactly on the bisector of a segment you have drawn. The two tools you need are your ruler (for drawing straight lines) and your compass (for drawing circles and arcs). Keep the compass opening fixed whenever you want two arcs that are exactly the same size.

Before you start, set out your tools. Place the ruler on your paper, and with a sharp pencil draw a long straight line across it. Label this line with two letters, for example AB. Mark a point P somewhere above the line. You will construct the perpendicular from P down to the line, meeting it at a new point you will call M.

The steps below build a perpendicular step by step. Follow them slowly with your own line and point, and check each step against your drawing as you go.

Worked Example 1 — Dropping a perpendicular from a point above a line

We construct the perpendicular from point P down to the line AB.

Step 1: With the point of your compass on P, open the compass a little wider than the distance down to the line. Draw an arc that cuts the line AB in two places. Call these two cut points X and Y. (Choosing a compass opening bigger than the drop makes sure the arc actually reaches the line.)

Step 2: Put the compass point on X. Open the compass to about two-thirds of the distance between X and Y, and draw an arc below the line, roughly beneath the middle of XY.

Step 3: Keeping the compass at exactly the same opening, put the point on Y and draw another arc below the line. This second arc crosses the first. Call the crossing point Q.

Step 4: Use your ruler to draw the straight line from P to Q. Where this line crosses AB, call the point M.

The line PM is perpendicular to AB. Check it: PM meets AB at right angles, and the small corner between them is a perfect square. The point M is exactly beneath P, and PM stands upright on AB.

Worked Example 2 — Erecting a perpendicular at a point on the line

Sometimes the point where the perpendicular must stand is already on the line. Suppose point O lies on the line AB, and we want to raise a perpendicular straight up from O.

Step 1: Put the compass point on O. With any convenient opening, draw arcs that cut AB on both sides of O. Call these two cuts X (on the left) and Y (on the right). The opening can be anything, but X and Y must be equal distances from O.

Step 2: Open the compass wider. Put the point on X and draw an arc above the line.

Step 3: Keeping the same wider opening, put the point on Y and draw another arc above the line. The two arcs cross. Call the crossing point R.

Step 4: Draw the straight line from O through R with your ruler. Extend it well above the line.

The line OR is perpendicular to AB, standing straight up from O. Again, the corner at O is a right angle, marked by a small square.

practice.prompt: Draw a line AB on your paper. Mark a point P above it. Write down the first two steps you would take to drop a perpendicular from P down to meet AB.
practice.answer: Step 1: Put the compass point on P, open it a little wider than the distance from P down to the line, and draw an arc that cuts AB in two places, X and Y. Step 2: Put the compass point on X and draw an arc below the line.
practice.worked_solution: The perpendicular is built with two equal arcs. First, from P draw one arc that reaches the line and cuts it twice — those two cuts give you X and Y. Then you begin the equal-arc step by drawing an arc from X below the line.

practice.prompt: In Worked Example 2, when you erect a perpendicular at point O on line AB, why must the two cuts X and Y be equal distances from O?
practice.answer: Because they are drawn with the same compass opening from O, so XO and OY are equal. That equality is what places the perpendicular exactly above the middle, standing straight up from O.
practice.worked_solution: Both arcs in Step 1 are made with the same compass opening centred on O, so the distances OX and OY are the same. A perpendicular erected at O must come up from the midpoint of the segment between the two arc cuts, and equal cuts give exactly that midpoint.

practice.prompt: After you have drawn the arc from X below the line in a perpendicular construction, what must you do with your compass before drawing the arc from Y, and why?
practice.answer: Keep the compass at exactly the same opening as the arc from X. Then the arc from Y will cross the first one, and the two arcs are the same size so the crossing point sits on the perpendicular.
practice.worked_solution: The two lower arcs must be identical in size so that they are symmetric about the perpendicular. If you changed the opening, the crossing point would drift off the line that should be perpendicular. Keeping the opening fixed guarantees the arcs meet at a point directly below the starting point.

practice.prompt: Explain in one sentence what it means for a constructed line to be perpendicular to another, and name the two tools you used to build it.
practice.answer: A perpendicular line meets the other line at a right angle of 90°, and it is built using only a ruler and a compass.

sections_json.title: Cutting a Line Segment into Two Equal Halves

blocks.text:
To **bisect** a line segment means to cut it into two exactly equal parts. The point where it is cut is called the **midpoint**, and it lies exactly halfway between the two ends. We also use the word "bisect" for angles (cutting an angle into two equal angles), but here we focus on the line segment itself.

You will need a ruler, a sharp pencil, and a pair of compasses. Here is the way to bisect a line segment, step by step.

**Step 1 — Draw the segment.** Use your ruler to draw a straight line segment AB. We want to find the point exactly in the middle of A and B.

**Step 2 — Open the compasses.** Set the compasses to a width a little more than half the length of AB. How do you know it is more than half? Guess roughly where the middle is, and open the compasses wider than that guess. (If you use a width less than half, the two arcs you are about to draw will not meet.)

**Step 3 — Draw the first arc.** Place the compass point on A. Draw an arc that swings above and below the segment. Keep the compasses at the same setting — do not change the width.

**Step 4 — Draw the second arc.** Without changing the compass width, place the point on B and draw another arc above and below. The two arcs cross at two points: one above the segment and one below it. Mark these two crossing points.

**Step 5 — Join the crossings.** Use your ruler to draw a straight line through the two crossing points. This line is called the **perpendicular bisector**: it crosses AB at a right angle, and the point where it meets AB is the midpoint. That midpoint bisects (cuts into two equal halves) the segment.

The line you drew through the two arc crossings is exactly halfway along AB, so the two smaller segments on either side of the midpoint are equal in length. Try measuring them with your ruler — they will match.

**Worked example — Bisecting a 6 cm segment**

Let us bisect a line segment AB that measures 6 cm.

1. Draw AB with your ruler so that it is 6 cm long. Label the left end A and the right end B.
2. Set your compasses to a width of about 4 cm. This is more than half of 6 cm, which is 3 cm, so the arcs will meet. (Anything wider than 3 cm works.)
3. Place the compass point on A and draw a wide arc that curves above and below AB.
4. Without changing the width, place the point on B and draw another arc. The two arcs cross at two points — one above the segment and one below it. Call the top crossing P and the bottom crossing Q.
5. Draw a straight line through P and Q. Where this line meets AB is the midpoint, M.

Now check: AM should measure 3 cm and MB should measure 3 cm. The line PQ has cut the 6 cm segment into two equal 3 cm pieces, so AB is bisected. The line PQ is also perpendicular to AB, which is why it is called the perpendicular bisector — but our goal here, the midpoint M, is what bisects the segment.

practice.prompt: A line segment CD is 10 cm long. You follow the bisection steps: draw an arc from C, draw a matching arc from D, join the two crossing points, and the joining line meets CD at point M. How long is CM, and how long is MD?
practice.answer: CM = 5 cm and MD = 5 cm. Bisecting cuts the segment into two equal halves, so each half is 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.
practice.worked_solution: The midpoint M splits CD into two equal parts. So CM = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm and MD = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm. The two halves must be equal, which is the whole point of bisecting.

practice.prompt: While bisecting segment PQ, you set your compasses so that the width is 1 cm, but PQ is 5 cm long. What goes wrong when you try to draw the arcs, and why?
practice.answer: The arcs do not meet, so you cannot find the crossing points. The compass width must be more than half the length of the segment (more than 2.5 cm for a 5 cm segment) or the two arcs drawn from P and Q will not cross.
practice.worked_solution: Half of 5 cm is 2.5 cm. With the compasses set to only 1 cm, the arc drawn from P stays within 1 cm of P, and the arc drawn from Q stays within 1 cm of Q. There is a gap in the middle between 1 cm and 4 cm along the segment, so the arcs never touch. The compass width always has to be more than half the segment length for the two arcs to meet.

practice.prompt: A perpendicular bisector is drawn on a line segment XY, and it meets XY at the midpoint N. If XN measures 7 cm, what is the full length of XY?
practice.answer: XY = 14 cm. Since N is the midpoint, XN and NY are equal, so NY = 7 cm, and the whole segment is 7 + 7 = 14 cm.
practice.worked_solution: The perpendicular bisector meets the segment at its midpoint, which cuts it into two equal halves. So NY = XN = 7 cm. Adding the two equal halves gives XY = 7 + 7 = 14 cm.

blocks.text:
A right angle is an angle of exactly 90°. It is the angle you see at the corner of a sheet of paper or a building. When two lines meet at 90°, we call them perpendicular. In construction work, we use a ruler and a pair of compasses to draw a 90° angle without needing a protractor, and it comes out very accurately every time.

Here is the idea behind the construction. We start with a straight line and a point on it. From that point we build a right angle using the same compass-and-ruler moves that bisect a straight angle. If you follow the steps in order, you will always finish with two lines that meet at exactly 90°.

What you need:
• A sharp pencil
• A ruler (with straight edges)
• A pair of compasses

The construction has five steps. Take your time with each one and keep the compass opening the same where the steps tell you to.

Step 1 – Draw a horizontal line across your page with the ruler. Mark a point on it and call it A. This is where the corner of your 90° angle will sit.

Step 2 – Put the compass point on A and open it to any convenient width. Draw an arc that crosses the line on both sides of A. Call the two points where the arc meets the line B (left of A) and C (right of A).

Step 3 – Without changing the compass opening, put the compass point on B and draw an arc above the line, roughly in the middle between B and C.

Step 4 – Keeping the compass opening the same, put the compass point on C and draw another arc above the line. This arc must cross the one you just drew. Call the point where the two arcs meet D.

Step 5 – Use your ruler to draw a straight line from A through D. The angle between this new line and your original line at A is exactly 90°.

Why does this work? Because B and C are equal distances from A, and the two arcs above the line are drawn with the same compass opening, so B and C are equally far from D as well. That makes the line AD perfectly upright, meeting the horizontal line at a right angle.

Worked Example

Construct a 90° angle at a point P on a horizontal line.

Step 1 – Draw a horizontal line and mark point P on it.
Step 2 – With the compass point on P, draw an arc that cuts the line on both sides. Call the cuts Q (left) and R (right).
Step 3 – Without changing the compass opening, put the point on Q and draw an arc above the line.
Step 4 – With the same opening, put the point on R and draw an arc above the line so it crosses the first arc. Call the crossing point S.
Step 5 – Join P to S with your ruler.

The line PS makes an angle of 90° with the horizontal line. The angle between your horizontal line and PS at point P is the right angle you wanted.

practice.prompt: On a fresh part of your page, draw a horizontal line and mark a point T in the middle of it. Using only your ruler and compasses, construct a 90° angle at T. Describe each step you took, and name the points you used, so that someone reading your steps could build the same angle.
practice.answer: Construct the 90° angle at T exactly as in the worked example: (1) draw an arc centred at T cutting the line at two points; (2) keeping the same opening, draw arcs from each of those two points above the line so they cross; (3) join T to the crossing point. The line you draw meets the original horizontal line at 90°.
practice.worked_solution:
Step 1 – Draw the horizontal line and mark T.
Step 2 – Put the compass point on T and draw an arc that cuts the line on both sides. Call the cuts U (left) and V (right).
Step 3 – Without changing the opening, put the point on U and draw an arc above the line.
Step 4 – With the same opening, put the point on V and draw an arc above the line so it crosses the first one. Call the crossing point W.
Step 5 – Join T to W with the ruler. The angle between the horizontal line and TW is exactly 90°.

practice.prompt: Look at the construction you have been doing. In Step 3 you drew an arc from one side of A, and in Step 4 you drew an arc from the other side of A with the same compass opening. Why must the compass opening stay exactly the same between these two steps?
practice.answer: Because the two points on the line (like Q and R) must be equally far from the crossing point above the line. If the opening changed, the crossing point would be closer to one side, and the line you finally draw would lean over and not be at 90°.
practice.worked_solution: In Step 3, the arc centred at Q marks every point that is a fixed distance from Q. In Step 4, the arc centred at R marks every point the same distance from R, but only if the compass opening has not changed. Their crossing point D is therefore the same distance from Q and from R. Since Q and R are themselves equally far from A, the line AD stands exactly upright and meets the horizontal line at 90°. Changing the opening would break the equal distances and tilt the final line.

blocks.text:
A 60° angle is one of the special angles you can build with just a compass and a straightedge (ruler). The trick is to use the fact that a circle is made up of 360°, and each of the six equal "wedges" around a point spans 60°.

Here is the method, step by step.

Step 1 — Draw a ray.
On your paper, draw a ray starting at a point A and passing through a point B. This gives you a straight line to work from. The point A is where your 60° angle will sit (the vertex).

Step 2 — Make the first arc.
Put the metal point of the compass exactly on A. Open the compass to any convenient width, and draw a short arc that crosses the ray AB. Call the point where the arc cuts the ray P.

Step 3 — Make the second arc.
Do not change the compass opening at all — keep it exactly the same width. Now move the compass point onto P and draw another arc. It will cross your first arc. Call this crossing point Q.

Step 4 — Join A to Q.
Draw a straight ray from A through Q. The angle between the ray AB and the ray AQ is 60°.

Why does this work? Because in Steps 2 and 3 you kept the compass opening the same, the distance AP equals PQ equals AQ. So triangle APQ has all three sides equal — it is an equilateral triangle. Every angle in an equilateral triangle is 60°, so the angle at A is 60°.

The two most common slips are changing the compass width between Steps 2 and 3 (everything falls apart), and drawing the second arc on the wrong side of the ray. Make sure both arcs are drawn with the same opening, and it works first time.

Worked example: Construct a 60° angle at the point A on a line.

Setup: Draw a ray AB on your paper.

1. Place the compass point on A and draw an arc crossing AB. Mark this crossing point P.
2. Keep the compass exactly as it is. Place the point on P and draw a second arc, so it crosses the first arc. Mark the crossing Q.
3. Draw the ray from A through Q.

The angle BAQ is your 60° angle. If you have a protractor handy, you can check it — it should read 60°.

Notice what you must never do between steps 2 and 3: you must not widen or narrow the compass. Keeping the opening fixed is what makes AP = PQ = AQ, which is what forces the angle to be exactly 60°.

practice.prompt: Draw a ray starting at point A. Using only a compass and a ruler, construct a 60° angle at A. In your own words, write down the four steps you took.
practice.answer: 1. Draw the ray AB. 2. With the compass point on A, draw an arc crossing AB; mark the crossing P. 3. Keeping the same compass opening, put the point on P and draw an arc crossing the first; mark the crossing Q. 4. Draw the ray from A through Q. The angle BAQ is 60°.
practice.worked_solution: The key point is that the compass opening stays the same the whole way, so AP = PQ = AQ. That makes triangle APQ equilateral, so its angle at A is 60°.

practice.prompt: A friend tries to construct a 60° angle but after drawing the first arc they open the compass wider before drawing the second arc. Explain, in your own words, why this will not give a 60° angle.
practice.answer: If the compass width is changed, then the distances AP, PQ and AQ are no longer all equal, so triangle APQ is no longer equilateral and its angle at A is no longer 60°.
practice.worked_solution: The 60° angle comes from building an equilateral triangle, and an equilateral triangle needs all three sides equal. Changing the compass opening breaks that equality.

practice.prompt: After constructing a 60° angle at A between ray AB and ray AQ, how many times does the angle 60° fit into a full turn of 360° around point A? Use this to explain why six copies of your angle fill a full circle.
practice.answer: 360° ÷ 60° = 6, so a 60° angle fits exactly six times around a point, filling a full turn.
practice.worked_solution: A full turn is 360°. Since each angle is 60°, six of them give 6 × 60° = 360°, which is exactly one full turn.

blocks.text: Parallel lines are lines in the same plane that never meet, however far they are extended. Two things you will use to draw them are a ruler and a set square (the triangle from your mathematical set). Here is the idea behind the method: a set square has straight edges that meet at right angles. If you slide the set square along a straight edge without turning it, any line you draw along one of its edges will stay at the same angle to the edge you slid along. Lines drawn at the same angle to the same line are parallel to each other. To draw a line parallel to a given line, follow these steps with your ruler and set square: 1. Draw your given line across your page with the ruler and label it (for example, call it line AB). 2. Place the ruler beside line AB so that one long edge of the ruler lies exactly along the line. Keep the ruler firmly in this position — it is your guide, and it must not move. 3. Rest one edge of the set square against the ruler's edge. The set square should touch the ruler so that its own edges make a right angle with the ruler's edge. 4. Holding the ruler still, slide the set square along the ruler to the place where you want the new parallel line to be. 5. Draw a straight line along the edge of the set square that is furthest from the ruler. That new line is parallel to your given line. Because the set square slid without turning, its edge drew a line that makes exactly the same angle with the ruler as the given line does. Two lines that make the same angle with a third line are parallel, so your new line is parallel to line AB.

Worked example — draw a line parallel to line CD. Suppose you have drawn line CD and you want a parallel line about 5 cm below it. - Place your ruler so that one long edge lies exactly along line CD. Hold it there firmly. - Set the set square against the ruler's edge, with its edges at a right angle to the ruler. - Keeping the ruler still, slide the set square down the ruler until it is where you want the new line (about 5 cm below CD). - Draw along the set square's free edge. Label the new line, for instance EF. Line EF is parallel to line CD. If you slide the set square to several positions and draw each time, every line you draw will be parallel to CD — and therefore parallel to one another.

practice.prompt: Using your ruler and set square, draw a line AB across your page. Then construct a second line parallel to AB, about 3 cm above it, and label it PQ.
practice.answer: The line PQ you drew should be parallel to AB: lay your ruler along AB, slide the set square along it (without turning it) to about 3 cm above, and draw along the set square's free edge.
practice.worked_solution: 1. Draw line AB with the ruler. 2. Place the ruler's long edge exactly along AB and hold it still. 3. Rest the set square against the ruler's edge so its edges meet the ruler at a right angle. 4. Slide the set square up the ruler to about 3 cm above AB, keeping the ruler fixed. 5. Draw along the edge of the set square furthest from the ruler and label it PQ. Since the set square never turned, PQ makes the same angle with the ruler as AB does, so PQ is parallel to AB.

practice.prompt: Explain in your own words why, when you slide a set square along a ruler, every line you draw is parallel to the first line you drew.
practice.answer: Because the set square slides without turning, its drawing edge keeps the same angle to the ruler all the way along. Every line drawn along that edge therefore makes the same angle with the ruler as the first line, and lines that make the same angle with a third line are parallel.

blocks.text: When two lines cross and the four angles where they meet are all right angles (each exactly 90°), the lines are called perpendicular. One quick way to recognise a pair of perpendicular lines is to look for a right-angle corner, like the corner of your set square, sitting neatly in the gap where the two lines meet. You can construct a perpendicular line with just your set square and ruler. Here is the idea: the set square already has a built-in right angle, so if you line up one edge of that right angle with your given line and draw along the other edge, the new line you draw will meet the given line at a perfect right angle. Follow these steps to draw a line perpendicular to a given line through a point on that line: 1. Draw a straight line and mark a point P on it. This point is where your perpendicular will cross the line. 2. Place your set square so that one edge of its right-angle corner lies exactly along the line, with the corner of the right angle sitting on point P. 3. Holding the set square steady, draw a straight line along the other edge of the right angle, starting from P. 4. The new line now meets the first line at P, and the corner where they meet is a right angle. Your two lines are perpendicular. To check your work, slide the corner of the set square into the angle between the two lines. If the corner fits exactly with no gap, your lines are perpendicular.

Worked example: Construct a line perpendicular to AB at the point P on it. Step 1. Draw a horizontal line and label its ends A and B. Mark a point P somewhere along AB. Step 2. Take your set square and place it so that the edge of its right-angle corner lies along AB, with the corner of the right angle resting on point P. Step 3. Keep the set square firmly in place and draw a straight line upward from P along the other edge of the right-angle corner. Step 4. Check the corner: the angle between AB and your new line is a right angle, so the new line is perpendicular to AB through P.

practice.prompt: Draw a horizontal line and mark a point Q on it. Using your set square and ruler, construct a line perpendicular to the horizontal line through Q. What should you check to confirm your construction is correct?
practice.answer: You draw the new line through Q along the other edge of the set square's right-angle corner, with the corner resting on Q and one edge lying on the horizontal line. To check it, slide the corner of the set square into the angle where the two lines meet — if it fits exactly with no gap, your construction is correct because the lines meet at a right angle.
practice.worked_solution: Line the set square's right-angle edge along the horizontal line with the corner on Q, then draw upward along the other right-angle edge. The two lines meet at Q at 90°, so they are perpendicular.

practice.prompt: Two lines cross at a point, and when you check the corner with your set square it fits exactly with no gap. Are the two lines perpendicular? Explain why.
practice.answer: Yes. The set square's corner is a right angle (90°). If it fits exactly in the angle where the lines meet, that angle is 90°, and two lines that meet at a right angle are perpendicular.

blocks.text:
To bisect a line segment means to cut it into two equal parts. When you bisect a segment, the point where the two equal parts meet is called the midpoint. The line that cuts the segment into equal halves crosses it at a right angle, so the construction also gives you a perpendicular through the middle of the segment. You only need your mathematical set — a ruler and a pair of compasses. The compasses are the key tool here: instead of measuring the segment, you use equal radii (the opening of the compass) to locate the two points that sit exactly the same distance from each end. Here is the plan you will follow every time:
  1. Open your compasses to a radius greater than half the length of the segment. Keeping this radius fixed, place the point of the compasses on one end of the segment and draw an arc that passes above and below the segment.
  2. Without changing the compass opening, move the point to the other end of the segment and draw another arc. The two arcs cross each other in two places — one above the segment and one below it.
  3. Using your ruler, join those two crossing points with a straight line. This line passes through the midpoint of the segment and crosses it at a right angle.
  4. The point where your new line meets the original segment is its midpoint, and it divides the segment into two equal parts.
The reason the arcs must be drawn with the same opening is that every point on an arc is the same distance from the compass point at the centre. Because you used the same radius from each end, each crossing point is the same distance from both ends — and a point that is equally far from the two ends lies exactly on the perpendicular bisector.

Worked example: Bisect a line segment AB that is about 8 cm long.
  1. Draw a segment AB, about 8 cm long, with your ruler.
  2. Open your compasses so the opening is a little more than half of AB — about 5 cm for an 8 cm segment.
  3. Place the compass point on A. Draw an arc that curves above AB and another below it, using the same opening.
  4. Move the compass point to B without changing the opening. Draw an arc above and below AB again. The new arcs cross the first pair in two points.
  5. With your ruler, draw a straight line through the two crossing points. This line meets AB at its midpoint and stands at a right angle to it.
  6. Label the midpoint M. You have now bisected AB: AM and MB are equal.
To check your work, measure AM and MB with the ruler. If you drew your arcs carefully with a fixed compass opening, the two lengths will be exactly equal.

practice.prompt: Using only your ruler and compasses, bisect the line segment CD below (draw a segment of any convenient length first). Mark the midpoint and label it M, then write down the two equal parts it creates.
practice.answer: The construction produces a perpendicular line through the midpoint M of CD, so the segment is cut into two equal parts CM and MD, with CM = MD.
practice.worked_solution: Draw CD. Open the compasses wider than half of CD, draw an arc above and below CD from point C, then with the same opening draw arcs from point D. Join the two crossing points with a straight line. Where this line meets CD is the midpoint M, dividing the segment into two equal halves CM and MD.

practice.prompt: A builder wants to find the exact middle of a plank that is 120 cm long, without measuring it with a tape. Which instrument would she use to bisect the plank, and what is the length of each of the two equal parts?
practice.answer: She would use a pair of compasses and a ruler (her mathematical set) to bisect the plank. Each equal part is 120 cm ÷ 2 = 60 cm.
practice.worked_solution: Bisecting means cutting into two equal parts. Half of 120 cm is 60 cm, and bisection finds that exact middle point.

practice.prompt: When you bisect a line segment, you draw two arcs from each end of the segment. Why must the compass opening stay the same for all four arcs?
practice.answer: The same opening keeps the radius equal from both ends, so each crossing point of the arcs is the same distance from both ends. That places the crossing points exactly on the perpendicular bisector, which passes through the midpoint and cuts the segment into two equal parts.
practice.worked_solution: Every point on an arc is the same distance from the compass point. Using one fixed radius from both ends makes each intersection equally far from both A and B, so the line through the intersections is the perpendicular bisector that lands exactly on the midpoint.

blocks.text:
An angle of 90° is a right angle. Its two arms stand perpendicular to one another, like the corner of a book or the corner of this page. You can build one yourself with a compass and a ruler on any straight line.

Here is the method you will use:
1. Draw a straight line and mark a point on it where you want the 90° angle to sit.
2. Put the compass point on that point and draw an arc that cuts the line at two places, one on each side of your point.
3. Open the compass a little wider. Put the compass point on one of the two cuts and draw an arc above the line. Keep the opening the same, put the point on the other cut, and draw another arc above the line. The two arcs meet at a point above the line.
4. Draw a straight line from your marked point through that meeting point.
5. The angle between this new line and the original line is exactly 90°.

Let us construct a 90° angle at a point P on a straight line.

Step 1 — Draw a straight line and mark P somewhere along it.

Step 2 — Put the compass point on P and draw an arc that crosses the line on both sides of P. Call the two crossings A (on the left) and B (on the right).

Step 3 — Widen the compass a little. Put the point on A and draw an arc above the line. Keeping the compass exactly the same width, put the point on B and draw another arc above the line. The two arcs cross each other at a point C.

Step 4 — Use your ruler to draw a straight line from P up through C.

The angle between PC and the original line is 90°. Mark it with the ∟ symbol.

practice.prompt: Using your ruler and compass, construct an angle of 90° on a straight line you draw yourself. Mark the point where the angle is made, and label the constructed right angle with the symbol ∟.
practice.answer: Your construction should show a point on a line, an arc cutting the line on both sides of that point, two wider arcs meeting above the line at a single crossing, and a straight line from the point up through that crossing. The angle between the new line and the original line is exactly 90°, marked with the ∟ symbol.
practice.worked_solution:
1. Draw a straight line and mark a point P on it.
2. With the compass point on P, draw an arc cutting the line at A (left) and B (right).
3. Widen the compass. From A draw an arc above the line; keep the width fixed, from B draw another arc above the line so the two arcs meet at C.
4. Draw the straight line from P through C. The angle between PC and the original line is 90°, so mark it with ∟.

practice.prompt: Look at this construction for an angle at point P: an arc from P cuts the line at A and B, and two wider arcs from A and B meet above the line at C. Without drawing anything else, what is the size of the angle APC?
practice.worked_solution: The two wider arcs from A and B meet at C, and the line from P through C was drawn through that meeting point. This is exactly the construction for a right angle, so angle APC measures 90°.

sections_json.title: Constructing a 60° Angle with a Compass

blocks.text:
A 60° angle is one of the angles you can build with just a straight edge and a compass — no protractor needed. The secret is that an equilateral triangle has three equal sides, and every one of its angles is exactly 60°. So if you draw an equilateral triangle, you have built a 60° angle for free.

You will need your mathematical set: a sharp pencil, a ruler (or straight edge), and a compass. Keep the compass setting fixed at the same radius through the whole construction — that is what makes the triangle equilateral.

Here is the whole construction in words before you try it yourself.

1. Draw a straight line and mark a point on it. Call that point A. This will be the vertex of your angle.
2. Set your compass to a comfortable radius. With the compass point on A, draw an arc that crosses the line. Call the point where the arc meets the line B.
3. Keep the compass at exactly the same radius. Now put the compass point on B and draw a second arc that cuts the first arc. Call the point where the two arcs meet C.
4. Use your ruler to join C to A with a straight line.

The line AC makes an angle of 60° with the line AB at A. Done — you have constructed a 60° angle.

Let's build a 60° angle together, step by step.

Start: Draw a line and mark point A on it. Set your compass to a radius of, say, 4 cm — any radius will work, as long as you never change it.

Step 1 — Draw the first arc. With the compass point on A, draw an arc that crosses the line. The point where the arc meets the line is B.

Step 2 — Draw the second arc. Without changing the compass radius, place the point on B and draw another arc so that it crosses the first arc. Where the two arcs meet, mark point C.

Step 3 — Join C to A. Use your ruler to draw the straight line from C back to A.

Now look at triangle ABC. The two arcs used the same radius, so AB = AC = BC. That makes triangle ABC equilateral, and every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°. So the angle at A, between line AB and line AC, is exactly 60°. The construction is complete.

practice.prompt: Using only your ruler and compass, construct a 60° angle. Follow the construction: draw a line, mark point A, set a compass radius, draw a first arc to meet the line at B, keep the same radius, draw a second arc from B to cut the first at C, then join C to A. When you finish, measure your angle with a protractor to check it is about 60°.
practice.answer: Your constructed angle at A should measure approximately 60°. It is exactly 60° if you kept the compass radius fixed throughout, because triangle ABC is then equilateral with all its sides equal, and every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°.
practice.worked_solution: Draw line AB, set the compass to a fixed radius, draw an arc from A to cross the line at B, then from B draw another arc of the same radius to cut the first at C. Join C to A. Because both arcs used the same radius, AB = AC = BC, so triangle ABC is equilateral and angle BAC = 60°.

practice.prompt: Why must you keep the compass at the same radius when you draw the second arc from point B?
practice.answer: Keeping the same radius makes AC equal to AB and equal to BC, so triangle ABC has three equal sides. Only then is it an equilateral triangle, and only an equilateral triangle has all angles equal to 60°. If you changed the radius, the two sides would not be equal and the angle at A would not be 60°.

sections_json.title: Constructing a Line Parallel to Another

blocks.text:
Two straight lines are parallel when they never meet, however far you draw them, and stay the same distance apart all along their length. In this construction you are given a straight line AB and a point P, and your job is to draw a second line through P that is parallel to AB — a line that runs alongside AB, the same distance away at every point, never crossing it.

You will need a set square and a ruler. The set square has a right angle in one corner, and it is that corner (marked in the figures) that makes the construction work. Study fig-01: the line AB lies flat across the page, with the point P marked above it. Your first task is to line up the set square with AB, and the right angle is the part that keeps it true.

blocks.caption: Line $AB$, with a point $P$ marked above it. A set square is drawn below $AB$ with one edge along the line: the right angle is at the left end of that edge, one leg runs down from it, and the hypotenuse closes back to a point on $AB$ to the right.

blocks.text: Construct a line through P parallel to AB. (a) Place the set square so that one of its straight edges lies accurately along the line AB, as in fig-01. (b) Put the ruler against one of the other edges of the set square — the left-hand edge if you are right-handed. In fig-02 the ruler lies along the set square's downward edge; in fig-03 it rests against the sloping edge instead. Which edge you choose does not matter: the only thing that matters is that the ruler is held firmly against the set square and does not move once it is in place. (c) Hold the ruler firmly and slide the set square along it towards P. Keep sliding until the edge that was lying along AB reaches P. Then draw a line along that edge of the set square, through P — this is shown in fig-04 and fig-05. Why does this work? Sliding the set square along the held ruler moves it without turning it, so the edge that lay on AB keeps exactly the same direction the whole way. A line drawn through P along that edge therefore runs parallel to AB, the same distance away all along — which is precisely the line you wanted, as fig-05 shows.

blocks.caption: The same slide as fig-04, made against the leaning ruler of fig-03. The set square is drawn twice: once with its edge on $AB$, and once slid along the ruler until that edge passes through $P$. The two positions are congruent and point the same way — sliding along a held ruler moves the set square without turning it — so the edge through $P$ stays parallel to $AB$. The arrow gives the direction of the slide, along the ruler's edge, and the right angle is marked in both positions.

The vertical ruler held fixed, with the set square drawn twice — once with its edge on $AB$ and once higher up, its edge on a second line parallel to $AB$ — and an arrow between the two positions pointing up along the ruler.

The same set square on $AB$ as in fig-02, with the ruler moved to rest against its sloping edge instead of its upright one. The set square has not moved; only the ruler has, so it now leans across $AB$, running from lower left to upper right. The right angle is still where the edge on $AB$ meets the short upright edge, and it is marked there. The ruler's inclination does not affect the construction. The set square is drawn at one particular size, and with its right angle at one particular end; neither is part of the method. Any set square works, either way round, so long as one edge lies along $AB$ and the ruler rests against another.

The same set square on $AB$, with the ruler now drawn as a long strip lying along the set square's downward edge. The right angle marked at the corner is the set square's own, between the edge lying along $AB$ and the edge running down from it.

practice.prompt: You are given a line AB and a point P above it. What is the first step in constructing a line through P parallel to AB?
practice.answer: Place the set square so that one of its straight edges lies accurately along the line AB.

practice.prompt: After the set square is lying on AB, what do you do with the ruler before you slide the set square?
practice.answer: Place the ruler against one of the other edges of the set square (for example the left-hand edge if you are right-handed) and hold it firmly so it does not move.

practice.prompt: While sliding the set square along the ruler towards P, what must you be careful to do, and why does that keep the line you draw parallel to AB?
practice.answer: Hold the ruler firmly so that it does not move. This makes the set square slide without turning, so the edge that was on AB keeps the same direction — and the line drawn through P along that edge stays parallel to AB.

blocks.text:
Two lines are said to be perpendicular to each other when they meet at a right angle — that is, at an angle of \(90^\circ\).

Look at fig-06. The line \(XY\) crosses the line \(AB\), with \(X\) above and \(Y\) below. The small square drawn at the crossing marks the right angle in the upper right quadrant. Because \(XY\) meets \(AB\) at \(90^\circ\), the two lines are perpendicular to each other.

blocks.caption: Line $AB$ with a second line $XY$ crossing it, $X$ above and $Y$ below, and a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant at the crossing.

blocks.text: Let us construct a line perpendicular to a given line, using a set square and a ruler. Step 1 — Draw the line and mark the point. Draw a line \(AB\) as in fig-07, and mark a point \(Q\) on the line where you want the perpendicular line to pass. Step 2 — Place the set square. Place the edge of the set square on line \(AB\), so it sits on the line as shown in fig-08. Now hold the ruler so that its edge meets the hypotenuse (the long sloping edge) of the set square, as the figure shows. Step 3 — Slide and draw. Pressing firmly on the ruler so it does not move, slide the set square down along the hypotenuse until the third edge of the set square touches point \(Q\). Then draw a line along that edge, from \(X\) above the line down to \(Y\) below it. Fig-09 shows the result: the line \(XY\) now crosses \(AB\) at a right angle, marked with the small square. Because the third edge of the set square is perpendicular to its base, the line you drew is perpendicular to \(AB\). The two lines meet at \(90^\circ\), so \(XY \perp AB\).

blocks.caption: Line $AB$ with the set square standing on it as a narrow right-angled triangle: a short base along $AB$, the upright edge rising from the right end of that base with the right angle marked there, and the hypotenuse closing back down to the left.
A plain line with a stroke at each end, labelled $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right.

blocks.text: The key point to remember: a line drawn perpendicular to another line meets it at a right angle, which is \(90^\circ\). The set square has a built-in right angle, so sliding it along the ruler and drawing along its third edge gives you a line that is exactly perpendicular to your line.

blocks.caption: Line $AB$ with $XY$ now drawn across it, $X$ above and $Y$ below, and a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant.

practice.prompt: When are two lines said to be perpendicular to each other?
practice.answer: Two lines are perpendicular when they meet at a right angle, which is \(90^\circ\).

practice.prompt: Name the two instruments you use to construct a line perpendicular to a given line.
practice.answer: A set square and a ruler.

practice.prompt: In the construction of a perpendicular line, what do you press firmly on so that it does not move while you slide the set square?
practice.answer: You press firmly on the ruler.

practice.prompt: A line \(PQ\) is drawn so that it crosses line \(AB\) and makes an angle of \(90^\circ\) with it. What is the relationship between \(PQ\) and \(AB\)?

blocks.text: To bisect a line segment means to divide it into two equal halves. The point where the segment is cut into those two equal halves is called its midpoint. Using a pair of compasses and a ruler, you can find that midpoint exactly — and, as a bonus, the line you draw to do it meets the segment at a right angle (90°). You need a mathematical set for this. Here is the whole procedure. Step 1. Draw the line segment you want to bisect and label its ends, say $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right (fig-10). Step 2. Open your pair of compasses so that the radius (the gap between the sharp point and the pencil) is about $\frac{3}{4}$ of the length of $AB$. Step 3. Place the sharp point of the compasses on $A$. Draw two arcs: one above the middle of $AB$ and one below the middle of $AB$. Step 4. Keeping the same radius (do not change the compass opening), place the sharp point of the compasses on $B$. Draw two more arcs so that they cut the first pair of arcs — one crossing above $AB$ and one crossing below. Label the upper crossing $P$ and the lower crossing $Q$ (fig-11). Each small X is a point where an arc from $A$ meets an arc from $B$. Step 5. Join $P$ to $Q$ with your ruler (fig-12). Step 6. The line $PQ$ crosses $AB$ at $M$. $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$, so $AM = MB$, and $PQ$ meets $AB$ at $90^\circ$.

blocks.caption: The same arcs with $P$ joined to $Q$, the joining line crossing $AB$ at its middle at $M$ and carrying a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant.
The segment $AB$ with arc pairs crossing above and below it, the upper crossing labelled $P$ and the lower one $Q$. Each crossing is drawn as a small X where an arc from $A$ meets an arc from $B$.
The line segment $AB$, a stroke at each end, $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right.

blocks.text: Worked example — bisecting the segment $XY$ Suppose you have a segment $XY$ and you want to bisect it. 1. Open your compasses so the radius is about $\frac{3}{4}$ of $XY$. 2. Put the sharp point on $X$. Draw one arc above the middle of $XY$ and one below it. 3. Without changing the compass opening, put the sharp point on $Y$. Draw two more arcs so they cut the first pair — one crossing above and one crossing below. 4. The upper crossing is $P$ and the lower crossing is $Q$. 5. Join $P$ to $Q$ with a ruler. This line crosses $XY$ at its midpoint $M$. 6. Read off the result: $XM = MY$, and $PQ$ meets $XY$ at $90^\circ$.

practice.prompt: 1. What does it mean to bisect a line segment $AB$? Where is the point where the bisecting line crosses $AB$?
practice.answer: To bisect $AB$ means to divide it into two equal halves. The point where the bisecting line $PQ$ crosses $AB$ is its midpoint $M$, so $AM = MB$.

practice.prompt: 2. You draw the two arcs from $A$ with a certain compass opening. When you move the sharp point to $B$, what must you do with the compasses before drawing the second pair of arcs, and why?
practice.answer: You must keep the same radius — do not change the compass opening. This way the arcs from $B$ cut the arcs from $A$ at $P$ above and $Q$ below, so $P$ and $Q$ are the crossings that the joining line runs through.

practice.prompt: 3. After you join $P$ to $Q$ with a ruler, the line $PQ$ crosses $AB$ at $M$. What two facts do you know about $M$ and about how $PQ$ meets $AB$?
practice.answer: $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$, so $AM = MB$, and $PQ$ meets $AB$ at $90^\circ$.

practice.prompt: 4. A segment $PQ$ is 12 cm long. If you bisect it, how long is each half, and what angle does the bisecting line make with $PQ$?
practice.answer: Each half is 6 cm, and the bisecting line meets $PQ$ at $90^\circ$.

blocks.text:
You can build a $90^\circ$ angle with nothing but your ruler and compasses. The idea is to raise a perpendicular from a point on a straight line. Here is how it works, one step at a time.

1. Draw a straight line and mark a point $C$ on it — that is the point where the $90^\circ$ angle is to be built. In the figure (fig-13) the line runs from $A$ on the left to $B$ on the right, and $C$ sits near the middle.
2. Put the point of your compasses at $C$ and draw an arc that cuts the line at two points. Call those two points $D$ and $E$, one on each side of $C$.
3. Now open your compasses WIDER than the width $DC$ you used in step 2. This wider setting is essential: if you kept the old width, arcs drawn from $D$ and $E$ would only meet back at $C$ itself, and that gives you nothing new. With the compasses at $D$ at this new wider setting, draw an arc above the line.
4. Keeping the compasses at the same wider setting, place the point at $E$ and draw another arc above the line, cutting the first arc at a point $F$.
5. Join $C$ to $F$ with your ruler.
6. The line $CF$ is perpendicular to $AB$, so the angle between $CF$ and the line, $\angle FCB$, is exactly $90^\circ$.

blocks.caption: A line with a stroke at each end, $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right, and four short strokes standing on the line, a pair towards $A$ and a pair towards $B$. A perpendicular rises from a point near the middle, with a right-angle mark at its foot, and two short strokes cross each other near its top.

blocks.text:
Let's watch the whole construction come together. In fig-13 you can see a line $AB$ with a point $C$ marked on it. Starting from $C$, an arc is drawn that cuts the line in two places — the four short strokes standing on the line show those two cuts, a pair towards $A$ and a pair towards $B$; together they are the two points $D$ and $E$.

Then the compasses are opened wider than the first width, and arcs are struck from $D$ and $E$ above the line. The two short strokes crossing each other near the top of the perpendicular show where those wider arcs meet — that is point $F$.

Finally a ruler joins $C$ to $F$. The perpendicular rises from $C$, and the little square at its foot marks the right angle: $\angle FCB = 90^\circ$.

The key move to remember is step 3 — you must open the compasses wider than $DC$ before drawing the arcs from $D$ and $E$. With the old width the two arcs would only meet back at $C$, so you would never reach $F$.

practice.prompt: Write down the steps, in order, you would take to construct a $90^\circ$ angle at a point $C$ on a straight line $AB$.
practice.answer: 1. Mark point $C$ on the line $AB$. 2. With compasses at $C$, draw an arc cutting the line at two points $D$ and $E$. 3. Open the compasses wider than $DC$, and with the point at $D$ draw an arc above the line. 4. With the same wider setting at $E$, draw another arc cutting the first at $F$. 5. Join $C$ to $F$ with a ruler. 6. $CF$ is perpendicular to $AB$, so $\angle FCB = 90^\circ$.
practice.worked_solution: Follow the six steps of the construction exactly, ending with the perpendicular $CF$.

practice.prompt: In constructing a $90^\circ$ angle at point $C$ on a line, you first draw an arc with compasses at $C$ to mark points $D$ and $E$. Explain why you must open the compasses WIDER than $DC$ before drawing the next arcs from $D$ and $E$.
practice.answer: With the original width $DC$, the arcs drawn from $D$ and $E$ would only meet again back at $C$ itself, so you would not reach the new point $F$. Opening wider lets the two arcs meet at a point $F$ above the line, which is what joins to $C$ to make the perpendicular.
practice.worked_solution: The step-2 width is exactly the distance from $C$ to each of $D$ and $E$, so arcs of that width centred at $D$ and $E$ both pass through $C$ and meet only there. A wider opening makes them cross at a fresh point $F$ above the line.

practice.prompt: You have carried out the construction and joined $C$ to $F$, where $F$ is where the two wider arcs met. What can you say about the angle between $CF$ and the original line $AB$? What is the size of $\angle FCB$?
practice.worked_solution: Since $CF$ was drawn perpendicular to $AB$, the angle at the foot of the perpendicular is a right angle, $90^\circ$.

blocks.text:
An angle of 60° is one you can build with just a ruler and a pair of compasses, using two arcs of the same radius. The key idea: when you swing an arc of a fixed radius from a point, every point on that arc is the same distance from the centre. Two arcs of the *same* radius from two different centres will meet at a point that is that same distance from both — and that equal spacing is what makes the angle 60°.

The construction needs just three moves. You can follow them on fig-14.

blocks.caption: The line $BC$ with $B$ at the left, a stroke marking $X$ part way along, a long arc swung from $B$ through $X$ and up to the left, a shorter arc swung from $X$ cutting it, and a straight line from $B$ to that crossing.

blocks.text:
**Constructing a 60° angle at B, along the line BC**

1. **Draw the line.** Draw a line segment and mark a point B on it where the angle will sit. Mark the far end of the line C. Set your compasses to any convenient radius — it can be any size that fits comfortably on your page.

2. **First arc from B.** With the compass point on B, draw an arc that cuts the line BC at a point. Call that point X. (On fig-14 this is the long arc swung from B through X.)

3. **Second arc from X.** Keep the compasses at exactly the *same* radius — do not change the setting. Now put the compass point on X and draw another arc that cuts the first arc. Call the point where the two arcs cross A. (On fig-14 this is the shorter arc swung from X cutting the first.)

4. **Join A to B.** Draw a straight line from B to A.

The angle between line BC and line BA is exactly 60°. Because both arcs were drawn with the same radius, the distance from B to A equals the distance from B to X, which equals the distance from X to A — so the triangle BAX has all three sides equal, and a triangle with three equal sides has all three angles 60°.

practice.prompt: Construct a 60° angle at the left-hand end of a horizontal line, following the steps above. Label the line, the first arc's cutting point, and the crossing point of the two arcs, then join up to complete the angle.
practice.answer: Your finished figure should show a line segment with B at the left, an arc from B cutting the line at X, a second arc from X (same radius) cutting the first at A, and a line from B to A. The angle between BA and the original line is 60°.
practice.worked_solution: Draw the line and mark B at its left end and C at its right. Set your compasses to any convenient radius. With the point on B, swing an arc that cuts the line at X. Without changing the radius, put the point on X and swing another arc so it crosses the first; mark that crossing A. Join B to A. Because BX, XA and BA are all equal, triangle BAX is equilateral and the angle at B is 60°.

findings_text: lo-t3w06-03: "If you change the radius after drawing from $A$, the arcs will not cross properly, and $P$ and $Q$ will not line up." — This is false. With different radii the arcs can still intersect, and the two intersection points lie on a line perpendicular to AB (they are vertically aligned). What actually fails is that the line through P and Q no longer passes through the midpoint of AB.

lo-t3w06-04: "To do this you only need a point on the line and a compass." — This is false: the construction cannot be completed with only a point and a compass. A ruler (straightedge) is needed to draw the line and, as Step 5 says, to join C to F.

lo-t3w06-05: "The two arcs cross only because you kept the same radius for both." — This is false as stated. Two arcs drawn from B and X with different radii can also intersect; keeping the same radius is what makes the intersection point exactly the same distance from both centres and therefore makes triangle ABX equilateral. The equal radius is not what makes the arcs cross at all.

lo-t3w06-02: "Now hold your ruler so that its edge meets the hypotenuse of the set square, as shown in fig-08." — The section's own description of fig-08 shows only the set square standing on AB—its base, upright edge, hypotenuse, and right-angle mark—with no ruler shown, so the instruction points to a detail the figure does not provide.

lo-t3w06-01: "The same slide as fig-04, made against the leaning ruler of fig-03. The set square is drawn twice: once with its edge on $AB$, and once slid along the ruler until that edge passes through $P$. The two positions are congruent and point the same way — sliding along a held ruler moves the set square without turning it — so the edge through $P$ stays parallel to $AB$. The arrow gives the direction of the slide, along the ruler's edge, and the right angle is marked in both positions." — This is figure-caption narration describing a diagram and referencing other figures; it is not written for the learner as part of the construction instructions.

lo-t3w06-01: "The same set square on $AB$ as in fig-02, with the ruler moved to rest against its sloping edge instead of its upright one. The set square has not moved; only the ruler has, so it now leans across $AB$, running from lower left to upper right. The right angle is still where the edge on $AB$ meets the short upright edge, and it is marked there. The ruler's inclination does not affect the construction. The set square is drawn at one particular size, and with its right angle at one particular end; neither is part of the method. Any set square works, either way round, so long as one edge lies along $AB$ and the ruler rests against another." — This is a figure caption/label that describes an illustration and refers to fig-02; it narrates the diagram rather than addressing the learner.

lo-t3w06-01: "Line $AB$, with a point $P$ marked above it. A set square is drawn below $AB$ with one edge along the line: the right angle is at the left end of that edge, one leg runs down from it, and the hypotenuse closes back to a point on $AB$ to the right." — This is the fig-01 caption embedded as body text; it is descriptive caption text, not learner-facing instruction.

lo-t3w06-01: "The same set square on $AB$, with the ruler now drawn as a long strip lying along the set square's downward edge. The right angle marked at the corner is the set square's own, between the edge lying along $AB$ and the edge running down from it." — This is a figure caption describing the drawing in fig-02, meant for someone looking at the figure, not for the learner doing the construction.

lo-t3w06-01: "The vertical ruler held fixed, with the set square drawn twice — once with its edge on $AB$ and once higher up, its edge on a second line parallel to $AB$ — and an arrow between the two positions pointing up along the ruler." — This is the fig-04 caption; it describes the diagram and labels its parts instead of being addressed to the learner.

lo-t3w06-03: "The same arcs with $P$ joined to $Q$, the joining line crossing $AB$ at its middle at $M$ and carrying a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant.

The segment $AB$ with arc pairs crossing above and below it, the upper crossing labelled $P$ and the lower one $Q$. Each crossing is drawn as a small X where an arc from $A$ meets an arc from $B$.

The line segment $AB$, a stroke at each end, $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right." — These are figure captions/alt-text descriptions, not instructions or explanation for the learner; they narrate what the diagrams show and should not appear as standalone lesson text.
later_round_findings: lo-t3w06-01: "The set square has a right angle — a square corner — and that corner is what makes the method work." — This is an invented reason. The method works because the set square is slid along a held ruler, so it is translated without being turned and its edge keeps pointing the same way. The right angle is not what makes the construction work, and the section later allows the ruler to rest against the sloping edge, where the right-angle corner is not doing the work.
