blocks.text: Two lines are parallel when they run side by side and never meet, however far you extend them. In this lesson you will learn a neat way to draw a line through a given point $P$ that is parallel to another line $AB$. To do this you need only two tools from your mathematical set: a set square and a ruler. The set square has a right angle — a square corner — but what makes the method work is sliding the set square along a held ruler, so its edge keeps pointing the same way. You can use either edge of the set square and hold the ruler against either of the other two edges; it does not matter which, as long as one edge lies along $AB$ and the ruler rests against a different edge.

Example. Construct a line through point $P$ so that it is parallel to $AB$. Step 1 — Lay the set square on the line. Place your set square so that one of its edges lies exactly along $AB$, with the corner of the right angle at one end of that edge (fig-01). Step 2 — Put the ruler against another edge. Hold the set square still and lay the ruler along one of its other edges, so the ruler presses against it (fig-02). If you are right-handed, use the left-hand edge of the set square; left-handed people use the right-hand edge. It does not matter which edge you use — the ruler can even rest against the sloping edge of the set square (fig-03) — so long as the set square does not move. Step 3 — Slide the set square up to $P$. Keep the ruler pressed firmly in place with one hand, so it does not move. With your other hand, slide the set square along the ruler towards $P$, just as fig-04 and fig-05 show. Sliding along a held ruler moves the set square without turning it, so the edge that lay on $AB$ keeps pointing the same way. Step 4 — Stop and draw. Stop when the edge that was lying on $AB$ passes exactly through $P$. Now draw a line along that edge through $P$. Because the set square slid without turning, this new line points the same way as $AB$, so it is parallel to it.

blocks.caption: The same slide as fig-04, made against the leaning ruler of fig-03. The set square is drawn twice: once with its edge on $AB$, and once slid along the ruler until that edge passes through $P$. The two positions are congruent and point the same way — sliding along a held ruler moves the set square without turning it — so the edge through $P$ stays parallel to $AB$. The arrow gives the direction of the slide, along the ruler's edge, and the right angle is marked in both positions.

The vertical ruler held fixed, with the set square drawn twice — once with its edge on $AB$ and once higher up, its edge on a second line parallel to $AB$ — and an arrow between the two positions pointing up along the ruler.

The same set square on $AB$ as in fig-02, with the ruler moved to rest against its sloping edge instead of its upright one. The set square has not moved; only the ruler has, so it now leans across $AB$, running from lower left to upper right. The right angle is still where the edge on $AB$ meets the short upright edge, and it is marked there. The ruler's inclination does not affect the construction. The set square is drawn at one particular size, and with its right angle at one particular end; neither is part of the method. Any set square works, either way round, so long as one edge lies along $AB$ and the ruler rests against another.

The same set square on $AB$, with the ruler now drawn as a long strip lying along the set square's downward edge. The right angle marked at the corner is the set square's own, between the edge lying along $AB$ and the edge running down from it.

Line $AB$, with a point $P$ marked above it. A set square is drawn below $AB$ with one edge along the line: the right angle is at the left end of that edge, one leg runs down from it, and the hypotenuse closes back to a point on $AB$ to the right.

practice.prompt: Draw a line $CD$. Mark a point $Q$ above it. Using your set square and ruler, construct a line through $Q$ that is parallel to $CD$. In your own words, write the four steps you followed.
practice.answer: Place one edge of the set square exactly along $CD$; lay the ruler firmly against another edge of the set square; slide the set square along the ruler until the edge that was on $CD$ passes through $Q$; draw a line along that edge through $Q$. The line you drew is parallel to $CD$.
practice.worked_solution: Follow the same four steps as in the example: (1) set square on the line $CD$; (2) ruler against another edge, held firm; (3) slide the set square along the ruler up to $Q$ without turning it; (4) stop when the edge passes through $Q$ and draw the line. Because sliding along the held ruler does not turn the set square, the drawn line points the same way as $CD$ and is therefore parallel to it.

practice.prompt: When you slide the set square along the ruler to reach $P$, why must you hold the ruler firmly? What could go wrong if you let the ruler move?
practice.answer: You hold the ruler firm so the set square slides along a fixed straight path without turning. If the ruler moves, the set square may turn as it slides, so the edge through $P$ would no longer point the same way as $AB$ and the new line would not be parallel.
practice.worked_solution: The whole method works because sliding along a held ruler moves the set square without turning it. If the ruler shifts, the set square can rotate as it slides, changing the direction of its edge. That edge would then no longer make a line parallel to $AB$.

blocks.text:
Two lines are said to be **perpendicular** to each other when they meet at a right angle, that is, at $90^\circ$. Look at fig-06: line $AB$ is crossed by a second line $XY$, with $X$ above the line and $Y$ below it. At the crossing there is a small square mark in the upper right quadrant — that mark is the right-angle sign, and it tells you the two lines meet at exactly $90^\circ$.

In this section you will learn to construct perpendicular lines yourself, using just a set square and a ruler.

blocks.caption: Line $AB$ with a second line $XY$ crossing it, $X$ above and $Y$ below, and a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant at the crossing.

blocks.text:
Follow these steps to draw a line perpendicular to a given line through a point on it. You need your set square and your ruler.

**Step 1 — Draw the line and mark your point.** Draw a line $AB$ (fig-07), then mark a point $Q$ somewhere on the line.

**Step 2 — Place the set square.** Put the edge of the set square flat on line $AB$. Now hold your ruler so that its edge meets the hypotenuse of the set square. The set square stands on the line like a narrow right-angled triangle: its short base lies along $AB$, its upright edge rises from one end of that base, and the hypotenuse closes back down to the left.

**Step 3 — Slide the set square to your point.** Press firmly on the ruler so it does not move. Slide the set square down along the hypotenuse side until the third edge of the set square touches point $Q$.

**Step 4 — Draw the line.** Keeping everything still, draw a line $XY$ along the third edge of the set square, with $X$ above the line and $Y$ below it (fig-09). Add the little right-angle mark at the crossing to record that the lines meet at $90^\circ$.

Line $XY$ now crosses line $AB$ at a right angle, so $XY$ is perpendicular to $AB$.

blocks.caption: Line $AB$ with $XY$ now drawn across it, $X$ above and $Y$ below, and a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant.
A plain line with a stroke at each end, labelled $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right.

Line $AB$ with the set square standing on it as a narrow right-angled triangle: a short base along $AB$, the upright edge rising from the right end of that base with the right angle marked there, and the hypotenuse closing back down to the left.

practice.prompt: When do we say that two lines are perpendicular to each other?
practice.answer: Two lines are perpendicular when they meet at a right angle, that is, at $90^\circ$.

practice.prompt: A line $PQ$ is drawn, and you mark a point $R$ on it. In your own words, list the steps you take to draw a line through $R$ that is perpendicular to $PQ$.
practice.answer: Place the edge of the set square on line $PQ$. Hold the ruler so its edge meets the hypotenuse of the set square. Pressing firmly on the ruler, slide the set square along the hypotenuse until the third edge touches point $R$. Draw a line along that third edge. The line you draw crosses $PQ$ at a right angle, so it is perpendicular to $PQ$.

blocks.text: To bisect a line segment means to cut it into two equal halves. You can find the exact middle point of any line segment using just a pair of compasses and a ruler. You already know how to draw a straight line with a ruler. Now you will use the compasses to mark out two points, one above the line and one below it, and join them. The line you join them with will pass exactly through the middle of the segment, and it will meet the segment at a right angle (90°). Take your line segment and label its ends A (left) and B (right).

How to bisect line segment AB Step 1. Open your compasses so that the radius is about three-quarters of the length of AB. Step 2. Place the sharp point on A. Draw two arcs — one above the line and one below it — each reaching toward the middle of AB (fig-11). Step 3. Without changing the radius, place the sharp point on B. Draw two more arcs so that they cross the first two arcs. The arc from A and the arc from B that are above the line meet at a point you label P. The two arcs below the line meet at a point you label Q (fig-11). Step 4. Using a ruler, join P to Q with a straight line (fig-12). Step 5. The line PQ crosses AB at the point M. This point M is the midpoint of AB, so the two halves are equal: AM = MB. The line PQ also meets AB at a right angle, 90° (fig-12).

blocks.caption: The same arcs with $P$ joined to $Q$, the joining line crossing $AB$ at its middle at $M$ and carrying a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant.
The segment $AB$ with arc pairs crossing above and below it, the upper crossing labelled $P$ and the lower one $Q$. Each crossing is drawn as a small X where an arc from $A$ meets an arc from $B$.
The line segment $AB$, a stroke at each end, $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right.

practice.prompt: Draw a line segment AB about 8 cm long. Bisect it using your compasses and ruler. When you have finished, what single word names the point M where the line PQ crosses AB, and what is true about AM and MB?
practice.answer: M is the midpoint of AB, and AM = MB (the two halves are equal).
practice.worked_solution: Open the compasses to about three-quarters of the length of AB. With the point on A, draw an arc above and one below the middle. Keeping the same radius, put the point on B and draw two arcs that cross the first pair. Label the upper crossing P and the lower Q. Join P to Q with a ruler; where it crosses AB is M, the midpoint, so AM = MB.

practice.prompt: When bisecting a line segment AB, you first draw arcs from A above and below the line. What must you keep the same (not change) before drawing the next pair of arcs from B?
practice.answer: The radius of the compasses must stay the same (you must not change the radius between drawing the arcs from A and the arcs from B).

practice.prompt: You have bisected line segment AB and found the midpoint M. Apart from cutting the segment into two equal halves, what else is special about the way the line PQ meets AB at M?
practice.answer: The line PQ meets AB at M at a right angle (90°).

blocks.text:
An angle of 90° is a right angle — the corner of a square or a rectangle. You can construct it exactly using only a ruler and a pair of compasses, with no protractor at all. The trick is to draw a line that stands perpendicular to a given line: where the two lines meet, the angle between them is 90°.

To do this you need a point on the line, a pair of compasses, and a ruler. As you go, compare your work with fig-13 to check each step.

blocks.caption: A line with a stroke at each end, $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right, and four short strokes standing on the line, a pair towards $A$ and a pair towards $B$. A perpendicular rises from a point near the middle, with a right-angle mark at its foot, and two short strokes cross each other near its top.

blocks.text:
Construct an angle of 90° at a point C on the line AB.

Step 1 — Draw a straight line AB and mark a point C on it, where the 90° angle is to be constructed.

Step 2 — Put the point of the compasses at C and draw an arc that cuts the line at two points. Label these two points D and E.

Step 3 — Now open the compasses WIDER than DC, the width you used in step 2. This wider setting is important: arcs drawn with the step-2 width meet only at C itself, so they would not give you a new crossing point. With the compasses at D at this new wider setting, draw an arc above the line.

Step 4 — Keep the compasses at the same wider setting, put the point at E, and draw another arc above the line. This arc cuts the first one at a point F.

Step 5 — Join C to F with a ruler.

Step 6 — The line CF is perpendicular to AB, so the angle between CF and CB is a right angle: ∠FCB = 90°. Mark the little square at C, as in fig-13, to show the right angle.

practice.prompt: Construct an angle of 90° at a point C on a line AB, following the compass-and-ruler method. What is the name of the angle you have drawn, and what is the line CF called in relation to AB?
practice.answer: The angle is a right angle, 90°. The line CF is perpendicular to AB (so ∠FCB = 90°).
practice.worked_solution: Draw line AB and mark point C on it. Put the compasses at C and draw an arc cutting AB at D and E. Open the compasses wider than DC, put the point at D and draw an arc above the line. Keeping the same wider setting, put the point at E and draw another arc cutting the first at F. Join C to F. Since CF stands perpendicular to AB, the angle between CF and CB is a right angle of 90°.

practice.prompt: In the construction of an angle of 90°, explain why the compasses must be opened wider than DC for steps 3 and 4, instead of keeping the width used in step 2.
practice.answer: With the step-2 width, arcs drawn from D and E would meet only at C itself, giving no new crossing point to mark the perpendicular. A wider setting makes the two arcs meet at a new point F above the line.

blocks.text:
An angle of 60° is special: it is one of the angles of an equilateral triangle, and an equilateral triangle has all three sides equal. That is the secret of this construction — if you can draw a triangle with three equal sides, each of its angles must be 60°.

Here is the idea you will use. You set your compass to one fixed radius, and you keep that same radius for every arc. Where two arcs cross, you have found a point that is exactly the fixed radius away from both centres. Join that point back to the starting end of your line, and you have an equilateral triangle — and therefore a 60° angle.

You need only your mathematical set: a sharp pencil, a ruler, and a compass.

Follow these steps to construct an angle of 60°. Step 1 — draw the base line. Draw a line segment and label it BC, with B on the left. This is the side your 60° angle will sit on, with its vertex at B. Step 2 — swing the first arc. Place the point of your compass at B, open it to any convenient radius, and draw an arc that cuts the line at a point you label X. Keep the compass open at exactly this radius for the whole construction — do not change it. Step 3 — swing the second arc. Without changing the radius, move the compass point to X and draw another arc. Let it cut the first arc at a point you label A. Step 4 — join. Draw a straight line from B to A. The angle ABC — the angle at B between the line BC and the line BA — is 60°.

Worked example — construct angle ABC = 60°. 1. Draw a line segment BC with B on the left. Set your compass to a convenient radius, say about 4 cm. 2. Put the compass point at B and swing an arc so that it cuts the line. Mark where it crosses the line as X. (See fig-14: the long arc swings up and to the left from B, passing through X.) 3. Keep the radius exactly the same. Move the compass point to X and swing another arc so that it cuts the first arc. Mark that crossing point as A. 4. Draw a straight line from B through A and extend it. You have now drawn the triangle ABX. Its three sides — BX, XA and AB — are all equal, because every arc was drawn at the same radius. So triangle ABX is equilateral, and the angle ABC is 60°. The two arcs cross at A because the second arc is drawn from X with the same radius as the first, so A is the same distance from X as it is from B. That is what makes triangle ABX equilateral. If the second arc missed the first, check that your compass did not slip open.

blocks.caption: The line $BC$ with $B$ at the left, a stroke marking $X$ part way along, a long arc swung from $B$ through $X$ and up to the left, a shorter arc swung from $X$ cutting it, and a straight line from $B$ to that crossing.

practice.prompt: Construct an angle of 60° at point B on a line segment BC. Write the three steps you follow, and name the angle that measures 60°.
practice.answer: The angle ABC measures 60°. The three steps are: (1) draw line BC and swing an arc from B cutting it at X; (2) keeping the same radius, swing an arc from X to cut the first arc at A; (3) join B to A.
practice.worked_solution: Set your compass to any radius, draw an arc from B crossing the line at X, then without changing the radius draw an arc from X to meet the first at A. Drawing BA completes the equilateral triangle ABX, so angle ABC is 60°.

practice.prompt: You set your compass to 4 cm, drew an arc from B cutting the line at X, then moved the point to X and drew a second arc that cut the first at A. Why is the angle ABC exactly 60°, and what do you call the triangle ABX?
practice.answer: Triangle ABX is equilateral — all three sides are equal because every arc used the same 4 cm radius — and every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°, so angle ABC is 60°.
practice.worked_solution: BX is 4 cm (the arc from B), and both XA and AB are also 4 cm (each drawn at the same radius). Equal sides mean equal angles, and three equal angles add to 180°, so each is 60°.

sections_json.title: What Statistics Is For: Collecting and Reading Data

blocks.text: Every day we are surrounded by facts and figures: how many goals a team scored, the marks in a test, the number of people in your street, the price of food in the market. These facts and figures, collected together, are called data. Statistics is the branch of mathematics that deals with collecting, organising, and reading data so that it can be understood and used. What is statistics for? Statistics has several clear purposes. First, it helps us collect information in a careful and fair way, instead of guessing. Second, it helps us organise a large amount of information so that it is not a confusing jumble. Third, it helps us compare things — for example, which fruit is most liked by students. Fourth, it helps us find patterns and trends, such as whether rainfall increases in a certain month. Finally, it helps us make decisions and predictions — a shopkeeper uses data on what people buy to decide what to stock, and a government uses data on population to plan schools and hospitals. How is data collected? Data can be gathered by counting (how many books on a shelf), by measuring (the heights of your classmates), by asking questions (a survey or questionnaire), by observing (watching traffic pass a road), or by reading existing records (a school register). How is data tabulated? Once data is collected, it is put into a table. A table arranges the information neatly in rows and columns so that you can see at a glance how often each item occurs. The number of times an item appears is its frequency. A table that shows each item together with its frequency is called a frequency table.

Worked example 1 — Collecting and tabulating data A class wants to know the favourite sport among 15 students. Each student names one sport. The answers collected are: Football, Tennis, Football, Volleyball, Football, Tennis, Basketball, Football, Volleyball, Football, Tennis, Football, Basketball, Tennis, Football Step 1 — Collect. The data is gathered by asking each student one question. The answers above are the raw data. Step 2 — Tally. To organise it, we make a tally table. For each answer we draw one stroke. Every fifth stroke is drawn across the previous four to make counting easier (a group of five, like IIII). Sport | Tally | Frequency -------------|--------|---------- Football | IIII II| 7 Tennis | IIII | 4 Volleyball | II | 2 Basketball | II | 2 Step 3 — Interpret. Reading the table, Football has the highest frequency (7), so Football is the most popular sport in the class. Basketball and Volleyball are equally popular, each with 2. Worked example 2 — Reading and comparing data in a table The table below shows the marks scored by students in a Mathematics test. Marks | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 -----------|----|----|----|----|---- Frequency | 3 | 5 | 8 | 6 | 2 Read the table to answer: (a) How many students scored 40? (b) Which mark was scored by most students? (c) How many students took the test? (a) The frequency below 40 is 6, so 6 students scored 40. (b) The largest frequency is 8, under the mark 30, so most students scored 30. (c) Add all the frequencies: 3 + 5 + 8 + 6 + 2 = 24 students.

practice.prompt: 1. State three purposes of statistics, and name one way in which data can be collected.
practice.answer: Answers may vary. Three purposes of statistics include: collecting information carefully, organising data into a neat form, comparing things, finding patterns or trends, and making decisions or predictions. One way data can be collected: counting, measuring, asking questions (survey), observing, or reading existing records.
practice.worked_solution: Statistics helps us collect, organise, compare, find patterns, and make decisions. Data can be gathered by counting, measuring, asking questions, observing, or reading records — any one of these is correct.

practice.prompt:
2. A teacher asked 12 students their favourite colour. The answers were: Red, Blue, Red, Green, Blue, Red, Red, Blue, Green, Red, Blue, Red.
(a) Make a frequency table of these colours.
(b) Which colour is the most popular?
practice.answer:
(a) Frequency table: Red — 6, Blue — 4, Green — 2.
(b) Red is the most popular, with frequency 6.
practice.worked_solution: Count each colour. Red appears at positions 1, 3, 6, 7, 10 and 12, so 6 times. Blue appears at 2, 5, 8, 11, so 4 times. Green appears at 4 and 9, so 2 times. The table shows Red (6), Blue (4), Green (2). The highest frequency is 6, so Red is most popular.

practice.prompt:
3. The frequency table below shows the number of siblings of some students.

Number of siblings | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4
-------------------|----|----|----|----|----
Frequency          | 4 | 7 | 9 | 5 | 2

(a) How many students have exactly 2 siblings?
(b) How many students in total were asked?
(c) Which number of siblings is the most common?
practice.answer:
(a) 9 students.
(b) 4 + 7 + 9 + 5 + 2 = 27 students.
(c) 2 siblings, because it has the highest frequency of 9.
practice.worked_solution:
(a) Read the frequency below the "2" column: 9.
(b) Add all frequencies: 4 + 7 + 9 + 5 + 2 = 27.
(c) The largest frequency is 9, which sits under "2 siblings", so the most common number of siblings is 2.

sections_json.title: Making Sense of Numbers with Tables

blocks.text:
When we collect a lot of numbers, they can be hard to read. Statistics is the way we organise those numbers so they start to tell us something useful. One of the most helpful tools for doing this is a table.

A table takes rows of information and lines them up in columns, so you can see at a glance what is there. For example, suppose a class counted how many books each student read in a month. Instead of listing twenty separate numbers, we can put them in a table like this:

| Number of books read | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|----------------------|---|---|---|---|
| Number of students   | 4 | 7 | 6 | 3 |

To read a table, you ask yourself simple questions and let the numbers answer them.

Question: How many students read exactly 3 books? Look down the "Number of books read" row until you find 3. The number underneath it, 7, tells you that 7 students read 3 books.

Question: How many students were counted altogether? Add every number in the bottom row: 4 + 7 + 6 + 3 = 20 students.

Question: How many students read 4 or 5 books? Add the students in those two columns: 6 + 3 = 9 students.

So a table lets you compare groups, find totals, and answer questions quickly. The columns and rows are your signposts — always read the headings first so you know what each number is counting.

Example — Favourite fruits

A shop asked its customers which fruit they liked most and recorded the answers in this table:

| Fruit      | Apple | Banana | Mango | Orange |
|------------|-------|--------|-------|--------|
| Customers  | 12    | 8      | 15    | 5      |

Let's read a few facts from it.

Step 1: Which fruit was liked most?
Look for the biggest number in the "Customers" row. The biggest is 15, which sits under Mango. So mango was the favourite fruit.

Step 2: How many customers chose banana or orange?
Add the customers for those two fruits: 8 + 5 = 13 customers.

Step 3: How many customers answered altogether?
Add the whole "Customers" row: 12 + 8 + 15 + 5 = 40 customers.

Step 4: How many more customers chose apple than orange?
The apple column has 12 and the orange column has 5. The difference is 12 − 5 = 7 more customers chose apple.

Notice how each answer came straight from reading the numbers in the table. The headings told us what the numbers meant, and the numbers answered our questions.

To interpret a table confidently, use these three steps every time:

1. Read the headings. The row and column headings tell you what the numbers are counting. Without them, numbers have no meaning.

2. Find the right column or row. Put your finger on the heading you are interested in and follow it to the number you need.

3. Do the arithmetic the question asks for. Sometimes you just read one number. Sometimes you add columns together, or subtract one from another to find a difference.

A table is a summary: it takes a messy list of data and turns it into answers you can find. Once you can read a table, you can interpret statistical data — which simply means turning the numbers back into a clear description of what they show.

practice.prompt:
A sports club asked its members which sport they play most often. The results are shown in this table:

| Sport    | Football | Basketball | Tennis | Swimming |
|----------|----------|------------|--------|----------|
| Members  | 18       | 10         | 6      | 14       |

(a) How many members play tennis?
(b) How many members were asked altogether?
(c) Which sport is played by the most members?
(d) How many more members play football than basketball?
practice.answer: (a) 6 members play tennis. (b) 18 + 10 + 6 + 14 = 48 members. (c) Football, with 18 members. (d) 18 − 10 = 8 more members play football than basketball.
practice.worked_solution:
(a) Read the number under Tennis: it is 6.
(b) Add the whole Members row: 18 + 10 + 6 + 14 = 48.
(c) Find the largest number in the Members row: 18 is the biggest, and it is under Football.
(d) Subtract the smaller from the larger: 18 − 10 = 8.

practice.prompt:
A farmer recorded how many baskets of oranges each tree gave. The table shows the results:

| Tree       | Tree A | Tree B | Tree C | Tree D |
|------------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| Baskets    | 9      | 12     | 7      | 15     |

(a) Which tree gave the fewest baskets?
(b) How many baskets did Tree B and Tree C give together?
(c) How many more baskets did Tree D give than Tree A?
practice.answer: (a) Tree C, with 7 baskets. (b) 12 + 7 = 19 baskets. (c) 15 − 9 = 6 more baskets.
practice.worked_solution:
(a) The smallest number in the Baskets row is 7, under Tree C.
(b) Add the baskets for Tree B and Tree C: 12 + 7 = 19.
(c) Subtract Tree A's baskets from Tree D's: 15 − 9 = 6.

blocks.text:
You already know how to count things and record what you find — how many bottles are in the crate, how many pencils are in the tin. Statistics is the way we turn that kind of counting and recording into something useful.

Statistics is the branch of mathematics that deals with collecting, organising, and interpreting information. It is not just about counting for the sake of counting. The whole point is to take information that is scattered around — a list of names, a pile of counters, a row of marks — and arrange it so that it tells you something clear.

Think about it in three parts:

1. Collecting — you gather the information, like counting how many of your classmates are present.
2. Organising — you arrange that information in a neat way, such as putting the numbers in a table or a list.
3. Interpreting — you read the organised information to understand what it means, like seeing which day had the most pupils in school.

So the purpose of statistics is simple: it helps us collect, organise, and make sense of information. Whenever you have a lot of facts or numbers and you want to understand them, statistics is the tool you use to do it.

practice.prompt: In your own words, what is statistics, and what is its purpose?
practice.answer: Statistics is the branch of mathematics that deals with collecting, organising, and interpreting information. Its purpose is to help us collect, organise, and make sense of information.

practice.prompt: Name the three things statistics helps us do with information.
A teacher counts the number of pupils present in each class and writes the results in a table so she can see which class has the most pupils. Which two parts of statistics is she doing?
practice.answer: She is collecting the information (counting the pupils) and organising it (putting the results in a table) so she can interpret it.

sections_json.title: Making Sense of a Frequency Table

blocks.text:
Statistics is the branch of mathematics that helps us gather information, organise it, and make sense of it. When we want to answer a question like "Which colour do most students in my class like best?" or "How many children are in each family?", we first have to collect the data — that is, gather the facts or numbers. We can collect data by counting, by asking people (a questionnaire), by watching, or by recording what we observe. Once the data is collected, it usually looks like a long, messy list. To understand it, we need to organise it. One of the best ways is to build a frequency table. A frequency table shows us each different value and how many times it appears. That "how many times" is called the frequency.

Here is the simple idea behind a frequency table: we take every piece of data, and for each value we make a mark. We often use tally marks — four vertical strokes, with the fifth drawn across them as a diagonal line, so we can count quickly in groups of five. After we have marked every piece of data, we count the marks for each value and write the total. That total is the frequency.

When the table is finished, we can interpret it — we can read the table to answer questions about the data, such as which value is the most common, which is the least common, or how many pieces of data there are altogether (the total of all the frequencies).

Worked example

A teacher asked each child in a class to say how many pets they have. Here are the answers from the class:

2, 1, 3, 2, 1, 0, 2, 3, 1, 2, 0, 2, 1, 3, 2

Step 1 — List the different values.
The answers we saw are 0, 1, 2 and 3. Write these in a column in order (smallest first): 0, 1, 2, 3.

Step 2 — Tally the data.
Go through the list one number at a time and put a tally mark next to that value. For the first five numbers, "2, 1, 3, 2, 1":

  • 0: no mark yet
  • 1: || (two marks — the 1s in positions 2 and 5)
  • 2: || (two marks — the 2s in positions 1 and 4)
  • 3: | (one mark — the 3 in position 3)

Now continue through the rest of the list — "0, 2, 3, 1, 2, 0, 2, 1, 3, 2" — adding a mark each time. When you finish, count the marks for each value:

  • 0 appears in positions 6 and 11 → 2 marks
  • 1 appears in positions 2, 5, 9, 13 → 4 marks
  • 2 appears in positions 1, 4, 7, 10, 12, 15 → 6 marks
  • 3 appears in positions 3, 8, 14 → 3 marks

Write these as tally marks in a second column and the counts as a third column called Frequency:

Number of petsTallyFrequency
0||2
1||||4
2~~~|6
3|||3

Check your tally.
The frequencies must add up to the total number of pieces of data. Here, 2 + 4 + 6 + 3 = 15, and there are exactly 15 numbers in the list — so the table is correct. If the frequencies did not add up to 15, we would know to re-tally.

Interpreting the table.
Now we can read answers straight from the table:

  • The most common number of pets is 2, because it has the highest frequency (6).
  • The least common number of pets is 0, because it has the lowest frequency (2).
  • The total number of children asked is 2 + 4 + 6 + 3 = 15.

practice.prompt:

First tally the data, then write the frequencies in a table with columns for "Number of children", "Tally" and "Frequency". Check that your frequencies add up to the total number of families.

Tally each number: - 1 appears in positions 1, 2, 12 → 3 marks → frequency 3 - 2 appears in positions 7, 8, 13 → 3 marks → frequency 3 - 3 appears in positions 3, 6, 9, 10 → 4 marks → frequency 4 - 4 appears in positions 4, 5, 11 → 3 marks → frequency 3 Check: 3 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 13, and the list has 13 numbers, so the tally is correct.
Number of childrenTallyFrequency
1|||3
2|||3
3||||4
4|||3

practice.prompt:
A class counted the number of books each student read last term and recorded these results:

3, 1, 2, 3, 4, 2, 1, 3, 2, 4, 2, 3

Use the data to answer these questions without re-counting the whole list:
(a) What is the highest number of books read by any student?
(b) What is the lowest number of books read?
(c) Which number of books was read most often?
(d) How many students are in the class?
practice.answer: (a) 4 books  (b) 1 book  (c) 3 books (it occurs 4 times)  (d) 12 students
practice.worked_solution:
(a) The largest value in the list is 4, so the highest number of books read is 4.
(b) The smallest value in the list is 1, so the lowest number of books read is 1.
(c) Count how many times each number appears:
- 1 appears in positions 2 and 7 → twice
- 2 appears in positions 3, 5, 9, 11 → 4 times
- 3 appears in positions 1, 4, 8, 12 → 4 times
- 4 appears in positions 6 and 10 → twice
The most common is 3 (tied with 2 at 4 times). 
(d) The number of students equals the total of the data: there are 12 numbers in the list, so 12 students.

(Note: the "most often" answer reads from the frequency table — both 2 and 3 occur 4 times, the highest frequency.)

sections_json.title: What Is Statistics and Why Do We Need It?

blocks.text:
Every day we come across lots of information. The number of students in your class, how many bottles of water were sold at a shop in a week, the heights of your friends — these are all pieces of information. When we collect such facts together for a particular reason, we call them data. Data are facts or information collected for a particular purpose. Statistics is the science of collecting, organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting data. So statistics is not just about gathering numbers — it is the whole way of handling information so that it becomes useful. Notice the five actions in that definition:
  • Collecting — gathering the information you need.
  • Organising — putting that information in order so it is easy to work with.
  • Presenting — showing the information clearly, for example in a table.
  • Analysing — studying the information to see what it tells you.
  • Interpreting — explaining what the information means.
Why do we need statistics? It helps us to:
  • Collect information — it shows us how to gather facts in an orderly way.
  • Organise information — it lets us arrange the facts neatly so nothing is lost.
  • Compare information — it lets us look at two sets of facts and see which is bigger, faster or more.
  • Make decisions — with facts organised, we can choose wisely instead of guessing.
  • Present information clearly — it lets us show others our findings in a way they can understand.

Worked example — seeing statistics in action Suppose your class wants to know how many students come to school by bus, by bicycle and on foot. Here is how statistics helps at each step:
  • Collect: You ask every student in the class how they travel and write down each answer.
  • Organise: You group the answers — all the "bus" answers together, all the "bicycle" answers together, all the "foot" answers together.
  • Present: You put the totals in a table so anyone can read them at a glance.
  • Analyse and interpret: You look at the table and see that most students come by bus, so you can explain that to your class.
That last point is an example of a decision: seeing that most students travel by bus, your class might arrange a bus pick-up point. Statistics turned scattered answers into something useful.

practice.prompt: In your own words, what are data? Give one example of data you might collect at home.
practice.answer: Data are facts or information collected for a particular purpose. An example could be the number of plates washed each evening, or the amount of time spent on homework each day — any facts you collect for a purpose.

practice.prompt: Define statistics by naming the five actions it involves.
practice.answer: Statistics is the science of collecting, organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting data.

practice.prompt: List three ways statistics helps us. For each one, say in a sentence how it is useful.
practice.answer: Three of: it helps us collect information (gather facts in an orderly way), organise information (arrange facts neatly), compare information (see which set is bigger or more), make decisions (choose wisely instead of guessing), and present information clearly (show others our findings).

practice.prompt: A shop owner writes down how many loaves of bread she sells each day for a week. Write the five steps of statistics in the order she would use them, from collecting the data to explaining what the data mean.
practice.answer: Collect (write down the daily sales), organise (arrange the figures, for example from smallest to largest or by day), present (show the figures clearly, for example in a table), analyse (study the figures to see patterns), interpret (explain what the figures mean, such as which day sells most bread).
practice.worked_solution: The definition of statistics lists the five actions in order: collecting, organising, presenting, analysing, then interpreting. So the shop owner first collects her daily sales figures, then organises them neatly, then presents them clearly in a table, then analyses them to spot patterns, and finally interprets them — explaining what they tell her, such as the busiest day.

blocks.text: Statistics is the study of information — called data — gathered about people, things or events. Before we can read and understand a table of numbers, the data must first be collected, and then set out neatly. There are four common ways to collect data: 1. Observation — you watch something happen and note what you see. 2. Counting — you count how many of each item there are. 3. Interview — you ask people questions face to face and record their answers. 4. Questionnaire — you give people a set of written questions to answer. Whichever method you use, you end up with a list of items. For example, counting the vehicles passing a school might give you this list: bus, car, car, car, lorry, bicycle, bicycle, car, car, lorry, bicycle, car. A list like this is hard to read, so we use tally marks to record the data as it is collected.

Tally marks are short strokes used to record each item as it is counted. Every time you see one more of an item, you add a stroke. Strokes are grouped in fives: four upright strokes, then a fifth stroke drawn across them like ||||/. This grouping makes it easy to count the total at a glance. Let's record the vehicle data with tally marks. The data is: bus, car, car, car, lorry, bicycle, bicycle, car, car, lorry, bicycle, car. - car appears 6 times → tally ||||/ |, total 6 - bus appears 1 time → tally |, total 1 - lorry appears 2 times → tally ||, total 2 - bicycle appears 3 times → tally |||, total 3 When the tally is finished, you can count up the strokes for each item and write the total in the last column. A table that shows how many times each item occurs in a set of data is called a frequency table. In a frequency table, the last column is the frequency — the number of times each item occurs.

Let's set the vehicle data out as a complete frequency table. First list each different vehicle in its own row, record the tally marks as you count, then write the total. | Vehicles | Tally | Total | |---|---|---| | car | \|\|\|\|\|/ \| | 6 | | bus | \| | 1 | | lorry | \|\| | 2 | | bicycle | \|\|\| | 3 | The frequency table shows at a glance that car is the most common vehicle (6), and bus the least common (1). A frequency table does not always need a tally column — sometimes it just shows each item and its frequency. For example, a survey of students' favourite colours gives this frequency table: | colour | frequency | |---|---| | Red | 18 | | Blue | 20 | | Green | 14 | | Yellow | 16 | | White | 15 | | Pink | 30 | Here the most popular colour is Pink (30 students) and the least popular is Green (14 students). By setting data out in a table like this, you can read it quickly and answer questions about it easily.

practice.prompt: State three methods of collecting data.
practice.answer: Observation, counting, interview and questionnaire (any three of these).

practice.prompt: Prepare a frequency table for the following data: 1, 1, 3, 4, 4, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 1, 2.
practice.worked_solution: Count how many times each number appears. The number 1 appears at positions 1, 2 and 12 → 3 times. The number 2 appears at positions 7, 8 and 13 → 3 times. The number 3 appears at positions 5, 6, 9 and 10 → 4 times. The number 4 appears at positions 4, 5 and 11 → 3 times. Set these counts in a table with a Number column and a Frequency column.

practice.prompt: The favourite colours of students are recorded with these frequencies: Red 18, Blue 20, Green 14, Yellow 16, White 15, Pink 30. Which colour is the most popular and which is the least popular?
practice.answer: Pink is the most popular (30), and Green is the least popular (14).

findings_text: lo-t3w09-02: "| car | |||/| | 6 |" — The tally table gives a total of 6 for car, and the working text says a five-group plus one more gives six tally marks, but the Tally cell only shows |||/|, which is one five-stroke group. Six tally marks should be shown as the five-group plus one extra stroke.

sections_json.title: What is Statistics, and Why Do We Need It?

blocks.text: Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, presenting, analyzing and interpreting data. The word data sits at the heart of it all, so let's be clear about what data means. Data are facts or information collected for a particular purpose. The number of pupils in your class, the scores you got in your last test, or the amount of rain that fell each day last week are all examples of data. Each is a set of facts gathered for a reason — to answer a question or find something out. Wherever facts are gathered for a purpose, statistics is at work.

Why do we need statistics? Because it helps us to do five important things: (a) Collect information — bring facts together in one place. (b) Organize information — put the facts in order so they are easy to read and handle. (c) Compare information — look at two or more sets of facts side by side. (d) Make decisions — use the facts to choose what to do. (e) Present information clearly — show the facts in a way that others can understand. These five are the purpose of statistics: it turns scattered facts into useful, clear information that helps us decide and act.

Example. Your class wants to know how many pupils walk to school. First you collect information by asking every pupil how they travel. Then you organize information by counting how many walk, how many ride a bicycle, and how many are dropped off by car. Now you can compare information to see which way most pupils travel, and present it clearly in a small table. Finally, you can make a decision — for instance, whether the school should ask for more bicycle racks. Every step you just took — collecting, organizing, comparing, presenting and deciding — is statistics.

practice.prompt: What is statistics?
practice.answer: Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, presenting, analyzing and interpreting data.

practice.prompt: State what data are.
practice.answer: Data are facts or information collected for a particular purpose.

practice.prompt: Your father records the amount he spends on food, transport and school fees each month, so he can see which costs him the most. Which two purposes of statistics is he using?
practice.answer: He is collecting information (recording the amounts) and comparing information (seeing which cost is the most).
practice.worked_solution: Recording the amounts each month is collecting information. Looking at the amounts to see which is the largest is comparing information. He could also be making a decision about where to spend less.

practice.prompt: List the five ways that statistics helps us.
practice.answer: It helps us to (a) collect information, (b) organize information, (c) compare information, (d) make decisions, and (e) present information clearly.

blocks.text: When you want to find out something about a group, you first need to gather information about them. That gathered information is called data. There are four main ways to collect data: 1. Observation — you watch and note what you see, such as counting how many cars pass a spot. 2. Counting — you count items one by one. 3. Interview — you ask people questions and record their answers. 4. Questionnaire — you give people a written set of questions and collect their written answers. Once you have collected data, you need a neat way to record it as it comes in. Tally marks are quick marks used to record data while you are collecting it. For every item you count, you draw one stroke. When you reach the fifth stroke, you draw it across the previous four to make a group like this: |||/| (four strokes with the fifth crossing them). Each group of five tally marks is easy to count later. After tallying, you can set the data out in a frequency table. A frequency table is a table showing how many times each item occurs in a set of data. The column that lists each item's count is called the frequency.

Worked example — recording data with tally marks Imagine you record the vehicles that pass by as: bus, car, car, car, lorry, bicycle, bicycle, car, car, lorry, bicycle, car. To record this with tally marks, go through the list one item at a time. Start with the car column, adding a stroke for each car you meet. As you count the cars — car, car, car, car, car, car — you draw |||/| (five) then one more, giving six tally marks for car. Continue for the other vehicles. Your tally table looks like this: | Vehicles | Tally | Total | |---|---|---| | car | |||/|| | 6 | | bus | | | 1 | | lorry | || | 2 | | bicycle | ||| | 3 | | motor bike | | | 0 | Read the last column (the Total) as the count for each item: car occurs 6 times, bus 1 time, lorry 2 times and bicycle 3 times. Notice the motor bike appears in the table with a total of 0 because it did not occur in the data. Worked example — a frequency table A class is asked their favourite colour, and the counts are collected. The results are set out in a frequency table: | Colour | Frequency | |---|---| | Red | 18 | | Blue | 20 | | Green | 14 | | Yellow | 16 | | White | 15 | | Pink | 30 | The frequency column tells you how many students chose each colour. For instance, 30 students chose Pink and 14 chose Green. To check your table, you can add all the frequencies together to find the total number of students who answered.

So the whole process has three steps. First, collect the data using observation, counting, an interview or a questionnaire. Second, record the data with tally marks as it is collected. Third, tabulate — set the data out in a frequency table so you can read how many times each item occurs at a glance. Now try building a frequency table yourself.

practice.prompt: State three methods of collecting data.
practice.answer: Any three of: observation, counting, interview, questionnaire.

practice.prompt: Prepare a frequency table for the following data: 1, 1, 3, 4, 4, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 1, 2.
practice.worked_solution: Go through the list and count how many times each number appears. The number 1 appears three times (1, 1, 1), 2 appears three times (2, 2, 2), 3 appears four times (3, 3, 3, 3) and 4 appears three times (4, 4, 4). Write each number once in the first column and its count in the frequency column.

sections_json.title: The Right Order for Algebraic Expressions

blocks.text: When you simplify an algebraic expression, you must deal with the operations in a fixed order. This order is often remembered by the word BODMAS: - Brackets first - Order (powers such as squares and cubes) - Division and Multiplication (work from left to right) - Addition and Subtraction (work from left to right) The key idea is that you never just work from left to right. Brackets always come first, then powers, then multiply or divide, and only at the end do you add or subtract. Multiplication and division are treated as equal in rank, so when you meet them together you simply work left to right. Addition and subtraction are also equal in rank, so when you meet them together you work left to right too. Here is how the same steps work when the numbers are replaced by letters. For example, in the expression 3 + 2x, the multiplication 2x is done before the addition, because multiplication comes before addition. So 3 + 2x already means "2 times x, then add 3" — never "3 + 2, then times x". The letter x stands for a number, and the ordinary order of operations still applies to it. A useful habit is to rewrite each term clearly. A term like 4y ÷ 2 means "4 times y, divided by 2", so it simplifies to 2y because 4 ÷ 2 = 2, then the y is carried along. Always work out the numbers first and keep the letter with its term.

Worked example 1 — multiply and divide, then add Simplify 6x ÷ 2 + 4x. Step 1: Deal with the division first, because division comes before addition. 6x ÷ 2 = 3x Step 2: Now add the terms. 3x + 4x = 7x So 6x ÷ 2 + 4x = 7x.

Worked example 2 — brackets come first Simplify 3(x + 2y) − y. Step 1: Deal with the bracket first. Multiply everything inside the bracket by the 3 in front. 3(x + 2y) = 3x + 6y Step 2: Now subtract the y that is outside the bracket. 3x + 6y − y = 3x + 5y So 3(x + 2y) − y = 3x + 5y.

Worked example 3 — powers come before multiply Simplify 2x × x. Here the expression has no brackets, but remember that x × x is x² (a power). Multiplication of the letters gives a power. Step 1: Multiply the letters. 2x × x = 2x² So 2x × x = 2x².

practice.prompt: Simplify 4a × 3 + 5a.
practice.worked_solution:
Multiplication comes before addition, so do 4a × 3 first.
4a × 3 = 12a
Now add: 12a + 5a = 17a.

practice.prompt: Simplify 2(3p + q) − 2q.
practice.worked_solution:
Brackets come first. Multiply everything inside the bracket by 2:
2(3p + q) = 6p + 2q
Now subtract the outside term: 6p + 2q − 2q = 6p.

practice.prompt: Simplify 8y ÷ 2 + y.
practice.worked_solution:
Division comes before addition, so do 8y ÷ 2 first.
8y ÷ 2 = 4y
Now add: 4y + y = 5y.

practice.prompt: Simplify 5m + 2 + 2m, making sure to collect like terms in the right order.
practice.worked_solution:
Addition and subtraction have equal rank, so work from left to right.
5m + 2m = 7m, then keep the +2.
So the expression is 7m + 2.

blocks.text: Brackets are a way of grouping parts of an expression so we know what to deal with together. In algebra they do exactly the same job as in arithmetic: everything inside the brackets is treated as one group. When a letter or number sits right in front of a bracket with no sign between them, it means multiply. For example, 3(x + 2) means 3 lots of (x + 2), which is the same as 3 × x + 3 × 2. To remove brackets, we multiply the term outside the bracket by every term inside it. This is sometimes called expanding the bracket. Once the brackets are gone, we often collect the like terms (the terms with the same letter) to finish the simplification.

Watch a full example of removing brackets and then simplifying. Example: Simplify 3(x + 2) + 4x. Step 1 — Remove the bracket by multiplying 3 by each term inside: 3 × x + 3 × 2 = 3x + 6 Step 2 — Bring down the rest of the expression: 3x + 6 + 4x Step 3 — Collect like terms (the x terms together, the number terms together): 3x + 4x + 6 = 7x + 6 So 3(x + 2) + 4x = 7x + 6.

Worked Example 1 — Removing two brackets Simplify 2(x + 3) − 3(x − 1). Step 1 — Remove the first bracket: 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 Step 2 — Remove the second bracket. The minus sign in front means we subtract 3 × (x − 1), so the −1 inside becomes −3 × −1 = +3: −3(x − 1) = −3x + 3 Step 3 — Put it together: 2x + 6 − 3x + 3 Step 4 — Collect like terms: 2x − 3x + 6 + 3 = −x + 9 So 2(x + 3) − 3(x − 1) = −x + 9.

Inserting brackets (also called factorising) is the reverse of removing them. We look at every term and find the highest common factor — the largest number and the largest letter power that divides into all the terms. For example, in 6x + 9, both 6x and 9 divide by 3. So we write the 3 outside the brackets and put the remaining parts inside: 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3) Check: 3 × 2x = 6x and 3 × 3 = 9, so it works.

Worked Example 2 — Inserting brackets Factorise 8y + 12. Step 1 — Find the highest common factor of 8y and 12. The largest number that divides both 8 and 12 is 4. Step 2 — Divide each term by 4: 8y ÷ 4 = 2y and 12 ÷ 4 = 3 Step 3 — Put the 4 outside the bracket: 8y + 12 = 4(2y + 3) Step 4 — Check by expanding: 4 × 2y = 8y and 4 × 3 = 12. Correct. Worked Example 3 — A bracket with a letter factor Factorise 5a + 10a². Both terms have a factor of 5 and also an a. The highest common factor is 5a. 5a ÷ 5a = 1 and 10a² ÷ 5a = 2a So 5a + 10a² = 5a(1 + 2a).

practice.prompt: Remove the brackets and simplify: 4(x + 5) + 2x
practice.worked_solution: Remove the bracket: 4(x + 5) = 4x + 20. Bring down the rest: 4x + 20 + 2x. Collect like terms: 4x + 2x + 20 = 6x + 20.

practice.prompt: Remove the brackets and simplify: 5(y − 2) − 2(y + 1)
practice.worked_solution: Remove the first bracket: 5(y − 2) = 5y − 10. Remove the second: −2(y + 1) = −2y − 2. Together: 5y − 10 − 2y − 2. Collect like terms: 5y − 2y − 10 − 2 = 3y − 12.

practice.prompt: Insert brackets to factorise: 10x + 15
practice.worked_solution: The highest common factor of 10x and 15 is 5. Divide each term by 5: 10x ÷ 5 = 2x and 15 ÷ 5 = 3. Write 5 outside the bracket: 5(2x + 3). Check: 5 × 2x = 10x and 5 × 3 = 15.

practice.prompt: Insert brackets to factorise: 6m + 9m²
practice.worked_solution: Both terms share a factor of 3 and of m, so the highest common factor is 3m. Divide: 6m ÷ 3m = 2 and 9m² ÷ 3m = 3m. Write: 6m + 9m² = 3m(2 + 3m). Check by expanding: 3m × 2 = 6m and 3m × 3m = 9m².

practice.prompt: Remove the brackets and simplify: 2(3a + 4) + 3(a − 2)
practice.worked_solution: Remove the first bracket: 2(3a + 4) = 6a + 8. Remove the second: 3(a − 2) = 3a − 6. Together: 6a + 8 + 3a − 6. Collect like terms: 6a + 3a + 8 − 6 = 9a + 2.

sections_json.title: Order of Operations, Brackets, and Algebra in Words

blocks.text:
When an algebraic expression contains several operations, you work through them in a fixed order. This order is the same one you use with numbers:

1. Do whatever is inside **brackets** first.
2. Then do **multiplication** and **division** from left to right.
3. Finally do **addition** and **subtraction** from left to right.

For example, in the expression \(5 + 3 \times 2x\), there are no brackets, so you multiply before you add:
\(5 + 3 \times 2x = 5 + 6x\).
The answer is \(5 + 6x\) — you cannot add 5 and 6x because they are not like terms.

If we put brackets in, the order changes. In \((5 + 3) \times 2x\), you work out the bracket first:
\((5 + 3) \times 2x = 8 \times 2x = 16x\).

So brackets can change the meaning of an expression completely. Always clear them out first.

To **remove a bracket**, multiply each term inside the bracket by what sits in front of it. This is called expanding the bracket.

\(3(2x + 4) = 3 \times 2x + 3 \times 4 = 6x + 12\)

When there is a minus sign in front of the bracket, it multiplies every term inside, so every sign flips:
\(- (3x - 5) = -3x + 5\)

Here is a longer simplification that puts everything together:
\[\n2(3x + 1) - (x - 4)\n\]
Remove both brackets:
\[\n= 6x + 2 - x + 4\n\]
Collect the like terms (the \(x\) terms, then the numbers):
\[\n= (6x - x) + (2 + 4) = 5x + 6\n\]

Always simplify fully so no like terms are left over.

Algebra is useful for solving **word problems**. To turn words into an algebraic expression, follow these steps:

1. Choose a letter to stand for the unknown amount.
2. Translate each phrase into a piece of algebra:
   - "three times a number" means \(3x\)
   - "five more than a number" means \(x + 5\)
   - "a number decreased by two" means \(x - 2\)
   - "the sum of a number and four" means \(x + 4\)
3. Combine the pieces using the order of operations and brackets.

Here is an example. "A number is multiplied by 3, then 7 is added to the result." The number is \(x\), so:
\[\n\text{result} = 3x + 7\n\]

Brackets matter in word problems too. "The sum of a number and 4, all multiplied by 2" is written as \(2(x + 4)\), not \(2x + 4\). The words "the sum of ... all multiplied by" tell you to add first, so the addition goes inside the bracket.

Worked example 1 — Order of operations
Simplify \(6 + 4 \times 3a\).

There are no brackets, so multiply before adding:
\(4 \times 3a = 12a\).
Then \(6 + 12a\).
\(6\) and \(12a\) are not like terms, so the answer is \(6 + 12a\).

Worked example 2 — Removing brackets
Simplify \(5(2x - 3) - 2(x + 4)\).

Expand the first bracket: \(5(2x - 3) = 10x - 15\).
Expand the second: \(-2(x + 4) = -2x - 8\).
Put them together:
\[\n10x - 15 - 2x - 8\n\]
Collect like terms:
\[\n(10x - 2x) + (-15 - 8) = 8x - 23\n\]
Answer: \(8x - 23\).

Worked example 3 — Word problem
"Twice the sum of a number and 5" — write this as an expression and simplify it.

Let the number be \(x\).
"The sum of a number and 5" is \(x + 5\).
"Twice" means multiply by 2, so the whole sum goes inside a bracket:
\[\n2(x + 5)\n\]
Expand:
\[\n2x + 10\n\]
So the expression is \(2x + 10\).

practice.prompt: Simplify: \(9 + 2 \times 4x\)
practice.worked_solution: Multiply before adding: \(2 \times 4x = 8x\). Then \(9 + 8x\). 9 and 8x are not like terms, so the answer is \(9 + 8x\).

practice.prompt: Remove the brackets and simplify: \(3(2x + 1) + (x - 5)\)
practice.worked_solution: Expand: \(3(2x+1) = 6x + 3\) and \((x-5) = x - 5\). Together: \(6x + 3 + x - 5\). Collect like terms: \((6x+x) + (3-5) = 7x - 2\).

practice.prompt: A number \(x\) is increased by 3, and then the result is multiplied by 4. Write this as an algebraic expression and simplify it.
practice.worked_solution: "Increased by 3" gives \(x + 3\). "Then multiplied by 4" means the whole sum goes inside a bracket: \(4(x + 3)\). Expanding gives \(4x + 12\).

practice.prompt: The difference between a number \(y\) and 2 is multiplied by 5. Write this as an algebraic expression and simplify it.
practice.worked_solution: "The difference between a number \(y\) and 2" means \(y - 2\). "Multiplied by 5" means the whole difference goes inside a bracket: \(5(y - 2)\). Expanding gives \(5y - 10\).

sections_json.title: Getting the Order Right in Algebra

blocks.text:
When an algebraic expression mixes different operations, you cannot just work from left to right — the order you do them in changes the answer. In algebra, just as in arithmetic, you follow a fixed order:

1. **B**rackets first — work out whatever is inside them.
2. **O**rders (powers and roots), if any.
3. **D**ivision and **M**ultiplication, from left to right.
4. **A**ddition and **S**ubtraction, from left to right.

You can remember this as **BODMAS**. The key rule for algebra is that multiplication and division are done *before* addition and subtraction. So in an expression like `4n + 3n × 10`, you do not add `4n + 3n` first — you must multiply `3n × 10` before you add anything. Brackets, when they appear, override everything and are worked out first.

**Simplify `4n + 3n × 10`.**

There are no brackets, so multiplication comes first.

- Multiply first: `3n × 10 = 30n`
- Now add: `4n + 30n = 34n`

So `4n + 3n × 10 = 34n`. If you had wrongly added first you would have got `7n × 10 = 70n` — a very different result, so the order really matters.

**Simplify `7 × 3a − (3a + 5a) × 2`.**

Here there is a bracket, and BODMAS says it comes first.

- Work out the bracket: `3a + 5a = 8a`
- The expression is now `7 × 3a − 8a × 2`
- Multiply first: `7 × 3a = 21a` and `8a × 2 = 16a`
- Now subtract: `21a − 16a = 5a`

So `7 × 3a − (3a + 5a) × 2 = 5a`.

practice.prompt: Simplify `4n + 3n × 10`.
practice.worked_solution: Multiplication comes before addition: `3n × 10 = 30n`, then `4n + 30n = 34n`.

practice.prompt: Simplify `32 + 8x ÷ 2`.
practice.worked_solution: Division comes before addition: `8x ÷ 2 = 4x`, then `32 + 4x` (the `32` and the `4x` are unlike terms, so they cannot be combined).

practice.prompt: Simplify `3 × 5x + 4x ÷ 2`.
practice.worked_solution: Do the multiplication and division first, left to right: `3 × 5x = 15x` and `4x ÷ 2 = 2x`. Then add: `15x + 2x = 17x`.

practice.prompt: Simplify `36y ÷ 6 + y + 2 × 4y`.
practice.worked_solution: Do the division and multiplication first, left to right: `36y ÷ 6 = 6y` and `2 × 4y = 8y`. The expression becomes `6y + y + 8y`. Now add: `6y + y + 8y = 15y`.

practice.prompt: Simplify `7 × 3a − (3a + 5a) × 2`.
practice.worked_solution: Work out the bracket first: `3a + 5a = 8a`. Now the expression is `7 × 3a − 8a × 2`. Multiply first: `7 × 3a = 21a` and `8a × 2 = 16a`. Then subtract: `21a − 16a = 5a`.

sections_json.title: Removing and Inserting Brackets in Algebra

blocks.text: Brackets are used in algebra to group terms together. When a whole expression sits inside a bracket, everything inside must be treated as one unit. To simplify an expression containing brackets, you first remove the brackets, and then you add or subtract the like terms. The sign that sits just in front of a bracket tells you what to do with the terms inside: - When a plus sign sits in front of the bracket, you may remove the bracket and write each term inside with the sign it already has. - When a minus sign sits in front of the bracket, removing the bracket changes the sign of every term inside: a plus becomes a minus, and a minus becomes a plus. Think of it this way: subtracting a group is the same as subtracting each member of that group one by one. So $-(a + b)$ means $-a - b$, and $-(a - b)$ means $-a + b$. Once the brackets are gone, you simplify by collecting like terms — terms that have exactly the same letter. Add or subtract their numbers and keep the letter unchanged.

Example 1: Simplify $(12a - 7) + (4 - 5a)$. A plus sign is in front of each bracket, so we remove the brackets and keep every sign the same: $$(12a - 7) + (4 - 5a) = 12a - 7 + 4 - 5a$$ Now collect like terms. The terms in $a$ are $12a$ and $-5a$, and the plain numbers are $-7$ and $4$: $$12a - 5a - 7 + 4 = 7a - 3$$ So $(12a - 7) + (4 - 5a) = 7a - 3$. Example 2: Simplify $(8x - 2y) - (9x - 4y)$. The first bracket has a plus sign in front, so its terms stay as they are. The second bracket has a minus sign in front, so every sign inside it must change: $9x$ becomes $-9x$ and $-4y$ becomes $+4y$. $$(8x - 2y) - (9x - 4y) = 8x - 2y - 9x + 4y$$ Collect the like terms: $$8x - 9x - 2y + 4y = -x + 2y$$ So $(8x - 2y) - (9x - 4y) = -x + 2y$, which is often written $2y - x$.

Inserting a bracket is the reverse process. When you need to put brackets around part of an expression, you work out what sign must go in front of the bracket so that the expression inside changes correctly. - To insert a bracket with a plus sign in front, simply write the bracket and keep every term's sign the same as it was. - To insert a bracket with a minus sign in front, every term that goes inside must have its sign changed — because removing that bracket later would flip the signs back to what you started with. For example, suppose you want to factor a pair of terms out of $10a - 5b - 3$ so that the last two terms sit in a bracket after a minus sign. You want to write $$10a - (5b + 3)$$ Check it: removing the bracket gives $10a - 5b - 3$, exactly the original expression. Because the minus sign is in front, the $5b$ and the $3$ both had their signs changed (both were plus in the bracket, and both come out as minus). That is how you know the bracket was inserted correctly.

practice.worked_solution:
The first number $12$ has no bracket around it, so it stays. The first bracket has a minus sign in front, so $7 - 2f$ becomes $-7 + 2f$. The second bracket also has a minus sign in front, so $3 - f$ becomes $-3 + f$. Together:

$$12 - (7 - 2f) - (3 - f) = 12 - 7 + 2f - 3 + f$$

Collect the plain numbers $12 - 7 - 3 = 2$, and collect the $f$ terms $2f + f = 3f$:

$$12 - 7 + 2f - 3 + f = 2 + 3f$$

practice.prompt: Simplify $(8a - 5) + (14 - 3a)$.
practice.worked_solution:
A plus sign is in front of each bracket, so remove them and keep every sign the same:

$$(8a - 5) + (14 - 3a) = 8a - 5 + 14 - 3a$$

Collect the $a$ terms $8a - 3a = 5a$, and collect the numbers $-5 + 14 = 9$:

$$8a - 5 + 14 - 3a = 5a + 9$$

practice.prompt: Insert a bracket around the last two terms of $14a - 6b - 4$ so that a minus sign stands in front of the bracket, keeping the value the same.
practice.worked_solution:
Write the first term $14a$ as it is, then place the bracket after the minus sign. The two terms that go inside are $-6b$ and $-4$, but because a minus sign will sit in front of the bracket, their signs must be changed inside the bracket: $-6b$ becomes $+6b$ and $-4$ becomes $+4$. So the result is

$$14a - (6b + 4)$$

Check by removing the bracket: $14a - 6b - 4$, which matches the original expression.

sections_json.title: Turning Word Problems into Algebraic Expressions

blocks.text:
A word problem gives you information in sentences, and your job is to turn those sentences into algebra before you do any simplifying. The key is to read carefully and decide what each part means.

Here is how to translate common phrases:

- "A pen costs h naira" — the unknown quantity h stands for the pen's price.
- "20 less than a pen" — take the pen's price and subtract 20, so it becomes h − 20.
- "A crayon costs ₦20 less than a pen" — the crayon costs h − 20 naira.
- "The total cost of the two" — add the two costs together.
- "3 more than something" — add 3; "3 less than something" — subtract 3.
- "twice a number" — multiply by 2; "half of a number" — divide by 2.

So a sentence like "a pencil costs ₦5 less than a pen that costs h naira" becomes h − 5. Once you have written the algebra, you simplify it the same way you have been doing all along.

Example 1
A pen costs h naira and a crayon costs ₦20 less than a pen.

(a) Find the cost of a crayon.
The crayon costs ₦20 less than the pen, so subtract 20 from the pen's price:
Cost of a crayon = h − 20 naira.

(b) Find the total cost of a crayon and a pen.
Add the pen's cost and the crayon's cost:
Total = h + (h − 20) = h + h − 20 = 2h − 20 naira.

Example 2
Envelopes cost d naira per pack, and 4 notebooks cost ₦20 more than a pack of envelopes. Find the total cost of a pack of envelopes and the notebooks.

The envelopes cost d naira.
The notebooks cost ₦20 more than the envelopes, so they cost d + 20 naira.
Total cost = d + (d + 20) = d + d + 20 = 2d + 20 naira.

Notice in both examples that you write the phrase as an expression first, then collect the like terms to simplify.

practice.prompt: A pencil costs ₦x and a pen costs ₦8 more than a pencil. Write an expression for the total cost of the pencil and the pen, and simplify it.
practice.worked_solution: The pen costs ₦8 more than the pencil, so the pen costs x + 8. The total is the pencil plus the pen: x + (x + 8) = x + x + 8 = 2x + 8.

practice.prompt: A packet of biscuits costs k naira and a loaf of bread costs ₦12 less than a packet of biscuits. Find, in terms of k, the total cost of the biscuit packet and the loaf of bread.
practice.worked_solution: The bread costs ₦12 less than the biscuits, so it costs k − 12. The total is k + (k − 12) = k + k − 12 = 2k − 12.

practice.prompt: A pen and a pencil together cost ₦x. If the pen costs ₦y, write an expression for the cost of 3 pencils.
practice.worked_solution: The pen and pencil together cost x, and the pen costs y, so one pencil costs x − y. Three pencils cost 3 × (x − y) = 3(x − y) naira.

blocks.text: When an algebraic expression contains several operations, you must do them in a fixed order so that everyone gets the same answer. Work out any **brackets** first, then do **multiplication and division** from left to right, and finally **addition and subtraction** from left to right. In algebra, remember that a term like $3x$ means $3 \times x$. So $3x \times 2$ really means $3 \times x \times 2$, and $17y - 5 \times 2y$ means you must do the multiplication $5 \times 2y$ before you subtract. Likewise, $7x \div x$ means $7 \times x \div x$, which simplifies because the $x$'s cancel.

**Example 1 — finding values in order** (a) $18 - 6 \times 2$ Multiply first: $6 \times 2 = 12$, then subtract. $18 - 12 = 6$ (b) $6 - 18 \div 3$ Divide first: $18 \div 3 = 6$, then subtract. $6 - 6 = 0$ (c) $6 \times 2 - 2 - 40 \div 4$ Do the multiplication and division first: $6 \times 2 = 12$ and $40 \div 4 = 10$, then subtract left to right. $12 - 2 - 10 = 10 - 10 = 0$

**Example 2 — simplifying expressions** (a) $3x \times 2 + 5x$ Multiply first: $3x \times 2 = 6x$. Then add the like terms. $6x + 5x = 11x$ (b) $17y - 5 \times 2y$ Multiply first: $5 \times 2y = 10y$. Then subtract the like terms. $17y - 10y = 7y$

**Example 3 — division and brackets** (a) $7x \div x + 5$ Divide first: $7x \div x = 7$ (the $x$'s cancel). Then add. $7 + 5 = 12$ (b) $4x - (6 \div 3)$ Work inside the bracket first: $6 \div 3 = 2$. Then subtract. $4x - 2$ (c) $(24x \div 6) + x + (1 \times 5x)$ Work the brackets first: $24x \div 6 = 4x$ and $1 \times 5x = 5x$. Then add the like terms. $4x + x + 5x = 5x + 5x = 10x$

practice.prompt: Simplify $4n + 3n \times 10$
practice.worked_solution: Multiply first: $3n \times 10 = 30n$. Then add the like terms: $4n + 30n = 34n$.

practice.prompt: Simplify $32 + 8x \div 2$
practice.worked_solution: Divide first: $8x \div 2 = 4x$. Then add: $32 + 4x$. The terms are not alike, so they cannot be combined further.

practice.prompt: Simplify $3 \times 5x + 4x \div 2$
practice.worked_solution: Do the multiplication and division first: $3 \times 5x = 15x$ and $4x \div 2 = 2x$. Then add the like terms: $15x + 2x = 17x$.

practice.prompt: Simplify $36y \div 6 + y + 2 \times 4y$
practice.worked_solution: Do the division and multiplication first: $36y \div 6 = 6y$ and $2 \times 4y = 8y$. Then add the like terms: $6y + y + 8y = 15y$.

blocks.text: When an algebraic expression has brackets, you often want to remove them so you can collect like terms. Two rules tell you exactly what happens when the bracket comes off. Rule 1 — a + sign in front of a bracket. A plus sign before a bracket does not change any sign inside the bracket. Every term inside keeps its own sign as the bracket is removed. Rule 2 — a − sign in front of a bracket. A minus sign before a bracket changes every sign inside it: each + becomes −, and each − becomes +. Before you start, always check whether the terms inside the bracket can be simplified first — if they can, do that first, then remove the bracket.

Example 1 — removing a bracket after a + Simplify 6x + (3 - x). The + before the bracket keeps the signs unchanged: 6x + (3 - x) = 6x + 3 - x Now collect the like terms: 6x - x + 3 = 5x + 3 So 6x + (3 - x) = 5x + 3. Example 2 — removing a bracket after a − Simplify 10d - (9c - 4d). The − before the bracket flips every sign inside: +9c becomes -9c and -4d becomes +4d. 10d - (9c - 4d) = 10d - 9c + 4d Collect the like terms: 10d + 4d - 9c = 14d - 9c So 10d - (9c - 4d) = 14d - 9c. Example 3 — two brackets Simplify (6x - y) - (4x - 5y). Remove the first bracket: the + in front of it keeps signs unchanged, so it stays 6x - y. Remove the second bracket: the − flips each sign, so 4x becomes -4x and -5y becomes +5y. 6x - y - 4x + 5y Collect the like terms: 6x - 4x + 5y - y = 2x + 4y = 2(x + 2y) So (6x - y) - (4x - 5y) = 2x + 4y, or 2(x + 2y).

practice.prompt: Simplify $(12a - 7) + (4 - 5a)$.
practice.worked_solution: Remove the bracket: the $+$ before it keeps every sign unchanged, so $12a - 7 + 4 - 5a$. Collect like terms: $12a - 5a = 7a$ and $-7 + 4 = -3$. So the expression is $7a - 3$.

practice.prompt: Simplify $(8x - 2y) - (9x - 4y)$.
practice.worked_solution: Remove the first bracket (a $+$ before it): $8x - 2y$. Remove the second bracket (a $-$ before it): each sign flips, so $-(9x - 4y)$ becomes $-9x + 4y$. Together: $8x - 2y - 9x + 4y$. Collect like terms: $8x - 9x = -x$ and $-2y + 4y = 2y$. So the expression is $-x + 2y$.

Remove the first bracket (a $-$ before it): $12 - 7 + 2f$. Remove the second bracket (also a $-$ before it): $-(3 - f)$ becomes $-3 + f$. Together: $12 - 7 + 2f - 3 + f$. Collect like terms: the numbers give $12 - 7 - 3 = 2$, and the $f$ terms give $2f + f = 3f$. So the expression is $2 + 3f$.

practice.prompt: Simplify $(8a - 5) + (14 - 3a)$.
practice.worked_solution: Remove the bracket (a $+$ before it keeps every sign unchanged): $8a - 5 + 14 - 3a$. Collect like terms: $8a - 3a = 5a$ and $-5 + 14 = 9$. So the expression is $5a + 9$.

sections_json.title: Turning Word Problems into Algebraic Expressions

blocks.text:
A word problem describes a situation in words, and your job is to turn those words into an algebraic expression. To do this, you decide what each unknown letter stands for, then use the words to build an expression step by step. Two phrases come up again and again:
  • "...less than a..." means you subtract. If a pen costs P naira and a pencil costs 15 naira less, the pencil costs ₦(P − 15).
  • "...more than a..." means you add. If a pencil costs x naira and a rubber costs 40 naira more, the rubber costs ₦(x + 40).
Once you have each separate cost as an expression, you add them together and then simplify by collecting like terms. When an item "joins" a group, add it; when an item "leaves", subtract it.

Example 1 A pen costs ₦P and a pencil costs 15 naira less than a pen. (a) Find the cost of a pencil. (b) Find the cost of a pen and a pencil. Solution Cost of a pen = ₦P (a) A pencil is 15 naira less than a pen, so subtract 15: cost of a pencil = ₦(P − 15) (b) To find both together, add the two costs: cost of a pen and a pencil = ₦P + ₦(P − 15) = ₦P + ₦P − ₦15 = ₦2P − ₦15 = ₦(2P − 15)

Example 2 A pencil costs ₦x and a rubber costs 40 naira more than a pencil. (a) Find the cost of a rubber. (b) Find the cost of a pencil and a rubber. Solution (a) Cost of a pencil = ₦x. A rubber is 40 naira more, so add 40: cost of a rubber = ₦(x + 40) (b) Add the two costs: cost of a pencil and a rubber = ₦x + ₦(x + 40) = ₦(x + x + 40) = ₦(2x + 40)

Example 3 In a class there are x boys and y girls. This semester, 5 boys join and 3 girls leave the class. How many students are now in this class? Solution Total number = number of boys + number of girls. 5 boys join, so the number of boys becomes x + 5. 3 girls leave, so the number of girls becomes y − 3. Total number = (x + 5) + (y − 3) = x + y + 5 − 3 = x + y + 2 So there are now (x + y + 2) students in the class.

practice.prompt: A pen costs h naira and a crayon costs ₦20 less than a pen. (a) Find the cost of a crayon. (b) Find the cost of a crayon and a pen.
practice.worked_solution: A crayon is 20 naira less than a pen, so subtract 20 from the pen's cost: crayon = ₦(h − 20). Together, pen + crayon = ₦h + ₦(h − 20) = ₦h + ₦h − ₦20 = ₦2h − ₦20 = ₦(2h − 20).

practice.prompt: Envelopes cost d naira per pack. A notepad costs 20 naira more than a pack of envelopes. Find the total cost of a pack of envelopes and a notepad.
practice.worked_solution: A notepad is 20 naira more than a pack of envelopes, so it costs ₦(d + 20). Total = pack of envelopes + notepad = ₦d + ₦(d + 20) = ₦(d + d + 20) = ₦(2d + 20).

practice.prompt: A pen and a pencil together cost ₦x. A pen costs ₦y. Find the cost of 3 pencils.
practice.worked_solution: A pen and a pencil cost ₦x, and the pen costs ₦y, so one pencil costs ₦x − ₦y = ₦(x − y). Three pencils cost 3 × ₦(x − y) = ₦3(x − y).
