practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a square whose sides are 8 cm.
practice.worked_solution: Perimeter of a square $= 4L = 4 \times 8 = 32\ \mathrm{cm}$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a rectangle of length 7 cm and breadth 4 cm.
What is the perimeter of a regular pentagon with sides 5 cm?
practice.worked_solution: A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides, so perimeter $= 5 \times 5 = 25\ \mathrm{cm}$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a regular hexagon with sides 5 cm.
practice.worked_solution: A regular hexagon has 6 equal sides, so perimeter $= 6 \times 5 = 30\ \mathrm{cm}$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a parallelogram whose base is 6 cm and sides are 5 cm.
A rectangle is such that its length is twice its breadth. If the breadth is $d$, write down the total length of all four sides in terms of $d$.
practice.worked_solution: Length $= 2d$, breadth $= d$. Perimeter $= 2(\text{length} + \text{breadth}) = 2(2d + d) = 2(3d) = 6d$.

practice.prompt: The circumference of a circle is 22 cm. Find the radius, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.
practice.worked_solution: $2\pi r = 22$, so $2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = 22$, giving $\frac{44r}{7} = 22$. Cross-multiply: $44r = 154$, so $r = \frac{154}{44} = 3.5\ \mathrm{cm}$.

sections_json.title: Cubes and Cuboids: Faces, Edges and Vertices

blocks.text:
Solid shapes that are not flat are called three-dimensional (3D) shapes because they have length, width and height. Two 3D shapes you meet everywhere are the cube and the cuboid. Think of a dice, a Rubik's cube or a box of salt — these are all 3D shapes. To describe any 3D shape, you use three special parts:
  • A face is a flat surface of the shape. When you feel the top of a box, you are touching one of its faces.
  • An edge is a straight line where two faces meet. Run your finger along the corner of a book and you are tracing an edge.
  • A vertex (plural vertices) is a corner, where three or more edges meet. The sharp points of a box are its vertices.
Now let us look closely at a cube. A cube is a special 3D shape where every face is a square and every edge is the same length. Because all its faces are equal squares, a cube looks exactly the same no matter which face you look at. A cube has these properties:
  • 6 faces — all of them squares and all of them the same size.
  • 12 edges — all the same length.
  • 8 vertices — every corner where three edges meet.
A cuboid, sometimes called a rectangular prism or a rectangular box, is like a stretched cube. Its faces are rectangles (though some may be squares), and opposite faces are equal to each other. A shoe box or a book is a cuboid. A cuboid has these properties:
  • 6 faces — they are rectangles; the two opposite faces are equal to each other.
  • 12 edges — but not all the same length; edges come in sets of four equal ones.
  • 8 vertices.
Notice the important difference: both a cube and a cuboid have 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. The difference is in their faces. Every face of a cube is a square, while the faces of a cuboid are rectangles (only some of them might be squares).

Worked Example 1: Describing a cube A student picks up a die. How many faces, edges and vertices does it have, and what shape are its faces? Solution: A die is a cube. A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. Since every face of a cube is a square, the faces are all squares, and they are all the same size. Worked Example 2: Cube or cuboid? Look at these two boxes.
  • Box A is a salt container with all its sides the same length and square faces.
  • Box B is a shoe box with rectangular faces, where opposite faces match.
Which one is a cube and which one is a cuboid? Solution: Box A has equal edges and square faces, so it is a cube. Box B has rectangular faces where only opposite faces are equal, so it is a cuboid. Worked Example 3: Counting edges on a cuboid A cuboid has faces that come in three pairs of equal rectangles. How many edges does it have, and how do the edges group? Solution: A cuboid has 12 edges. They are not all equal. There are four edges along the length, four along the width and four along the height. So the 12 edges come in three sets of 4 equal edges.

practice.prompt: A Rubik's cube is a cube. How many faces, edges and vertices does it have, and what shape are all its faces?
practice.answer: 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices; all faces are squares.
practice.worked_solution: A Rubik's cube is a cube, so it has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. Because every face of a cube is a square, all 6 faces are squares and they are all the same size.

practice.prompt:
State whether each shape is a cube or a cuboid, and give one reason for your choice.
(a) A gift box where every face is a rectangle and opposite faces are equal.
(b) A block where every face is a square and every edge is the same length.
practice.answer: (a) Cuboid — its faces are rectangles with opposite faces equal. (b) Cube — every face is a square and every edge is the same length.
practice.worked_solution: For (a), the faces are rectangles (not all squares) and only opposite faces match, which is the property of a cuboid. For (b), every face is a square and all edges are equal, which is exactly the property of a cube.

practice.prompt: A cuboid has 6 faces and 8 vertices. How many edges does it have? Explain whether all these edges are the same length.
practice.answer: 12 edges. They are not all the same length; they come in three sets of 4 equal edges (length, width and height).
practice.worked_solution: A cuboid, like a cube, has 12 edges. But unlike a cube, the edges are not all equal: there are 4 edges of one length, 4 of another and 4 of a third, matching the three pairs of opposite faces.

sections_json.title: Pyramids and Cones: Faces, Edges and Vertices

blocks.text:
We have looked at cubes and cuboids, where every face is flat and every face is a rectangle or square. Pyramids and cones are different: they rise up to a single point. That point is called the apex (you can also call it the vertex at the top).

Pyramids

A pyramid has one flat base, which can be any polygon (a triangle, a square, a pentagon, and so on). Every other face of a pyramid is a triangle, and all those triangles meet together at the apex above the base. To count the parts of a pyramid, look at the shape of its base. Suppose the base has n sides:
  • Faces: the base is 1 face, plus one triangular face for each side of the base, so the total is n + 1 faces.
  • Edges: the base has n edges around its rim, and each of those base corners sends one sloping edge up to the apex, giving another n edges. Total is 2n edges.
  • Vertices: the base has n corners, plus the apex at the top, giving n + 1 vertices.
For example, a square-based pyramid has a square base, so n = 4. That gives 4 + 1 = 5 faces, 2 × 4 = 8 edges, and 4 + 1 = 5 vertices.

Cones

A cone is like a pyramid, but its base is a circle. A cone has:
  • Faces: one flat circular base and one curved surface that tapers to the apex. That is 2 faces.
  • Edge: one edge — the circular rim where the base meets the curved surface.
  • Vertices: just the apex point at the top, so 1 vertex.
Notice the difference: a pyramid's sloping sides are flat triangles, while a cone's sloping surface is curved and smooth, with no corners along the sides.

Example 1 — A triangular-based pyramid A triangular-based pyramid (also called a tetrahedron) has a triangular base, so n = 3.
  • Faces: n + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4 faces (the triangular base plus three triangular sloping faces).
  • Edges: 2n = 2 × 3 = 6 edges.
  • Vertices: n + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4 vertices.
Example 2 — A cone A cone has a circular base, so it is not counted with the formula above (a circle has no corners).
  • Faces: 2 (one circular base and one curved surface).
  • Edges: 1 (the circular rim around the base).
  • Vertices: 1 (the apex at the top).

practice.prompt: A square-based pyramid has a square base. How many faces, edges, and vertices does it have?
practice.worked_solution: The base is a square, so n = 4. Faces = n + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5. Edges = 2n = 2 × 4 = 8. Vertices = n + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5.

practice.prompt: A hexagonal-based pyramid has a hexagonal base (a base with 6 sides). Find the number of faces, edges, and vertices of this pyramid.
practice.worked_solution: The base has n = 6 sides. Faces = n + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7. Edges = 2n = 2 × 6 = 12. Vertices = n + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7.

practice.prompt: State the number of faces, edges, and vertices of a cone.
practice.worked_solution: A cone has one flat circular base and one curved surface: that is 2 faces. The circular rim where the base meets the curved surface is its 1 edge. Its only vertex is the apex at the top.

sections_json.title: Cubes and Cuboids: Faces, Edges and Vertices

blocks.text:
In this section you will learn to pick out the properties of a cube and a cuboid. You already know that a cube and a cuboid are different — here we will look at exactly what makes each one what it is.

Every solid shape can be described by three kinds of parts:
- A **face** is a flat surface of the shape.
- An **edge** is a line where two faces meet.
- A **vertex** (plural **vertices**) is a corner where edges meet.

Now let us examine the cube.

**The cube**

A cube has 6 faces. Every face is a square, and all six squares are exactly the same size. This is what makes a cube a cube — every face is an identical square.

A cube has 12 edges. All 12 edges are the same length, because every face is the same square.

A cube has 8 vertices. Each corner of the cube is a vertex, and there are 8 of them (4 on top and 4 at the bottom).

So a cube has:
- 6 faces (all squares, all equal)
- 12 edges (all equal)
- 8 vertices

**The cuboid**

A cuboid also has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices — the same numbers as a cube. So what is the difference?

The difference is the shape of the faces. A cuboid's faces are **rectangles**, not squares. Usually the faces come in matching pairs: the two faces at the front and back are the same, the two at the sides are the same, and the two at the top and bottom are the same. The edges are not all equal — the cuboid has a length, a breadth and a height, and each is a different size.

So a cuboid has:
- 6 faces (all rectangles, in matching pairs)
- 12 edges (not all equal — length, breadth and height)
- 8 vertices

The handy way to remember the numbers: a cube and a cuboid both have **6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices**. They differ only in the shape of their faces — squares for the cube, rectangles for the cuboid.

**Worked example: reading the properties off a cuboid**

Think of a cuboid like a shoe box. Count its parts.

- **Faces:** a shoe box has a top, a bottom, a front, a back, and two sides — that is 6 faces. The front and back are the same rectangle, the two sides are the same rectangle, and the top and bottom are the same rectangle.
- **Edges:** every face is a rectangle with 4 sides, but each edge is shared by two faces. Count them by going around: 4 edges around the top, 4 around the bottom, and 4 joining the top to the bottom. That gives 12 edges in total.
- **Vertices:** there are 4 corners on the top and 4 on the bottom — 8 vertices in total.

So the cuboid has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices, exactly like a cube. The only difference is that its faces are rectangles (in matching pairs), and its edges are not all equal.

practice.prompt: How many vertices has a cuboid?

A cube and a cuboid both have the same number of faces, edges and vertices. Write down those three numbers, and then state the one thing that makes a cube different from a cuboid.
practice.answer: Both have 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. The cube's 6 faces are all equal squares, while the cuboid's 6 faces are rectangles (in matching pairs).

Each has 6 faces (the cube's are equal squares, the cuboid's are rectangles in matching pairs), 12 edges (the cube's are all equal, the cuboid's are not all equal), and 8 vertices. The difference is the shape of the faces: squares for the cube, rectangles for the cuboid.

sections_json.title: Pyramids and Cones: Meeting Their Parts

blocks.text:
A pyramid and a cone both taper up to a single point, but their bases are different, and that changes what you can count on them.

Start with a pyramid. A pyramid has a flat base that is a polygon — a triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, and so on. From each side of that base rises a triangular face, and all those triangular faces lean in to meet at one point on top, called the apex. So a pyramid is named by the shape of its base: a pyramid with a square base is a square-based pyramid, one with a hexagonal base is a hexagonal-based pyramid.

You can count the parts of any pyramid from its base:
- Faces: the base plus one triangular face for every side of the base. A square-based pyramid has 1 square base + 4 triangles = 5 faces.
- Vertices: the apex plus one corner for each corner of the base. A square-based pyramid has 1 + 4 = 5 vertices.
- Edges: the edges around the base, plus one edge from each base corner up to the apex. A square-based pyramid has 4 + 4 = 8 edges.

A special pyramid is the tetrahedron — a triangular-based pyramid. Its base is a triangle, so it has 1 + 3 = 4 faces, 1 + 3 = 4 vertices, and 3 + 3 = 6 edges.

A cone is different from a pyramid because its base is a circle, not a polygon. A cone has:
- One circular base.
- One curved surface that sweeps from the rim of the circle up to the apex — the pointed tip.
- One vertex, the apex itself.
- One edge — the circular rim where the curved surface meets the base.

So the quickest difference to remember: a pyramid is built from flat faces on a polygon base, while a cone is built from one flat circular base and one curved surface.

Worked example — a square-based pyramid

Take a pyramid whose base is a square. List its faces, vertices and edges.

The base is a square, which has 4 sides. The pyramid has that 1 square base, plus 1 triangular face rising from each of the 4 sides, so the faces are 1 + 4 = 5.

The vertices are the apex at the top plus the 4 corners of the square base: 1 + 4 = 5.

The edges are the 4 edges around the square base plus the 4 edges joining each base corner to the apex: 4 + 4 = 8.

So a square-based pyramid has 5 faces, 5 vertices and 8 edges.

blocks.text:
Some shapes are solid: they have length, breadth and height, so they take up space. These are called **three-dimensional** shapes or **solid shapes**. A cube of sugar, a drink can and a match box are all solid shapes.

To describe a solid shape we talk about its **faces**, its **edges** and its **vertices** (one is a *vertex*).

- A **face** (or surface) is a flat or curved side of the shape.
- An **edge** is a line where two faces meet. It may be straight or curved.
- A **vertex** is a point corner where edges meet.

In this section you will learn the properties of a **cube** and a **cuboid** — that is, how many faces, edges and vertices each one has.

A **cube** is the solid shape you know from a cube of sugar. All of its faces are squares, and they are all the same size.

Look at fig-01, which shows a cube drawn as a see-through solid. Count its parts and you will find these properties:

1. It is a solid shape.
2. It has **6 square faces** — every face is a square.
3. It has **12 edges**.
4. It has **8 vertices**.

A **cuboid** is a solid shape like a match box. Its faces are rectangles, and opposite faces are the same size. Fig-02 shows a cuboid, with leader lines naming its **face**, one of its **vertices** and one of its **edges**. A cuboid has these properties:

1. It has **6 faces**.
2. It has **12 edges**.
3. It has **8 vertices**.

blocks.caption: A cube drawn as a see-through solid: two equal squares, the nearer one offset down and to the right of the farther one, with the four pairs of corresponding corners joined.

blocks.text:
**Worked example**

Look at fig-01, the cube. Let us count its properties step by step.

- **Faces.** A face is a flat side. The cube has a top, a bottom, and four sides around it — that is 1 + 1 + 4 = **6** square faces.
- **Edges.** An edge is a line where two faces meet. Each of the two squares in fig-01 has four sides, and the four corners are joined, so the cube has 4 + 4 + 4 = **12 edges**.
- **Vertices.** A vertex is a point corner where edges meet. The two squares in fig-01 have four corners each, so the cube has 4 + 4 = **8 vertices**.

Now look at fig-02, the cuboid. It has the same number of parts: **6** faces (all rectangles), **12** edges and **8** vertices. The only difference is that a cube's faces are all squares, while a cuboid's faces are rectangles.

blocks.text: A pyramid is named after the shape of its base. Look at fig-03, fig-04, fig-05 and fig-06: the triangular base pyramid (fig-03), the square base pyramid (fig-04), the pentagonal based pyramid (fig-05) and the rectangular based pyramid (fig-06). blocks.text:
Three-dimensional shapes are shapes that have length, breadth and height. Because they have all three, they are also called solid shapes. A solid shape can be regular or irregular. Regular shapes have a tidy, fixed form — a cube of sugar, a can of drink and a match box are all regular shapes. Irregular shapes are not tidy — a stone or a tree is irregular.

In this section you will learn the properties of two regular solids: the cube and the cuboid.

Before you read the properties, settle three words that describe any solid: - A face (or surface) is a flat or curved side of a solid. - An edge is a line where two faces meet. It may be straight or curved. - A vertex is a point corner where edges meet. The plural of vertex is vertices.

Look at fig-01. It shows a cube drawn as a see-through solid — two equal squares, one nearer to you and one farther away, with the four pairs of matching corners joined. Every face of a cube is an equal square.

A cube has these properties:

1. It is a solid shape.
2. It has 6 square faces.
3. It has 12 edges.
4. It has 8 vertices.

Count them on fig-01 if you like: six faces, twelve edges and eight vertices.

blocks.caption: A cube drawn as a see-through solid: two equal squares, the nearer one offset down and to the right of the farther one, with the four pairs of corresponding corners joined.

blocks.text:
Now look at fig-02, a cuboid drawn the same way — wide and shallow. Three leader lines point to the top face, the nearer top-right vertex, and the nearer right-hand vertical edge, so you can see where the faces, vertices and edges sit.

A cuboid has these properties:

1. It has 6 faces.
2. It has 12 edges.
3. It has 8 vertices.

Notice the counts: the cube and the cuboid both have 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. What makes a cube special is that all six of its faces are equal squares; a cuboid's faces can be rectangles, so it does not have to be the same on every side.

practice.answer: Face (a flat or curved side), edge (a line where two faces meet), vertex (a point corner where edges meet).

sections_json.title: Pyramids and Cones: Faces, Edges and Vertices

blocks.text: A pyramid gets its name from the shape of its base. Look at the triangular based pyramid in fig-03, the square based pyramid in fig-04, the pentagonal based pyramid in fig-05, and the rectangular based pyramid in fig-06. In every one, the sides rise from the base and meet at a single point at the top, called the apex. So a pyramid with a square base is called a square based pyramid, a pyramid with a triangular base is a triangular based pyramid, and so on. A triangular based pyramid has a special name of its own — a tetrahedron.

blocks.caption: A rectangular based pyramid, drawn like the square one but on a base wider than it is tall.

A pentagonal based pyramid. The base is drawn as a pentagon standing on one side with its fifth vertex uppermost, and the apex above is joined to that vertex, to the two vertices either side of it, and to the lower-right vertex — four edges from the apex, the last of them crossing the face of the solid.
A square base pyramid. The base is drawn as an upright rectangle and the apex above is joined to all four of its corners, so two edges run outside the rectangle and two cross it.
A triangular base pyramid. The base triangle is drawn in perspective, its third vertex raised into the middle of the figure, and the apex above is joined to all three base vertices.

blocks.text:
Every solid shape can be described by counting its faces (the flat surfaces), its edges (the lines where two faces meet), and its vertices (the corners). The table below counts these for the pyramids you have seen.

| Shape | Faces | Edges | Vertices |
|---|---|---|---|
| Triangular based Pyramid | 4 | 6 | 4 |
| Square based Pyramid | 5 | 8 | 5 |
| Pentagonal base Pyramid | 6 | 10 | 6 |
| Rectangular based Pyramid | 5 | 8 | 5 |

Notice the pattern: the number of faces, edges and vertices all grow together as the base gains more sides. A square based pyramid and a rectangular based pyramid each have the same counts — 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices — because each base has four sides. A pentagonal based pyramid, with a five-sided base, has one more of each: 6 faces, 10 edges and 6 vertices.

A cone is different from a pyramid, as you can see in fig-07. Its base is a flat circular face, and from it a single curved surface runs up to a pointed top. A cone has:

1. Two faces — one curved face and one flat face.
2. One edge — the circular line where the flat base meets the curved surface.
3. One vertex — the pointed top.

blocks.caption: Two drawings side by side. On the left an upright cone: an elliptical base with the two slant sides running up from the ends of the ellipse to the apex. On the right a cone lying on its side, apex at the left, its two slant sides reaching a narrow upright ellipse whose top and bottom then continue as two parallel lines to a second narrow ellipse further right.

blocks.text:
Example. A hexagonal based pyramid has a base with six sides. How many faces, edges and vertices does it have?

Follow the pattern you saw in the table. The number of sides on the base gives the number of vertices: the base has six corners, and the apex adds one more, so the pyramid has 6 + 1 = 7 vertices. Its faces are the six triangular side faces plus the base itself, giving 6 + 1 = 7 faces. Each of the six base vertices joins the apex with one edge, and the base itself has six edges around it, so the pyramid has 6 + 6 = 12 edges.

So a hexagonal based pyramid has 7 faces, 12 edges and 7 vertices.

The circular line where the flat base meets the curved surface is the single edge, and the pointed top is the single vertex.

practice.worked_solution: A tetrahedron is a triangular based pyramid. From the table, a triangular based pyramid has 4 vertices.

blocks.text: Two solid shapes you meet all the time are the cylinder and the sphere. Let's look closely at what makes each one special, so you can pick them out anywhere. A cylinder has two identical flat circular faces, one at the top and one at the bottom. These two circles are called the bases. The two bases are joined by a single curved surface that wraps all the way around. A cylinder has no sharp points (no vertices), but it does have two edges — the two circular rims where the curved surface meets each base. Because of that curved surface, a cylinder can roll along the ground, but only in a straight line (it rolls end over end, not in all directions). Think of a tin of baked beans or a drinking glass. A sphere is perfectly round — every point on its surface is exactly the same distance from its centre. That fixed distance is called the radius. A sphere has no flat faces, no edges, and no vertices at all. Because it has only one continuous curved surface, a sphere rolls in every direction. Think of a football or a tennis ball. Here is a quick way to tell them apart: a sphere is the only shape that rolls freely in every direction and has no flat face, no edge, and no corner. A cylinder has exactly two flat circular faces, two circular edges, and no corners.

Volume is the amount of space a solid takes up, and we measure it in cubic units such as cm³ or m³. Three box-like solids have a simple volume formula you can rely on. A cube is a solid where every edge is the same length. If its edge is s, then its volume is: Volume of cube = s × s × s = s³ A cuboid (a rectangular box) has three different edges — length l, width w and height h. Its volume is: Volume of cuboid = l × w × h A prism is any solid that has the same shape all the way through from one end to the other. The two ends are identical polygons, and they are joined by flat rectangular faces. The volume of any prism is: Volume of prism = area of the cross‑section × length The cross‑section is the shape of the two identical ends — for example, if a prism has a triangular end, you first find the area of that triangle and then multiply by the prism's length. So a cuboid is actually a prism whose cross‑section is a rectangle, and the rule "area of cross‑section × length" gives the same result as l × w × h.

Worked Example 1 — Properties of a cylinder A tin of soup has two flat circular ends and one curved surface that joins them. How many faces, edges and vertices does it have? The two circular ends are flat faces, and the curved surface is not flat but it is still one surface. So there are 3 faces in total. There are two circular edges — the rim where the curved surface meets each circular base. There are no vertices, because no flat faces meet at a point. Worked Example 2 — Volume of a cube Find the volume of a cube with edge 4 cm. Volume = s × s × s = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cm³. Worked Example 3 — Volume of a cuboid A box is 5 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm high. Find its volume. Volume = l × w × h = 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 cm³. Worked Example 4 — Volume of a prism A triangular prism has a triangular end whose area is 8 cm² and a length of 6 cm. Find its volume. Volume = area of cross‑section × length = 8 × 6 = 48 cm³.

practice.answer: It is a sphere, because a sphere has no flat faces, no edges and no vertices, and it rolls freely in every direction.

practice.worked_solution: Volume of a cube = s × s × s = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 cm³.

practice.worked_solution: Volume of a cuboid = l × w × h = 8 × 4 × 3 = 96 cm³.

sections_json.title: Volume of Cubes, Cuboids and Prisms

blocks.text:
Volume is the amount of space a solid takes up. It is measured in cubic units, like cubic centimetres (cm³) or cubic metres (m³).

A **cube** has every edge the same length. If the edge is \(a\), then:
\[ \text{Volume} = a \times a \times a = a^3 \]

A **cuboid** (a rectangular box) has three different edge lengths: length \(l\), width \(w\) and height \(h\). Its volume is:
\[ \text{Volume} = l \times w \times h \]

A **prism** is a solid with the same shape (a face) all the way through. A cube and a cuboid are both prisms. For any prism, the volume is found by multiplying the area of the end face (the cross-section) by the length (or height):
\[ \text{Volume} = \text{area of cross-section} \times \text{length} \]

So the same rule works for a cube, a cuboid and any other prism: find the area of the end face, then multiply by how long the prism is.

**Example 1: a cube**
A cube has edges of length 5 cm. Find its volume.

\[ \text{Volume} = a^3 = 5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125 \]
The volume is **125 cm³**.

**Example 2: a cuboid**
A cuboid is 8 cm long, 3 cm wide and 4 cm high. Find its volume.

\[ \text{Volume} = l \times w \times h = 8 \times 3 \times 4 = 96 \]
The volume is **96 cm³**.

**Example 3: a prism**
A triangular prism has a triangular end face with area 12 cm² and is 7 cm long. Find its volume.

\[ \text{Volume} = \text{area of cross-section} \times \text{length} = 12 \times 7 = 84 \]
The volume is **84 cm³**.

practice.worked_solution: Volume of a cube = edge × edge × edge = 6 × 6 × 6 = 216. The volume is 216 cm³.

practice.worked_solution: Volume of a cuboid = length × width × height = 10 × 4 × 3 = 120. The volume is 120 cm³.

sections_json.title: Cylinders and Spheres: Getting to Know Their Shapes

blocks.text:
Two shapes you see every day are the cylinder and the sphere. A tin of baked beans or a toilet roll is a cylinder; a football or an orange is a sphere. They are three-dimensional shapes, so they take up space, and each has its own special set of properties. Let us look at each one carefully. The cylinder Picture a tin of baked beans. A cylinder has two flat circular faces — one at the top and one at the bottom. These two circles are equal in size and lie parallel to each other. Between them runs a curved surface that joins the two circles, like the curved side of the tin. So a cylinder has:
  • two circular faces (the top and the bottom), equal and parallel;
  • one curved surface (the side);
  • no vertices (no sharp corner points);
  • two circular edges (the rims where each circular face meets the curved side).
If you count all the surfaces, a cylinder has 2 flat circular faces and 1 curved surface — 3 surfaces in all. The sphere Now picture a football. A sphere is perfectly round — every point on its surface is the same distance from its centre. A sphere has no flat faces, no edges and no corners. It is just one single curved surface that curves all the way around, with no starting or ending point.

Worked example Is this statement true or false? “A cylinder has two circular faces and one curved surface.” Answer: True. The two circular faces are the top and bottom of the cylinder, and the curved surface is the side that joins them. The statement describes the cylinder correctly. Worked example A ball has no flat faces, no edges and no vertices. Name the three-dimensional shape it is, and say how many surfaces it has. Answer: The ball is a sphere. It has just one surface — a single curved surface that wraps all the way around it.

practice.prompt: A solid cylinder has two circular faces (the top and the bottom) and one curved surface. How many faces does a cylinder have altogether?
practice.answer: A cylinder has 2 faces (the two circular faces — the top and the bottom). The curved side is a curved surface, not counted as a flat face.
practice.worked_solution: The word "faces" means the flat circular surfaces. A cylinder has one at the top and one at the bottom, so it has 2 faces. The curved side is a curved surface, not a flat face, so it is not included in the count of faces.

practice.prompt: How many circular faces does a solid cylinder have?
practice.answer: A solid cylinder has 2 circular faces — one at the top and one at the bottom.

practice.prompt: A sphere has no flat faces, no edges and no vertices. What is the name of its only surface?
practice.answer: It is a curved surface — one single curved surface that wraps all the way around the sphere.

sections_json.title: Finding the Volume of Cubes, Cuboids and Prisms

blocks.text:
Volume tells you how much space a solid shape takes up. You measure it in cubic units, such as cubic centimetres (cm³) or cubic metres (m³). To find the volume of a cube or a cuboid, you multiply its length, its width and its height together. Think of a cuboid as a stack of cubes. A cuboid that is 4 cm long, 2 cm wide and 3 cm high can be pictured as 3 layers, each layer holding 4 × 2 = 8 cubes. That gives 3 × 8 = 24 cubes, so its volume is 24 cm³. What you have done is simply multiply the three dimensions:
Volume of a cuboid = length × width × height
A cube is just a cuboid whose length, width and height are all the same size. So if a cube has edges of length s, its volume is:
Volume of a cube = s × s × s = s³
A prism is a solid with two identical, parallel faces (its bases) joined by flat rectangular sides. The volume of any prism is found by multiplying the area of one base by the height of the prism:
Volume of a prism = area of base × height
A cuboid is itself a prism whose base is a rectangle, so its base area is length × width, and multiplying by the height gives exactly the same formula as before.

Worked example 1: the volume of a cuboid Find the volume of a cuboid that is 8 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high. Use Volume = length × width × height. Volume = 8 × 4 × 3 = 32 × 3 = 96 cm³. So the cuboid takes up 96 cm³ of space. Worked example 2: the volume of a cube Find the volume of a cube whose edges are each 4 cm long. Use Volume = s³ = s × s × s. Volume = 4 × 4 × 4 = 16 × 4 = 64 cm³. So the cube takes up 64 cm³ of space. Worked example 3: the volume of a prism A triangular prism has a base of area 12 cm² and a height of 5 cm. Find its volume. Use Volume = area of base × height. Volume = 12 × 5 = 60 cm³. So the prism takes up 60 cm³ of space.

practice.prompt: Find the volume of a cuboid that is 8 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high.
practice.worked_solution: Volume = length × width × height = 8 × 4 × 3 = 96 cm³.

practice.prompt: Find the volume of a cuboid with dimensions 5 m by 2 m by 3 m.
practice.worked_solution: Volume = length × width × height = 5 × 2 × 3 = 30 m³.

practice.prompt: What is the volume of a cube of edges 4 cm × 4 cm × 4 cm?
practice.worked_solution: Volume of a cube = s³ = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cm³.

practice.prompt: A rectangular tank is 6 m long and 2 m wide and holds 36 m³ of water when full. How deep is the water in the tank?
practice.worked_solution: The tank is a cuboid, so Volume = length × width × depth. Here 36 = 6 × 2 × depth = 12 × depth. So depth = 36 ÷ 12 = 3 m.

sections_json.title: Cylinders and Spheres: Shapes That Are Curved

blocks.text: Two three-dimensional shapes you meet all the time are the cylinder and the sphere. A drinks tin is a cylinder; a ball is a sphere. Even though they look quite different from the cubes and cuboids you already know, you can describe each one by its faces, edges and vertices. Look at the cylinder in fig-01. A cylinder stands on a circular base and has a circular top. That means it has two circular faces — one on the top and one on the bottom. Around the outside, between those two circles, runs a single smooth surface that curves all the way round: the curved face. So a solid cylinder has three faces altogether — two circular and one curved. Now count edges and vertices. The curved face meets the top circle along one edge and the bottom circle along another, so a cylinder has two curved edges. But where do the faces come together to make a point? They never do — the curved face simply wraps around. So a cylinder has no vertex.

blocks.caption: A cylinder drawn upright: an ellipse for the top face, two vertical sides falling from its ends, and a curve closing the base.

blocks.text: Now turn to the sphere in fig-02. A sphere is the shape of a ball — every point on its surface is the same distance from its centre. Because of that, a sphere looks identical from every direction: it is symmetrical from all directions. Unlike the cylinder, a sphere has no flat face at all. Its whole surface is one single curved surface. And because there is nothing flat and no line where faces meet, a sphere has no edge and no vertex.

blocks.caption: A sphere drawn as a circle with an ellipse across its middle to show the curved surface.

practice.prompt: 1. How many circular faces does a solid cylinder have?
practice.answer: A solid cylinder has 2 circular faces — one on the top and one on the bottom.

practice.prompt: 2. How many faces does a cylinder have altogether?
practice.answer: A cylinder has 3 faces altogether: 2 circular faces and 1 curved face.

practice.prompt: 3. Does a sphere have any edges or vertices?
practice.answer: No. A sphere has no edge and no vertex — its whole surface is one curved surface.

sections_json.title: Volume of a Cube, a Cuboid and a Prism

blocks.text:
Volume is the amount of space a three-dimensional shape fills, and we measure it in cubic units such as cm³ or m³. For a cuboid, think of the base as being made of layers that are stacked up to the height, so the volume is found by multiplying its three dimensions together:

Volume of cuboid = length × breadth × height = l × b × h

A cube is a special cuboid whose three sides are all the same length, so we simply multiply the side by itself three times:

Volume of cube = length × length × length = l³

Calculate the volume of a cuboid of length 3cm, breadth 2cm and height 8cm.

Volume of cuboid = l × b × h
= 3cm × 2cm × 8cm
= 48cm³

Sometimes you know the volume and the base, and you need to find the height. The volume of a cuboid is 24cm³ and its base is 6cm by 2cm. Find its height.

Volume = l × b × h
24cm³ = 6cm × 2cm × h
24cm³ = 12cm² × h

Divide both sides by 12cm²:
24cm³ ÷ 12cm² = h
2cm = h

So the height of the cuboid is 2cm.

Calculate the volume of a cube of side 3cm.

Volume of cube = l³
= 3cm × 3cm × 3cm
= 27cm³

A prism has a uniform cross-section, so its volume is found by multiplying the area of its base by the height (the distance it runs back). Look at the triangular prism in fig-03. Its end is a triangle with base 5m and height 3m, and the prism runs back 10m.

First find the area of the triangular face:
Area of triangle = ½ × b × h = ½ × 5m × 3m = 7.5m²

Then find the volume:
Volume of prism = area of base × height
= 7.5m² × 10m
= 75m³

blocks.caption: A triangular prism lying on its rectangular face. The triangular end has a base of 5 m and a height of 3 m, and the prism runs back 10 m.

practice.worked_solution: Volume = l × b × h = 5m × 2m × 3m = 30m³.

practice.worked_solution: Volume = l³ = 4cm × 4cm × 4cm = 64cm³.

blocks.text:
In this section you will learn to identify the properties of two solid shapes: the cylinder and the sphere. You already know the cube, cuboid, pyramid and cone; now we look at shapes whose faces curve.

A **cylinder** looks like a tin can or a drum. Look at the cylinder in fig-01: it has a circular top, a circular base, and a curved side joining them. From the figure you can read off its properties:

1. It has **two circular faces** (the top and the base) and **one curved face**.
2. It has **no vertex** (no corner where edges meet).
3. It has **two curved edges** (the circles where the curved face meets the top face and the base).
4. Altogether it has **three faces**.

A **sphere** looks like a ball. Look at the sphere in fig-02. Its properties are:

1. It is **symmetrical from all directions** — turn it any way and it looks the same.
2. It has **no edge** and **no vertex**.
3. It has **one curved surface**.

blocks.caption: A sphere drawn as a circle with an ellipse across its middle to show the curved surface.
A cylinder drawn upright: an ellipse for the top face, two vertical sides falling from its ends, and a curve closing the base.

blocks.text:
Let us compare a cylinder and a sphere side by side.

**Example.** Count the faces, edges and vertices of a cylinder.

In fig-01 you can see the two circular ends and the curved side between them. So the cylinder has:

- Faces: two circular faces plus one curved face = **3 faces**
- Edges: two curved edges (where the curved face meets each circular face)
- Vertices: none

**Example.** Count the faces, edges and vertices of a sphere.

In fig-02 the sphere has only its curved surface. So:

- Faces: **1 curved face**
- Edges: none
- Vertices: none

Notice the difference: the cylinder has two curved edges and no vertex, while the sphere has no edge at all.

practice.prompt: 1. How many circular faces does a solid cylinder have?
practice.worked_solution: A solid cylinder has a circular top and a circular base. Each is a circular face, so there are 2 circular faces.

practice.prompt: 2. A cylinder has how many faces altogether?
practice.answer: Three faces (two circular faces and one curved face).
practice.worked_solution: The cylinder has two circular faces (top and base) plus one curved face joining them. So altogether it has 2 + 1 = 3 faces.

practice.prompt: 3. How many vertices does a sphere have?
practice.answer: None — a sphere has no vertex and no edge.
practice.worked_solution: A sphere is only a curved surface, so it has no corners and no edges.

practice.prompt: 4. Name two properties that tell a cylinder apart from a sphere.
practice.answer: A cylinder has two circular faces and two curved edges; a sphere has one curved surface and no edges.
practice.worked_solution: The cylinder has faces that are circles and two curved edges, while the sphere has only a curved surface with no edges and no vertices.

sections_json.title: Volume of Cubes, Cuboids and Prisms

blocks.text:
The volume of a solid tells you how much space it takes up. You already know the units — when you measure in centimetres, volume is in cubic centimetres (cm³), and when you measure in metres, it is in cubic metres (m³).

For a cuboid, the volume is found by multiplying the area of its base by its height:

Volume of cuboid = area of base × height
                 = length × breadth × height
                 = lbh

Remember that length, breadth and height are all measured in the same unit, and you multiply them together.

A cube is a special cuboid where every edge is the same length, l. So all three dimensions equal l, and

Volume of cube = l × l × l = l³

You can read l³ as "l cubed".

The same idea — volume equals area of base × height — also works for a prism. A prism has two identical parallel faces joined by a constant cross-section. So for any prism:

Volume of prism = area of base × height

You first find the area of the base face, then multiply it by the height (the distance the prism runs).

**Example 1.** Find the volume of a cuboid of length 3 cm, breadth 2 cm and height 8 cm.

Volume of cuboid = L × b × h

length = 3 cm, breadth = 2 cm, height = 8 cm

Volume = 3 cm × 2 cm × 8 cm
       = 48 cm³

So the cuboid has volume 48 cm³.

**Example 2.** A cuboid has volume 24 cm³. Its base is 6 cm by 2 cm. Find its height.

Volume of cuboid = L × b × h

length = 6 cm, breadth = 2 cm, height = ?

Volume = 24 cm³

24 cm³ = 6 cm × 2 cm × h
24 cm³ = 12 cm² × h

Divide both sides by 12 cm²:

24 cm³ ÷ 12 cm² = h
2 cm = h

So the height is 2 cm.

**Example 3.** Find the volume of a cube of side 3 cm.

Volume of cube = l³

V = (3 cm)³
V = 3 cm × 3 cm × 3 cm
V = 27 cm³

So the cube has volume 27 cm³.

**Example 4.** Find the volume of the triangular prism. Its triangular end has a base of 5 m and a height of 3 m, and the prism runs back 10 m.

First find the area of the triangular base:

Area of triangle = ½ × b × h
                = ½ × 5 × 3
                = 7.5 m²

Then volume = area of base × height
            = 7.5 m² × 10 m
            = 75 m³

So the prism has volume 75 m³.

practice.worked_solution: Volume = L × b × h = 8 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm = 96 cm³.

practice.worked_solution: Volume = L × b × h = 5 m × 2 m × 3 m = 30 m³.

practice.worked_solution: Volume of cube = l³ = 4 cm × 4 cm × 4 cm = 64 cm³.
