practice.worked_solution: Volume = L × b × h, so 36 m³ = 6 m × 2 m × h = 12 m² × h. Dividing both sides by 12 m² gives h = 36 m³ ÷ 12 m² = 3 m.

blocks.text: When you look at railway tracks stretching into the distance, the two rails never cross no matter how far they go. Lines that stay exactly the same distance apart and never meet are called parallel lines. They are written with the symbol ∥, so you would read AB ∥ CD as "line AB is parallel to line CD." In this section you will learn to construct a line that is parallel to a given line and passes through a chosen point, using only a ruler and a pair of compasses. Constructing means drawing it accurately with these tools, not just sketching it by eye. This is a skill you will use again and again, because parallel lines appear all over geometry.

Here is the method for constructing a parallel line. Suppose you are given a line AB and a point P above it, and you want to draw the line through P that is parallel to AB. Step 1. Draw the given line AB and mark the point P somewhere above it. Step 2. Place the point of your compass on A and open it to the point P. Without changing this opening, swing an arc that crosses the line AB. Call the crossing point C. Step 3. Now move the compass point to C and draw an arc above the line (still keeping the same opening) so that it passes through P. This arc marks out the path a circle would take through P at the same distance from the line. Step 4. Without changing the compass opening, place the compass point on P and draw an arc that crosses the line AB. Call this new point D. Step 5. Measure the distance from C to D with your compass. Then, keeping that same opening, put the compass point on P and draw an arc that crosses the first arc you drew through P. Call that crossing Q. Step 6. Draw a straight line from P to Q with your ruler. This line is parallel to AB. You can check it: the arcs you drew guarantee that CP and DQ are equal in length, which is exactly what makes the two lines stay the same distance apart.

Worked example. Construct a line through the point P that is parallel to the given line AB. Solution. Follow the six steps in order. 1. Draw line AB and mark point P above it. 2. Put the compass point on A, open it to P, and swing an arc down to cut the line at C. 3. Move the compass to C and, keeping the opening fixed, draw an arc upward through P. 4. Still keeping the same opening, put the compass point on P and draw an arc down to cut the line at D. 5. Measure the gap from C to D with the compass. Keep that opening, put the point on P, and draw an arc that crosses the arc from Step 3. Mark the crossing Q. 6. Join P and Q with a ruler. The line PQ you have drawn is parallel to AB, so you can label it PQ ∥ AB. The key to the whole construction is that you kept the compass opening the same each time, which copies distances exactly onto your page.

practice.prompt: What symbol do we use to show that two lines are parallel? Write it down and use it to write "line XY is parallel to line MN".
practice.answer: The parallel symbol is ∥, and "line XY is parallel to line MN" is written XY ∥ MN.

practice.prompt: In the construction of a parallel line, you kept your compass opening exactly the same while drawing the arcs. Why is keeping the compass opening fixed so important in this construction?
practice.answer: Keeping the compass opening fixed copies the same distance onto the page each time, so the two segments that control the spacing are equal. Equal spacing is what makes the two lines stay the same distance apart and therefore parallel.

practice.prompt: Draw a line and label its ends A and B. Mark a point P above the line. Then construct the line through P that is parallel to AB, using a ruler and compasses. Describe each step you take in the order you do them.
practice.answer: Steps: (1) Place the compass point on A, open to P, and swing an arc down to cut AB at C. (2) Put the point on C and draw an arc up through P. (3) Put the point on P and draw an arc down to cut AB at D. (4) Measure CD with the compass, then put the point on P and draw an arc crossing the arc from step 2 at Q. (5) Draw PQ with the ruler. PQ is parallel to AB.

practice.prompt: Two lines are drawn so that they never meet, no matter how far they are extended, and the distance between them stays the same all the way along. What are these two lines called?

blocks.text:
Two lines are **perpendicular** when they cross at a right angle — a square corner of exactly 90°. You meet perpendicular lines all the time: the floor meets the wall, the page edge meets its top edge, the rungs of a ladder meet the side rails.

You can construct a perpendicular line with just a **ruler** and a **compass** — no measuring of angles needed. The trick is that the compass draws equal distances, and equal distances force the corner to come out exactly right.

Here is the construction to draw a line perpendicular to a given line through a point on it.

**Step 1.** Draw a line and mark a point P on it where you want the perpendicular to stand.

**Step 2.** Put the compass point on P and open it a little. Draw an arc that crosses the line on both sides of P. Where that arc cuts the line, mark the two points A and B. Because you did not move the compass between the two cuts, PA and PB are exactly equal.

**Step 3.** Open the compass a little wider. Put the point on A and draw a small arc above the line. Without changing the compass opening, put the point on B and draw another small arc. The two arcs meet at a point C above the line.

**Step 4.** Join P to C with your ruler. The line PC is perpendicular to the original line.

Why does this work? In Step 3 the point C is exactly the same distance from A as from B. So C is perched perfectly above the middle of the segment AB, and the line from P to C stands straight up from the line — meeting it at exactly 90°.

Sometimes you need a perpendicular that comes down **onto** the line from a point above it. This is the same idea, flipped around.

**Step 1.** Draw a line and mark a point P **above** the line, off it.

**Step 2.** Put the compass point on P and open it wide enough that the arc will reach the line. Draw an arc that cuts the line in two places. Mark those two cuts A and B.

**Step 3.** Put the compass point on A and draw a small arc below the line. Without changing the compass opening, put the point on B and draw another small arc. The two arcs meet at a point C below the line.

**Step 4.** Join P to C. This line crosses the line at a right angle — it is perpendicular to the line and it passes through P.

Whether the point P sits on the line or above it, the method is the same: mark two equal distances from the line, find the point where the two wider arcs cross, and join. The crossing point is always exactly above the middle of your two marks, which forces the perpendicular.

A good habit before you finish any construction is to look at the corner where the two lines meet. If you have been careful, the corner should look like a clean square corner — and when you check later, it will measure exactly 90°.

**Example: construct a perpendicular to line XY at the point P.**

We follow the four steps with the line already drawn and P marked on it.

1. Put the compass point on P and draw an arc that cuts the line at A on the left and B on the right. The compass is not moved between the two cuts, so PA = PB.
2. Widen the compass a little. Draw an arc from A, then an arc from B with the same opening. They cross at C above the line.
3. Use the ruler to join P to C.

The line PC now stands on the line AB at a square corner. We have constructed a perpendicular line at P. If we check the corner with a set square or later construct a 90° angle there, it comes out exactly right because C was found at equal distances from A and B, putting it directly above the middle of AB.

practice.prompt: Draw a horizontal line and mark a point P on it. Using only a ruler and compass, construct the line perpendicular to your line through P. In your working, say what you did in each of the four steps.
practice.answer: Draw the line and mark P. With the compass point on P, draw an arc cutting the line at A (left) and B (right). Widen the compass and draw an arc from A and an arc from B with the same opening; mark where they cross as C. Join P to C with the ruler. PC is the perpendicular at P.
practice.worked_solution: Step 1: draw the line and mark P. Step 2: compass on P, draw an arc that cuts the line at A and B, keeping the opening fixed so PA = PB. Step 3: widen the compass, draw arcs from A and from B with the same opening, meeting at C above the line. Step 4: join P to C. Because C is equally distant from A and B, PC meets the line at exactly 90°, so PC is perpendicular.

practice.prompt: Draw a line and mark a point P above the line, off it. Using only a ruler and compass, construct the perpendicular from P down onto the line. Describe each step you took.
practice.answer: Put the compass point on P and draw an arc wide enough to cut the line at A and B. Then, keeping the opening fixed, draw an arc from A and an arc from B below the line; mark where they cross as C. Join P to C. The line PC crosses the original line at a right angle and passes through P, so it is the required perpendicular.
practice.worked_solution: With the compass on P, draw an arc reaching the line and cutting it at A and B (P is equally distant from both cuts). Without changing the opening, draw an arc from A and an arc from B below the line; they meet at C. Joining P to C gives a line through P that meets the original line at exactly 90°, since C lies directly below the middle of AB.

sections_json.title: Finding the Midpoint: Bisecting a Line Segment

blocks.text:
When we **bisect** a line segment, we cut it into two equal halves. The point where the two halves meet is called the **midpoint** — it sits exactly halfway along the segment. Bisecting a segment also gives us a new line that meets the segment at a right angle (90°), so the line we draw is called the **perpendicular bisector**.

To bisect a line segment you need only a ruler and a pair of compasses. Follow these steps:

1. Draw the line segment AB.
2. Open your compass to **more than half** the length of AB.
3. Place the compass point on A and draw an arc that sweeps **above and below** the segment.
4. Without changing the compass opening, place the point on B and draw arcs that sweep above and below, crossing the first two arcs.
5. Use your ruler to join the two points where the arcs cross. This new line is the **perpendicular bisector**. It crosses AB at the midpoint M, and it does so at a right angle, so AM = MB.

Why must the compass be opened to more than half the length? If the opening were less than half, the arcs drawn from A and from B would not reach each other, and there would be no crossing points to join. The two crossing points are the key: the line drawn through them is exactly what splits AB into two equal parts.

**Example: Bisect a line segment 6 cm long.**

1. Draw a line segment AB that is 6 cm long.
2. Open the compass to 4 cm (more than half of 6 cm).
3. With the compass point on A, draw an arc that sweeps above and below the segment.
4. Keeping the same opening, put the point on B and draw arcs above and below that cross the first two.
5. Join the two crossing points with a straight line. This is the perpendicular bisector.

The perpendicular bisector crosses AB at point M. Since it cuts AB into two equal parts, AM = MB = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm. Each half is 3 cm long, and the bisector meets AB at a right angle (90°).

practice.prompt: Draw a line segment 8 cm long and bisect it with compasses. How long is each half after you bisect it?
practice.worked_solution: The perpendicular bisector cuts the segment into two equal parts. Half of 8 cm is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm, so AM = MB = 4 cm.

practice.prompt: When you bisect a line segment, the line you draw crosses the segment at what kind of angle, and what is that point called?
practice.answer: The line crosses the segment at a right angle (90°), and the point where it crosses is the midpoint.

practice.prompt: You are bisecting a segment AB that is 10 cm long. You open your compass to only 3 cm before drawing the arcs. Explain why your construction will fail, and state the smallest opening that would work.
practice.answer: 3 cm is less than half of 10 cm, so the arcs drawn from A and from B will not reach each other and there will be no crossing points to join. The smallest opening that works is anything more than 5 cm (more than half of 10 cm).
practice.worked_solution: For the arcs to cross, the compass opening must be more than half the length of the segment. Half of 10 cm is 5 cm, so the opening must be greater than 5 cm, for example 6 cm. With 3 cm the arcs never meet, so no crossing points exist and the bisector cannot be drawn.

practice.prompt: You bisect a segment and find that one of the two halves is 7 cm long. What was the total length of the original segment?
practice.worked_solution: Bisecting splits the segment into two equal halves. If one half is 7 cm, the other half is also 7 cm. Total length = 7 cm + 7 cm = 14 cm.

sections_json.title: Building a Perfect Right Angle: Constructing 90°

blocks.text: A right angle measures exactly 90°, and you can build one with only a ruler and a compass. The secret is to think of a straight line as a flat angle of 180°. If you split a straight line exactly in half at a point, each half is 90°. Here is the construction that does exactly that. You will need a pencil, a ruler, and a compass. Constructing a 90° angle at a point O on a line Step 1 – Draw the baseline. Use your ruler to draw a straight line. Choose a point O on that line. This is where the 90° angle will sit. Step 2 – Make two marks at equal distances. Put the point of your compass at O. Set the opening to any comfortable width and draw an arc that crosses the line. The arc cuts the line at two points, A on the left of O and B on the right of O. Because one arc drew them both, OA and OB are the same length. Step 3 – Widen the compass. Open the compass so its width is bigger than OA (more than half of AB). This wider opening is important – it is what makes the two arcs you are about to draw cross each other. Step 4 – Draw two arcs that meet. Keep the compass at this wider opening. Put the point at A and draw a gentle arc above O. Then, without changing the opening, put the point at B and draw another arc. The two arcs cross at a point above O – call it P. Step 5 – Join the top. Use your ruler to draw a straight line from O through P. The line OP stands straight up from the baseline, so the angle between OP and the line (angle POA) is exactly 90°. The key idea: the two equal arcs from A and B meet at P because P is the same distance from A as it is from B, and O is the midpoint of AB. So P is exactly halfway around the flat line from A to B – and halfway around 180° is 90°.

Worked example: Construct a 90° angle at point O. Here is the full construction, one step at a time, so you can see exactly what your drawing should look like as you go. 1. Draw a horizontal line with your ruler. Mark a point O somewhere on it. 2. With the compass point at O, draw an arc crossing the line on both sides. It touches the line at A (left) and B (right). OA = OB. 3. Widen the compass so the opening is clearly larger than OA. 4. Keeping that wider opening, put the point at A and draw an arc above the line. Without changing the opening, put the point at B and draw a second arc. The two arcs cross above O – mark the crossing P. 5. Draw a straight line from O through P with your ruler. The finished drawing has a vertical line OP standing on the horizontal line, with the corner at O. The angle between the baseline and OP, measured on either side, is 90°. Check it with the corner of your set square: it fits exactly.

practice.prompt: Describe, in the right order, the five steps you take to construct a 90° angle at a point O on a straight line. (You may use a ruler and compass.)
practice.answer: 1. Draw a straight line and mark point O on it. 2. With the compass point at O, draw an arc crossing the line at A (left) and B (right), so OA = OB. 3. Widen the compass so its opening is larger than OA. 4. With the wider opening, draw an arc from A above O, then without changing the opening draw an arc from B; the arcs cross at P. 5. Draw the straight line from O through P. Angle POA = 90°.
practice.worked_solution: The construction builds a 90° angle by halving the flat 180° line. Draw the baseline and pick O. One arc from O marks equal distances A and B. A wider compass then draws two arcs from A and B that meet at P. Joining O to P splits the straight line exactly in half, so the angle between OP and the baseline is 90°.

practice.prompt: In the 90° construction, you draw a first arc from O that cuts the line at A and B, then you draw two further arcs from A and B that meet at P. Why must the two arcs you draw from A and from B use exactly the same compass opening?
practice.answer: They must use the same opening so that AP and BP are equal in length. That makes P the same distance from A as from B, so the line OP passes exactly through the middle of the flat 180° line, giving 90°.
practice.worked_solution: An arc drawn with the compass point at A and a fixed opening reaches every point the same distance AP from A. A second arc with the same opening from B reaches every point the same distance BP from B. Where the two arcs cross, AP = BP. So P is balanced between A and B, and joining O (the midpoint) to P cuts the straight angle in half to give 90°.

practice.prompt: After constructing your 90° angle, you measure the other angle on the other side of OP, between the baseline and OP but on the opposite side. How big is that angle, and why?
practice.answer: It is also 90°. The whole line is a straight angle of 180°, and OP divides it into two equal angles, so each is 90°.
practice.worked_solution: A straight line forms a flat angle of 180°. The perpendicular line OP splits it into two equal angles on either side. Half of 180° is 90°, so both the angle on one side and the angle on the other side are 90°.

sections_json.title: Drawing a 60° Angle with a Compass

blocks.text:
An angle of 60° is special because it is one of the angles you can build using only a ruler and a compass — no protractor needed. It turns out that if you draw an equilateral triangle (a triangle where all three sides are equal), then all three of its angles measure 60°. So the trick is to use the compass to mark a point that is the same distance from two points on your line, and the lines joining them will meet at 60°.

Here is the method, step by step. You will need a sharp pencil, a ruler, and a compass.

Step 1: Draw a straight line and pick a point on it. Let us call the line ℓ and the point A. The angle you build will have its corner (its vertex) at A.

Step 2: Put the point of the compass at A and open it to any convenient width. Draw an arc that crosses the line ℓ. Call the point where the arc meets the line B. Keep the compass at exactly this same width for the next step — do not change it.

Step 3: Keeping the compass at that same width, put its point on B and draw an arc that passes through A and goes up above the line. Where this new arc crosses your first arc, mark that point C.

Step 4: Use the ruler to draw a straight line from A through C and extend it. The angle between your original line ℓ and this new line AC is 60°.

Why does this work? The compass keeps the distance AB the same everywhere, so AB = AC = BC. That makes triangle ABC an equilateral triangle, and every angle in an equilateral triangle is 60°. The angle at A between lines ℓ and AC is therefore 60°.

Example: Construct a 60° angle at point P on a line.

1. Draw a line and mark a point P on it. This line will be the bottom side of your angle.
2. Put the compass point on P and open it to a comfortable width (about halfway across your paper is fine). Draw an arc crossing the line to the right of P. Where the arc meets the line, call it Q.
3. Do not change the compass width. Put the point on Q and draw an arc that passes over P and rises up above the line. Where this new arc crosses the first arc, call it R.
4. Use the ruler to draw a straight line from P through R, extending it beyond R.
5. The angle between your original line PQ and the new line PR is 60°.

Check your work: PR is a radius of the first arc, so it equals PQ. And RQ is a radius of the second arc, so it also equals PQ. That means PQ = PR = RQ, so triangle PQR has three equal sides — it is equilateral, and every angle inside it is 60°. The angle you drew at P is the 60° one.

practice.prompt: You are constructing a 60° angle at point M on a straight line. After drawing the first arc that crosses the line at point N, you must keep the compass at the same width. In the next step you put the compass point on N. How far should the compass be opened, and what single property of the figure does keeping it this width guarantee?
practice.answer: The compass must stay open to the same width as when you drew the first arc (the distance from M to N). Keeping it the same width guarantees that the three sides of the triangle you build are equal, so the triangle is equilateral and every angle inside it measures 60°. The angle you construct at M is therefore 60°.
practice.worked_solution: When you set the compass at M and mark N, the compass width equals the distance MN. If you never change this width, then the next point you mark (call it P) is also at distance MN from both M and N. So MN = NP = PM, and triangle MNP has three equal sides. An equilateral triangle has three equal angles that add to 180°, so each is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°.

practice.prompt: A classmate says: "To construct a 60° angle, I draw the first arc, then I can use any compass width for the remaining arcs — it doesn't matter if I change it." Explain whether this is correct, and say what happens to the angle if the compass width is changed partway through.
practice.answer: It is not correct. To get exactly 60° you must keep the compass at the same width for every arc. If you change the width partway through, the three marked points will not all be the same distance from each other, so the triangle will not be equilateral. The angle you draw will no longer be exactly 60° — it could be smaller or larger, but it will not be 60°.
practice.worked_solution: The 60° result comes entirely from the triangle having three equal sides. If every arc uses the same width, then each side of the triangle equals that width, so the triangle is equilateral and all its angles are 60°. If the width changes, one or more sides have different lengths, the triangle is no longer equilateral, and the constructed angle is not 60°. Keeping the width fixed is what makes the construction reliable.

blocks.text:
Two lines are **parallel** when they stay the same distance apart all along their length — they never meet, no matter how far you extend them. In construction we draw parallel lines using a **set square** and a **ruler**.

The trick is that the set square has one straight edge, and the ruler gives you a straight, fixed line to slide the set square along. When you slide the set square along a ruler, the edge of the set square that you draw along keeps the same direction the whole time — so every line you draw with it stays parallel to every other line you draw with it.

Here is the rule to remember: **the ruler does not move, and the set square slides against it.**

You will need: a sharp pencil, a ruler, and a set square from your mathematical set.

**Example — construct a line through point P parallel to line AB**

**Step 1.** Draw the line AB with your ruler. Mark a point P anywhere above it. This is the point through which your new parallel line must pass.

**Step 2.** Place the set square so that one of its straight edges lies exactly on the line AB.

**Step 3.** Hold the set square firmly in that position. Place the ruler against one of the *other* edges of the set square, so the ruler is snug against it and the set square can still slide.

**Step 4.** Press the ruler down hard so it does not move. Now slide the set square along the ruler — up toward point P. As you slide, the edge that was on AB stays pointing in the same direction.

**Step 5.** Slide the set square until that edge reaches point P. Draw a line along the edge of the set square through P.

That new line is parallel to AB, because it was drawn with the very same edge of the set square that lay on AB, so both lines have the same direction.

practice.prompt: Draw a horizontal line XY about 6 cm long. Using your set square and ruler, construct a line through a point Q that you mark above the line, so that the new line is parallel to XY. Explain in one sentence why your new line is parallel to XY.
practice.answer: Your new line through Q is parallel to XY because it was drawn with the same edge of the set square that lay on XY, so it keeps the same direction all along — the two lines never meet, no matter how far they are extended.
practice.worked_solution: Place the set square so one edge lies exactly on XY, put the ruler against another edge and hold it still, slide the set square up to Q, then draw along the set square's edge through Q. Since the set square only slid (it did not turn), the drawing edge kept its direction, so the line through Q has the same direction as XY — that is what makes them parallel.

practice.prompt: Draw a slanted line AB. Construct a line through a point P below it that is parallel to AB. Which piece of your mathematical set must you hold still the whole time, and which piece slides?
practice.answer: The ruler must be held still the whole time, and the set square slides along it. The edge of the set square that was on AB keeps its direction as it slides, so the line drawn through P is parallel to AB.

blocks.text: Two lines are perpendicular when they meet at a right angle — that is, at an angle of 90°. You can think of the corner of a book or a sheet of paper: the two edges that meet there are perpendicular to each other. The best tool for drawing a perpendicular line is the set square, because it has one right-angled corner. You will use it together with a ruler, so that your drawn line stays straight. Here is the plan for drawing a perpendicular line at a chosen point on a straight line. 1. Draw the given line. Use your ruler to draw a straight line. Mark the point where you want the perpendicular to meet it. 2. Line up the set square. Put one edge of the set square along your drawn line, with the right-angle corner sitting on your marked point. The set square's other right-angle edge should stand up from the line. 3. Draw the perpendicular. Hold the set square firmly and draw along the standing edge. The line you draw rises from your point and makes a right angle with the first line. Because the set square's corner is exactly 90°, the new line is perpendicular to the old one. Check your work: the two lines should form four right angles where they cross, just like the corner of a page.

Worked example Construct a perpendicular to the line below at the point marked P. You will do this on paper with your ruler and set square. P .___________________ Solution 1. Place the ruler along the given line so one long edge lies exactly on it. 2. Put the set square on top of the ruler so that one of its right-angle edges lies against the ruler's edge, and the right-angle corner touches the ruler where point P is. 3. Keeping the set square pressed against the ruler, draw along the set square's upright edge, starting at P and going upwards. 4. The upright line and the original line meet at P, and the corner between them is a right angle. Your drawing should now look like this, with a little square drawn in the corner to mark the right angle: | | |________ P The line you drew is perpendicular to the original line.

practice.prompt: 1. Draw a straight horizontal line about 10 cm long. Mark a point in the middle of it. Using your ruler and set square, construct a perpendicular line at that point. What angle do the two lines make where they meet?
practice.answer: 90° (a right angle). The lines meet at four right angles.
practice.worked_solution: After drawing the horizontal line, place the set square so one right-angle edge lies along the line and the right-angle corner sits on the marked point. Draw along the upright edge. The two lines form a right angle at the meeting point, which measures 90°.

practice.prompt: 2. Which tool do you use to draw a perpendicular line, and why is it suitable?
practice.answer: The set square (with the ruler to keep the line straight), because it has a right-angled corner that is exactly 90°.
practice.worked_solution: A set square has one corner that is exactly a right angle. Lining that corner up on the given line guarantees the new line is perpendicular.

blocks.text: To bisect a line segment means to divide it into two equal parts. The point that cuts the segment into two equal halves is its midpoint. You can find it exactly with a pair of compasses, without measuring. Here is the method for a segment from point A to point B: 1. Draw the line segment AB. 2. Open the compass to a distance more than half the length of AB. (If you open it less than half, the arcs below will not meet.) 3. Place the compass point on A. Draw an arc that swings over the line and one that swings under the line. 4. Keeping the compass opening exactly the same, place the compass point on B. Draw arcs that cross the first two — one above the line and one below it. 5. The two crossing points — one above the line and one below it — mark where the arcs meet. 6. Draw a straight line through those two crossing points. Where this line meets AB is its midpoint, M. The segment has been bisected: AM and MB are equal. The secret of the method is that you never change the compass opening between steps 3 and 4. That is what makes the two crossing points line up exactly through the midpoint.

Worked example — bisecting PQ Follow each step on your own paper with your compass set. • Draw a segment and label its ends P and Q. • Open the compass to a little more than half the length of PQ. • Put the point on P and swing an arc above the segment and an arc below it. • Without changing the compass opening, put the point on Q and swing arcs that cross the first two — one above, one below. • You now have two crossing points, one on each side of the segment. Draw the straight line through both crossings. • The line you drew cuts PQ at its midpoint. Label it M. Measure PM and MQ with a ruler — they are equal.

practice.prompt: Draw a segment AB of any length. Bisect it with a pair of compasses, then label the midpoint M. State what you can say about the lengths AM and MB.
practice.worked_solution: Draw AB, then with the compass opened more than half of AB, draw arcs above and below from A, then the same arcs from B. Draw the line through the two crossing points; its meeting with AB is M. Because the construction keeps the compass opening the same, M lies exactly at the middle, so AM = MB.

practice.prompt: To bisect a segment CD, you open your compass to a distance. Must this distance be less than, equal to, or more than half the length of CD? Explain why.
practice.worked_solution: If the opening were less than half of CD, the arcs drawn from C and D would not reach across to meet one another on both sides of the segment. Opening it more than half guarantees the arcs from the two ends cross, giving the two crossing points the bisecting line passes through.

practice.prompt: While bisecting a segment, after drawing arcs from the first end you change the compass opening before drawing arcs from the second end. Will the line through the two crossing points still cut the segment exactly in half? Give a reason.
practice.answer: No — the bisector must be drawn with the same compass opening at both ends.
practice.worked_solution: The whole construction works because both pairs of arcs are swung at the same distance from the two ends, so the crossing points sit equally far from A and B and therefore line up through the midpoint. If the opening changes, the crossing points shift off that central line, so the drawn line no longer passes through the midpoint.

blocks.text:
A right angle measures exactly 90°, and you can build one wherever you like on a straight line using only your mathematical set. Here you will construct the 90° angle at a chosen point on a line, and you will use compass arcs to do it.

Every angle you draw needs two arms meeting at a point (the vertex). To construct 90° you will raise a new arm straight up from a point that already sits on your line, so that the new arm and the original line make a perfect right angle.

The whole trick is to work on both sides of your point with the compass, then join across. The steps you will follow are:

1. Draw a straight line and mark a point P on it — P is where the right angle will sit.
2. Place your compass point on P and open it to a convenient radius. Draw one arc cutting the line on the left of P and one arc cutting the line on the right of P. Call these two cuts M and N. (M and N are now equal distances from P.)
3. Open your compass a little wider than before. Place the point on M and draw an arc above the line.
4. Keep the same radius, move the compass point to N, and draw another arc above the line so that it crosses the first arc. Call the crossing point C.
5. Use your ruler to draw a straight line from P through C.

The line PC is now at right angles to your original line, so the angle where P, the line and PC meet is exactly 90°. Because you used the same compass opening for both arcs in step 3 and 4, C stands exactly above P, and that is what guarantees the right angle.

Let us construct the 90° angle together on a fresh line, so you can see the full construction before you try one alone.

Take a ruler and draw a straight horizontal line across your page. Mark a point P about halfway along it.

Now set your compass to a comfortable radius (about 3 cm) and place the metal point on P. Swing the compass so the pencil draws one small arc that cuts the line to the left of P, and then swing it again to cut the line to the right of P. Label the left cut M and the right cut N. Because you did not change the compass opening, PM and PN are equal.

Next, open your compass a little wider (say 4 cm). Put the point on M and draw a fair-sized arc that rises above the line. Without changing the opening, move the point to N and draw another arc above the line. The two arcs should cross somewhere above P — call that crossing point C.

Finally, lay your ruler so its edge passes through P and C, and draw the straight line PC, letting it run above and below P.

The two lines now cross at P, and the angle between the right-hand side of your original line and the arm PC is 90°. You have constructed a right angle.

practice.prompt: On a fresh line, construct a 90° angle at a point P that lies on the line. When you are finished, explain how you know the angle you drew is exactly 90°.
practice.answer: The angle at P between the original line and the line drawn from P through C is exactly 90° because C was located by two equal compass arcs swung from M and N, which sit at equal distances on either side of P. That places C directly above P, so the new arm PC is perpendicular to the original line, making the angle a right angle.
practice.worked_solution: 1. Draw a straight line and mark point P on it. 2. Set the compass to a fixed radius, place the point on P, and cut the line at M (left) and N (right). 3. Open the compass wider; from M draw an arc above the line, then from N (same opening) draw an arc crossing it at C. 4. Draw the line from P through C. Since M and N are equidistant from P and the two arcs used the same radius, C lies directly above P, so PC is perpendicular to the line and the angle is 90°.

practice.prompt: When constructing a 90° angle at a point P on a line, you first cut the line at two points M and N using one fixed compass opening. Why must you keep the compass at the same opening for these two cuts, and what does that guarantee about M and N?
practice.answer: Keeping the compass at the same opening for the two cuts guarantees that PM and PN are equal — that is, M and N are the same distance from P on opposite sides. This balance is what places the crossing point C directly above P, so the line drawn from P through C stands perpendicular to the original line and the angle is exactly 90°.
practice.worked_solution: A compass swung at a fixed opening draws points that are all the same distance from the centre point. So cutting at M with opening r gives PM = r, and cutting at N with the same opening r gives PN = r. Equal distances on either side of P balance the construction so the arc crossing C lands straight above P.

blocks.text: A 60° angle is one of the special angles you can draw with just a ruler and a pair of compasses — no protractor needed. The whole trick is to build an equilateral triangle: a triangle whose three sides are all equal. In an equilateral triangle, every angle is 60°. So if you draw an equilateral triangle and keep one of its angles, that angle is your 60°. Here is the construction, step by step. You will need a sharp pencil, a ruler, and your compasses (part of your mathematical set). Step 1. Draw a straight line. Choose a point near one end of it and call it A. This point will be the corner where your 60° angle sits. Step 2. Set your compasses to any radius that fits on your page — the size does not matter, as long as it stays the same throughout. Place the compass point on A and draw an arc that crosses the line. Call the point where the arc meets the line B. Step 3. Without changing the compass setting, place the compass point on B and draw another arc. Make it cross the first arc. Call the point where the two arcs meet C. Step 4. Use your ruler to draw a straight line from A to C. The angle between the original line and the line AC — that is, angle BAC — is 60°. Why does this work? In Step 2, the distance from A to B is your chosen radius, so AB is one radius long. In Step 3, the second arc is drawn with the same radius from B, so BC is also one radius long. And in Step 4, the line AC reaches the point C that lies on the first arc from A, so AC is one radius long too. That means AB = BC = AC: the triangle is equilateral, and every angle in it, including angle BAC, is exactly 60°.

Worked example — construct a 60° angle at point A. 1. Draw a horizontal line on your page and mark a point A near the middle. 2. Set your compasses to a radius of about 4 cm (any size works). Put the point on A and draw an arc that crosses the line to the right of A. Mark where it lands as B. 3. Keep the compasses exactly as they are. Put the point on B and draw an arc. Make sure it crosses the first arc above the line. Mark the meeting point as C. 4. Draw a straight line from A through C, extending it a little. You now have angle BAC between the original line and line AC. Measure it with your protractor to check — it should read 60°. The two arcs must use the same radius, so never change your compass setting between Step 2 and Step 3.

practice.prompt: Construct a 60° angle following the compass-arc method you have just learned. Use your protractor afterwards to check the size of your angle. What should your angle measure?
practice.worked_solution: Draw a line, mark a point A, draw an arc from A to meet the line at B, draw an equal arc from B to meet the first arc at C, then join A to C. The angle between the original line and line AC is 60°, because AB, BC and AC are all equal radii, forming an equilateral triangle.

practice.prompt: In the construction of a 60° angle, the three points A, B and C form a triangle whose three sides are all equal. What is the name of this kind of triangle, and what is the size of each of its angles?
practice.answer: It is an equilateral triangle, and each of its angles is 60°.

practice.prompt: Suppose you set your compasses to a radius of 5 cm and complete the full construction of a 60° angle. How long is each side of the triangle formed by points A, B and C?
practice.worked_solution: The radius you chose is used for every arc, so AB is one radius (5 cm), BC is one radius (5 cm), and AC is one radius (5 cm). All three sides are equal, so each is 5 cm.

sections_json.title: Drawing a Parallel Line Through a Point

blocks.text: Two lines are parallel when they run side by side and never meet, no matter how far they are extended. You are going to draw a line that passes through a given point P and stays parallel to a given line AB. You will need only a set square and a ruler from your mathematical set.

Example: Construct a line through the point P so that it is parallel to AB. Step 1. Place the set square so that one of its edges lies exactly along the line AB (fig-01). Step 2. Place the ruler along one of the other edges of the set square. If you are right-handed, use the left-hand edge (fig-02). You may rest the ruler against the set square's sloping edge instead of its upright one (fig-03) — either works, and the ruler's slant does not affect the construction. What matters is that one edge of the set square lies along AB and the ruler rests against a different edge of the set square. Step 3. Hold the ruler firmly so it does not move. Slide the set square along the ruler, towards P. Sliding along a held ruler moves the set square without turning it, so its edge keeps the same direction (fig-04 and fig-05). Stop when the edge that was lying on AB reaches P. Step 4. Draw a line along that edge of the set square, through P. Because the set square was slid, not turned, this edge keeps the same direction as AB, so the line you draw through P is parallel to AB.

blocks.caption: The same slide as fig-04, made against the leaning ruler of fig-03. The set square is drawn twice: once with its edge on $AB$, and once slid along the ruler until that edge passes through $P$. The two positions are congruent and point the same way — sliding along a held ruler moves the set square without turning it — so the edge through $P$ stays parallel to $AB$. The arrow gives the direction of the slide, along the ruler's edge, and the right angle is marked in both positions.

The vertical ruler held fixed, with the set square drawn twice — once with its edge on $AB$ and once higher up, its edge on a second line parallel to $AB$ — and an arrow between the two positions pointing up along the ruler.

The same set square on $AB$ as in fig-02, with the ruler moved to rest against its sloping edge instead of its upright one. The set square has not moved; only the ruler has, so it now leans across $AB$, running from lower left to upper right. The right angle is still where the edge on $AB$ meets the short upright edge, and it is marked there. The ruler's inclination does not affect the construction. The set square is drawn at one particular size, and with its right angle at one particular end; neither is part of the method. Any set square works, either way round, so long as one edge lies along $AB$ and the ruler rests against another.

The same set square on $AB$, with the ruler now drawn as a long strip lying along the set square's downward edge. The right angle marked at the corner is the set square's own, between the edge lying along $AB$ and the edge running down from it.

Line $AB$, with a point $P$ marked above it. A set square is drawn below $AB$ with one edge along the line: the right angle is at the left end of that edge, one leg runs down from it, and the hypotenuse closes back to a point on $AB$ to the right.

practice.prompt: Draw a horizontal line AB about 8 cm long with a point P marked about 3 cm above it. Construct a line through P that is parallel to AB, using only your set square and ruler.
practice.answer: The line through P runs horizontally (parallel to AB), never meeting AB however far extended. Check it by eye: it is the same distance from AB all the way along.
practice.worked_solution: Place one edge of the set square exactly along AB. Rest the ruler firmly against another edge of the set square. Hold the ruler still and slide the set square along it until the edge that was on AB reaches P. Draw a line along that edge through P. Since the slide moved the set square without turning it, the drawn line keeps the direction of AB.

practice.prompt: You have placed the set square with one edge along AB and the ruler against another of its edges. Before drawing, you must do two things in order. What are they?
practice.answer: First hold the ruler firmly so it cannot move, then slide the set square along the ruler until the edge that was on AB reaches P. Only then draw the line along that edge through P.

blocks.text:
Two lines are said to be **perpendicular** to each other when they meet at a right angle — that is, at $90^\circ$. In fig-06 you can see line $AB$ crossed by line $XY$; the small square drawn at the crossing marks the right angle, so $XY$ is perpendicular to $AB$.

To construct a perpendicular line yourself, you need only your ruler and set square. Here is the way to do it.

**Step 1 — Draw the line and mark the point.** Draw a line $AB$ and mark a point $Q$ somewhere on it, as in fig-07. This point $Q$ is where your new perpendicular line will cross $AB$.

**Step 2 — Place the set square.** Put the edge of the set square on line $AB$. Now place your ruler so that its edge meets the hypotenuse (the long sloping edge) of the set square, as in fig-08. Notice how the set square stands upright on $AB$, with its right angle sitting on the line.

**Step 3 — Slide and draw.** Pressing firmly on the ruler so it cannot move, slide the set square down along the hypotenuse until the third edge of the set square touches point $Q$. Now draw a line $XY$ along that third edge, letting $X$ lie above $AB$ and $Y$ below it, as in fig-09.

Because you slid the set square without turning it, its right angle is preserved, so the line you draw crosses $AB$ at exactly $90^\circ$. The two lines $AB$ and $XY$ are perpendicular.

blocks.caption: Line $AB$ with $XY$ now drawn across it, $X$ above and $Y$ below, and a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant.

Line $AB$ with the set square standing on it as a narrow right-angled triangle: a short base along $AB$, the upright edge rising from the right end of that base with the right angle marked there, and the hypotenuse closing back down to the left.
A plain line with a stroke at each end, labelled $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right.
Line $AB$ with a second line $XY$ crossing it, $X$ above and $Y$ below, and a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant at the crossing.

blocks.text:
**Example — construct a line perpendicular to $PQ$ at the point $R$ on it.**

1. Draw line $PQ$ and mark point $R$ on it.
2. Lay the edge of the set square along $PQ$, then place the ruler against the hypotenuse of the set square and hold it firm.
3. Pressing down on the ruler, slide the set square along the hypotenuse until its third edge touches $R$.
4. Draw line $XY$ along that third edge so that $X$ is above $PQ$ and $Y$ is below it.

Check your result: the small right-angle mark at the crossing of $PQ$ and $XY$ shows the two lines meet at $90^\circ$, so they are perpendicular.

practice.prompt: Draw a line $AB$ and mark a point $Q$ on it. Using your ruler and set square, construct a line through $Q$ that is perpendicular to $AB$. What do you look for to confirm that your line is perpendicular?
practice.answer: The constructed line meets $AB$ at a right angle ($90^\circ$), shown by the small right-angle mark at the crossing.
practice.worked_solution: Lay the edge of the set square along $AB$, hold the ruler against the hypotenuse, and slide the set square until its third edge touches $Q$. Draw the line along that third edge. The two lines meet at $90^\circ$, so they are perpendicular.

practice.prompt: Two lines $XY$ and $UV$ meet at a point and the angle between them is $90^\circ$. In your own words, what do you call these two lines?
practice.answer: Perpendicular — two lines that meet at a right angle ($90^\circ$) are perpendicular to each other.

blocks.text: To bisect a line segment means to divide it into two equal halves. The point where the two halves meet is called the midpoint, and it lies exactly in the middle of the segment. Here is how you bisect a given line segment with a pair of compasses and a ruler. Start with your segment, say AB (fig-10). You will need a pair of compasses, a ruler and a sharp pencil. 1. Open your compasses so that the radius is about three-quarters of the length of AB. The exact opening is not critical, but it must be more than half of AB, otherwise the arcs below will not cross. 2. Place the sharp point of the compass on A. Draw two arcs, one above the line and the other below the line, near the middle of AB. 3. Keeping the compasses at the same radius, move the sharp point to B. Draw two more arcs so that they cut the first pair of arcs. The upper pair of arcs crosses at a point P, and the lower pair crosses at a point Q (fig-11). 4. With your ruler, join P to Q. The line PQ crosses AB at a point M (fig-12). The point M is the midpoint of AB. That means the two halves are equal: AM = MB. So you have cut the segment into two equal halves, and PQ meets AB at a right angle, 90°.

blocks.caption: The same arcs with $P$ joined to $Q$, the joining line crossing $AB$ at its middle at $M$ and carrying a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant.
The segment $AB$ with arc pairs crossing above and below it, the upper crossing labelled $P$ and the lower one $Q$. Each crossing is drawn as a small X where an arc from $A$ meets an arc from $B$.
The line segment $AB$, a stroke at each end, $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right.

blocks.text: Worked example — bisecting segment CD Suppose you are asked to bisect the segment CD. Follow the steps in order. 1. Draw the segment CD, with C on the left and D on the right. 2. Open the compasses to about three-quarters of the length of CD — more than half of it. 3. Put the sharp point on C. Draw an arc above the line and an arc below the line, near the middle. 4. Keep the same radius. Move the sharp point to D. Draw an arc above the line and an arc below the line, so that they cut the first arcs. Mark where the upper arcs cross as P and where the lower arcs cross as Q. 5. Join P to Q with a ruler. Where PQ meets CD, mark the point M. M is the midpoint of CD, so CM = MD, and the two halves are equal. PQ meets CD at a right angle.

practice.prompt: Bisect the line segment AB shown in fig-10. What does the word "bisect" mean, and what must be true of the two halves after you finish?
practice.answer: To bisect means to divide into two equal halves. After bisecting, the two halves are equal, so AM = MB, where M is the midpoint.
practice.worked_solution: Open the compasses to about three-quarters of the length of AB (more than half). Draw two arcs from A, one above and one below the line. Keeping the same radius, draw two arcs from B so that they cut the first arcs at P (above) and Q (below). Join P to Q with a ruler. The crossing point M on AB is the midpoint, so AM = MB.

practice.prompt: In the construction in fig-12, the line PQ crosses AB at M. What does the point M divide AB into, and at what angle does PQ meet AB?
practice.answer: M is the midpoint of AB, so it divides AB into two equal halves AM and MB. PQ meets AB at a right angle, 90°.

practice.prompt: When bisecting a segment, your compasses must be open to more than half the length of the segment. Why is that important?
practice.answer: If the compasses were open to less than half the length, the arcs drawn from the two ends would not cross each other above and below the line, so you would not get the crossing points P and Q to join up.

blocks.text:
A right angle — an angle of exactly 90° — is one you can build for yourself with just a ruler and a pair of compasses. The trick is that a perpendicular line and a right angle are the same thing: if a line rises straight up from a point on another line so that the two are perpendicular, the angle where they meet is 90°. So to construct a 90° angle you construct a perpendicular.

Look at fig-13. A straight line AB has been drawn, and a point C marked on it where the right angle is wanted. A perpendicular rises from C, and where it meets the line there is the small square mark that tells you the angle is a right angle. The two short strokes crossing each other near the top of the perpendicular are construction marks from the compass — they show the steps used to build it. You will make those same marks yourself.

What matters is the order: first place the point C on the line, then sweep one arc from C, then two wider arcs from the points that arc makes, and finally join C to where those two arcs cross.

blocks.caption: A line with a stroke at each end, $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right, and four short strokes standing on the line, a pair towards $A$ and a pair towards $B$. A perpendicular rises from a point near the middle, with a right-angle mark at its foot, and two short strokes cross each other near its top.

blocks.text:
Construct a 90° angle at a point C on the line AB, and follow along with fig-13.

1. Draw a straight line AB and mark a point C on it where the 90° angle is to be constructed.

2. Put the point of the compasses at C and draw an arc that cuts the line at two points, D and E — one on each side of C. These two points are now marked on the line, at equal distances from C.

3. Open the compasses WIDER than DC (the width used in step 2 will not work, because arcs drawn at that width from D and E meet only at C itself). With the compasses at D at this new, wider setting, draw an arc above the line.

4. Keep the compasses at the same wider setting from step 3, place them at E, and draw another arc above the line. This second arc cuts the first one at a point F.

5. Join C to F with a ruler.

6. CF is perpendicular to AB, so the angle formed between CF and the line at C is a right angle: ∠FCB = 90°.

The one step to be careful with is the third: the second setting of the compasses must be wider than the distance DC. That is exactly why the two arcs from D and E cross each other at F instead of meeting at C — the wider setting pushes their crossing point up above the line, and joining that point back to C gives you a line standing straight up at 90°.

practice.prompt: Construct a 90° angle at a point C on a line AB, and write down, in the correct order, the two widths you set the compasses to.
practice.answer: The two widths are: first, the width used to draw the arc from C that cuts the line at D and E; second, a WIDER setting (wider than DC) used for the arcs from D and E that cross at F. The final angle at C is 90°.
practice.worked_solution: After drawing line AB and marking C, set the compasses at C and draw an arc cutting the line at D and E (width 1). Then open the compasses wider than DC (width 2), put the point at D and draw an arc above the line, then keep width 2 and do the same from E so the arcs cross at F. Join C to F; CF is perpendicular to AB, so ∠FCB = 90°.

practice.prompt: In the construction of a 90° angle, why must the compasses be opened wider for the second set of arcs than for the first?
practice.answer: Because the two wider arcs need to meet at a point F above the line. If the compasses stayed at the first width (DC), the arcs drawn from D and E would meet only at C itself — right on the line — and that would not give a perpendicular rising from C.

blocks.text:
You can construct a 60° angle using only a ruler and a pair of compasses, by drawing arcs of equal radius. Here is the idea: if you swing two arcs of the same radius so that one cuts the other, the crossing point lies exactly on the ray that makes 60° with your original line.

Start with a line segment BC, with B on the left. Place the point of your compasses on B, open them to any convenient radius, and swing an arc that cuts BC at a point X (see fig-14). Keep this same radius — it stays fixed for the whole construction, and that equal radius is what makes the angle work out to 60°.

Now place the point of your compasses on X and, with the same radius as before, swing a second arc that cuts the first arc. Call the point where the two arcs cross A.

Finally, draw the straight line from B to A. The angle ABC is a 60° angle.

blocks.caption: The line $BC$ with $B$ at the left, a stroke marking $X$ part way along, a long arc swung from $B$ through $X$ and up to the left, a shorter arc swung from $X$ cutting it, and a straight line from $B$ to that crossing.

blocks.text:
Let us build a 60° angle step by step.

Step 1 — Draw a line segment and mark B. Label the left end B and the right end C.

Step 2 — With your compasses' point on B, choose any convenient radius and swing an arc that cuts BC. Mark where it cuts BC as X.

Step 3 — Without changing the radius, move the compasses' point to X and swing a second arc that cuts the first arc. Label the crossing point A.

Step 4 — Join B to A with a straight line. The angle ABC (between BA and BC) is 60°.

Check your work in fig-14: the long arc from B through X, the shorter arc from X cutting it, and the straight line from B up to A. Your three points B, X and A are all the same distance apart because the radius never changed — and a triangle whose three sides are equal always has a 60° angle at each corner.

practice.prompt: Write down, in the correct order, the steps you follow to construct a 60° angle at B on a line segment BC.
practice.answer: 1. Swing an arc from B with any convenient radius to cut BC at X. 2. With the same radius, swing an arc from X to cut the first arc at A. 3. Join B to A. The angle ABC is 60°.

practice.prompt: In constructing a 60° angle, you swing a second arc from X using the same radius as the first arc. Why must the two radii be equal?
practice.answer: Because equal radii make the three points B, X and A all the same distance apart, forming an equilateral triangle whose angles are each 60°.
