sections_json.title: Drawing a line parallel to a given line through a point

blocks.text:
Two lines are **parallel** when they run side by side, the same distance apart all the way along, and never meet — like the two rails of a railway track. In construction we draw a line through a given point so that it stays the same distance from an existing line. The tool that does this for us is the **set square** working against a **ruler**: the ruler gives the slide a fixed direction, and the set square slides along it without turning, so the edge you draw through always keeps the same direction as the line you started with.

Here is the whole construction, on a line $AB$ with a point $P$ marked above it (fig-01).

1. **Lay the set square on $AB$.** Place the set square so that one of its edges lies exactly along the line $AB$.
2. **Put the ruler against another edge.** Place your ruler along one of the set square's other edges. If you are right-handed, use the left-hand edge. Now the set square cannot turn — it can only slide up and down the ruler (fig-02 and fig-03).
3. **Slide the set square up to $P$.** Hold the ruler firmly in place and slide the set square along it towards $P$. Stop when the edge that was on $AB$ passes through $P$ (fig-04).
4. **Draw the line.** Draw a line along that edge of the set square through $P$. Because sliding moved the set square without turning it, this new edge keeps exactly the same direction as it had on $AB$ — so the line you draw through $P$ is parallel to $AB$ (fig-05).

The set square is drawn at one size with its right angle at one end in the figures, but neither matters: any set square works, either way round, so long as one edge lies along $AB$ and the ruler rests against another edge. The ruler's own angle does not affect the result either — it just steadies the slide.

blocks.caption: The same slide as fig-04, made against the leaning ruler of fig-03. The set square is drawn twice: once with its edge on $AB$, and once slid along the ruler until that edge passes through $P$. The two positions are congruent and point the same way — sliding along a held ruler moves the set square without turning it — so the edge through $P$ stays parallel to $AB$. The arrow gives the direction of the slide, along the ruler's edge, and the right angle is marked in both positions.

The vertical ruler held fixed, with the set square drawn twice — once with its edge on $AB$ and once higher up, its edge on a second line parallel to $AB$ — and an arrow between the two positions pointing up along the ruler.

The same set square on $AB$ as in fig-02, with the ruler moved to rest against its sloping edge instead of its upright one. The set square has not moved; only the ruler has, so it now leans across $AB$, running from lower left to upper right. The right angle is still where the edge on $AB$ meets the short upright edge, and it is marked there. The ruler's inclination does not affect the construction. The set square is drawn at one particular size, and with its right angle at one particular end; neither is part of the method. Any set square works, either way round, so long as one edge lies along $AB$ and the ruler rests against another.

The same set square on $AB$, with the ruler now drawn as a long strip lying along the set square's downward edge. The right angle marked at the corner is the set square's own, between the edge lying along $AB$ and the edge running down from it.

Line $AB$, with a point $P$ marked above it. A set square is drawn below $AB$ with one edge along the line: the right angle is at the left end of that edge, one leg runs down from it, and the hypotenuse closes back to a point on $AB$ to the right.

blocks.text:
**Worked example.** Construct a line through point $P$ parallel to the line $CD$.

*Step 1.* Place the set square on the line $CD$, one edge lying exactly along it.
*Step 2.* Hold the ruler against the set square's other edge (the left-hand edge if you are right-handed), so the set square is locked to the slide.
*Step 3.* Hold the ruler firmly and slide the set square along it towards $P$, until the edge that was on $CD$ reaches $P$.
*Step 4.* Draw a line along that edge through $P$.

The line you have drawn through $P$ keeps the direction of $CD$, because the set square slid without turning. It is parallel to $CD$.

practice.prompt: Draw a horizontal line $PQ$ about 8 cm long and mark a point $R$ about 3 cm above it. Construct a line through $R$ parallel to $PQ$. Describe the steps you used.
practice.answer: The constructed line through $R$ is parallel to $PQ$: it runs side by side with $PQ$, the same distance apart all the way along, and never meets it.
practice.worked_solution: Place one edge of the set square exactly along $PQ$. Hold the ruler against the set square's other edge (the left-hand one if you are right-handed) so the set square cannot turn. Hold the ruler firm and slide the set square along it towards $R$, stopping when the edge that was on $PQ$ passes through $R$. Draw a line along that edge through $R$. Since the set square slid without turning, the drawn line has the same direction as $PQ$ and is therefore parallel to it.

practice.prompt: In the construction of a line through a point parallel to a given line, why must you hold the ruler firmly while you slide the set square along it? What would happen if the ruler moved?
practice.answer: The ruler sets the direction of the slide. Holding it firm means the set square can only move straight along it without turning, so the new edge keeps the same direction as the line it started on. If the ruler moved, the set square's slide would change direction and the drawn line would no longer be parallel.

blocks.text:
Two lines are said to be **perpendicular** to each other when they meet at a right angle, that is, at $90^\circ$. Look at fig-06: line $AB$ has a second line $XY$ crossing it, with $X$ above and $Y$ below, and the little square at the crossing marks the right angle. Whenever two lines meet and the angle between them is a right angle, the lines are perpendicular.

A set square has one corner that is exactly a right angle. Because of this, you can use it, together with a ruler, to draw a line perpendicular to another line through any point on it.

blocks.caption: Line $AB$ with a second line $XY$ crossing it, $X$ above and $Y$ below, and a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant at the crossing.

blocks.text:
Let's construct a line perpendicular to $AB$ through a point $Q$ on it.

**Step 1.** Draw the line $AB$ and mark a point $Q$ on it, as in fig-07.

**Step 2.** Place the edge of the set square on line $AB$, so that its base lies along the line. Let the edge of the ruler meet the hypotenuse of the set square, as shown in fig-08 — the set square stands on $AB$ like a narrow right-angled triangle, with the upright edge rising from the line and the right angle marked there.

**Step 3.** Pressing firmly on the ruler, slide the set square down along the hypotenuse side until the third edge touches point $Q$. Then draw a line $XY$ along that third edge. Because the set square's upright edge is a right angle, the line you draw crosses $AB$ at a right angle.

Fig-09 shows the result: line $XY$ crosses $AB$ with $X$ above and $Y$ below, and the right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant confirms the two lines meet at $90^\circ$. The line $XY$ is perpendicular to $AB$.

blocks.caption: Line $AB$ with the set square standing on it as a narrow right-angled triangle: a short base along $AB$, the upright edge rising from the right end of that base with the right angle marked there, and the hypotenuse closing back down to the left.
A plain line with a stroke at each end, labelled $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right.
Line $AB$ with $XY$ now drawn across it, $X$ above and $Y$ below, and a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant.

practice.prompt: Two lines are perpendicular when they meet at a right angle. What is the size, in degrees, of the angle between two perpendicular lines?
Using your set square and ruler, construct a line perpendicular to the line $AB$ through a point $Q$ on it. Name the perpendicular line $XY$.
practice.answer: The line $XY$ you draw must cross $AB$ at $Q$ and meet it at a right angle; check with the right-angle corner of your set square that the two lines meet at $90^\circ$.
practice.worked_solution: 1. Draw the line $AB$ and mark the point $Q$ on it. 2. Place the edge of the set square on $AB$ so its base lies along the line, and rest the ruler against the hypotenuse of the set square. 3. Press firmly on the ruler, slide the set square along until its third (upright) edge touches $Q$, and draw the line $XY$ along that edge. Since the set square's upright edge makes a right angle with its base, $XY$ meets $AB$ at $90^\circ$.

blocks.text: To bisect a line segment means to divide it into two equal halves. When you bisect a segment AB, you find the point M exactly at its middle, so that AM = MB. The construction uses a pair of compasses and a ruler, and the line that crosses AB meets it at a right angle (90°). The two crossing points you make with the compasses are labelled P and Q, and joining them gives you the line that cuts AB in half.

Follow these steps to bisect the line segment AB (fig-10 shows the starting segment, with A on the left and B on the right). Step 1. Open the pair of compasses so that the radius is about ¾ of the length of AB. Step 2. Place the sharp point of the compasses on A and draw two arcs — one above and the other below the middle of AB. Step 3. Keeping the same radius, place the sharp point on B and draw two more arcs so that they cut the first arcs at P (above AB) and Q (below AB), as in fig-11. Each crossing is where an arc from A meets an arc from B. Step 4. Join P to Q with a ruler (fig-12). Step 5. The line PQ crosses AB at M. M is the midpoint of AB, so AM = MB, and PQ meets AB at 90°. Your segment is now bisected.

blocks.caption: The same arcs with $P$ joined to $Q$, the joining line crossing $AB$ at its middle at $M$ and carrying a right-angle mark in the upper right quadrant.
The segment $AB$ with arc pairs crossing above and below it, the upper crossing labelled $P$ and the lower one $Q$. Each crossing is drawn as a small X where an arc from $A$ meets an arc from $B$.
The line segment $AB$, a stroke at each end, $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right.

practice.prompt: When you bisect a line segment AB, the crossing line PQ meets AB at the point M. What does M being the midpoint of AB tell you about the two halves of the segment, and at what angle does PQ meet AB?
practice.answer: M is the midpoint, so AM = MB (the segment is divided into two equal halves), and PQ meets AB at 90°.

practice.prompt: When constructing the bisection of segment AB, what must you do to the pair of compasses after drawing the two arcs from A, before you draw the arcs from B?
practice.answer: Keep the same radius (the compass opening) as you used from A, so that the arcs from B cut the first arcs at P and Q.

practice.prompt: List, in order, the first three steps you take to bisect a line segment AB with a pair of compasses.
practice.answer: 1. Open the compasses so the radius is about ¾ of the length of AB. 2. Place the sharp point on A and draw two arcs, one above and one below the middle of AB. 3. Keeping the same radius, place the sharp point on B and draw two arcs so they cut the first arcs at P and Q.

blocks.text:
A 90° angle is a right angle — the kind you see at the corner of a book or a sheet of paper. You can construct one exactly with your compasses and ruler, without measuring it. The trick is that a line drawn perpendicular to another line always makes a right angle where it meets it, and the compasses can help you find the point the perpendicular must pass through.

Here is the construction. You will need your compasses, your ruler and a pencil.

**Step 1.** Draw a straight line and label its ends $A$ and $B$. Mark a point $C$ on the line, at the place where you want the right angle to stand.

**Step 2.** Put the point of your compasses at $C$ and draw an arc. This arc cuts the line at two points — label them $D$ and $E$, one on each side of $C$.

**Step 3.** Now open your compasses **wider** than the distance $DC$ from step 2. (The width you used in step 2 will not work here: arcs drawn with it from $D$ and $E$ would only meet again at $C$ itself.) With this new, wider setting, place the compasses at $D$ and draw an arc above the line.

**Step 4.** Keep the compasses at that same wider setting. Move them to $E$ and draw another arc, cutting the first arc at a point $F$ above the line.

**Step 5.** Use your ruler to join $C$ to $F$ with a straight line.

**Step 6.** The line $CF$ is perpendicular to $AB$, so the angle where they meet is a right angle: $\angle FCB = 90^\circ$.

Let us follow the construction through once together, watching what each arc does.

Draw line $AB$. Mark point $C$ in the middle of it. With the compasses at $C$, draw an arc that cuts the line at two points. Call the left one $D$ and the right one $E$ — notice the arc has cut the line exactly twice, once at $D$ and once at $E$.

Now widen the compasses. This is the key move: the new opening must be **larger** than the distance $DC$. With this wider opening, put the point at $D$ and draw a long arc rising above the line. Then, without changing the compasses, put the point at $E$ and draw another arc rising above the line. The two arcs cross each other above the line — that crossing point is $F$.

With your ruler, draw the straight line from $C$ up to $F$. The line $CF$ meets $AB$ at a perfect right angle, and the little square you could draw at $C$ between $CF$ and $CB$ is the right-angle mark. So $\angle FCB = 90^\circ$.

Check your own drawing: the two crossed strokes at the top of your figure mark where the two wider arcs met at $F$, and $CF$ rises straight up from the line to meet it at a right angle.

blocks.caption: A line with a stroke at each end, $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right, and four short strokes standing on the line, a pair towards $A$ and a pair towards $B$. A perpendicular rises from a point near the middle, with a right-angle mark at its foot, and two short strokes cross each other near its top.

practice.prompt: After you draw the arc from $C$ that cuts the line at $D$ and $E$, you must change the compasses before drawing the two arcs that meet at $F$. What change do you make, and why is it needed?
practice.answer: You open the compasses wider than the distance $DC$. The width used in step 2 would not work, because arcs drawn with it from $D$ and $E$ would meet only at $C$ itself.

practice.prompt: In this construction, the arc drawn with the compasses at $C$ cuts the line $AB$ at exactly two points. What are the two points labelled?
practice.answer: The two points are labelled $D$ and $E$, one on each side of $C$.

practice.prompt: Having joined $C$ to $F$ with your ruler, state the size of $\angle FCB$ and the name given to the line $CF$ in relation to $AB$.

Place these steps of the construction in the correct order by numbering them 1 to 5:

(a) With the compasses at $D$ at the wider setting, draw an arc above the line.
(b) Draw a straight line $AB$ and mark a point $C$ on it.
(c) With the compasses at $E$ at the same wider setting, draw an arc cutting the first at $F$.
(d) With the compasses at $C$, draw an arc cutting the line at $D$ and $E$.
(e) Join $C$ to $F$ with a ruler, so that $\angle FCB = 90^\circ$.
practice.worked_solution: First you draw the line and mark the point where the angle will stand — that is (b). Next, with the compasses at $C$, you draw the arc that cuts the line at $D$ and $E$ — that is (d). Then you widen the compasses and draw the first arc from $D$ — (a). Keeping that wider setting, you draw the arc from $E$ so it cuts the first at $F$ — (c). Finally you join $C$ to $F$ and you have the right angle — (e).

blocks.text:
A 60° angle can be drawn using only a ruler and a pair of compasses. The trick is that an equilateral triangle has three equal sides, and every angle in it is 60°. By swinging arcs of the same radius, you build two sides of an equilateral triangle, and the angle you open up between them is exactly 60°.

Here is the construction.

**Step 1.** Draw a straight line segment, say BC, with B at the left and C at the right. Put the point of your compasses on B and open them to any convenient radius. Draw an arc so that it cuts BC — mark where it cuts the line as X.

**Step 2.** Now put the point of your compasses on X, keeping exactly the same radius you used from B. Draw an arc so that it cuts the first arc. Call the point where the two arcs cross A.

**Step 3.** Draw the straight line from B to A.

The angle between the line BA and the line BC, measured at B, is 60°. Because you used the same radius for both arcs, BX and XA are equal in length, and BA equals them too — so the three points form an equilateral triangle, and an equilateral triangle has a 60° angle at every corner.

blocks.caption: The line $BC$ with $B$ at the left, a stroke marking $X$ part way along, a long arc swung from $B$ through $X$ and up to the left, a shorter arc swung from $X$ cutting it, and a straight line from $B$ to that crossing.

practice.prompt: Follow the construction to draw a 60° angle at a point B on a straight line.
practice.answer: The two arcs, swung from B and from X with the same radius, cross at A, and the angle ABC between the line BA and the line BC is 60°.
practice.worked_solution:
1. Draw line segment BC. Put the compasses on B, open to any convenient radius, and swing an arc cutting BC at X.
2. Keep the same radius, put the compasses on X, and swing an arc to cut the first arc. Mark the crossing A.
3. Draw the straight line from B to A. The angle between BA and BC at B is 60°.

practice.prompt: In the construction, why must the angle at B come out to exactly 60°?
practice.answer: The two arcs cut at A, and drawing BA closes the shape ABX. All three sides — BX, XA and BA — are equal, so ABX is an equilateral triangle, and the angle at B is 60°.
practice.worked_solution: The compasses keep the same radius for both arcs, so the distance BX (from B to the cut on BC) and the distance XA (the second arc, swung from X) are equal. Since A lies on the first arc centred at B, BA equals the same radius as well. With BX = XA = BA, the triangle ABX has three equal sides — it is equilateral. Every angle in an equilateral triangle is 60°, so the angle at B is 60°.

blocks.text:
Think about how much information surrounds you every day. In one morning you might see how many cars pass your house, how many goals your favourite team scored last season, or how much your school spends on books each term. All of these are numbers, but numbers on their own are not very useful. The job of statistics is to turn those scattered numbers into something you can understand and use. Statistics is the branch of mathematics that deals with collecting, organising, analysing, and interpreting data. Data simply means the information or facts that you collect, usually as numbers. The word statistics can mean two things: the whole process of handling data, or the numbers themselves once they have been organised. What is the purpose of statistics? The main purpose is to make sense of information so that we can make better decisions. Statistics helps us in several ways:
  • To summarise large amounts of information. If your teacher lists the marks of all 40 students in your class, that is a lot of numbers. Statistics lets you group them into a table so you can quickly see, for example, how many students scored above 60.
  • To compare. Statistics lets you compare things fairly, such as the attendance of two classes or the rainfall of two months.
  • To spot patterns and trends. When data is organised, you can see whether something is increasing, decreasing, or staying the same over time.
  • To support decisions. Governments, companies, and schools all use statistics to plan. A shop uses sales data to decide which goods to stock; a school uses exam data to decide where learners need more help.
  • To predict. From organised data, you can often make a reasonable guess about what might happen next.
Collecting and tabulating data. The first step in statistics is gathering the data. You can collect it by counting, by measuring, or by asking questions. Once you have the raw data — that is, the data just as you collected it, in no particular order — you organise it into a table. Tabulating means arranging the data into rows and columns so that it is neat and easy to read. A well-made table is the starting point for all the analysis that comes later.

Worked example 1: Seeing the purpose of statistics. Suppose your school wants to buy sports kits and needs to know which sport learners prefer. The school asks 20 learners and records each learner's choice: Football, Tennis, Football, Swimming, Tennis, Football, Swimming, Football, Tennis, Football, Swimming, Football, Tennis, Football, Football, Swimming, Tennis, Football, Swimming, Football These are the raw data — 20 answers in the order they were collected. On their own they are hard to read. Now let's tabulate them. We count how many learners chose each sport. Football appears 10 times, Tennis appears 4 times, and Swimming appears 6 times.
SportNumber of learners (frequency)
Football10
Tennis4
Swimming6
Total20
The table immediately shows the purpose of statistics: the messy list has been summarised into a clear picture. We can see at a glance that Football is the most popular and Tennis is the least popular. With this organised data, the school can decide how many kits of each sport to buy. Notice also that the frequencies add up to 20, which confirms we counted every learner.

Worked example 2: Reading and interpreting a table. A farmer records the number of eggs collected from her hens on each day of one week.
DayNumber of eggs
Monday25
Tuesday28
Wednesday22
Thursday30
Friday26
Saturday24
Sunday27
What can this table tell us? Interpreting means reading meaning out of the organised data.
  • Thursday had the highest number of eggs, with 30.
  • Wednesday had the lowest number of eggs, with 22.
  • The eggs collected each day are between 22 and 30, so the hens are fairly steady producers.
Now suppose the farmer wants to know roughly how many eggs she gets in a week. She can add the numbers: 25 + 28 + 22 + 30 + 26 + 24 + 27 = 182. So in one week the hens produced 182 eggs. This total is itself a useful statistic. The farmer could compare this week's total with next week's to spot whether the hens are producing more or fewer eggs — a trend that helps her plan for selling the eggs.

practice.prompt:
A class of 15 learners is asked which of three subjects they enjoy most: Mathematics, English, or Basic Science. Their answers, in order, are:

English, Science, Maths, Maths, English, Science, Maths, English, Maths, Science, Maths, English, Science, Maths, English

a) Count how many learners chose each subject and write the results in a table with columns for Subject and Number of learners.
b) Which subject is most popular, and which is least popular?
c) What is the total number of learners shown by your table? Why must this total be 15?
practice.answer:
a) Table: Mathematics = 6, English = 5, Basic Science = 4, Total = 15.
b) Mathematics is most popular (6 learners); Basic Science is least popular (4 learners).
c) The total is 15, which must equal the number of learners asked, because every learner chose exactly one subject and each was counted once.
practice.worked_solution:
Count each subject from the list. Mathematics appears 6 times, English appears 5 times, and Basic Science appears 4 times. Write these in a table:

Subject | Number of learners
Mathematics | 6
English | 5
Basic Science | 4
Total | 15

Adding the frequencies: 6 + 5 + 4 = 15. This confirms every one of the 15 learners has been counted exactly once. The largest frequency is 6 (Mathematics), so it is most popular; the smallest is 4 (Basic Science), so it is least popular.

practice.prompt:
The table below shows the number of books borrowed from a school library each day of one week.

Day | Books borrowed
Monday | 40
Tuesday | 35
Wednesday | 45
Thursday | 50
Friday | 30

a) Which day had the most books borrowed, and which had the fewest?
b) How many books were borrowed altogether that week?
c) Give one way the librarian could use this information to make a decision about the library.
practice.answer:
a) Most: Thursday (50 books); fewest: Friday (30 books).
b) 40 + 35 + 45 + 50 + 30 = 200 books.
c) Accept any sensible decision, for example the librarian could open earlier or longer on the busiest days, or buy more copies of the kinds of books that are borrowed most.
practice.worked_solution:
a) Compare the numbers in the table: the largest is 50 on Thursday, so Thursday had the most books borrowed. The smallest is 30 on Friday, so Friday had the fewest.
b) Add all the daily totals: 40 + 35 + 45 + 50 + 30 = 200. So 200 books were borrowed that week.
c) The purpose of statistics is to support decisions. The librarian can see which days are busiest and which are quiet, and can use that to plan staffing, opening hours, or which books to stock more of.

practice.prompt: In your own words, explain what the purpose of statistics is, and mention at least two ways that organising data into a table helps people understand it.
practice.answer: Accept an answer in the learner's own words. It should state that the purpose of statistics is to make sense of information so that better decisions can be made. It should mention at least two of: it summarises large amounts of data; it makes comparison easy; it helps spot patterns and trends; it supports decisions and predictions. A table helps because it arranges data neatly into rows and columns so it is easy to read and compare.

sections_json.title: Reading Tables to Make Sense of Data

blocks.text:
After data is collected, it is often arranged into a table. A table is a tidy way of showing information in rows and columns so that the numbers are easy to read and compare. Reading a table means looking carefully at its headings to understand what each row and each column stands for, and then pulling out the information you need to answer a question.

Let's look at the parts of a table. The top row (the heading row) tells you what each column contains. The first column usually names the things being counted, and the other columns hold the numbers. To interpret a table, ask yourself three things:

1. What does the table count? (Look at the headings.)
2. Which row or column do I need? (Find the right place.)
3. What does the number actually mean? (Read it with the heading.)

Below is a table showing how 40 students in a school travel to school each morning.

The table below shows how 40 students travel to school.

| Mode of travel | Number of students |
|----------------|--------------------|
| Walking        | 18                 |
| Bicycle        | 10                 |
| Bus            | 8                  |
| Car            | 4                  |

We can use this table to answer questions.

Example 1: How many students walk to school?
Find the row "Walking". The number beside it is 18. So 18 students walk.

Example 2: How many more students walk than come by car?
Walking is 18 and car is 4. Difference: 18 − 4 = 14. So 14 more students walk than come by car.

Example 3: The total of all the numbers is 18 + 10 + 8 + 4 = 40, which matches the total number of students. This is a quick way to check that the table is correct.

So a table lets us find exact numbers and compare them quickly.

practice.prompt:
The table below shows the favourite subjects of 30 students in a class.

| Subject | Number of students |
|---------|--------------------|
| Mathematics | 12 |
| English | 6 |
| Science | 8 |
| Social Studies | 4 |

(a) How many students chose Science?
(b) Which subject did the most students choose, and how many chose it?
(c) How many more students chose Mathematics than English?
practice.answer:
(a) 8 students chose Science.
(b) Mathematics; 12 students chose it.
(c) 12 − 6 = 6, so 6 more students chose Mathematics than English.
practice.worked_solution:
(a) Read across the "Science" row to the number column: 8.
(b) Compare the numbers 12, 6, 8 and 4. The largest is 12, which sits in the Mathematics row.
(c) Subtract the English number from the Mathematics number: 12 − 6 = 6.

practice.prompt:
A fruit seller recorded the number of fruits he sold in one day.

| Fruit | Number sold |
|-------|-------------|
| Oranges | 45 |
| Apples | 30 |
| Bananas | 25 |
| Mangoes | 20 |

(a) How many apples did he sell?
(b) How many more oranges than mangoes did he sell?
(c) Altogether, how many fruits did he sell that day?
practice.answer:
(a) 30 apples.
(b) 45 − 20 = 25 more oranges than mangoes.
(c) 45 + 30 + 25 + 20 = 120 fruits in all.
practice.worked_solution:
(a) Find the "Apples" row and read the number beside it: 30.
(b) Subtract the mangoes from the oranges: 45 − 20 = 25.
(c) Add all four numbers: 45 + 30 + 25 + 20 = 120.

blocks.text: Every day you meet information all around you: how many learners came to school, how many goals a team scored, how much rain fell in a week, how many people voted. On its own, a jumbled list of such facts is hard to make sense of. Statistics is the method of collecting and organising information so that it can be understood and used. Its purpose is not to gather numbers for their own sake. When information is collected and arranged neatly, it becomes easy to see what is happening, to compare one thing with another, and to make sensible decisions. A teacher collects the number of learners present each day; arranged in order, that information shows which day of the week attendance was best. A shopkeeper records what was sold; organised into a table, it shows which items are most wanted. This is what statistics is for: turning scattered information into something clear enough to read and act on. So the heart of statistics is two steps: collecting the information, and organising it so that its meaning can be seen.

Suppose a class wants to know which colour of pencil is most common among its learners. First the information is collected: each learner names their pencil colour — blue, red, blue, green, red, blue, blue, green, red, blue. That list alone is hard to read, so the information is then organised. Write each colour once, and count how many times it appears: - Blue: 5 - Red: 3 - Green: 2 Now the meaning is clear at a glance: blue is the most common pencil colour. Statistics collected the information and organised it so a decision — which colour to buy more of — could be made easily.

practice.prompt: Explain in your own words what statistics is, and state its two main steps.
practice.answer: Statistics is the method of collecting and organising information so that it can be understood and used. Its two main steps are collecting the information and organising it.

practice.prompt: A gardener notes the number of tomatoes picked from a plant each day: 4, 6, 4, 5, 6, 4, 5, 6. Organise this information by counting how many times each number appears.
practice.answer: 4 appears 3 times, 5 appears 2 times, 6 appears 3 times.
practice.worked_solution: Count each number in the list: 4, 6, 4, 5, 6, 4, 5, 6. There are three 4s, two 5s and three 6s. Organising it this way shows that 4 and 6 were equally common, and 5 was least common.

sections_json.title: From Tallies to a Frequency Table

blocks.text: When a statistician wants to find out something — say, how many brothers and sisters your classmates have, or how many bottles were collected for recycling — the first thing to do is collect the information. Every single piece of information you gather is called a piece of data. But a long list of numbers is hard to read at a glance. To understand it, you need to organise it into a table, and the most useful table for this is a frequency table. A frequency table records three things for each different value: the value itself, how you counted it using tally marks, and the frequency — the number of times that value appears. Let's look at how tally marks work. Each time a value appears, you draw one short vertical stroke |. When you reach the fifth mark, you draw it across the four as a diagonal stroke, making a bundle of five: ||||. This bundle makes it much easier to count your marks at the end. So: - four marks are |||| (four strokes) - five marks are |||| (four strokes and one across) - seven marks are |||| || - ten marks are |||| |||| To build a frequency table, you go through your data one value at a time. For each value you meet, find its row in the table and add one tally mark. When you have finished the whole list, you count the tallies in each row and write that number in the frequency column. The tally and the frequency must always match, so counting carefully is the whole skill.

Let's follow one small collection of data all the way through. Ten students recorded how many pencils each had on their desk, and here is the list: 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3, 2 There are ten students, so there are ten numbers. The values that appear are 1, 2 and 3. We set up a frequency table with a row for each of these values. Start with a blank tally column. Now go through the list in order and add a mark each time a value appears. - First number is 3: add one mark in row 3. - Next is 1: add a mark in row 1. - Next is 2: add a mark in row 2. - Next is 3: add a mark in row 3. - Next is 1: add a mark in row 1. - Next is 3: add a mark in row 3. - Next is 2: add a mark in row 2. - Next is 1: add a mark in row 1. - Next is 3: add a mark in row 3. - Last is 2: add a mark in row 2. Now count each row of tallies. - Row 1: three marks, so frequency 3. - Row 2: three marks, so frequency 3. - Row 3: four marks, so frequency 4. The completed frequency table looks like this: | Number of pencils | Tally | Frequency | |---|---|---| | 1 | \|\|\| | 3 | | 2 | \|\|\| | 3 | | 3 | \|\|\|\| | 4 | | Total | | 10 | Check your work: the frequencies should add up to the total number of pieces of data. Here 3 + 3 + 4 = 10, and there were indeed ten students. If they did not add up, you missed a mark or counted one wrongly — go back and find the mistake.

Here is a complete example for you to follow. Twelve students in a class were asked their shoe size, and the results were recorded as follows: 6, 7, 5, 6, 6, 7, 5, 6, 7, 5, 6, 7 Step 1 — Set up the table. The values that appear are 5, 6 and 7, so give each its own row. Step 2 — Tally the data. Go through the list in order and add one mark per value. - 6: one mark in row 6 - 7: one mark in row 7 - 5: one mark in row 5 - 6: one mark in row 6 - 6: one mark in row 6 - 7: one mark in row 7 - 5: one mark in row 5 - 6: one mark in row 6 - 7: one mark in row 7 - 5: one mark in row 5 - 6: one mark in row 6 - 7: one mark in row 7 Step 3 — Count the tallies. - Row 5 has four marks, so frequency 4. - Row 6 has five marks (a full bundle of five), so frequency 5. - Row 7 has three marks, so frequency 3. Step 4 — Check the total. 4 + 5 + 3 = 12, which matches the twelve students. The table is correct. | Shoe size | Tally | Frequency | |---|---|---| | 5 | \|\|\|\| | 4 | | 6 | \|\|\|\|\| | 5 | | 7 | \|\|\| | 3 | | Total | | 12 | Once the table is complete you can read answers straight off it. The most common shoe size is 6, because it has the highest frequency (5). Five students wore size 6, four wore size 5, and three wore size 7.

practice.prompt:
Copy the tally marks below and write the frequency of each. Then find the total.

| Colour | Tally |
|---|---|
| Red | \|\|\| |
| Blue | \|\|\|\| |
| Green | \|\| |

What is the frequency of each colour, and how many pieces of data are there in total?
practice.answer: Red: 3, Blue: 4 (a full bundle of five counts as 5, but here \|\|\|\| is four strokes), Green: 2. Total = 3 + 4 + 2 = 9.
practice.worked_solution: Count the strokes in each row. Red has three strokes, so frequency 3. Blue has \|\|\|\| which is four strokes, so frequency 4. Green has two strokes, so frequency 2. Add them: 3 + 4 + 2 = 9 pieces of data.

practice.prompt:
Prepare a frequency table for the following data, showing the value, the tally and the frequency:

1, 1, 3, 4, 4, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 1, 2
practice.worked_solution:
List the values that appear: 1, 2, 3 and 4. Go through the list in order and tally each.

For 1: first 1, then 1 (fifth number), then 1 (twelfth number) — three 1s, frequency 3.
For 2: the seventh, eighth and thirteenth numbers are 2 — three 2s, frequency 3.
For 3: the third, sixth, ninth and tenth numbers are 3 — four 3s, frequency 4.
For 4: the fourth, fifth and eleventh numbers are 4 — three 4s, frequency 3.

Check the total: 3 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 13, which matches the 13 numbers given.

blocks.text: Let's see statistics at work with a small example. Aminu asks five friends how many brothers each of them has. The answers are: 2, 1, 3, 1, 2. - Collecting: Aminu asked the friends and wrote down their answers — the facts were gathered. - Organising: He sorts them into a table, listing each number and how many friends gave it. So "1" appears twice, "2" appears twice, and "3" appears once. - Presenting clearly: He now sees the organised table at a glance, so anyone reading it understands the answers without re-asking. - Comparing and deciding: He can compare the answers and see that more friends have 1 or 2 brothers than have 3. If he needs to guess a typical answer, he has the facts to decide on.

practice.prompt: In your own words, what is statistics?
practice.answer: Statistics is the science of collecting, organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting data.
practice.worked_solution: Recall the full meaning: statistics is not just gathering numbers — it is the whole science of collecting, organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting data.

practice.prompt: What are data?
practice.answer: Data are facts or information collected for a particular purpose.

practice.prompt: Name three ways statistics helps us, and give one example of your own for each.
practice.answer: Any three of: collect information, organise information, compare information, make decisions, present information clearly. Examples should match the ones you chose (for example, "compare information" — checking which month had the most rainfall).
practice.worked_solution: Look back at the list of five uses of statistics. Choose any three and think of your own everyday example for each, such as counting books in your bag (collecting) or writing a table of scores (presenting clearly).

sections_json.title: From Collected Data to a Frequency Table

blocks.text: Before you can make sense of a set of facts, you need to gather them first. In statistics, the facts we collect are called **data**, and data can be collected in four main ways: 1. **Observation** — watching and noting what happens. 2. **Counting** — counting objects one by one. 3. **Interview** — asking people questions and writing down their answers. 4. **Questionnaire** — giving people a written list of questions to fill in. For example, if you want to know which vehicles pass your school gate in one morning, you might watch and count each one as it goes by. That is collecting data. Once you have collected your data, you need to record it clearly as it comes in. A handy way to do this is with **tally marks**. A tally is a small stroke you make every time an item appears. You make four upright strokes, and the fifth stroke crosses the four to make a bundle of five, like this: ||||. This makes the final count easy to read. A **frequency table** is a table that shows how many times each item occurs in a set of data. Each different item is listed once, and next to it you write its **frequency** — the number of times that item appears. Let's see how a set of data becomes a frequency table.

**Example — collecting data with tally marks** One morning you note the vehicles that pass your gate in this order: bus, car, car, car, lorry, bicycle, bicycle, car, car, lorry, bicycle, car Go through the list from the start. Each time you see a vehicle, add one tally mark beside its name. When you reach five marks for one vehicle, bundle them as a crossed group of five, and start a new group. Car appears at positions 2, 3, 4, 8, 9 and 12 — six times, so it gets five marks bundled plus one extra: |||| | Bus appears once: | Lorry appears at positions 5 and 10 — twice: || Bicycle appears at positions 6, 7 and 11 — three times: ||| Now count each group of tally marks and write the result in the **Total** column. This gives the tally table: | Vehicles | Tally | Total | |---|---|---| | car | |||| | | 6 | | bus | | | 1 | | lorry | || | 2 | | bicycle | ||| | 3 | | Motor Bike | | | 0 | The **Total** column is the frequency of each vehicle — how many times it appeared in your data. You can check your work by adding the totals: 6 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 12, which matches the twelve vehicles you collected.

**Example — a frequency table**

When you already have the collected data and want to know how often each item occurs, you set it out in a frequency table. Suppose a class of students is asked their favourite colour, and their answers are counted. The frequency table records each colour once and shows how many students chose it:

| Colour | Frequency |
|---|---|
| Red | 18 |
| Blue | 20 |
| Green | 14 |
| Yellow | 16 |
| White | 15 |
| Pink | 30 |

The frequency of Blue is 20, which means 20 students chose blue as their favourite colour. The frequency of Pink is 30, the highest, so pink was the most popular. Reading a frequency table like this lets you analyse and interpret your data at a glance.

blocks.text: Whenever you need to know something about a group — how many pupils are in your class, how many bottle tops you have, which scores your classmates got in a test — you are working with data. Data are facts or information collected for a particular purpose. The collection on its own is not enough: the information is only useful once you can see what it means. Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, presenting, analyzing and interpreting data. It is the whole journey your information takes, from the moment you gather it to the moment you understand what it tells you. Statistics matters because it helps you to: - Collect information — gather the facts you need. - Organize information — arrange it so it is easy to look through. - Compare information — see how one thing stands against another. - Make decisions — choose sensibly from what the information shows. - Present information clearly — show it so others can understand it too. A single fact is just a fact. But when you collect facts, organize them and present them clearly, they become something you can compare and decide on. That is the purpose of statistics.

practice.prompt: Define statistics in your own words.
practice.answer: Statistics is the process of gathering facts, arranging them in an orderly way, showing them clearly, and using them to understand and make decisions.

practice.answer: Data are facts or information collected for a particular purpose.

practice.prompt: State two ways that statistics helps you.
practice.answer: Any two of: it helps you to collect information, organize information, compare information, make decisions, or present information clearly. (For example, it helps you to compare information and to make decisions.)

sections_json.title: From Raw Data to a Frequency Table

blocks.text: Very often we want to answer a question about a group of things, like "which vehicle passes our school most often?" or "what is the favourite colour in our class?". To answer that, we first need data — that is, pieces of information we have collected. Data can be collected in a few different ways:

Four common ways to collect data are:
  • Observation — watching and noting what you see, for example watching the road to record passing vehicles.
  • Counting — counting the items you want to know about, for example counting the pencils on each desk.
  • Interview — asking people questions and recording their answers.
  • Questionnaire — giving people a written list of questions to answer.

Once you have collected data, you need a neat way to record it as it comes in. That is what tally marks are for. A tally is a small stroke | written for each item you record. When you reach the fifth stroke, you draw it across the other four, like this: ||||/ (which counts as 5).

When the tallying is finished, we can count the strokes for each item and write down how many times it occurred. A frequency table is a table that shows how many times each item occurs in a set of data. The number of times an item occurs is called its frequency. For example, the favourite colours of a group of students can be shown in a frequency table: | Colour | Frequency | |---|---| | Red | 18 | | Blue | 20 | | Green | 14 | | Yellow | 16 | | White | 15 | | Pink | 30 |

Let's put this all together with the data collected by watching vehicles pass:

car, car, car, car, car, car, bus, lorry, lorry, bicycle, bicycle, bicycle

We record each vehicle with a tally mark as it appears. The tally for "car" builds up as six strokes, which we group as five and one extra: ||||/ |, so its total is 6. The other vehicles follow the same way.

Now we read the totals from the tally to make a frequency table. The vehicle that occurs most often has the largest frequency, and the one that occurs least often has the smallest:

| Vehicles | Tally | Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| car | \|\|\|\|\|/ \| | 6 |
| bus | \| | 1 |
| lorry | \|\| | 2 |
| bicycle | \|\|\| | 3 |

Reading the table tells us: car appeared 6 times, bus 1 time, lorry 2 times and bicycle 3 times. The car is the most common vehicle, and the bus is the least common.
